Literature summary: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer*. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it.

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance.

Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer*. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy. === abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0007734 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.001957 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. The ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while recent work questions the validity of this research line compared to simpler linear models [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation and representing multivariate series as graphs, yet tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [14, 20, 22]. Furthermore, transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [32]. This uncertainty motivates a rigorous examination of specific architectural modifications intended to stabilize learning across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds.

A key open problem is determining what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects. One proposed mechanism is enforcing consistency across network depth, based on the hypothesis that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data and that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [17, 18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in various contexts to strengthen layer interactions or refine activation steering [15, 34]. However, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. Existing studies test whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy, but results remain unsettled [1]. This work addresses this gap by testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling.

Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. This paper provides a calibrated testbed to evaluate this hypothesis without conflating implementation details with architectural effects.

- We execute a preregistered experiment testing cross-layer query consistency loss on a subject-disjoint time-series benchmark.
- We report results from both a primary cohort and a confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds.
- We clarify the role of layer-specific adaptation versus stability in subject-disjoint generalization for time-series transformers.

The preregistered prediction states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Specifically, we predict the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14, 20]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [15, 34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28].

This study positions itself against these themes by isolating the effect of cross-layer query weight consistency from other regularization forms. While [17] and [18] suggest consistency aids domain adaptation and overfitting, [3] reports inconclusive results for spectral entropy minimization in a similar setting. The disagreement between works proposing cross-layer mechanisms [15, 34] and those questioning transformer efficacy [5] motivates our boundary test. We do not claim attention stability from accuracy contrasts alone, nor do we generalize beyond the subject-disjoint setting defined in the preregistration.

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights. The hypothesis posits that stabilizing attention query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization. The operator is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight during loss computation of every optimization step. The operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it.

The operator retrieves reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. It computes the element-wise difference between the target weights and the reference weights, squares these differences, and sums them over all elements to compute the raw loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed consistency_coefficient of 0.01 to prevent the loss_term from dominating the classification objective. The resulting loss_term is stored for harness aggregation and returned for addition to the training objective. Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients, ensuring the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

The baseline condition serves as the comparator. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation.

The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This condition tests whether any observed effect arises from the regularization term itself or the specific cross-layer relationship. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. The method isolates the effect of the consistency loss from implementation variance by ensuring the only difference between the proposed condition and the baseline is the presence of the loss term.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification.** The experimental design employs a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization to unseen subjects, which a random split would not. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. This distinction is critical because generalization across subjects with different movement styles and sensor characteristics is the primary challenge in this domain. A random split would allow information leakage between training and testing sets via subject identity, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to test the robustness of the architectural bias.

**Pairing and Controls.** Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance attributable to initialization and data ordering, allowing for a more precise estimate of the intervention's effect. Each negative control's intended alternative explanation is that compute matching or regularization magnitude, rather than cross-layer consistency, drives any observed change. The observed contrast supports distinguishing meaningful structural regularization from arbitrary penalty terms. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds provides sufficient power to detect effects exceeding the registered margin, distinguishing zero-null detection from exceeding the margin. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin.

**Analysis Plan.** The analysis distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations. Here, replication is on new seeds within the same dataset and architecture, confirming stability across sampling variation. We report both primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately, state each preregistered decision, and never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance, but the registered margin provides a consistent decision rule. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort.** In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). There was no statistically significant difference, as the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Table 1 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition (0.9062), the baseline (0.9054), and the first negative control (0.9051). Figure 2 visualizes these means with error bars representing 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Figure 3 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions, showing the paired mean difference over 43 seeds with the registered worthwhile threshold marked. The lower confidence bound does not exceed the threshold.

**Replication Cohort.** In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). There was no statistically significant difference, as the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Table 2 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition (0.9055), the baseline (0.9035), and the first negative control (0.9043). Figure 5 visualizes these means for the replication cohort. Figure 6 plots the mean difference, showing the paired mean difference over 43 seeds. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold; support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it, which it does not.

**Training Dynamics.** Figure 4 and Figure 7 show the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. The curves for the conditions coincide closely, distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern. No value is jittered. The training dynamics do not suggest divergence in convergence behavior between the proposed condition and the baseline. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive regarding the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency improves accuracy.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Both the primary and replication cohorts produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. This suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

**Mechanism and Alternatives.** A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class, allowing deeper layers to refine features differently than shallower layers. An alternative mechanism is that the consistency coefficient was too small to influence learning, or that the Frobenius norm penalty does not align with the relevant feature space for subject-disjoint generalization. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment, and we do not claim attention stability from an accuracy contrast alone. The negative control confirms that the compute cost of the penalty term itself does not drive performance changes, as its accuracy was comparable to the baseline.

**Replication Value.** The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is not due to a specific seed configuration. The replication cohort mean difference (0.001957) was slightly larger than the primary (0.0007734), but both remained within noise relative to the margin. This consistency across cohorts strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if any, is below the threshold of practical importance defined in the preregistration.

**Relation to Cited Work.** These findings agree with [3], which reported inconclusive results for spectral entropy minimization in a similar setting. They conflict with the hypothesis that consistency regularization universally improves generalization as suggested by [17], though [17] focused on machine translation tasks. They are not comparable to [18] in terms of intervention, task, data regime or evaluation, as [18] addressed domain adaptive semantic segmentation. The results support the view that transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32], and that architectural modifications require careful verification [5]. We do not rely on [2] due to its retracted status.

**Future Directions.** What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks with deeper architectures or different regularization strengths. Future work should also measure attention maps directly to verify if stability is achieved even if accuracy does not improve.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency would work on different corpora, sensors, tasks, or deployment distributions. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects, but is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. The study is limited to a 2-block transformer on the UCI HAR dataset; deeper models might exhibit different behavior regarding layer consistency. The registered margin reflects measurement precision and does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. A null result here does not prove the mechanism is invalid, only that it did not exceed the margin under these conditions. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism, which this study does not include.

=== conclusion ===
This study found that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin for held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or replication cohorts. The results are inconclusive, suggesting that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. For someone choosing between these methods, standard training remains preferable unless further evidence arises, as the intervention adds computational cost without demonstrated benefit. What would settle the question next is testing on deeper architectures and measuring attention stability directly. These findings indicate layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0007734 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.001957 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. The ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while recent work questions the validity of this research line compared to simpler linear models [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation and representing multivariate series as graphs, yet tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [14, 20, 22]. Furthermore, transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [32]. This uncertainty motivates a rigorous examination of specific architectural modifications intended to stabilize learning across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds.

A key open problem is determining what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects. One proposed mechanism is enforcing consistency across network depth, based on the hypothesis that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data and that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [17, 18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in various contexts to strengthen layer interactions or refine activation steering [15, 34]. However, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. Existing studies test whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy, but results remain unsettled [1]. This work addresses this gap by testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling.

Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. This paper provides a calibrated testbed to evaluate this hypothesis without conflating implementation details with architectural effects.

- We execute a preregistered experiment testing cross-layer query consistency loss on a subject-disjoint time-series benchmark.
- We report results from both a primary cohort and a confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds.
- We clarify the role of layer-specific adaptation versus stability in subject-disjoint generalization for time-series transformers.

The preregistered prediction states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Specifically, we predict the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14, 20]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [15, 34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28].

This study positions itself against these themes by isolating the effect of cross-layer query weight consistency from other regularization forms. While [17] and [18] suggest consistency aids domain adaptation and overfitting, [3] reports inconclusive results for spectral entropy minimization in a similar setting. The disagreement between works proposing cross-layer mechanisms [15, 34] and those questioning transformer efficacy [5] motivates our boundary test. We do not claim attention stability from accuracy contrasts alone, nor do we generalize beyond the subject-disjoint setting defined in the preregistration.

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights. The hypothesis posits that stabilizing attention query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization. The operator is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight during loss computation of every optimization step. The operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it.

The operator retrieves reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. It computes the element-wise difference between the target weights and the reference weights, squares these differences, and sums them over all elements to compute the raw loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed consistency_coefficient of 0.01 to prevent the loss_term from dominating the classification objective. The resulting loss_term is stored for harness aggregation and returned for addition to the training objective. Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients, ensuring the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

The baseline condition serves as the comparator. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation.

The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This condition tests whether any observed effect arises from the regularization term itself or the specific cross-layer relationship. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. The method isolates the effect of the consistency loss from implementation variance by ensuring the only difference between the proposed condition and the baseline is the presence of the loss term.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification.** The experimental design employs a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization to unseen subjects, which a random split would not. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. This distinction is critical because generalization across subjects with different movement styles and sensor characteristics is the primary challenge in this domain. A random split would allow information leakage between training and testing sets via subject identity, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to test the robustness of the architectural bias.

**Pairing and Controls.** Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance attributable to initialization and data ordering, allowing for a more precise estimate of the intervention's effect. Each negative control's intended alternative explanation is that compute matching or regularization magnitude, rather than cross-layer consistency, drives any observed change. The observed contrast supports distinguishing meaningful structural regularization from arbitrary penalty terms. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds provides sufficient power to detect effects exceeding the registered margin, distinguishing zero-null detection from exceeding the margin. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin.

**Analysis Plan.** The analysis distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations. Here, replication is on new seeds within the same dataset and architecture, confirming stability across sampling variation. We report both primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately, state each preregistered decision, and never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance, but the registered margin provides a consistent decision rule. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort.** In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). There was no statistically significant difference, as the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Table 1 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition (0.9062), the baseline (0.9054), and the first negative control (0.9051). Figure 2 visualizes these means with error bars representing 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Figure 3 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions, showing the paired mean difference over 43 seeds with the registered worthwhile threshold marked. The lower confidence bound does not exceed the threshold.

**Replication Cohort.** In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). There was no statistically significant difference, as the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Table 2 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition (0.9055), the baseline (0.9035), and the first negative control (0.9043). Figure 5 visualizes these means for the replication cohort. Figure 6 plots the mean difference, showing the paired mean difference over 43 seeds. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold; support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it, which it does not.

**Training Dynamics.** Figure 4 and Figure 7 show the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. The curves for the conditions coincide closely, distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern. No value is jittered. The training dynamics do not suggest divergence in convergence behavior between the proposed condition and the baseline. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive regarding the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency improves accuracy.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Both the primary and replication cohorts produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. This suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

**Mechanism and Alternatives.** A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class, allowing deeper layers to refine features differently than shallower layers. An alternative mechanism is that the consistency coefficient was too small to influence learning, or that the Frobenius norm penalty does not align with the relevant feature space for subject-disjoint generalization. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment, and we do not claim attention stability from an accuracy contrast alone. The negative control confirms that the compute cost of the penalty term itself does not drive performance changes, as its accuracy was comparable to the baseline.

**Replication Value.** The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is not due to a specific seed configuration. The replication cohort mean difference (0.001957) was slightly larger than the primary (0.0007734), but both remained within noise relative to the margin. This consistency across cohorts strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if any, is below the threshold of practical importance defined in the preregistration.

**Relation to Cited Work.** These findings agree with [3], which reported inconclusive results for spectral entropy minimization in a similar setting. They conflict with the hypothesis that consistency regularization universally improves generalization as suggested by [17], though [17] focused on machine translation tasks. They are not comparable to [18] in terms of intervention, task, data regime or evaluation, as [18] addressed domain adaptive semantic segmentation. The results support the view that transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32], and that architectural modifications require careful verification [5]. We do not rely on [2] due to its retracted status.

**Future Directions.** What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks with deeper architectures or different regularization strengths. Future work should also measure attention maps directly to verify if stability is achieved even if accuracy does not improve.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency would work on different corpora, sensors, tasks, or deployment distributions. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects, but is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. The study is limited to a 2-block transformer on the UCI HAR dataset; deeper models might exhibit different behavior regarding layer consistency. The registered margin reflects measurement precision and does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. A null result here does not prove the mechanism is invalid, only that it did not exceed the margin under these conditions. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism, which this study does not include.

=== conclusion ===
This study found that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin for held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or replication cohorts. The results are inconclusive, suggesting that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. For someone choosing between these methods, standard training remains preferable unless further evidence arises, as the intervention adds computational cost without demonstrated benefit. What would settle the question next is testing on deeper architectures and measuring attention stability directly. These findings indicate layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [8, 18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [6, 12, 21]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15].

This study positions itself against these themes by isolating the effect of cross-layer query weight consistency from other regularization forms. While [9] and [10] suggest consistency aids domain adaptation and overfitting, [3] reports inconclusive results for spectral entropy minimization in a similar setting. The disagreement between works proposing cross-layer mechanisms [8, 18] and those questioning transformer efficacy [4] motivates our boundary test. We do not claim attention stability from accuracy contrasts alone, nor do we generalize beyond the subject-disjoint setting defined in the preregistration.

Abstract: Recently, there has been a surge of Transformer-based solutions for the long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) task. Abstract: Unneeded elements in the attention’s context degrade performance. Among their salient benefits, Transformers enable modeling long dependencies between input sequence elements and support parallel processing of sequence as compared to recurrent networks, e.g., Long short-term memory. Although the feature pyramid network (FPN) is a multi-scale structure, its fusion mechanism inherently limits the extraction of fine-grained information. The Transformer architecture excels at capturing long-range dependencies through its self-attention mechanism. The innovative contribution of this paper is to embed three novel modules into the traditional CNN model. Firstly, we utilize the FPN to extract multi-scale features and design a fine feature aggregation module (RFA) to integrate complementary information from different layers to obtain more reliable and accurate features. Second, the efficient frequency transformer (EFT) is proposed to deeply mine global information, local spatial features, and edge detail information. Finally, the graph-aware fusion (GAF) module is proposed to model the relationships among regions in the feature graph by graph convolutional network (GCN), which enhances the intra-class feature consistency. A wide range of experiments have been carried out on three publicly accessible RS scene datasets. Positive results show that our CLFETNet framework outperforms many existing methods, has high robustness and superiority in remote sensing scene classification tasks, and can effectively handle complex scenes and meet multi-scale feature challenges.

[21] A survey of transformers
Abstract: Transformers have achieved great success in many artificial intelligence fields, such as natural language processing, computer vision, and audio processing. Therefore, it is natural to attract lots of interest from academic and industry researchers. Up to the present, a great variety of Transformer variants (a.k.a. Next, we introduce the various X-formers from three perspectives: architectural modification, pre-training, and applications. Finally, we outline some potential directions for future research.

This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00133 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by -0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

These findings indicate that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance.
