Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered calibration-derived decision threshold. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4, 20]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [11] and representing multivariate series as graphs [7]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [16].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [8], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [6, 12, 21]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15].

This study positions itself against these themes by isolating cross-layer query consistency in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. While prior work establishes that consistency regularization can mitigate overfitting [9] and domain gaps affect attention [10], the specific effect of query projection alignment on subject-disjoint generalization remains unsettled. The inconclusive outcomes in related spectral regularization studies [3] suggest that weight geometry modifications may not yield robust gains in this regime. We extend this inquiry by employing a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to test the stability of any observed effect.
Method: The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear projection (9 to 64 channels), a learned positional embedding (128 timesteps, 64 channels), and two transformer blocks. Each block contains LayerNorm, 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with query/key/value/output Linear projections (64 to 64), a residual connection, LayerNorm, and a feed-forward network (Linear 64->128->ReLU->Linear 128->64) with a residual connection. The encoder output is mean-pooled over time and passed through a Linear layer (64 to 6 classes) for activity prediction. Training proceeds for 12 epochs with batch size 128 using SGD (learning rate 0.05, momentum 0.9).

The hypothesis is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization. The intervention adds a loss term computed as the squared element-wise difference between the query projection weights of block 0 and block 1, scaled by a fixed coefficient. This regularization encourages deeper layer weights to remain close to shallower layer weights, testing whether attention stability across depth benefits generalization. The comparator neutralizes this effect by executing the identical code path but returning a zero loss term, ensuring that any difference in outcome is attributable to the regularization term rather than implementation artifacts.

The operator specification defines the precise mathematical expression of this hypothesis. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to the target parameter blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The reference weights are retrieved from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight and detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed at 0.01 across all steps and seeds. This design ensures that the penalty influences the optimization of the deeper block's query projections without altering the earlier block's learning dynamics via backpropagation through the reference.

A negative control penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute, isolating whether the effect arises from consistency specifically or merely from adding a weight penalty. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. The control arm leaves the registered target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, adding nothing to the training objective. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Experimental setup: The design employs a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization across unseen individuals, which a random split would not address. The UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset provides raw inertial signals in 128-timestep windows over 9 channels, with an official split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows from unseen subjects. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution.

Pairing conditions by seed controls for variance arising from initialization and data ordering. We use 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. Attributing variation to the seeds that produced them allows us to quantify the stability of the effect across training runs rather than conflating it with subject variability. The seed budget supports the registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targeting rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin.

The negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any observed gain arises from the mere presence of an additional loss term or compute load rather than the specific cross-layer consistency. Its observed contrast supports whether the consistency relationship is necessary for any effect. The baseline ensures the harness is unbiased by verifying that the control arm records zero operator activity. The registered margin provides a consistent decision rule. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign. The supplied power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Registered conditions.
- Proposed condition: Server-bound target blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight has stored tensor shape (64, 64). Add loss term that applies Frobenius norm consistency regularization to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Baseline: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Figure 1 shows the experimental flow, data ingestion, model architecture, registered conditions, the CrossLayerQueryConsistency intervention at the loss term, and subject-disjoint evaluation on the UCI HAR test split.

In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. Table 1 presents the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). Figure 2 visualizes these means with error bars representing 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimate is printed above each bar.

Table 2 reports the outcome for held-out classification accuracy in the primary cohort. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). This changes the choice for someone choosing between these methods by indicating that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class in subject-disjoint time-series tasks. The finding stands against hypotheses that attention stability across depth benefits generalization in this regime. What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks with larger architectures or different consistency targets.
Discussion: The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. In the primary cohort, the mean difference was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]), and in the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, it was 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). This result suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not stabilize attention across depth in a way that improves subject-disjoint generalization for this architecture and task. A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for transformers to accommodate different movement styles and sensor characteristics across subjects. An alternative explanation is that the regularization coefficient was too small to influence the optimization trajectory meaningfully, though the negative control matched compute and showed no advantage, suggesting the penalty itself was not the driver. The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is not an artifact of a specific seed set; calling it the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds clarifies that it is a disjoint set of seeds through the same pipeline.

The design does not establish whether cross-layer consistency would benefit larger models or different time-series domains. The margin reflects measurement precision, not practical importance, so we cannot claim the effect is practically negligible, only that it is undetectable given the calibration noise. What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks with larger architectures or different consistency targets, such as value or key projections.

The evaluation is limited to the UCI HAR dataset with 9 channels and 128-timestep windows; results may not generalize to different sensor modalities or sequence lengths. The margin reflects measurement precision, not practical importance, so we cannot claim the effect is practically negligible, only that it is undetectable given the calibration noise. The study does not measure attention maps directly, so claims about attention stability are mechanistic hypotheses rather than measured findings. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. If a reference tensor is detached inside a penalty, this stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient.

This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered calibration-derived decision threshold. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4, 20]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [11] and representing multivariate series as graphs [7]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [16].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [8], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [6, 12, 21]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15].

This study positions itself against these themes by isolating cross-layer query consistency in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. While prior work establishes that consistency regularization can mitigate overfitting [9] and domain gaps affect attention [10], the specific effect of query projection alignment on subject-disjoint generalization remains unsettled. The inconclusive outcomes in related spectral regularization studies [3] suggest that weight geometry modifications may not yield robust gains in this regime. We extend this inquiry by employing a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to test the stability of any observed effect.
Method: The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear projection (9 to 64 channels), a learned positional embedding (128 timesteps, 64 channels), and two transformer blocks. Each block contains LayerNorm, 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with query/key/value/output Linear projections (64 to 64), a residual connection, LayerNorm, and a feed-forward network (Linear 64->128->ReLU->Linear 128->64) with a residual connection. The encoder output is mean-pooled over time and passed through a Linear layer (64 to 6 classes) for activity prediction. Training proceeds for 12 epochs with batch size 128 using SGD (learning rate 0.05, momentum 0.9).

The hypothesis is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization. The intervention adds a loss term computed as the squared element-wise difference between the query projection weights of block 0 and block 1, scaled by a fixed coefficient. This regularization encourages deeper layer weights to remain close to shallower layer weights, testing whether attention stability across depth benefits generalization. The comparator neutralizes this effect by executing the identical code path but returning a zero loss term, ensuring that any difference in outcome is attributable to the regularization term rather than implementation artifacts.

The operator specification defines the precise mathematical expression of this hypothesis. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to the target parameter blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The reference weights are retrieved from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight and detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed at 0.01 across all steps and seeds. This design ensures that the penalty influences the optimization of the deeper block's query projections without altering the earlier block's learning dynamics via backpropagation through the reference.

A negative control penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute, isolating whether the effect arises from consistency specifically or merely from adding a weight penalty. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. The control arm leaves the registered target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, adding nothing to the training objective. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Experimental setup: The design employs a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization across unseen individuals, which a random split would not address. The UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset provides raw inertial signals in 128-timestep windows over 9 channels, with an official split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows from unseen subjects. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution.

Pairing conditions by seed controls for variance arising from initialization and data ordering. We use 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. Attributing variation to the seeds that produced them allows us to quantify the stability of the effect across training runs rather than conflating it with subject variability. The seed budget supports the registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targeting rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin.

The negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any observed gain arises from the mere presence of an additional loss term or compute load rather than the specific cross-layer consistency. Its observed contrast supports whether the consistency relationship is necessary for any effect. The baseline ensures the harness is unbiased by verifying that the control arm records zero operator activity. The registered margin provides a consistent decision rule. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign. The supplied power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Results: We walk through the evidence for the primary and confirmatory replication cohorts separately. Figure 1 shows the experimental flow, data ingestion, model architecture, registered conditions, the CrossLayerQueryConsistency intervention at the loss term, and subject-disjoint evaluation on the UCI HAR test split.

In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. Table 1 presents the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). Figure 2 visualizes these means with error bars representing 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimate is printed above each bar.

Table 2 reports the outcome for held-out classification accuracy in the primary cohort. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 3 plots the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds with error bars showing 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Zero marks no directional effect. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold (held-out classification accuracy: 0.0125098 proportion); support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it. The 95% CI includes zero, and the preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. Table 3 presents the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), while the baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). Figure 5 visualizes these means. Table 4 reports the outcome for held-out classification accuracy in the replication cohort. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 6 plots the paired mean difference. The 95% CI includes zero, and the preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the replication cohort.

Table 5 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for both cohorts. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered calibration-derived decision threshold.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This study found that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not improve held-out classification accuracy on the UCI HAR subject-disjoint split. The mean difference was 0.000773 in the primary cohort and 0.00196 in the replication cohort, with both 95% confidence intervals including zero. This changes the choice for someone choosing between these methods by indicating that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class in subject-disjoint time-series tasks. The finding stands against hypotheses that attention stability across depth benefits generalization in this regime. What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks with larger architectures or different consistency targets.
Discussion: The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. In the primary cohort, the mean difference was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]), and in the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, it was 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Both confidence intervals included zero, and neither lower bound exceeded the calibration-derived decision threshold. This consistency across cohorts strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if any, is below the threshold of measurement precision defined in the preregistration.

This result suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not stabilize attention across depth in a way that improves subject-disjoint generalization for this architecture and task. A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for transformers to accommodate different movement styles and sensor characteristics across subjects. An alternative explanation is that the regularization coefficient was too small to influence the optimization trajectory meaningfully, though the negative control matched compute and showed no advantage, suggesting the penalty itself was not the driver. The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is not an artifact of a specific seed set; calling it the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds clarifies that it is a disjoint set of seeds through the same pipeline.

These findings stand against specific cited papers. While *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting [9], our results suggest that this specific consistency constraint does not mitigate that risk in the subject-disjoint setting. This conflicts with the hypothesis that attention stability across depth is beneficial, aligning instead with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which found inconclusive results for weight geometry modifications [3]. It is not comparable to *CDAC*, which addresses domain adaptive semantic segmentation rather than subject-disjoint time-series classification [10]. The retracted notice on *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise* cautions against relying on unverified robustness claims [2].

The design does not establish whether cross-layer consistency would benefit larger models or different time-series domains. The margin reflects measurement precision, not practical importance, so we cannot claim the effect is practically negligible, only that it is undetectable given the calibration noise. What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks with larger architectures or different consistency targets, such as value or key projections.
Limitations: This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency would benefit larger models or different time-series domains. The evaluation is limited to the UCI HAR dataset with 9 channels and 128-timestep windows; results may not generalize to different sensor modalities or sequence lengths. The margin reflects measurement precision, not practical importance, so we cannot claim the effect is practically negligible, only that it is undetectable given the calibration noise. The study does not measure attention maps directly, so claims about attention stability are mechanistic hypotheses rather than measured findings. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. If a reference tensor is detached inside a penalty, this stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)

6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01

Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: name the directly recorded outcomes, and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. If a reference tensor is detached inside a penalty, this stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient. Use the registered CI classifications without equating nonsignificance with equality. If a CI crosses zero but lies below the worthwhile margin, preserve its registered label and separately explain that it excludes gains of that target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model. The supplied power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; do not claim the former guarantees the latter. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

LENGTH. Write a full paper, not an extended abstract. Aim for roughly: introduction 600-800 words; related work 600-900; method 500-800 (BEFORE the operator specification that is appended for you); experimental setup 300-500; results 500-800; discussion 500-800; limitations 200-300; conclusion 150-250; abstract 150-250. A section that is three sentences long has not done its job. Depth means argument and detail, never padding or repetition.
INTRODUCTION. Open with the problem and why it matters, say what is missing in the current literature, then state what this paper does. End it with an explicit contributions list ('- We ...') of two to four items, then state the preregistered prediction.
RELATED WORK — 600-900 words. Synthesise by theme: what papers establish together, where they disagree, and what remains unsettled. The failure this section keeps producing looks like this: 'X studies uncertainty [1]. Y studies approximations [2].' — a list with citations attached. Write instead: 'Uncertainty motivates Bayesian methods [1], but their tractable approximations lose guarantees [2], motivating our boundary test.' Use that argumentative structure only when the abstracts support it. End by positioning this study against the themes; omit irrelevant references and quoted or italicised paper titles. Each reference in a grouped citation must independently support the WHOLE sentence. If papers support different halves, use separate sentences and markers.
RESULTS. Walk the reader through the evidence: discuss each figure and each table where it is relevant to the point being made, rather than listing them at the end.
DO NOT RESTATE THE CONFIGURATION. The dataset, split, architecture, training budget and outcome definition are written for you into the Experimental Setup and the appendix. State them nowhere else — not in the Method, not a second time in the setup.
WHAT THE SETUP SECTION IS FOR is DESIGN justification (300-500 words): why a subject-disjoint split answers the question and a random split would not; benefits and costs of pairing conditions by seed; each negative control's intended alternative explanation and what its observed contrast supports; the seed budget and analysis. These arguments are not supplied by the configuration block.
The METHOD is about the OPERATOR — what it does, why that is the right expression of the hypothesis, and what its comparator neutralises.
The CONCLUSION (150-250 words) states what was found, what it changes for someone choosing between these methods, and what would settle the question next. Not a one-paragraph restatement of the abstract.
NAME THE ARMS AS THE TABLES DO: 'the proposed condition', 'the baseline', 'the first negative control', 'the second negative control'. Do not invent a parallel name such as 'Intervention' — the reader has to match your prose to the tables.
REGISTER. Never enumerate random seeds in the prose — they are in the appendix. Never annotate a sentence with the subsystem that produced it.

PAPER-QUALITY SKILLS (only those relevant to this task are loaded; everything the system can decide for itself is checked, not asked for):
[claim-language] Claim what the evidence carries, and no more. Keep four registers apart and make it obvious which one a sentence is in: a RESULT states a measured quantity; an INTERPRETATION says what it may mean and is marked as such ('suggests', 'is consistent with'); a LIMITATION says what this design cannot tell anyone; FUTURE WORK proposes what would settle the question, and is the only register in which a wider setting may appear. Be exact about who was held out: evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen SUBJECTS — name that population — and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution, so do not call it out-of-distribution or domain generalisation. Where an outcome did not reach the registered decision threshold, report it as measured; do not upgrade it with a verb of proof.
[discussion-depth] The discussion is where the study is interpreted, not summarised again. Cover, in whatever order the argument wants: the principal finding; what it means; what this design does and does NOT establish; a mechanism that would produce the observed result and at least one alternative that would too; what the independent replication cohort adds or fails to add; and how the finding stands against specific cited papers [n] — agreeing, conflicting, extending, or not comparable because the intervention, task, data regime or evaluation differ. Judge that relation from what each abstract says, never from a title. Close with what would settle the question next. A null, refuted or inconclusive outcome owes the reader every one of those and is never rewritten as a positive finding. Length is not the target: a paragraph repeating the results covers none of this, and padding reads worse than brevity.
[paper-structure] Give a long section the internal structure its content earns. Where a section covers two or three distinct matters, open each with a short bold run-in heading (**Like this**) and keep one idea per paragraph; where it makes a single continuous argument, leave it undivided. Break at the argument's own joints — never split one argument to hit a shape, and never add a heading a section has not earned. Paragraphs of 60-150 words read well; one past 200 is doing more than one job and should be split where it turns. This matters most in related work, method, experimental setup, results and discussion, which are the sections long enough to become a wall. Do not fragment: a heading over two sentences is decoration, and several of them are harder to read than the block they replaced.
