=== abstract ===

Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===

Time-series classification from wearable sensors enables continuous health monitoring, activity recognition, and human-computer interaction. The UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset represents a standard benchmark where inertial signals from smartphones must be classified into discrete activities across different subjects. Success in this setting requires models to generalize across individuals with different movement styles, sensor placements, and execution speeds—a subject-disjoint generalization challenge that remains difficult for deep architectures.

Transformers have attracted significant interest for time-series modeling due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies through self-attention mechanisms [38]. However, whether the architectural choices that make transformers effective in language and vision transfer to temporal domains remains contested. Some work questions whether transformers offer genuine advantages over simpler linear models for time-series forecasting [5], while others demonstrate successful applications in biosignal augmentation [20] and multivariate representation learning [14]. The uncertainty extends to architectural modifications: surveys document numerous transformer variants across domains [11, 21, 41], yet systematic evidence about which inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers remains limited.

One proposed mechanism for improving transformer generalization involves enforcing consistency across network depth. Deep transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17], and domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention patterns [18]. Cross-layer mechanisms have been explored in various contexts: layer attention retrieves information from previous layers [15], cross-layer fusion captures multi-scale features [23], and cross-layer consistency has been applied to activation engineering [34]. The hypothesis is that stabilizing attention patterns across depth could improve generalization by reducing layer-specific overfitting while preserving the representational capacity needed for temporal feature learning.

**Gap and contribution.** This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. Prior work has tested related regularization strategies—spectral entropy minimization of input projections [3] and entropy-maximized weight noise [2]—but cross-layer query consistency in time-series transformers has not undergone preregistered replication. The gap concerns whether this specific intervention, which penalizes divergence between query projection weights in successive transformer blocks, yields measurable accuracy improvements when evaluated on held-out subjects.

**What this paper does.** We report a preregistered experiment testing cross-layer query consistency regularization in a calibrated time-series transformer testbed. The study uses the official subject-disjoint split of UCI HAR, evaluates held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects, and includes both a primary cohort and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters.

- We test whether cross-layer query consistency regularization improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers, with a preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion in accuracy gain.
- We report results from both primary (43 seeds) and confirmatory replication (43 disjoint seeds) cohorts, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for all estimates.
- We include a negative control that penalizes divergence from a fixed random matrix, isolating whether any observed effect stems from meaningful cross-layer relationships versus generic regularization.

**Preregistered prediction.** The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===

Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. Transformers have achieved superior performances in natural language processing and computer vision, triggering interest in the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [38]. However, the validity of this research line has been questioned: one study found that simple linear models outperformed sophisticated transformer-based forecasting models across nine real-life datasets, attributing this to temporal information loss from permutation-invariant self-attention [5]. This tension motivates careful evaluation of whether transformer architectural modifications genuinely improve time-series performance or merely add complexity without benefit.

Specific applications demonstrate transformers can work in temporal domains. Biosignal data augmentation using transformer-based conditional GANs has shown promise for expanding limited medical datasets [20]. Multivariate time series have been represented as graphs with attention mechanisms capturing both intra- and inter-series correlations [14]. Yet large pre-trained time-series models remain less common than in language and vision, with most tasks still requiring separate models designed from scratch [22]. Domain adaptation for time-series transformers faces limitations including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges under data shift [32]. These findings suggest that while transformers can process temporal data, their advantages over simpler architectures remain context-dependent.

**Consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. Deep transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data, motivating regularization strategies that constrain the solution space [17]. Domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, leading to attention to spurious regions that deteriorate target domain accuracy [18]. Cross-layer interactions have been explored through mechanisms that strengthen layer interactions by retrieving query-related information from different receptive field levels [15]. Cross-layer consistency has also been applied to activation engineering, refining steering vectors through geometric stability across depth [34]. Cross-layer fusion has been utilized to capture multi-scale features in remote sensing classification [23]. These approaches share the hypothesis that coordinating representations across network depth improves generalization, though the specific mechanisms and target domains differ.

**Weight and spectral regularization.** Related work tests whether specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. Spectral entropy minimization of input projections was tested in a subject-disjoint time-series setting but yielded inconclusive results: neither primary nor replication cohorts exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero [3]. This suggests that enforcing low-entropy singular value spectra on input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. Entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise for subject-disjoint robustness carries a retracted notice because the executed intervention did not implement the preregistered intervention [2]. These null and retracted findings underscore the importance of faithful implementation and preregistered replication when evaluating regularization hypotheses.

**Attention mechanism modifications.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms provide context for architectural modifications. Selective attention reduces attention to unneeded elements through a parameter-free change, improving language modeling performance across model sizes [8]. External attention using two linear layers offers linear complexity while implicitly considering correlations between samples [33]. Depth-attention performs cross-layer value mixing inside the attention module itself, adding no persistent inference state beyond the standard key-value cache [37]. Surveys document transformer applications across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41], while empirical studies examine how different factors affect attention performance [28]. These works establish that attention mechanisms can be modified, but whether such modifications improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers requires direct testing.

**Positioning this study.** This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training [1]. Unlike cross-domain attention consistency which aligns attention maps across domains [18], or depth-attention which mixes values across layers [37], the intervention regularizes query projection weights between successive transformer blocks. The preregistered design with primary and confirmatory replication cohorts distinguishes this work from single-cohort evaluations. The subject-disjoint UCI HAR split tests generalization to unseen individuals rather than random held-out windows, addressing whether the intervention improves robustness to inter-subject variability in movement patterns and sensor characteristics.

=== method ===

**Operator design.** The CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator enforces Frobenius norm consistency between query projection weights in successive transformer blocks. The target parameter is blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight with shape (64, 64). The reference parameter is blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight, detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The operator computes element-wise subtraction between target and reference weights, squares each element, sums over all elements, and scales by a fixed coefficient of 0.01. This loss term is added to the classification objective during every optimization step, so the combined objective is differentiated and the target parameters are trained by it.

**Why this expression.** The hypothesis is that stabilizing query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization by reducing layer-specific overfitting while preserving representational capacity. Query projections determine which features each attention head attends to; if these projections diverge substantially across layers, deeper layers may learn idiosyncratic attention patterns that do not generalize to new subjects. Regularizing toward earlier layers tests whether consistent attention mechanisms across depth benefit temporal feature learning more than layer-specific adaptation. The Frobenius norm provides a differentiable measure of weight divergence that can be added to the training objective without modifying the architecture or inference path.

**Comparator and controls.** The baseline condition executes identical code but returns zero loss term, leaving the registered target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged. This control arm reaches every registered lifecycle point on the same inputs, ensuring that any difference between conditions stems from the loss term itself rather than implementation artifacts. The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute, testing whether any observed effect requires alignment between actual layer weights versus generic weight regularization.

**Gradient handling.** Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients from the consistency loss. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only, so block 1 query projections are trained toward block 0's current weights without modifying block 0 through this pathway. Block 0 still receives gradients from the classification objective through its own forward pass. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds. Detaching the reference tensor stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient.

**Model architecture.** The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear projection (9 to 64 channels), a learned positional embedding (128 timesteps, 64 channels), and two transformer blocks. Each block contains LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and residual connection. Final LayerNorm(64) is followed by mean-pool over time and Linear(64,6) for classification. The 9 input channels correspond to the raw inertial signals from the UCI HAR dataset.

**Training and evaluation.** Training runs for 12 epochs with batch size 128, SGD (lr=0.05, momentum=0.9). Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy as number of correct activity predictions divided by 2,947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them.

**Operator specification.** CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step.
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective.

Algorithm 1: (1) Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight. (2) Detach reference_weights from gradient graph. (3) Compute diff = target - reference_weights. (4) Compute squared_elements = diff * diff. (5) Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements). (6) Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01. (7) Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw. (8) Store loss_term in scratch dict. (9) Return loss_term to harness.

=== experimental_setup ===

**Subject-disjoint split justification.** The official UCI HAR subject-disjoint split separates training and test subjects entirely, with 7,352 training windows from some subjects and 2,947 held-out windows from different subjects. This design answers whether the intervention improves generalization to unseen individuals rather than merely fitting the training distribution better. A random split would hold out windows from the same subjects used in training, conflating within-subject temporal generalization with between-subject generalization. For activity recognition applications where models must work for new users without subject-specific fine-tuning, the subject-disjoint evaluation is the relevant test. The cost is higher variance: inter-subject variability in movement style, sensor placement, and execution speed increases outcome noise compared to random splits.

**Paired seed design.** Both conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. This pairing reduces variance from random initialization and batch ordering when estimating the contrast between conditions. The benefit is tighter confidence intervals for the paired difference; the cost is that seeds are not independent across conditions. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them, not to subjects (subjects are fixed by the dataset split). The seed budget comprises 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix.

**Negative control purpose.** The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This tests whether any observed effect requires alignment between actual layer weights versus generic weight regularization toward an arbitrary target. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, this would support the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency specifically (rather than any weight constraint) matters. If both perform similarly, the effect may stem from generic regularization rather than meaningful cross-layer relationships.

**Confidence interval computation.** All uncertainty estimates are bootstrap 95% confidence intervals computed over the paired seed differences. The analysis computed confidence intervals, not standard deviations. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance.

**Condition execution.** Recorded activity shows 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity for the proposed condition in both primary and replication cohorts. The baseline recorded 0/43 seeds with operator activity in both cohorts, confirming the control arm left the target parameter unchanged. The first negative control recorded 43/43 seeds with operator activity in both cohorts. Conformance and activation counts describe execution; they do not establish the mechanism or prove the absence of implementation bias.

=== results ===

**Primary cohort accuracy.** Figure 2 displays mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition, baseline, and first negative control in the primary cohort. Bars represent means over 43 paired seeds with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals as error bars. The proposed condition achieved 0.9062 mean accuracy (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]). The baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The first negative control achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). The proposed condition shows a numerically higher point estimate than baseline, but the confidence intervals overlap substantially, indicating the difference is not statistically distinguishable from zero.

**Primary cohort contrast.** Figure 3 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, so no statistically significant difference was detected. The green dash-dot marker in Figure 3 shows the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion; support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed this threshold. The lower bound of -0.00271 falls far below this threshold, so the preregistered decision was inconclusive.

**Replication cohort accuracy.** Figure 5 displays mean held-out classification accuracy for all three conditions in the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. The proposed condition achieved 0.9055 mean accuracy (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]). The baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). The first negative control achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]). Point estimates remain close across conditions, with overlapping confidence intervals.

**Replication cohort contrast.** Figure 6 shows the mean difference between proposed and baseline in the replication cohort. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, so no statistically significant difference was detected. The lower bound of -0.00196 does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098, so the preregistered decision was inconclusive. The effect size (Cohen's dz=0.15) is larger than in the primary cohort (dz=0.06) but remains small and nonsignificant.

**Training dynamics.** Figure 4 and Figure 7 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. The curves for all three conditions track closely throughout training, with no condition showing consistent separation from the others. This pattern suggests the intervention does not substantially alter the optimization trajectory or final convergence point.

**Summary table.** Table 1 summarizes mean accuracy and confidence intervals for all conditions in both cohorts. Table 2 summarizes the paired contrasts with p-values and effect sizes. Both tables confirm that neither cohort produced a statistically significant difference, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

=== discussion ===

**Principal finding.** The cross-layer query consistency intervention did not yield statistically significant improvements in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary cohort (mean difference 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]) or the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds (mean difference 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Both confidence intervals include zero, and neither lower bound exceeds the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The preregistered decision was inconclusive in both cohorts. This suggests that enforcing Frobenius norm consistency between query projection weights across transformer blocks does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this calibrated testbed.

**Interpretation.** These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation remains essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. If cross-layer consistency improved generalization, we would expect the proposed condition to outperform the baseline with a confidence interval excluding zero and exceeding the worthwhile margin. Instead, the point estimates are small (0.000773 and 0.00196) and the intervals span both negative and positive values. One interpretation is that different transformer layers benefit from learning distinct query projections that capture different temporal features or abstraction levels. Regularizing toward earlier layers may constrain this layer-specific specialization without providing compensating benefits.

**Alternative mechanisms.** An alternative explanation is that the consistency penalty was too weak to produce measurable effects. The coefficient of 0.01 was chosen to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective, but this may have rendered the regularization ineffective. However, the negative control also used the same coefficient and showed similar performance to the proposed condition, suggesting the issue is not merely penalty strength but rather the nature of the constraint itself. Another alternative is that two transformer blocks are insufficient depth for cross-layer consistency to matter; deeper networks might show different behavior. This claim is untestable on this calibrated testbed, which pins one architecture at one size.

**What the replication cohort adds.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds provides confidence that the null result is not an artifact of a specific seed set. Both cohorts show the same pattern: small, nonsignificant differences with confidence intervals including zero. The replication cohort's effect size (dz=0.15) is larger than the primary (dz=0.06), but both remain far from the threshold needed to claim the intervention exceeds the worthwhile margin. This consistency across seed sets strengthens the conclusion that the intervention does not produce robust accuracy gains in this regime.

**Relation to cited work.** These findings align with prior null results on weight geometry regularization in subject-disjoint time-series settings. Spectral entropy minimization of input projections also yielded inconclusive results with confidence intervals including zero in both primary and replication cohorts [3]. This suggests a broader pattern: enforcing specific weight structures does not reliably improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The findings contrast with cross-domain attention consistency work that reported improvements in domain adaptive semantic segmentation [18], but that study addressed a different problem (domain shift across datasets rather than subject disjointness within a dataset) and used attention-map alignment rather than weight alignment. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment.

**Mechanistic hypotheses.** Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. The study does not measure attention maps directly, so claims about attention stability are mechanistic hypotheses rather than measured findings. The intervention regularizes query projection weights, not attention outputs or attention maps. Whether weight consistency translates to attention stability depends on how query projections interact with key and value projections during the attention computation, which was not measured. Future work could directly measure attention map similarity across layers to test whether weight regularization produces the hypothesized attention stabilization.

**Scope of generalization.** All claims are scoped to the calibrated testbed: PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks, 64 hidden channels, 4-head attention, on UCI HAR with official subject-disjoint split. The findings do not establish whether cross-layer consistency would help in larger models, different architectures, or other time-series datasets. A claim about model scale or architecture family is untestable on this calibrated testbed. The single calibrated model at one size is what was tested; generalization to other settings requires separate experiments.

=== limitations ===

**Architecture and scale.** The study tests one architecture at one size: PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks and 64 hidden channels. Whether cross-layer query consistency would benefit deeper transformers, different attention mechanisms, or larger hidden dimensions remains unknown. Claims about larger models are untestable on this calibrated testbed. The intervention may behave differently in architectures where depth plays a more substantial role in representation learning.

**Attention mechanism not measured.** The study does not measure attention maps directly. Claims about attention stability across layers are mechanistic hypotheses rather than measured findings. The intervention regularizes query projection weights, but whether this produces more stable or consistent attention patterns was not assessed. Direct measurement of attention maps would be needed to test the hypothesized mechanism.

**Dataset specificity.** Results are limited to the UCI HAR dataset with its specific sensor modality (smartphone inertial signals), activity classes (6 activities), and subject population. Whether the findings generalize to other time-series domains (physiological signals, financial data, environmental sensors) or other subject-disjoint benchmarks requires separate testing. The subject-disjoint split tests generalization to unseen individuals within this dataset, not to different corpora, sensors, or tasks.

**Coefficient and penalty strength.** The consistency coefficient of 0.01 was fixed across all conditions. Whether different coefficient values would produce different results was not tested. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient; the actual penalty magnitude depends on the weight divergence, which varies during training. The chosen value may have been too weak to produce measurable effects or too strong and interfered with task learning.

=== conclusion ===

This preregistered study tested whether cross-layer query consistency regularization improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Across 43 primary seeds and 43 pre-specified confirmatory replication seeds on disjoint seeds, the intervention produced small, statistically nonsignificant accuracy differences (primary: 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]; replication: 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. For someone choosing between standard training and cross-layer query consistency regularization in this setting, the evidence does not support adopting the intervention. The findings suggest layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks in this architecture class. What would settle the question next: direct measurement of attention maps to test whether weight regularization produces attention stability, testing in deeper architectures where cross-layer effects might be more pronounced, and evaluation on additional subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks to assess whether the null result generalizes beyond UCI HAR.

=== appendix ===

**Seed identities.** The 43 primary seed identities and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seed identities are recorded in the experiment archive but not enumerated in the prose per registration requirements.

**Figure descriptions.** Figure 1: Methodology flow showing UCI HAR data processing through PreNormTransformerEncoder with CrossLayerQueryConsistency intervention at the loss term across registered conditions, evaluated on the official test split for classification accuracy. Figure 2: Mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Figure 3: Mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. Figure 4: Mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the primary cohort. Figure 5: Mean held-out classification accuracy for all conditions in the replication cohort. Figure 6: Mean difference between proposed and baseline in the replication cohort. Figure 7: Mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the replication cohort.

**Data availability.** UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K).

Be faithful to those numbers and do NOT invent results, references, or findings. Write clear, precise academic prose. CITE numbered references in square brackets (e.g. [1] or [2, 3]); the Introduction and Related Work MUST cite them inline. An automated auditor checks each cited sentence against its abstract: say what a paper actually establishes, not merely its topic. You are NOT required to cite every reference; unused references are removed. NEVER cite a paper as evidence for something it does NOT discuss, including a gap in a different setting. State a gap WITHOUT a marker, use the reviewed gap statement, or cite an abstract that identifies that gap itself. Never attribute the opposite of what an abstract says. Stay INSIDE the abstract's own wording: use its terms, do not generalise them or add an unstated mechanism, domain or consequence. Plausible extensions are unsupported claims too; if in doubt, write less about the paper. Refer to figures and tables by number (e.g. 'Figure 1', 'Table 1'). Report results quantitatively (state the effect, its confidence interval, and whether it is significant). When the analysis contains primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts, report BOTH separately, state each preregistered decision, and never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. REGISTERED OPERATOR (including gradient handling; do not infer that detaching one loss term freezes ordinary task-loss learning):
Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

=== abstract ===

Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===

Time-series classification from wearable sensors enables continuous health monitoring, activity recognition, and human-computer interaction. The UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset represents a standard benchmark where inertial signals from smartphones must be classified into discrete activities across different subjects. Success in this setting requires models to generalize across individuals with different movement styles, sensor placements, and execution speeds—a subject-disjoint generalization challenge that remains difficult for deep architectures.

Transformers have attracted significant interest for time-series modeling due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies through self-attention mechanisms [38]. However, whether the architectural choices that make transformers effective in language and vision transfer to temporal domains remains contested. Some work questions whether transformers offer genuine advantages over simpler linear models for time-series forecasting [5], while others demonstrate successful applications in biosignal augmentation [20] and multivariate representation learning [14]. The uncertainty extends to architectural modifications: surveys document numerous transformer variants across domains [11, 21, 41], yet systematic evidence about which inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers remains limited.

One proposed mechanism for improving transformer generalization involves enforcing consistency across network depth. Deep transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17], and domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention patterns [18]. Cross-layer mechanisms have been explored in various contexts: layer attention retrieves information from previous layers [15], cross-layer fusion captures multi-scale features [23], and cross-layer consistency has been applied to activation engineering [34]. The hypothesis is that stabilizing attention patterns across depth could improve generalization by reducing layer-specific overfitting while preserving the representational capacity needed for temporal feature learning.

**Gap and contribution.** This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. Prior work has tested related regularization strategies—spectral entropy minimization of input projections [3] and entropy-maximized weight noise [2]—but cross-layer query consistency in time-series transformers has not undergone preregistered replication. The gap concerns whether this specific intervention, which penalizes divergence between query projection weights in successive transformer blocks, yields measurable accuracy improvements when evaluated on held-out subjects.

**What this paper does.** We report a preregistered experiment testing cross-layer query consistency regularization in a calibrated time-series transformer testbed. The study uses the official subject-disjoint split of UCI HAR, evaluates held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects, and includes both a primary cohort and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters.

- We test whether cross-layer query consistency regularization improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers, with a preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion in accuracy gain.
- We report results from both primary (43 seeds) and confirmatory replication (43 disjoint seeds) cohorts, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for all estimates.
- We include a negative control that penalizes divergence from a fixed random matrix, isolating whether any observed effect stems from meaningful cross-layer relationships versus generic regularization.

**Preregistered prediction.** The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===

Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. Transformers have achieved superior performances in natural language processing and computer vision, triggering interest in the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [38]. However, the validity of this research line has been questioned: one study found that simple linear models outperformed sophisticated transformer-based forecasting models across nine real-life datasets, attributing this to temporal information loss from permutation-invariant self-attention [5]. This tension motivates careful evaluation of whether transformer architectural modifications genuinely improve time-series performance or merely add complexity without benefit.

Specific applications demonstrate transformers can work in temporal domains. Biosignal data augmentation using transformer-based conditional GANs has shown promise for expanding limited medical datasets [20]. Multivariate time series have been represented as graphs with attention mechanisms capturing both intra- and inter-series correlations [14]. Yet large pre-trained time-series models remain less common than in language and vision, with most tasks still requiring separate models designed from scratch [22]. Domain adaptation for time-series transformers faces limitations including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges under data shift [32]. These findings suggest that while transformers can process temporal data, their advantages over simpler architectures remain context-dependent.

**Consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. Deep transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data, motivating regularization strategies that constrain the solution space [17]. Domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, leading to attention to spurious regions that deteriorate target domain accuracy [18]. Cross-layer interactions have been explored through mechanisms that strengthen layer interactions by retrieving query-related information from different receptive field levels [15]. Cross-layer consistency has also been applied to activation engineering, refining steering vectors through geometric stability across depth [34]. Cross-layer fusion has been utilized to capture multi-scale features in remote sensing classification [23]. These approaches share the hypothesis that coordinating representations across network depth improves generalization, though the specific mechanisms and target domains differ.

**Weight and spectral regularization.** Related work tests whether specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. Spectral entropy minimization of input projections was tested in a subject-disjoint time-series setting but yielded inconclusive results: neither primary nor replication cohorts exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero [3]. This suggests that enforcing low-entropy singular value spectra on input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. Entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise for subject-disjoint robustness carries a retracted notice because the executed intervention did not implement the preregistered intervention [2]. These null and retracted findings underscore the importance of faithful implementation and preregistered replication when evaluating regularization hypotheses.

**Attention mechanism modifications.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms provide context for architectural modifications. Selective attention reduces attention to unneeded elements through a parameter-free change, improving language modeling performance across model sizes [8]. External attention using two linear layers offers linear complexity while implicitly considering correlations between samples [33]. Depth-attention performs cross-layer value mixing inside the attention module itself, adding no persistent inference state beyond the standard key-value cache [37]. Surveys document transformer applications across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41], while empirical studies examine how different factors affect attention performance [28]. These works establish that attention mechanisms can be modified, but whether such modifications improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers requires direct testing.

**Positioning this study.** This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training [1]. Unlike cross-domain attention consistency which aligns attention maps across domains [18], or depth-attention which mixes values across layers [37], the intervention regularizes query projection weights between successive transformer blocks. The preregistered design with primary and confirmatory replication cohorts distinguishes this work from single-cohort evaluations. The subject-disjoint UCI HAR split tests generalization to unseen individuals rather than random held-out windows, addressing whether the intervention improves robustness to inter-subject variability in movement patterns and sensor characteristics.

=== method ===

**Operator design.** The CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator enforces Frobenius norm consistency between query projection weights in successive transformer blocks. The target parameter is blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight with shape (64, 64). The reference parameter is blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight, detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The operator computes element-wise subtraction between target and reference weights, squares each element, sums over all elements, and scales by a fixed coefficient of 0.01. This loss term is added to the classification objective during every optimization step, so the combined objective is differentiated and the target parameters are trained by it.

**Why this expression.** The hypothesis is that stabilizing query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization by reducing layer-specific overfitting while preserving representational capacity. Query projections determine which features each attention head attends to; if these projections diverge substantially across layers, deeper layers may learn idiosyncratic attention patterns that do not generalize to new subjects. Regularizing toward earlier layers tests whether consistent attention mechanisms across depth benefit temporal feature learning more than layer-specific adaptation. The Frobenius norm provides a differentiable measure of weight divergence that can be added to the training objective without modifying the architecture or inference path.

**Comparator and controls.** The baseline condition executes identical code but returns zero loss term, leaving the registered target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged. This control arm reaches every registered lifecycle point on the same inputs, ensuring that any difference between conditions stems from the loss term itself rather than implementation artifacts. The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute, testing whether any observed effect requires alignment between actual layer weights versus generic weight regularization.

**Gradient handling.** Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients from the consistency loss. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only, so block 1 query projections are trained toward block 0's current weights without modifying block 0 through this pathway. Block 0 still receives gradients from the classification objective through its own forward pass. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds. Detaching the reference tensor stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient.

**Model architecture.** The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear projection (9 to 64 channels), a learned positional embedding (128 timesteps, 64 channels), and two transformer blocks. Each block contains LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and residual connection. Final LayerNorm(64) is followed by mean-pool over time and Linear(64,6) for classification. The 9 input channels correspond to the raw inertial signals from the UCI HAR dataset.

**Training and evaluation.** Training runs for 12 epochs with batch size 128, SGD (lr=0.05, momentum=0.9). Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy as number of correct activity predictions divided by 2,947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them.

**Operator specification.** CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step.
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective.

Algorithm 1: (1) Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight. (2) Detach reference_weights from gradient graph. (3) Compute diff = target - reference_weights. (4) Compute squared_elements = diff * diff. (5) Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements). (6) Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01. (7) Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw. (8) Store loss_term in scratch dict. (9) Return loss_term to harness.

A random split would hold out windows from the same subjects used in training, conflating within-subject temporal generalization with between-subject generalization. For activity recognition applications where models must work for new users without subject-specific fine-tuning, the subject-disjoint evaluation is the relevant test. The cost is higher variance: inter-subject variability in movement style, sensor placement, and execution speed increases outcome noise compared to random splits.

**Paired seed design.** Both conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. This pairing reduces variance from random initialization and batch ordering when estimating the contrast between conditions. The benefit is tighter confidence intervals for the paired difference; the cost is that seeds are not independent across conditions. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them, not to subjects (subjects are fixed by the dataset split). If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, this would support the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency specifically (rather than any weight constraint) matters. If both perform similarly, the effect may stem from generic regularization rather than meaningful cross-layer relationships.

**Confidence interval computation.** All uncertainty estimates are bootstrap 95% confidence intervals computed over the paired seed differences. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance.

The green dash-dot marker in Figure 3 shows the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion; support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed this threshold. The lower bound of -0.00271 falls far below this threshold, so the preregistered decision was inconclusive.

**Replication cohort accuracy.** Figure 5 displays mean held-out classification accuracy for all three conditions in the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. The proposed condition achieved 0.9055 mean accuracy (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]). The baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). The first negative control achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]). Point estimates remain close across conditions, with overlapping confidence intervals.

**Replication cohort contrast.** Figure 6 shows the mean difference between proposed and baseline in the replication cohort. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, so no statistically significant difference was detected. The lower bound of -0.00196 does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098, so the preregistered decision was inconclusive. The effect size (Cohen's dz=0.15) is larger than in the primary cohort (dz=0.06) but remains small and nonsignificant.

**Training dynamics.** Figure 4 and Figure 7 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. The curves for all three conditions track closely throughout training, with no condition showing consistent separation from the others. This pattern suggests the intervention does not substantially alter the optimization trajectory or final convergence point.

**Summary table.** Table 1 summarizes mean accuracy and confidence intervals for all conditions in both cohorts. Table 2 summarizes the paired contrasts with p-values and effect sizes. Both tables confirm that neither cohort produced a statistically significant difference, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

=== discussion ===

**Principal finding.** The cross-layer query consistency intervention did not yield statistically significant improvements in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary cohort (mean difference 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]) or the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds (mean difference 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Both confidence intervals include zero, and neither lower bound exceeds the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The preregistered decision was inconclusive in both cohorts. This suggests that enforcing Frobenius norm consistency between query projection weights across transformer blocks does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this calibrated testbed.

**Interpretation.** These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation remains essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. If cross-layer consistency improved generalization, we would expect the proposed condition to outperform the baseline with a confidence interval excluding zero and exceeding the worthwhile margin. Instead, the point estimates are small (0.000773 and 0.00196) and the intervals span both negative and positive values. One interpretation is that different transformer layers benefit from learning distinct query projections that capture different temporal features or abstraction levels. Regularizing toward earlier layers may constrain this layer-specific specialization without providing compensating benefits.

**Alternative mechanisms.** An alternative explanation is that the consistency penalty was too weak to produce measurable effects. The coefficient of 0.01 was chosen to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective, but this may have rendered the regularization ineffective. However, the negative control also used the same coefficient and showed similar performance to the proposed condition, suggesting the issue is not merely penalty strength but rather the nature of the constraint itself. Another alternative is that two transformer blocks are insufficient depth for cross-layer consistency to matter; deeper networks might show different behavior. This claim is untestable on this calibrated testbed, which pins one architecture at one size.

**What the replication cohort adds.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds provides confidence that the null result is not an artifact of a specific seed set. Both cohorts show the same pattern: small, nonsignificant differences with confidence intervals including zero. The replication cohort's effect size (dz=0.15) is larger than the primary (dz=0.06), but both remain far from the threshold needed to claim the intervention exceeds the worthwhile margin. This consistency across seed sets strengthens the conclusion that the intervention does not produce robust accuracy gains in this regime.

**Relation to cited work.** These findings align with prior null results on weight geometry regularization in subject-disjoint time-series settings. Spectral entropy minimization of input projections also yielded inconclusive results with confidence intervals including zero in both primary and replication cohorts [3]. This suggests a broader pattern: enforcing specific weight structures does not reliably improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The findings contrast with cross-domain attention consistency work that reported improvements in domain adaptive semantic segmentation [18], but that study addressed a different problem (domain shift across datasets rather than subject disjointness within a dataset) and used attention-map alignment rather than weight alignment. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment.

**Mechanistic hypotheses.** Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. The study does not measure attention maps directly, so claims about attention stability are mechanistic hypotheses rather than measured findings. The intervention regularizes query projection weights, not attention outputs or attention maps. Whether weight consistency translates to attention stability depends on how query projections interact with key and value projections during the attention computation, which was not measured. Future work could directly measure attention map similarity across layers to test whether weight regularization produces the hypothesized attention stabilization.

**Scope of generalization.** All claims are scoped to the calibrated testbed: PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks, 64 hidden channels, 4-head attention, on UCI HAR with official subject-disjoint split. The findings do not establish whether cross-layer consistency would help in larger models, different architectures, or other time-series datasets. A claim about model scale or architecture family is untestable on this calibrated testbed. The single calibrated model at one size is what was tested; generalization to other settings requires separate experiments.

=== limitations ===

**Architecture and scale.** The study tests one architecture at one size: PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks and 64 hidden channels. Whether cross-layer query consistency would benefit deeper transformers, different attention mechanisms, or larger hidden dimensions remains unknown. Claims about larger models are untestable on this calibrated testbed. The intervention may behave differently in architectures where depth plays a more substantial role in representation learning.

**Attention mechanism not measured.** The study does not measure attention maps directly. Claims about attention stability across layers are mechanistic hypotheses rather than measured findings. The intervention regularizes query projection weights, but whether this produces more stable or consistent attention patterns was not assessed. Direct measurement of attention maps would be needed to test the hypothesized mechanism.

**Dataset specificity.** Results are limited to the UCI HAR dataset with its specific sensor modality (smartphone inertial signals), activity classes (6 activities), and subject population. Whether the findings generalize to other time-series domains (physiological signals, financial data, environmental sensors) or other subject-disjoint benchmarks requires separate testing. The subject-disjoint split tests generalization to unseen individuals within this dataset, not to different corpora, sensors, or tasks.

**Coefficient and penalty strength.** The consistency coefficient of 0.01 was fixed across all conditions. Whether different coefficient values would produce different results was not tested. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient; the actual penalty magnitude depends on the weight divergence, which varies during training. The chosen value may have been too weak to produce measurable effects or too strong and interfered with task learning.

=== conclusion ===

This preregistered study tested whether cross-layer query consistency regularization improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Across 43 primary seeds and 43 pre-specified confirmatory replication seeds on disjoint seeds, the intervention produced small, statistically nonsignificant accuracy differences (primary: 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]; replication: 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. For someone choosing between standard training and cross-layer query consistency regularization in this setting, the evidence does not support adopting the intervention. The findings suggest layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks in this architecture class. What would settle the question next: direct measurement of attention maps to test whether weight regularization produces attention stability, testing in deeper architectures where cross-layer effects might be more pronounced, and evaluation on additional subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks to assess whether the null result generalizes beyond UCI HAR.

=== appendix ===

**Seed identities.** The 43 primary seed identities and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seed identities are recorded in the experiment archive but not enumerated in the prose per registration requirements.

**Figure descriptions.** Figure 1: Methodology flow showing UCI HAR data processing through PreNormTransformerEncoder with CrossLayerQueryConsistency intervention at the loss term across registered conditions, evaluated on the official test split for classification accuracy. Figure 2: Mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Figure 3: Mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. Figure 4: Mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the primary cohort. Figure 5: Mean held-out classification accuracy for all conditions in the replication cohort. Figure 6: Mean difference between proposed and baseline in the replication cohort. Figure 7: Mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the replication cohort.

**Data availability.** UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K).
