payload.title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers

payload.user:
Related-work section:
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. Transformers have achieved superior performances in natural language processing and computer vision, triggering interest in the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [20]. However, the validity of this research line has been questioned: one study found that simple linear models outperformed sophisticated transformer-based forecasting models across nine real-life datasets, attributing this to temporal information loss from permutation-invariant self-attention [4]. This tension motivates careful evaluation of whether transformer architectural modifications genuinely improve time-series performance or merely add complexity without benefit.

Specific applications demonstrate transformers can work in temporal domains. Biosignal data augmentation using transformer-based conditional GANs has shown promise for expanding limited medical datasets [11]. Multivariate time series have been represented as graphs with attention mechanisms capturing both intra- and inter-series correlations [7]. Yet large pre-trained time-series models remain less common than in language and vision, with most tasks still requiring separate models designed from scratch [13]. Domain adaptation for time-series transformers faces limitations including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges under data shift [16]. These findings suggest that while transformers can process temporal data, their advantages over simpler architectures remain context-dependent.

**Consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. Deep transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data, motivating regularization strategies that constrain the solution space [9]. Domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, leading to attention to spurious regions that deteriorate target domain accuracy [10]. Cross-layer interactions have been explored through mechanisms that strengthen layer interactions by retrieving query-related information from different receptive field levels [8]. Cross-layer consistency has also been applied to activation engineering, refining steering vectors through geometric stability across depth [18]. Cross-layer fusion has been utilized to capture multi-scale features in remote sensing classification [14]. These approaches share the hypothesis that coordinating representations across network depth improves generalization, though the specific mechanisms and target domains differ.

**Weight and spectral regularization.** Related work tests whether specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. Spectral entropy minimization of input projections was tested in a subject-disjoint time-series setting but yielded inconclusive results: neither primary nor replication cohorts exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero [3]. This suggests that enforcing low-entropy singular value spectra on input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. Entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise for subject-disjoint robustness carries a retracted notice because the executed intervention did not implement the preregistered intervention [2]. These null and retracted findings underscore the importance of faithful implementation and preregistered replication when evaluating regularization hypotheses.

**Attention mechanism modifications.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms provide context for architectural modifications. Selective attention reduces attention to unneeded elements through a parameter-free change, improving language modeling performance across model sizes [5]. External attention using two linear layers offers linear complexity while implicitly considering correlations between samples [17]. Depth-attention performs cross-layer value mixing inside the attention module itself, adding no persistent inference state beyond the standard key-value cache [19]. Surveys document transformer applications across vision, NLP, and audio [6, 12, 21], while empirical studies examine how different factors affect attention performance [15]. These works establish that attention mechanisms can be modified, but whether such modifications improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers requires direct testing.

**Positioning this study.** This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training [1]. Unlike cross-domain attention consistency which aligns attention maps across domains [10], or depth-attention which mixes values across layers [19], the intervention regularizes query projection weights between successive transformer blocks. The preregistered design with primary and confirmatory replication cohorts distinguishes this work from single-cohort evaluations. The subject-disjoint UCI HAR split tests generalization to unseen individuals rather than random held-out windows, addressing whether the intervention improves robustness to inter-subject variability in movement patterns and sensor characteristics.

Cited papers and their abstracts:
[1] Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00133 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by -0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

[2] Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness
Abstract: [EDITORIAL NOTICE — RETRACTED: this paper carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it. Stated reason: The numerical outputs reported in this paper remain computationally reproducible: an independent re-run from the archived reproducibility bundle reproduced all eight aggregate metrics within tolerance. A post-publication audit of the artifact source found that the executed intervention did not implement the preregistered intervention. The preregistration committed to a multiplicative weight perturbation applied BEFORE the forward pass, an entropy term added to the training OBJECTIVE, and a noise scale learned by BACKPROPAGATION, with held-out evaluation on the clean weights. The experiment har. Its conclusions may not be relied on; cite it only with its status stated.] Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic training often fails to provide calibrated confidence under distribution shift. This study investigates whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We preregistered a hypothesis that entropy maximization would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the baseline, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the intervention across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results refuted the preregistered hypothesis in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by 0.04805 proportion (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002) relative to the baseline. The replication cohort confirmed this degradation with a contrast of -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Negative controls involving entropy minimization and fixed noise performed comparably to the deterministic baseline. These findings indicate that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over explicit entropy maximization for robustness tasks in this regime.

[3] Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning
Abstract: Regularization design for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. This study tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy compared to standard weight decay in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would exceed a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion in accuracy gain. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset, we evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and two negative controls across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results were inconclusive: the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0004419 (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], p=0.75) in the primary cohort and 0.002549 (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], p=0.106) in the replication cohort. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. These findings suggest that spectral entropy minimization of input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks.

[4] Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?
Abstract: Recently, there has been a surge of Transformer-based solutions for the long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) task. Despite the growing performance over the past few years, we question the validity of this line of research in this work. Specifically, Transformers is arguably the most successful solution to extract the semantic correlations among the elements in a long sequence. However, in time series modeling, we are to extract the temporal relations in an ordered set of continuous points. While employing positional encoding and using tokens to embed sub-series in Transformers facilitate preserving some ordering information, the nature of the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss. To validate our claim, we introduce a set of embarrassingly simple one-layer linear models named LTSF-Linear for comparison. Experimental results on nine real-life datasets show that LTSF-Linear surprisingly outperforms existing sophisticated Transformer-based LTSF models in all cases, and often by a large margin. Moreover, we conduct comprehensive empirical studies to explore the impacts of various design elements of LTSF models on their temporal relation extraction capability. We hope this surprising finding opens up new research directions for the LTSF task. We also advocate revisiting the validity of Transformer-based solutions for other time series analysis tasks (e.g., anomaly detection) in the future.

[5] Selective Attention Improves Transformer
Abstract: Unneeded elements in the attention’s context degrade performance. We introduce Selective Attention, a simple parameter-free change to the standard attention mechanism which reduces attention to unneeded elements. Selective attention consistently improves language modeling and downstream task performance in a variety of model sizes and context lengths. For example, transformers trained with the language modeling objective on C4 with selective attention perform language modeling equivalently to standard transformers with ~2X more heads and parameters in their attention modules. Selective attention also allows decreasing the size of the attention’s context buffer, leading to meaningful reductions in the memory and compute requirements during inference. For example, transformers trained on C4 with context sizes of 512, 1,024, and 2,048 need 16X, 25X, and 47X less memory for their attention module, respectively, when equipped with selective attention, as those without selective attention, with the same validation perplexity.

[6] A Survey on Vision Transformer
Abstract: Transformer, first applied to the field of natural language processing, is a type of deep neural network mainly based on the self-attention mechanism. Thanks to its strong representation capabilities, researchers are looking at ways to apply transformer to computer vision tasks. In a variety of visual benchmarks, transformer-based models perform similar to or better than other types of networks such as convolutional and recurrent neural networks. Given its high performance and less need for vision-specific inductive bias, transformer is receiving more and more attention from the computer vision community. In this paper, we review these vision transformer models by categorizing them in different tasks and analyzing their advantages and disadvantages. The main categories we explore include the backbone network, high/mid-level vision, low-level vision, and video processing. We also include efficient transformer methods for pushing transformer into real device-based applications. Furthermore, we also take a brief look at the self-attention mechanism in computer vision, as it is the base component in transformer. Toward the end of this paper, we discuss the challenges and provide several further research directions for vision transformers.

[7] Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer
Abstract: A reliable and efficient representation of multivariate time series is crucial in various downstream machine learning tasks. In multivariate time series forecasting, each variable depends on its historical values and there are inter-dependencies among variables as well. Models have to be designed to capture both intra- and inter-relationships among the time series. To move towards this goal, we propose the Time Series Attention Transformer (TSAT) for multivariate time series representation learning. Using TSAT, we represent both temporal information and inter-dependencies of multivariate time series in terms of edge-enhanced dynamic graphs. The intra-series correlations are represented by nodes in a dynamic graph; a self-attention mechanism is modified to capture the inter-series correlations by using the super-empirical mode decomposition (SMD) module. We applied the embedded dynamic graphs to times series forecasting problems, including two real-world datasets and two benchmark datasets. Extensive experiments show that TSAT clearly outerperforms six state-of-the-art baseline methods in various forecasting horizons. We further visualize the embedded dynamic graphs to illustrate the graph representation power of TSAT. We share our code at https://github.com/RadiantResearch/TSAT.

[8] Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention
Abstract: More and more evidence has shown that strengthening layer interactions can enhance the representation power of a deep neural network, while self-attention excels at learning interdependencies by retrieving query-activated information. Motivated by this, we devise a cross-layer attention mechanism, called multi-head recurrent layer attention (MRLA), that sends a query representation of the current layer to all previous layers to retrieve query-related information from different levels of receptive fields. A light-weighted version of MRLA is also proposed to reduce the quadratic computation cost. The proposed layer attention mechanism can enrich the representation power of many state-of-the-art vision networks, including CNNs and vision transformers. Its effectiveness has been extensively evaluated in image classification, object detection and instance segmentation tasks, where improvements can be consistently observed. For example, our MRLA can improve 1.6% Top-1 accuracy on ResNet-50, while only introducing 0.16M parameters and 0.07B FLOPs. Surprisingly, it can boost the performances by a large margin of 3-4% box AP and mask AP in dense prediction tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/joyfang1106/MRLA.

[9] Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks
Abstract: The large-scale and deep-layer deep neural network based on the Transformer model is very powerful in sequence tasks, but it is prone to overfitting for small-scale training data. Moreover, the prediction result of the model with a small disturbance input is significantly lower than that without disturbance. In this work, we propose a double consistency regularization (DOCR) method for the end-to-end model structure, which separately constrains the output of the encoder and decoder during the training process to alleviate the above problems. Specifically, on the basis of the cross-entropy loss function, we build the mean model by integrating the model parameters of the previous rounds and measure the consistency between the models by calculating the KL divergence between the features of the encoder output and the probability distribution of the decoder output of the mean model and the base model so as to impose regularization constraints on the solution space of the model. We conducted extensive experiments on machine translation tasks, and the results show that the BLEU score increased by 2.60 on average, demonstrating the effectiveness of DOCR in improving model performance and its complementary impacts with other regularization techniques.

[10] CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation
Abstract: While transformers have greatly boosted performance in semantic segmentation, domain adaptive transformers are not yet well explored. We identify that the domain gap can cause discrepancies in self-attention. Due to this gap, the transformer attends to spurious regions or pixels, which deteriorates accuracy on the target domain. We propose Cross-Domain Attention Consistency (CDAC), to perform adaptation on attention maps using cross-domain attention layers that share features between source and target domains. Specifically, we impose consistency between predictions from cross-domain attention and self-attention modules to encourage similar distributions across domains in both the attention and output of the model, i.e., attention-level and output-level alignment. We also enforce consistency in attention maps between different augmented views to further strengthen the attention-based alignment. Combining these two components, CDAC mitigates the discrepancy in attention maps across domains and further boosts the performance of the transformer under unsupervised domain adaptation settings. Our method is evaluated on various widely used benchmarks and outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines, including GTAV-to-Cityscapes by 1.3 and 1.5 percent point (pp) and Synthia-to-Cityscapes by 0.6 pp and 2.9 pp when combining with two competitive Transformer-based backbones, respectively. Our code will be publicly available at https://github.com/wangkaihong/CDAC.

[11] TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation
Abstract: Signal measurement appearing in the form of time series is one of the most common types of data used in medical machine learning applications. Such datasets are often small in size, expensive to collect and annotate, and might involve privacy issues, which hinders our ability to train large, state-of-the-art deep learning models for biomedical applications. For time-series data, the suite of data augmentation strategies we can use to expand the size of the dataset is limited by the need to maintain the basic properties of the signal. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) can be utilized as another data augmentation tool. In this paper, we present TTS-CGAN, a transformer-based conditional GAN model that can be trained on existing multi-class datasets and generate class-specific synthetic time-series sequences of arbitrary length. We elaborate on the model architecture and design strategies. Synthetic sequences generated by our model are indistinguishable from real ones, and can be used to complement or replace real signals of the same type, thus achieving the goal of data augmentation. To evaluate the quality of the generated data, we modify the wavelet coherence metric to be able to compare the similarity between two sets of signals, and also conduct a case study where a mix of synthetic and real data are used to train a deep learning model for sequence classification. Together with other visualization techniques and qualitative evaluation approaches, we demonstrate that TTS-CGAN generated synthetic data are similar to real data, and that our model performs better than the other state-of-the-art GAN models built for time-series data generation.

[12] Transformers in Vision: A Survey
Abstract: Astounding results from Transformer models on natural language tasks have intrigued the vision community to study their application to computer vision problems. Among their salient benefits, Transformers enable modeling long dependencies between input sequence elements and support parallel processing of sequence as compared to recurrent networks, e.g., Long short-term memory. Different from convolutional networks, Transformers require minimal inductive biases for their design and are naturally suited as set-functions. Furthermore, the straightforward design of Transformers allows processing multiple modalities (e.g., images, videos, text, and speech) using similar processing blocks and demonstrates excellent scalability to very large capacity networks and huge datasets. These strengths have led to exciting progress on a number of vision tasks using Transformer networks. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the Transformer models in the computer vision discipline. We start with an introduction to fundamental concepts behind the success of Transformers, i.e., self-attention, large-scale pre-training, and bidirectional feature encoding. We then cover extensive applications of transformers in vision including popular recognition tasks (e.g., image classification, object detection, action recognition, and segmentation), generative modeling, multi-modal tasks (e.g., visual-question answering, visual reasoning, and visual grounding), video processing (e.g., activity recognition, video forecasting), low-level vision (e.g., image super-resolution, image enhancement, and colorization), and three-dimensional analysis (e.g., point cloud classification and segmentation). We compare the respective advantages and limitations of popular techniques both in terms of architectural design and their experimental value. Finally, we provide an analysis on open research directions and possible future works. We hope this effort will ignite further interest in the community to solve current challenges toward the application of transformer models in computer vision.

[13] Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks
Abstract: Large pre-trained models have been vital in recent advancements in domains like language and vision, making model training for individual downstream tasks more efficient and provide superior performance. However, tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model from scratch leveraging training data and domain expertise specific to the task. We tackle a significant challenge for pre-training a foundational time-series model from multi-domain time-series datasets: extracting semantically useful tokenized inputs to the model across heterogeneous time-series from different domains. We propose Large Pre-trained Time-series Models (LPTM) that introduces a novel method of adaptive segmentation that automatically identifies optimal dataset-specific segmentation strategy during pre-training. This enables LPTM to perform similar to or better than domain-specific state-of-art model when fine-tuned to different downstream time-series analysis tasks and under zero-shot settings. LPTM achieves superior forecasting and time-series classification results taking up to 40% less data and 50% less training time compared to state-of-art baselines.

[14] Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification
Abstract: Abstract The rapid development of deep learning, especially the application of CNN and Transformer, brings a new direction for remote sensing scene classification. CNN is challenging to capture multi-scale features due to the limitation of the receptive field. Although the feature pyramid network (FPN) is a multi-scale structure, its fusion mechanism inherently limits the extraction of fine-grained information. The Transformer architecture excels at capturing long-range dependencies through its self-attention mechanism. While the multihead self-attention mechanism allows it to concentrate on both global and local patterns, there is still room for improvement in explicitly enhancing the extraction of local spatial features and edge detail information. To overcome the above limitations, this paper proposes a novel end-to-end learning model, called cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network (CLFETNet), for remote sensing scene classification. The innovative contribution of this paper is to embed three novel modules into the traditional CNN model. Firstly, we utilize the FPN to extract multi-scale features and design a fine feature aggregation module (RFA) to integrate complementary information from different layers to obtain more reliable and accurate features. Second, the efficient frequency transformer (EFT) is proposed to deeply mine global information, local spatial features, and edge detail information. Finally, the graph-aware fusion (GAF) module is proposed to model the relationships among regions in the feature graph by graph convolutional network (GCN), which enhances the intra-class feature consistency. A wide range of experiments have been carried out on three publicly accessible RS scene datasets. Positive results show that our CLFETNet framework outperforms many existing methods, has high robustness and superiority in remote sensing scene classification tasks, and can effectively handle complex scenes and meet multi-scale feature challenges.

[15] An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks
Abstract: Attention mechanisms have become a popular component in deep neural networks, yet there has been little examination of how different influencing factors and methods for computing attention from these factors affect performance. Toward a better general understanding of attention mechanisms, we present an empirical study that ablates various spatial attention elements within a generalized attention formulation, encompassing the dominant Transformer attention as well as the prevalent deformable convolution and dynamic convolution modules. Conducted on a variety of applications, the study yields significant findings about spatial attention in deep networks, some of which run counter to conventional understanding. For example, we find that the query and key content comparison in Transformer attention is negligible for self-attention, but vital for encoder-decoder attention. A proper combination of deformable convolution with key content only saliency achieves the best accuracy-efficiency tradeoff in self-attention. Related-work section:
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. Transformers have achieved superior performances in natural language processing and computer vision, triggering interest in the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [20]. However, the validity of this research line has been questioned: one study found that simple linear models outperformed sophisticated transformer-based forecasting models across nine real-life datasets, attributing this to temporal information loss from permutation-invariant self-attention [4]. This tension motivates careful evaluation of whether transformer architectural modifications genuinely improve time-series performance or merely add complexity without benefit.

Specific applications demonstrate transformers can work in temporal domains. Biosignal data augmentation using transformer-based conditional GANs has shown promise for expanding limited medical datasets [11]. Multivariate time series have been represented as graphs with attention mechanisms capturing both intra- and inter-series correlations [7]. Yet large pre-trained time-series models remain less common than in language and vision, with most tasks still requiring separate models designed from scratch [13]. Domain adaptation for time-series transformers faces limitations including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges under data shift [16]. These findings suggest that while transformers can process temporal data, their advantages over simpler architectures remain context-dependent.

**Consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. Deep transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data, motivating regularization strategies that constrain the solution space [9]. Domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, leading to attention to spurious regions that deteriorate target domain accuracy [10]. Cross-layer interactions have been explored through mechanisms that strengthen layer interactions by retrieving query-related information from different receptive field levels [8]. Cross-layer consistency has also been applied to activation engineering, refining steering vectors through geometric stability across depth [18]. Cross-layer fusion has been utilized to capture multi-scale features in remote sensing classification [14]. These approaches share the hypothesis that coordinating representations across network depth improves generalization, though the specific mechanisms and target domains differ.

**Weight and spectral regularization.** Related work tests whether specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. Spectral entropy minimization of input projections was tested in a subject-disjoint time-series setting but yielded inconclusive results: neither primary nor replication cohorts exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero [3]. This suggests that enforcing low-entropy singular value spectra on input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. Entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise for subject-disjoint robustness carries a retracted notice because the executed intervention did not implement the preregistered intervention [2]. These null and retracted findings underscore the importance of faithful implementation and preregistered replication when evaluating regularization hypotheses.

**Attention mechanism modifications.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms provide context for architectural modifications. Selective attention reduces attention to unneeded elements through a parameter-free change, improving language modeling performance across model sizes [5]. External attention using two linear layers offers linear complexity while implicitly considering correlations between samples [17]. Depth-attention performs cross-layer value mixing inside the attention module itself, adding no persistent inference state beyond the standard key-value cache [19]. Surveys document transformer applications across vision, NLP, and audio [6, 12, 21], while empirical studies examine how different factors affect attention performance [15]. These works establish that attention mechanisms can be modified, but whether such modifications improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers requires direct testing.

**Positioning this study.** This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training [1]. Unlike cross-domain attention consistency which aligns attention maps across domains [10], or depth-attention which mixes values across layers [19], the intervention regularizes query projection weights between successive transformer blocks. The preregistered design with primary and confirmatory replication cohorts distinguishes this work from single-cohort evaluations. The subject-disjoint UCI HAR split tests generalization to unseen individuals rather than random held-out windows, addressing whether the intervention improves robustness to inter-subject variability in movement patterns and sensor characteristics.

To address this, we propose Global Evolutionary Refined Steering (GER-steer), a training-free framework that grounded in the geometric stability of the network's representation evolution. GER-steer exploits this global signal to rectify raw steering vectors, effectively decoupling robust semantic intent from orthogonal artifacts. Extensive evaluations confirm that GER-steer consistently outperforms baselines, delivering superior efficacy and generalization without layer-specific tuning, establishing a universal solution for reliable model alignment.

[19] Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models
Abstract: Self-attention selects information freely across the sequence, but across depth, Transformers merely add each layer's output to the residual stream, so later layers cannot selectively reuse earlier-layer representations. Recent cross-layer methods improve this flow but operate on hidden states outside attention, adding state beyond the key-value cache at inference--a cost that becomes increasingly salient as modern LLMs compress the cache with grouped-query and multi-head latent attention. We introduce Depth-Attention, which performs this selection inside the attention module itself: before a layer attends over the sequence, its query attends over the keys of earlier layers at the same token position and mixes their values into the value that self-attention then reads. Because Depth-Attention reuses the standard attention queries, keys, and value-cache slots, storing depth-mixed values in place of the original values, it adds no parameters and introduces no persistent inference state beyond the standard key-value cache--the same cache size as a vanilla decoder and less than hidden-state-based cross-layer methods. On Qwen3-style decoders at 1.5B and 3B parameters, Depth-Attention attains the lowest perplexity and the highest average downstream accuracy, improving over the vanilla Transformer by up to 2.3 accuracy points and surpassing strong cross-layer baselines in perplexity and average accuracy, while adding under 0.01% extra arithmetic FLOPs and no additional persistent inference state. The gains hold from 360M to 3B parameters and extend to looped Transformers.

[20] Transformers in Time Series: A Survey
Abstract: Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications. In this paper, we systematically review Transformer schemes for time series modeling by highlighting their strengths as well as limitations. In particular, we examine the development of time series Transformers in two perspectives. From the perspective of network structure, we summarize the adaptations and modifications that have been made to Transformers in order to accommodate the challenges in time series analysis. From the perspective of applications, we categorize time series Transformers based on common tasks including forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification. Empirically, we perform robust analysis, model size analysis, and seasonal-trend decomposition analysis to study how Transformers perform in time series. Finally, we discuss and suggest future directions to provide useful research guidance. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first work to comprehensively and systematically summarize the recent advances of Transformers for modeling time series data. We hope this survey will ignite further research interests in time series Transformers.

[21] A survey of transformers
Abstract: Transformers have achieved great success in many artificial intelligence fields, such as natural language processing, computer vision, and audio processing. Therefore, it is natural to attract lots of interest from academic and industry researchers. Up to the present, a great variety of Transformer variants (a.k.a. X-formers) have been proposed, however, a systematic and comprehensive literature review on these Transformer variants is still missing. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive review of various X-formers. We first briefly introduce the vanilla Transformer and then propose a new taxonomy of X-formers. Next, we introduce the various X-formers from three perspectives: architectural modification, pre-training, and applications. Finally, we outline some potential directions for future research.

Abstract: Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

Introduction: Time-series classification from wearable sensors enables continuous health monitoring, activity recognition, and human-computer interaction. The UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset represents a standard benchmark where inertial signals from smartphones must be classified into discrete activities across different subjects. Success in this setting requires models to generalize across individuals with different movement styles, sensor placements, and execution speeds—a subject-disjoint generalization challenge that remains difficult for deep architectures.

Transformers have attracted significant interest for time-series modeling due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies through self-attention mechanisms [20]. However, whether the architectural choices that make transformers effective in language and vision transfer to temporal domains remains contested. Some work questions whether transformers offer genuine advantages over simpler linear models for time-series forecasting [4], while others demonstrate successful applications in biosignal augmentation [11] and multivariate representation learning [7]. The uncertainty extends to architectural modifications: surveys document numerous transformer variants across domains [6, 12, 21], yet systematic evidence about which inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers remains limited.

One proposed mechanism for improving transformer generalization involves enforcing consistency across network depth. Deep transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [9], and domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention patterns [10]. Cross-layer mechanisms have been explored in various contexts: layer attention retrieves information from previous layers [8], cross-layer fusion captures multi-scale features [14], and cross-layer consistency has been applied to activation engineering [18]. The hypothesis is that stabilizing attention patterns across depth could improve generalization by reducing layer-specific overfitting while preserving the representational capacity needed for temporal feature learning.

**Gap and contribution.** This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. Prior work has tested related regularization strategies—spectral entropy minimization of input projections [3] and entropy-maximized weight noise [2]—but cross-layer query consistency in time-series transformers has not undergone preregistered replication. The gap concerns whether this specific intervention, which penalizes divergence between query projection weights in successive transformer blocks, yields measurable accuracy improvements when evaluated on held-out subjects.

**What this paper does.** We report a preregistered experiment testing cross-layer query consistency regularization in a calibrated time-series transformer testbed. The study uses the official subject-disjoint split of UCI HAR, evaluates held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects, and includes both a primary cohort and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters.

- We test whether cross-layer query consistency regularization improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers, with a preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion in accuracy gain.

This tension motivates careful evaluation of whether transformer architectural modifications genuinely improve time-series performance or merely add complexity without benefit.

Specific applications demonstrate transformers can work in temporal domains. Biosignal data augmentation using transformer-based conditional GANs has shown promise for expanding limited medical datasets [11]. Multivariate time series have been represented as graphs with attention mechanisms capturing both intra- and inter-series correlations [7]. Yet large pre-trained time-series models remain less common than in language and vision, with most tasks still requiring separate models designed from scratch [13]. Domain adaptation for time-series transformers faces limitations including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges under data shift [16]. These findings suggest that while transformers can process temporal data, their advantages over simpler architectures remain context-dependent.

**Consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. Deep transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data, motivating regularization strategies that constrain the solution space [9]. Domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, leading to attention to spurious regions that deteriorate target domain accuracy [10]. Cross-layer interactions have been explored through mechanisms that strengthen layer interactions by retrieving query-related information from different receptive field levels [8]. Cross-layer consistency has also been applied to activation engineering, refining steering vectors through geometric stability across depth [18]. Cross-layer fusion has been utilized to capture multi-scale features in remote sensing classification [14]. These approaches share the hypothesis that coordinating representations across network depth improves generalization, though the specific mechanisms and target domains differ.

**Weight and spectral regularization.** Related work tests whether specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. Spectral entropy minimization of input projections was tested in a subject-disjoint time-series setting but yielded inconclusive results: neither primary nor replication cohorts exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero [3]. This suggests that enforcing low-entropy singular value spectra on input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. Entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise for subject-disjoint robustness carries a retracted notice because the executed intervention did not implement the preregistered intervention [2]. These null and retracted findings underscore the importance of faithful implementation and preregistered replication when evaluating regularization hypotheses.

**Attention mechanism modifications.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms provide context for architectural modifications. Selective attention reduces attention to unneeded elements through a parameter-free change, improving language modeling performance across model sizes [5]. External attention using two linear layers offers linear complexity while implicitly considering correlations between samples [17]. Depth-attention performs cross-layer value mixing inside the attention module itself, adding no persistent inference state beyond the standard key-value cache [19]. Surveys document transformer applications across vision, NLP, and audio [6, 12, 21], while empirical studies examine how different factors affect attention performance [15]. These works establish that attention mechanisms can be modified, but whether such modifications improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers requires direct testing.

**Positioning this study.** This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training [1]. Unlike cross-domain attention consistency which aligns attention maps across domains [10], or depth-attention which mixes values across layers [19], the intervention regularizes query projection weights between successive transformer blocks. The preregistered design with primary and confirmatory replication cohorts distinguishes this work from single-cohort evaluations. The subject-disjoint UCI HAR split tests generalization to unseen individuals rather than random held-out windows, addressing whether the intervention improves robustness to inter-subject variability in movement patterns and sensor characteristics.
Method: **Operator design.** The CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator enforces Frobenius norm consistency between query projection weights in successive transformer blocks. The target parameter is blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight with shape (64, 64). The reference parameter is blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight, detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The operator computes element-wise subtraction between target and reference weights, squares each element, sums over all elements, and scales by a fixed coefficient of 0.01. This loss term is added to the classification objective during every optimization step, so the combined objective is differentiated and the target parameters are trained by it.

**Why this expression.** The hypothesis is that stabilizing query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization by reducing layer-specific overfitting while preserving representational capacity. Query projections determine which features each attention head attends to; if these projections diverge substantially across layers, deeper layers may learn idiosyncratic attention patterns that do not generalize to new subjects. Regularizing toward earlier layers tests whether consistent attention mechanisms across depth benefit temporal feature learning more than layer-specific adaptation. The Frobenius norm provides a differentiable measure of weight divergence that can be added to the training objective without modifying the architecture or inference path.

**Comparator and controls.** The baseline condition executes identical code but returns zero loss term, leaving the registered target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged. This control arm reaches every registered lifecycle point on the same inputs, ensuring that any difference between conditions stems from the loss term itself rather than implementation artifacts. The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute, testing whether any observed effect requires alignment between actual layer weights versus generic weight regularization.

**Gradient handling.** Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients from the consistency loss. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only, so block 1 query projections are trained toward block 0's current weights without modifying block 0 through this pathway. Block 0 still receives gradients from the classification objective through its own forward pass. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds. Detaching the reference tensor stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient.

**Model architecture.** The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear projection (9 to 64 channels), a learned positional embedding (128 timesteps, 64 channels), and two transformer blocks. Each block contains LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and residual connection. Final LayerNorm(64) is followed by mean-pool over time and Linear(64,6) for classification. The 9 input channels correspond to the raw inertial signals from the UCI HAR dataset.

**Training and evaluation.** Training runs for 12 epochs with batch size 128, SGD (lr=0.05, momentum=0.9). Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy as number of correct activity predictions divided by 2,947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them.

Experimental setup: **Subject-disjoint split justification.** The official UCI HAR subject-disjoint split separates training and test subjects entirely, with 7,352 training windows from some subjects and 2,947 held-out windows from different subjects. This design answers whether the intervention improves generalization to unseen individuals rather than merely fitting the training distribution better. A random split would hold out windows from the same subjects used in training, conflating within-subject temporal generalization with between-subject generalization. For activity recognition applications where models must work for new users without subject-specific fine-tuning, the subject-disjoint evaluation is the relevant test. The cost is higher variance: inter-subject variability in movement style, sensor placement, and execution speed increases outcome noise compared to random splits.

**Paired seed design.** Both conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. This pairing reduces variance from random initialization and batch ordering when estimating the contrast between conditions. The benefit is tighter confidence intervals for the paired difference; the cost is that seeds are not independent across conditions. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them, not to subjects (subjects are fixed by the dataset split). The seed budget comprises 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix.

**Negative control purpose.** The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This tests whether any observed effect requires alignment between actual layer weights versus generic weight regularization toward an arbitrary target. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, this would support the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency specifically (rather than any weight constraint) matters. If both perform similarly, the effect may stem from generic regularization rather than meaningful cross-layer relationships.

**Confidence interval computation.** All uncertainty estimates are bootstrap 95% confidence intervals computed over the paired seed differences. The analysis computed confidence intervals, not standard deviations. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance.

**Condition execution.** Recorded activity shows 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity for the proposed condition in both primary and replication cohorts. The baseline recorded 0/43 seeds with operator activity in both cohorts, confirming the control arm left the target parameter unchanged. The first negative control recorded 43/43 seeds with operator activity in both cohorts. Conformance and activation counts describe execution; they do not establish the mechanism or prove the absence of implementation bias.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Results: **Primary cohort accuracy.** Figure 2 displays mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition, baseline, and first negative control in the primary cohort. Bars represent means over 43 paired seeds with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals as error bars. The proposed condition achieved 0.9062 mean accuracy (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]). The baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The first negative control achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). The proposed condition shows a numerically higher point estimate than baseline, but the confidence intervals overlap substantially, indicating the difference is not statistically distinguishable from zero.

**Primary cohort contrast.** Figure 3 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.000773 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, so no statistically significant difference was detected. The green dash-dot marker in Figure 3 shows the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion; support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed this threshold. The lower bound of -0.00271 falls far below this threshold, so the preregistered decision was inconclusive.

**Replication cohort accuracy.** Figure 5 displays mean held-out classification accuracy for all three conditions in the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. The proposed condition achieved 0.9055 mean accuracy (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]). The baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). The first negative control achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]). Point estimates remain close across conditions, with overlapping confidence intervals.

**Replication cohort contrast.** Figure 6 shows the mean difference between proposed and baseline in the replication cohort. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00196 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, so no statistically significant difference was detected. The lower bound of -0.00196 does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098, so the preregistered decision was inconclusive. The effect size (Cohen's dz=0.15) is larger than in the primary cohort (dz=0.06) but remains small and nonsignificant.

**Training dynamics.** Figure 4 and Figure 7 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. The curves for all three conditions track closely throughout training, with no condition showing consistent separation from the others. This pattern suggests the intervention does not substantially alter the optimization trajectory or final convergence point.

**Summary table.** Table 1 summarizes mean accuracy and confidence intervals for all conditions in both cohorts. Table 2 summarizes the paired contrasts with p-values and effect sizes. Both tables confirm that neither cohort produced a statistically significant difference, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This preregistered study tested whether cross-layer query consistency regularization improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Across 43 primary seeds and 43 pre-specified confirmatory replication seeds on disjoint seeds, the intervention produced small, statistically nonsignificant accuracy differences (primary: 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]; replication: 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. For someone choosing between standard training and cross-layer query consistency regularization in this setting, the evidence does not support adopting the intervention. One possibility, which this experiment did not test, is that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks in this architecture class. What would settle the question next: direct measurement of attention maps to test whether weight regularization produces attention stability, testing in deeper architectures where cross-layer effects might be more pronounced, and evaluation on additional subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks to assess whether the null result generalizes beyond UCI HAR.
Discussion: **Principal finding.** The cross-layer query consistency intervention did not yield statistically significant improvements in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary cohort (mean difference 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]) or the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds (mean difference 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Both confidence intervals include zero, and neither lower bound exceeds the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The preregistered decision was inconclusive in both cohorts. This suggests that enforcing Frobenius norm consistency between query projection weights across transformer blocks does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this calibrated testbed.

**Interpretation.** These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation remains essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. If cross-layer consistency improved generalization, we would expect the proposed condition to outperform the baseline with a confidence interval excluding zero and exceeding the worthwhile margin. Instead, the point estimates are small (0.000773 and 0.00196) and the intervals span both negative and positive values. One interpretation is that different transformer layers benefit from learning distinct query projections that capture different temporal features or abstraction levels. Regularizing toward earlier layers may constrain this layer-specific specialization without providing compensating benefits.

**Alternative mechanisms.** An alternative explanation is that the consistency penalty was too weak to produce measurable effects. The coefficient of 0.01 was chosen to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective, but this may have rendered the regularization ineffective. However, the negative control also used the same coefficient and showed similar performance to the proposed condition, suggesting the issue is not merely penalty strength but rather the nature of the constraint itself. Another alternative is that two transformer blocks are insufficient depth for cross-layer consistency to matter; deeper networks might show different behavior. This claim is untestable on this calibrated testbed, which pins one architecture at one size.

**What the replication cohort adds.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds provides confidence that the null result is not an artifact of a specific seed set. Both cohorts show the same pattern: small, nonsignificant differences with confidence intervals including zero. The replication cohort's effect size (dz=0.15) is larger than the primary (dz=0.06), but both remain far from the threshold needed to claim the intervention exceeds the worthwhile margin. This consistency across seed sets strengthens the conclusion that the intervention does not produce robust accuracy gains in this regime.

**Relation to cited work.** These findings align with prior null results on weight geometry regularization in subject-disjoint time-series settings. Spectral entropy minimization of input projections also yielded inconclusive results with confidence intervals including zero in both primary and replication cohorts [3]. This suggests a broader pattern: enforcing specific weight structures does not reliably improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The findings contrast with cross-domain attention consistency work that reported improvements in domain adaptive semantic segmentation [10], but that study addressed a different problem (domain shift across datasets rather than subject disjointness within a dataset) and used attention-map alignment rather than weight alignment. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment.

**Mechanistic hypotheses.** Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. The study does not measure attention maps directly, so claims about attention stability are mechanistic hypotheses rather than measured findings. The intervention regularizes query projection weights, not attention outputs or attention maps. Whether weight consistency translates to attention stability depends on how query projections interact with key and value projections during the attention computation, which was not measured. Future work could directly measure attention map similarity across layers to test whether weight regularization produces the hypothesized attention stabilization.

**Scope of generalization.** All claims are scoped to the calibrated testbed: PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks, 64 hidden channels, 4-head attention, on UCI HAR with official subject-disjoint split. The findings do not establish whether cross-layer consistency would help in larger models, different architectures, or other time-series datasets. A claim about model scale or architecture family is untestable on this calibrated testbed. The single calibrated model at one size is what was tested; generalization to other settings requires separate experiments.
Limitations: **Architecture and scale.** The study tests one architecture at one size: PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks and 64 hidden channels. Whether cross-layer query consistency would benefit deeper transformers, different attention mechanisms, or larger hidden dimensions remains unknown. Claims about larger models are untestable on this calibrated testbed. The intervention may behave differently in architectures where depth plays a more substantial role in representation learning.

**Attention mechanism not measured.** The study does not measure attention maps directly. Claims about attention stability across layers are mechanistic hypotheses rather than measured findings. The intervention regularizes query projection weights, but whether this produces more stable or consistent attention patterns was not assessed. Direct measurement of attention maps would be needed to test the hypothesized mechanism.

**Dataset specificity.** Results are limited to the UCI HAR dataset with its specific sensor modality (smartphone inertial signals), activity classes (6 activities), and subject population. Whether the findings generalize to other time-series domains (physiological signals, financial data, environmental sensors) or other subject-disjoint benchmarks requires separate testing. The subject-disjoint split tests generalization to unseen individuals within this dataset, not to different corpora, sensors, or tasks.

**Coefficient and penalty strength.** The consistency coefficient of 0.01 was fixed across all conditions. Whether different coefficient values would produce different results was not tested. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient; the actual penalty magnitude depends on the weight divergence, which varies during training. The chosen value may have been too weak to produce measurable effects or too strong and interfered with task learning.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.
