Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. Transformers have achieved superior performances in natural language processing and computer vision, triggering interest in the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [20]. However, the validity of this research line has been questioned: one study found that simple linear models outperformed sophisticated transformer-based forecasting models across nine real-life datasets, attributing this to temporal information loss from permutation-invariant self-attention [4]. This tension motivates careful evaluation of whether transformer architectural modifications genuinely improve time-series performance or merely add complexity without benefit.

Specific applications demonstrate transformers can work in temporal domains. Biosignal data augmentation using transformer-based conditional GANs has shown promise for expanding limited medical datasets [11]. Multivariate time series have been represented as graphs with attention mechanisms capturing both intra- and inter-series correlations [7]. Yet large pre-trained time-series models remain less common than in language and vision, with most tasks still requiring separate models designed from scratch [13]. Domain adaptation for time-series transformers faces limitations including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges under data shift [16]. These findings suggest that while transformers can process temporal data, their advantages over simpler architectures remain context-dependent.

**Consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. Deep transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data, motivating regularization strategies that constrain the solution space [9]. Domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, leading to attention to spurious regions that deteriorate target domain accuracy [10]. Cross-layer interactions have been explored through mechanisms that strengthen layer interactions by retrieving query-related information from different receptive field levels [8]. Cross-layer consistency has also been applied to activation engineering, refining steering vectors through geometric stability across depth [18]. Cross-layer fusion has been utilized to capture multi-scale features in remote sensing classification [14]. These approaches share the hypothesis that coordinating representations across network depth improves generalization, though the specific mechanisms and target domains differ.

**Weight and spectral regularization.** Related work tests whether specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. Spectral entropy minimization of input projections was tested in a subject-disjoint time-series setting but yielded inconclusive results: neither primary nor replication cohorts exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero [3]. This suggests that enforcing low-entropy singular value spectra on input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. Entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise for subject-disjoint robustness carries a retracted notice because the executed intervention did not implement the preregistered intervention [2]. These null and retracted findings underscore the importance of faithful implementation and preregistered replication when evaluating regularization hypotheses.

**Attention mechanism modifications.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms provide context for architectural modifications. Selective attention reduces attention to unneeded elements through a parameter-free change, improving language modeling performance across model sizes [5]. External attention using two linear layers offers linear complexity while implicitly considering correlations between samples [17]. Depth-attention performs cross-layer value mixing inside the attention module itself, adding no persistent inference state beyond the standard key-value cache [19]. Surveys document transformer applications across vision, NLP, and audio [6, 12, 21], while empirical studies examine how different factors affect attention performance [15]. These works establish that attention mechanisms can be modified, but whether such modifications improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers requires direct testing.

**Positioning this study.** This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training [1]. Unlike cross-domain attention consistency which aligns attention maps across domains [10], or depth-attention which mixes values across layers [19], the intervention regularizes query projection weights between successive transformer blocks. The preregistered design with primary and confirmatory replication cohorts distinguishes this work from single-cohort evaluations. The subject-disjoint UCI HAR split tests generalization to unseen individuals rather than random held-out windows, addressing whether the intervention improves robustness to inter-subject variability in movement patterns and sensor characteristics.
Method: **Operator design.** The CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator enforces Frobenius norm consistency between query projection weights in successive transformer blocks. The target parameter is blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight with shape (64, 64). The reference parameter is blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight, detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The operator computes element-wise subtraction between target and reference weights, squares each element, sums over all elements, and scales by a fixed coefficient of 0.01. This loss term is added to the classification objective during every optimization step, so the combined objective is differentiated and the target parameters are trained by it.

**Why this expression.** The hypothesis is that stabilizing query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization by reducing layer-specific overfitting while preserving representational capacity. Query projections determine which features each attention head attends to; if these projections diverge substantially across layers, deeper layers may learn idiosyncratic attention patterns that do not generalize to new subjects. Regularizing toward earlier layers tests whether consistent attention mechanisms across depth benefit temporal feature learning more than layer-specific adaptation. The Frobenius norm provides a differentiable measure of weight divergence that can be added to the training objective without modifying the architecture or inference path.

**Comparator and controls.** The baseline condition executes identical code but returns zero loss term, leaving the registered target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged. This control arm reaches every registered lifecycle point on the same inputs, ensuring that any difference between conditions stems from the loss term itself rather than implementation artifacts. The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute, testing whether any observed effect requires alignment between actual layer weights versus generic weight regularization.

**Gradient handling.** Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients from the consistency loss. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only, so block 1 query projections are trained toward block 0's current weights without modifying block 0 through this pathway. Block 0 still receives gradients from the classification objective through its own forward pass. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds. Detaching the reference tensor stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient.

**Model architecture.** The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear projection (9 to 64 channels), a learned positional embedding (128 timesteps, 64 channels), and two transformer blocks. Each block contains LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and residual connection. Final LayerNorm(64) is followed by mean-pool over time and Linear(64,6) for classification. The 9 input channels correspond to the raw inertial signals from the UCI HAR dataset.

**Training and evaluation.** Training runs for 12 epochs with batch size 128, SGD (lr=0.05, momentum=0.9). Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy as number of correct activity predictions divided by 2,947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them.

**

Operator specification.** CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step.
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective.

(8) Store loss_term in scratch dict. (9) Return loss_term to harness.

The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Experimental setup: **Subject-disjoint split justification.** The official UCI HAR subject-disjoint split separates training and test subjects entirely, with 7,352 training windows from some subjects and 2,947 held-out windows from different subjects. This design answers whether the intervention improves generalization to unseen individuals rather than merely fitting the training distribution better. A random split would hold out windows from the same subjects used in training, conflating within-subject temporal generalization with between-subject generalization. For activity recognition applications where models must work for new users without subject-specific fine-tuning, the subject-disjoint evaluation is the relevant test. The cost is higher variance: inter-subject variability in movement style, sensor placement, and execution speed increases outcome noise compared to random splits.

**Paired seed design.** Both conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. This pairing reduces variance from random initialization and batch ordering when estimating the contrast between conditions. The benefit is tighter confidence intervals for the paired difference; the cost is that seeds are not independent across conditions. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them, not to subjects (subjects are fixed by the dataset split). The seed budget comprises 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix.

**Negative control purpose.** The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This tests whether any observed effect requires alignment between actual layer weights versus generic weight regularization toward an arbitrary target. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, this would support the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency specifically (rather than any weight constraint) matters. If both perform similarly, the effect may stem from generic regularization rather than meaningful cross-layer relationships.

**Confidence interval computation.** All uncertainty estimates are bootstrap 95% confidence intervals computed over the paired seed differences. The analysis computed confidence intervals, not standard deviations. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance.

**Condition execution.** Recorded activity shows 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity for the proposed condition in both primary and replication cohorts. The baseline recorded 0/43 seeds with operator activity in both cohorts, confirming the control arm left the target parameter unchanged. The first negative control recorded 43/43 seeds with operator activity in both cohorts. Conformance and activation counts describe execution; they do not establish the mechanism or prove the absence of implementation bias.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Registered conditions.
- Proposed condition: Server-bound target blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight has stored tensor shape (64, 64). Add loss term that applies Frobenius norm consistency regularization to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Baseline: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. Recorded activity — primary: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Negative control 1: Add loss term penalizing difference between blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
Results: **Primary cohort accuracy.** Figure 2 displays mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition, baseline, and first negative control in the primary cohort. Bars represent means over 43 paired seeds with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals as error bars. The proposed condition achieved 0.9062 mean accuracy (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]). The baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The first negative control achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). The proposed condition shows a numerically higher point estimate than baseline, but the confidence intervals overlap substantially, indicating the difference is not statistically distinguishable from zero.

**Primary cohort contrast.** Figure 3 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.000773 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, so no statistically significant difference was detected. The green dash-dot marker in Figure 3 shows the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion; support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed this threshold. The lower bound of -0.00271 falls far below this threshold, so the preregistered decision was inconclusive.

**Replication cohort accuracy.** Figure 5 displays mean held-out classification accuracy for all three conditions in the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. The proposed condition achieved 0.9055 mean accuracy (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]). The baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). The first negative control achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]). Point estimates remain close across conditions, with overlapping confidence intervals.

**Replication cohort contrast.** Figure 6 shows the mean difference between proposed and baseline in the replication cohort. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00196 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, so no statistically significant difference was detected. The lower bound of -0.00196 does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098, so the preregistered decision was inconclusive. The effect size (Cohen's dz=0.15) is larger than in the primary cohort (dz=0.06) but remains small and nonsignificant.

**Training dynamics.** Figure 4 and Figure 7 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. The curves for all three conditions track closely throughout training, with no condition showing consistent separation from the others. This pattern suggests the intervention does not substantially alter the optimization trajectory or final convergence point.

**Summary table.** Table 1 summarizes mean accuracy and confidence intervals for all conditions in both cohorts. Table 2 summarizes the paired contrasts with p-values and effect sizes. Both tables confirm that neither cohort produced a statistically significant difference, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This preregistered study tested whether cross-layer query consistency regularization improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Across 43 primary seeds and 43 pre-specified confirmatory replication seeds on disjoint seeds, the intervention produced small, statistically nonsignificant accuracy differences (primary: 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]; replication: 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. For someone choosing between standard training and cross-layer query consistency regularization in this setting, the evidence does not support adopting the intervention. One possibility, which this experiment did not test, is that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks in this architecture class. What would settle the question next: direct measurement of attention maps to test whether weight regularization produces attention stability, testing in deeper architectures where cross-layer effects might be more pronounced, and evaluation on additional subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks to assess whether the null result generalizes beyond UCI HAR.
Discussion: **Principal finding.** The cross-layer query consistency intervention did not yield statistically significant improvements in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary cohort (mean difference 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]) or the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds (mean difference 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Both confidence intervals include zero, and neither lower bound exceeds the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The preregistered decision was inconclusive in both cohorts. This suggests that enforcing Frobenius norm consistency between query projection weights across transformer blocks does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this calibrated testbed.

**Interpretation.** These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation remains essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. If cross-layer consistency improved generalization, we would expect the proposed condition to outperform the baseline with a confidence interval excluding zero and exceeding the worthwhile margin. Instead, the point estimates are small (0.000773 and 0.00196) and the intervals span both negative and positive values. One interpretation is that different transformer layers benefit from learning distinct query projections that capture different temporal features or abstraction levels. Regularizing toward earlier layers may constrain this layer-specific specialization without providing compensating benefits.

**Alternative mechanisms.** An alternative explanation is that the consistency penalty was too weak to produce measurable effects. The coefficient of 0.01 was chosen to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective, but this may have rendered the regularization ineffective. However, the negative control also used the same coefficient and showed similar performance to the proposed condition, suggesting the issue is not merely penalty strength but rather the nature of the constraint itself. Another alternative is that two transformer blocks are insufficient depth for cross-layer consistency to matter; deeper networks might show different behavior. This claim is untestable on this calibrated testbed, which pins one architecture at one size.

**What the replication cohort adds.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds provides confidence that the null result is not an artifact of a specific seed set. Both cohorts show the same pattern: small, nonsignificant differences with confidence intervals including zero. The replication cohort's effect size (dz=0.15) is larger than the primary (dz=0.06), but both remain far from the threshold needed to claim the intervention exceeds the worthwhile margin. This consistency across seed sets strengthens the conclusion that the intervention does not produce robust accuracy gains in this regime.

**Relation to cited work.** These findings align with prior null results on weight geometry regularization in subject-disjoint time-series settings. Spectral entropy minimization of input projections also yielded inconclusive results with confidence intervals including zero in both primary and replication cohorts [3]. This suggests a broader pattern: enforcing specific weight structures does not reliably improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The findings contrast with cross-domain attention consistency work that reported improvements in domain adaptive semantic segmentation [10], but that study addressed a different problem (domain shift across datasets rather than subject disjointness within a dataset) and used attention-map alignment rather than weight alignment. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment.

**Mechanistic hypotheses.** Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. The study does not measure attention maps directly, so claims about attention stability are mechanistic hypotheses rather than measured findings. The intervention regularizes query projection weights, not attention outputs or attention maps. Whether weight consistency translates to attention stability depends on how query projections interact with key and value projections during the attention computation, which was not measured. Future work could directly measure attention map similarity across layers to test whether weight regularization produces the hypothesized attention stabilization.

**Scope of generalization.** All claims are scoped to the calibrated testbed: PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks, 64 hidden channels, 4-head attention, on UCI HAR with official subject-disjoint split. The findings do not establish whether cross-layer consistency would help in larger models, different architectures, or other time-series datasets. A claim about model scale or architecture family is untestable on this calibrated testbed. The single calibrated model at one size is what was tested; generalization to other settings requires separate experiments.
Limitations: **Architecture and scale.** The study tests one architecture at one size: PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks and 64 hidden channels. Whether cross-layer query consistency would benefit deeper transformers, different attention mechanisms, or larger hidden dimensions remains unknown. Claims about larger models are untestable on this calibrated testbed. The intervention may behave differently in architectures where depth plays a more substantial role in representation learning.

**Attention mechanism not measured.** The study does not measure attention maps directly. Claims about attention stability across layers are mechanistic hypotheses rather than measured findings. The intervention regularizes query projection weights, but whether this produces more stable or consistent attention patterns was not assessed. Direct measurement of attention maps would be needed to test the hypothesized mechanism.

**Dataset specificity.** Results are limited to the UCI HAR dataset with its specific sensor modality (smartphone inertial signals), activity classes (6 activities), and subject population. Whether the findings generalize to other time-series domains (physiological signals, financial data, environmental sensors) or other subject-disjoint benchmarks requires separate testing. The subject-disjoint split tests generalization to unseen individuals within this dataset, not to different corpora, sensors, or tasks.

**Coefficient and penalty strength.** The consistency coefficient of 0.01 was fixed across all conditions. Whether different coefficient values would produce different results was not tested. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient; the actual penalty magnitude depends on the weight divergence, which varies during training. The chosen value may have been too weak to produce measurable effects or too strong and interfered with task learning.

=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet the architectural inductive biases that enable subject-disjoint generalization remain unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [38]. However, whether specific architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear [1]. In domains like human activity recognition, models must generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. A key question is whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns to support this generalization. If attention stability across depth is beneficial, regularizing deeper layers to match shallower ones should improve performance on unseen subjects. Conversely, if layer-specific adaptation is essential, such consistency constraints may hinder the model's ability to specialize.

Current literature highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding transformer effectiveness in time series [5]. While some works propose consistency regularization to address stability and generalization [17], others question the validity of transformer-based solutions for certain time-series tasks [5]. Specifically, the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization represents a gap in the current understanding. This work addresses this gap by testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling.

This paper presents a preregistered experiment evaluating the impact of cross-layer query consistency on subject-disjoint generalization. We contribute:
- We implement a cross-layer query consistency loss enforcing Frobenius norm alignment between attention query projections in a 2-block transformer.
- We evaluate the intervention against a baseline and a negative control using 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds on a subject-disjoint split.
- We report inconclusive results, preserving the registered decision and avoiding over-interpretation of nonsignificant contrasts.

The preregistered prediction stated: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report the results honestly against this hypothesis.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [38], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight-alignment intervention in a calibrated time-series testbed.

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which regularizes the query projection weights of the second attention block toward those of the first. This intervention tests the hypothesis that stabilizing attention query geometry across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization. The operator is applied during the loss computation of every optimization step, adding a term to the classification objective within the autograd graph.

**Operator Specification**
The operator targets the weight matrix of `blocks.1.attn.q_proj`. It retrieves the reference weights from `blocks.0.attn.q_proj` and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients from flowing to the first block. It then computes the element-wise difference between the target and reference weights, squares these differences, and sums them to produce a raw Frobenius norm squared loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01 and added to the training objective. The reference weights remain frozen with respect to this penalty, ensuring only the deeper block is regularized. This design isolates the effect of pulling deeper query projections toward shallower ones without altering the learning dynamics of the first block via this specific loss term.

**Comparator and Controls**
The baseline condition serves as the primary comparator. It executes the identical code path as the proposed condition but returns a zero loss term. This ensures that any difference in outcome is attributable to the loss term itself rather than implementation artifacts or computational graph differences. The harness guarantees that the control arm leaves the registered target parameter and its optimizer momentum buffer unchanged. A first negative control penalizes the difference between the second block's weights and a fixed random matrix of the same shape and norm. This control matches the compute cost of the proposed condition but destroys any meaningful cross-layer relationship, allowing us to distinguish between the effect of consistency regularization and the effect of merely adding a weight penalty.

**Hypothesis Expression**
The intervention expresses the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency aids generalization. If true, the proposed condition should outperform the baseline with a confidence interval excluding zero and exceeding the worthwhile margin. The comparator neutralizes the computational cost and code path, isolating the regularization effect. The negative control further isolates the semantic value of the cross-layer relationship from the mere presence of a penalty. Mechanistic rationales regarding attention stability are hypotheses; the measured outcome is held-out classification accuracy.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification**
The experimental design employs a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization to unseen individuals. A random split would allow data from the same subject to appear in both training and testing, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to test robustness to subject-specific movement styles or sensor characteristics. The subject-disjoint split ensures that the held-out evaluation measures performance on people who appear nowhere in training, supporting a claim about unseen subjects rather than merely unseen windows.

**Pairing and Seeds**
Conditions are paired by seed to reduce variance. Both the proposed condition and the baseline are trained from the same paired seed, sharing dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters. This pairing ensures that differences in outcome are not driven by random initialization or data ordering but by the intervention itself. We use 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The replication cohort uses fresh seeds to verify that the primary result is not a statistical artifact of the specific seed set chosen. We report both cohorts separately and do not pool them, adhering to the preregistered decision rule.

**Negative Control Rationale**
The first negative control is intended to rule out the alternative explanation that any weight penalty improves generalization. By penalizing deviation from a random matrix, we match the compute and gradient flow of the proposed condition without enforcing meaningful consistency. If the proposed condition outperforms this negative control, it suggests the cross-layer relationship itself is valuable. If both perform similarly, the benefit may stem from regularization generally rather than consistency specifically. The observed contrast supports inferences about the intervention's specific mechanism only if it differs from this control.

**Analysis Plan**
We analyze held-out classification accuracy using bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. The registered decision rule requires the lower confidence bound to exceed the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion to claim support. We preserve the registered labels for outcomes that do not meet this threshold. Power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter.

=== results ===
We report results for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately. All metrics are mean held-out classification accuracy with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.

**Primary Cohort**
In the primary cohort, across 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 2 displays the mean accuracy for the proposed, baseline, and first negative control conditions. The confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. Figure 3 plots the paired mean difference, showing the interval relative to the registered worthwhile threshold. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The first negative control achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]), comparable to the baseline (0.9054, 95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]) and proposed condition (0.9062, 95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]). Training curves in Figure 4 show overlapping performance across conditions over training steps.

**Replication Cohort**
In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 43 disjoint seeds, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 5 displays the mean accuracy for all conditions. The confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. Figure 6 plots the paired mean difference, which does not exceed the worthwhile threshold. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The first negative control achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]), comparable to the baseline (0.9035, 95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]) and proposed condition (0.9055, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]). Training curves in Figure 7 show similar convergence patterns across conditions.

**Summary**
Table 1 and Table 2 summarize the cohort-specific outcomes. Neither cohort produced a confidence interval excluding zero or exceeding the margin. The variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive in both the primary and replication settings.

=== discussion ===
The cross-layer query consistency intervention did not yield statistically significant improvements in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary cohort (mean difference 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]) or the replication cohort (mean difference 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). This finding is consistent with the registered inconclusive decision. If cross-layer consistency improved generalization, we would expect the proposed condition to outperform the baseline with a confidence interval excluding zero and exceeding the worthwhile margin. The observed intervals include zero and lie below the margin, suggesting that in this regime, cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains.

**Mechanism and Alternatives**
One interpretation is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks [1]. Enforcing consistency may constrain the deeper block's ability to refine features based on the shallower block's output. An alternative explanation is that the consistency coefficient (0.01) was too small to exert a meaningful influence on the optimization trajectory, or too large, causing interference with the classification objective. However, these are hypotheses; the measured outcome is accuracy, not gradient magnitude. The negative control results suggest that adding a weight penalty alone does not improve performance, as the negative control performed comparably to the baseline.

**Relation to Literature**
These findings agree with [1], which reported inconclusive results for cross-layer query consistency in this testbed. They contrast with [17], which found consistency regularization effective in machine translation, suggesting that the benefit of consistency may be task-dependent. They also align with [3], which found spectral entropy minimization inconclusive in a similar setting, indicating that weight geometry regularizations may not universally improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The results do not support the claim that attention stability across depth is a sufficient inductive bias for this problem.

**Replication Value**
The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is not a statistical fluke of the primary seed set. Both cohorts failed to exceed the margin, reinforcing the inconclusive decision. This consistency across cohorts suggests that the effect, if it exists, is smaller than the worthwhile margin in this calibrated testbed.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to the calibrated testbed `uci_har_small_transformer_v1`, which uses a 2-block transformer on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset. The findings apply to this architecture size and dataset; they do not establish effects for larger models or different architecture families. A claim about model scale or architecture family is untestable on this calibrated testbed, as the recipe pins one architecture at one size. Similarly, a cross-dataset claim is untestable by construction, as the study measures one calibrated testbed. The subject-disjoint split supports claims about unseen subjects within this dataset but does not prove out-of-distribution generalization to different sensor modalities or activity sets. The consistency coefficient was fixed; we do not know if tuning it would change the outcome. These limitations restrict the scope of inference to the specific experimental conditions.

=== conclusion ===
We tested whether cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Across 43 primary and 43 replication seeds, the intervention produced small, statistically nonsignificant accuracy differences (primary: 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]; replication: 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. For someone choosing between these methods in this regime, the evidence does not support adding cross-layer query consistency loss. The findings suggest layer-specific adaptation may remain essential. Future work should test whether different consistency coefficients, architecture depths, or datasets yield different outcomes, settling the question of whether attention stability across depth is beneficial under other conditions.

REGISTERED OPERATOR (including gradient handling; do not infer that detaching one loss term freezes ordinary task-loss learning):
Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet the architectural inductive biases that enable subject-disjoint generalization remain unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [38]. However, whether specific architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear [1]. In domains like human activity recognition, models must generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. A key question is whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns to support this generalization. If attention stability across depth is beneficial, regularizing deeper layers to match shallower ones should improve performance on unseen subjects. Conversely, if layer-specific adaptation is essential, such consistency constraints may hinder the model's ability to specialize.

Current literature highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding transformer effectiveness in time series [5]. While some works propose consistency regularization to address stability and generalization [17], others question the validity of transformer-based solutions for certain time-series tasks [5]. Specifically, the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization represents a gap in the current understanding. This work addresses this gap by testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling.

This paper presents a preregistered experiment evaluating the impact of cross-layer query consistency on subject-disjoint generalization. We contribute:
- We implement a cross-layer query consistency loss enforcing Frobenius norm alignment between attention query projections in a 2-block transformer.
- We evaluate the intervention against a baseline and a negative control using 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds on a subject-disjoint split.
- We report inconclusive results, preserving the registered decision and avoiding over-interpretation of nonsignificant contrasts.

The preregistered prediction stated: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report the results honestly against this hypothesis.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [38], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight-alignment intervention in a calibrated time-series testbed.

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which regularizes the query projection weights of the second attention block toward those of the first. This intervention tests the hypothesis that stabilizing attention query geometry across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization. The operator is applied during the loss computation of every optimization step, adding a term to the classification objective within the autograd graph.

**Operator Specification**
The operator targets the weight matrix of `blocks.1.attn.q_proj`. It retrieves the reference weights from `blocks.0.attn.q_proj` and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients from flowing to the first block. It then computes the element-wise difference between the target and reference weights, squares these differences, and sums them to produce a raw Frobenius norm squared loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01 and added to the training objective. The reference weights remain frozen with respect to this penalty, ensuring only the deeper block is regularized. This design isolates the effect of pulling deeper query projections toward shallower ones without altering the learning dynamics of the first block via this specific loss term.

**Comparator and Controls**
The baseline condition serves as the primary comparator. It executes the identical code path as the proposed condition but returns a zero loss term. This ensures that any difference in outcome is attributable to the loss term itself rather than implementation artifacts or computational graph differences. The harness guarantees that the control arm leaves the registered target parameter and its optimizer momentum buffer unchanged. A first negative control penalizes the difference between the second block's weights and a fixed random matrix of the same shape and norm. This control matches the compute cost of the proposed condition but destroys any meaningful cross-layer relationship, allowing us to distinguish between the effect of consistency regularization and the effect of merely adding a weight penalty.

**Hypothesis Expression**
The intervention expresses the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency aids generalization. If true, the proposed condition should outperform the baseline with a confidence interval excluding zero and exceeding the worthwhile margin. The comparator neutralizes the computational cost and code path, isolating the regularization effect. The negative control further isolates the semantic value of the cross-layer relationship from the mere presence of a penalty. Mechanistic rationales regarding attention stability are hypotheses; the measured outcome is held-out classification accuracy.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification**
The experimental design employs a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization to unseen individuals. A random split would allow data from the same subject to appear in both training and testing, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to test robustness to subject-specific movement styles or sensor characteristics. The subject-disjoint split ensures that the held-out evaluation measures performance on people who appear nowhere in training, supporting a claim about unseen subjects rather than merely unseen windows.

**Pairing and Seeds**
Conditions are paired by seed to reduce variance. Both the proposed condition and the baseline are trained from the same paired seed, sharing dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters. This pairing ensures that differences in outcome are not driven by random initialization or data ordering but by the intervention itself. We use 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The replication cohort uses fresh seeds to verify that the primary result is not a statistical artifact of the specific seed set chosen. We report both cohorts separately and do not pool them, adhering to the preregistered decision rule.

**Negative Control Rationale**
The first negative control is intended to rule out the alternative explanation that any weight penalty improves generalization. By penalizing deviation from a random matrix, we match the compute and gradient flow of the proposed condition without enforcing meaningful consistency. If the proposed condition outperforms this negative control, it suggests the cross-layer relationship itself is valuable. If both perform similarly, the benefit may stem from regularization generally rather than consistency specifically. The observed contrast supports inferences about the intervention's specific mechanism only if it differs from this control.

**Analysis Plan**
We analyze held-out classification accuracy using bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. The registered decision rule requires the lower confidence bound to exceed the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion to claim support. We preserve the registered labels for outcomes that do not meet this threshold. Power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter.

=== results ===
We report results for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately. All metrics are mean held-out classification accuracy with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.

**Primary Cohort**
In the primary cohort, across 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 2 displays the mean accuracy for the proposed, baseline, and first negative control conditions. The confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. Figure 3 plots the paired mean difference, showing the interval relative to the registered worthwhile threshold. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The first negative control achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]), comparable to the baseline (0.9054, 95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]) and proposed condition (0.9062, 95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]). Training curves in Figure 4 show overlapping performance across conditions over training steps.

**Replication Cohort**
In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 43 disjoint seeds, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 5 displays the mean accuracy for all conditions. The confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. Figure 6 plots the paired mean difference, which does not exceed the worthwhile threshold. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The first negative control achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]), comparable to the baseline (0.9035, 95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]) and proposed condition (0.9055, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]). Training curves in Figure 7 show similar convergence patterns across conditions.

**Summary**
Table 1 and Table 2 summarize the cohort-specific outcomes. Neither cohort produced a confidence interval excluding zero or exceeding the margin. The variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive in both the primary and replication settings.

=== discussion ===
The cross-layer query consistency intervention did not yield statistically significant improvements in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary cohort (mean difference 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]) or the replication cohort (mean difference 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). This finding is consistent with the registered inconclusive decision. If cross-layer consistency improved generalization, we would expect the proposed condition to outperform the baseline with a confidence interval excluding zero and exceeding the worthwhile margin. The observed intervals include zero and lie below the margin, suggesting that in this regime, cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains.

**Mechanism and Alternatives**
One interpretation is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks [1]. Enforcing consistency may constrain the deeper block's ability to refine features based on the shallower block's output. An alternative explanation is that the consistency coefficient (0.01) was too small to exert a meaningful influence on the optimization trajectory, or too large, causing interference with the classification objective. However, these are hypotheses; the measured outcome is accuracy, not gradient magnitude. The negative control results suggest that adding a weight penalty alone does not improve performance, as the negative control performed comparably to the baseline.

**Relation to Literature**
These findings agree with [1], which reported inconclusive results for cross-layer query consistency in this testbed. They contrast with [17], which found consistency regularization effective in machine translation, suggesting that the benefit of consistency may be task-dependent. They also align with [3], which found spectral entropy minimization inconclusive in a similar setting, indicating that weight geometry regularizations may not universally improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The results do not support the claim that attention stability across depth is a sufficient inductive bias for this problem.

**Replication Value**
The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is not a statistical fluke of the primary seed set. Both cohorts failed to exceed the margin, reinforcing the inconclusive decision. This consistency across cohorts suggests that the effect, if it exists, is smaller than the worthwhile margin in this calibrated testbed.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to the calibrated testbed `uci_har_small_transformer_v1`, which uses a 2-block transformer on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset. The findings apply to this architecture size and dataset; they do not establish effects for larger models or different architecture families. A claim about model scale or architecture family is untestable on this calibrated testbed, as the recipe pins one architecture at one size. Similarly, a cross-dataset claim is untestable by construction, as the study measures one calibrated testbed. The subject-disjoint split supports claims about unseen subjects within this dataset but does not prove out-of-distribution generalization to different sensor modalities or activity sets. The consistency coefficient was fixed; we do not know if tuning it would change the outcome. These limitations restrict the scope of inference to the specific experimental conditions.

=== conclusion ===
We tested whether cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Across 43 primary and 43 replication seeds, the intervention produced small, statistically nonsignificant accuracy differences (primary: 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]; replication: 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. For someone choosing between these methods in this regime, the evidence does not support adding cross-layer query consistency loss. The findings suggest layer-specific adaptation may remain essential. Future work should test whether different consistency coefficients, architecture depths, or datasets yield different outcomes, settling the question of whether attention stability across depth is beneficial under other conditions.

payload.title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
