Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet the architectural inductive biases that enable subject-disjoint generalization remain unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line, suggesting simple linear models may outperform complex architectures in some forecasting tasks [4, 22]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation and representing multivariate series as graphs [9, 13]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [15]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including generalization challenges and data shift issues [18].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data and proposes constraining encoder and decoder outputs [11]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention and imposes consistency between predictions from cross-domain attention and self-attention modules [12]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [10], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering, grounded in the geometric stability of the network's representation evolution [20]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [16]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it, and its conclusions may not be relied on [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [6]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [19]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [21]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio, though specific vision surveys limit their scope to computer vision tasks [7, 14, 23]. *Point Transformer* and *Transformer Tracking* explicitly focus on computer vision applications, investigating self-attention for point cloud processing and feature fusion in tracking, respectively [5, 8]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [17].

This study positions itself against these themes by isolating cross-layer query consistency in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. Unlike vision surveys that document broad application [7, 14], we focus on the mechanistic impact of weight regularization on generalization. Unlike domain adaptation works that align attention maps across domains [12], we regularize weights within a single domain to test stability. We extend the inquiry into consistency regularization [11] by testing a specific weight-based loss in a time-series transformer, distinct from output-level consistency.
Method: The core of this experiment is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces similarity between the query projection weights of the first and second attention blocks. The hypothesis is that stabilizing attention query patterns across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization by reducing layer-specific overfitting. The operator is applied during the loss computation of every optimization step, adding a regularization term to the classification objective.

The operator retrieves the reference weights from the first block's query projection (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight) and detaches them from the gradient graph. This detachment ensures that the regularization penalty does not induce gradients in the first block, isolating the effect to the target parameters in the second block (blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight). The operator computes the element-wise difference between the target weights and the detached reference weights, squares these differences, and sums them to form a raw loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01 and added to the training objective. The coefficient was chosen to prevent the consistency term from dominating the classification objective while remaining large enough to influence optimization.

The comparator for this intervention is the baseline condition, which executes the identical training code path but returns a zero loss term for the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, ensuring that dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. This pairing controls for variance arising from initialization and data sampling, allowing the contrast to isolate the effect of the loss term. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, recording operator activity to verify that the control arm leaves the target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged.

A first negative control is included to distinguish the effect of meaningful cross-layer relationship from mere compute matching. This condition penalizes the difference between the second block's weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as the first block's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the computational cost of the proposed condition. If the proposed condition outperforms this negative control, it suggests that the specific alignment to the first block's weights, rather than just the presence of a penalty, drives any observed effect.

The operator specification is fixed before any compute was spent. The reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients from this term. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds. This design ensures that any difference in outcome is attributable to the gradient signal imposed on the second block's query weights, not to changes in the first block or optimization dynamics unrelated to the penalty.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Experimental setup: The experimental design prioritizes a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization to unseen individuals. A random split would allow data from the same subject to appear in both training and testing sets, inflating accuracy estimates by leveraging subject-specific idiosyncrasies rather than generalizable temporal features. The subject-disjoint split ensures that the held-out evaluation measures performance on people who appear nowhere in training, supporting a claim about unseen subjects. This design choice is critical for assessing the utility of the intervention in real-world deployment where new users will not be represented in the training data.

Pairing conditions by seed is a key design feature to reduce variance. By deriving the dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters once and reusing them for both the proposed condition and the baseline, we isolate the effect of the intervention from the stochasticity of training. This pairing increases the statistical power to detect small effects, as the contrast is computed on paired differences rather than independent samples. The seed budget consists of 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. This budget was determined by a registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targeting 90% power to reject a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin.

The negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any regularization penalty, regardless of its target, might improve generalization by simply adding noise or constraining the optimization trajectory. By comparing the proposed condition to a negative control that penalizes against a random matrix, we test whether the specific cross-layer relationship is necessary. If the proposed condition does not outperform the negative control, it suggests that the meaningful alignment is not the active ingredient. The observed contrast supports or refutes the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency specifically, rather than regularization generally, drives improvement.

The analysis plan distinguishes between the primary cohort and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort. Results are reported separately for each, and they are never pooled. A result is only considered replicated if both cohorts show a statistically significant effect exceeding the worthwhile margin. This strict criterion prevents false positives arising from random variation in a single cohort. The power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; detecting a non-zero effect does not guarantee the effect is large enough to be practically important.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Registered conditions.
- Proposed condition: Server-bound target blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight has stored tensor shape (64, 64). Add loss term that applies Frobenius norm consistency regularization to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Baseline: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. Recorded activity — primary: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Negative control 1: Add loss term penalizing difference between blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
Results: We report the held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition, the baseline, and the first negative control across both cohorts. Figure 1 illustrates the methodology flow, showing the dataset, model, registered conditions, intervention application at the loss term, and subject-disjoint evaluation. The results are presented quantitatively, stating the effect, its confidence interval, and whether it is significant.

In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for all three conditions in the primary cohort. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The first negative control achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). The confidence interval for the difference includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. Figure 3 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098. The lower confidence bound does not exceed this threshold. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps, where the curves for all conditions coincide closely, distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern.

In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 5 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for all three conditions in the replication cohort. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), while the baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). The first negative control achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]). Figure 6 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The confidence interval includes zero and does not exceed the worthwhile margin. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the replication cohort, again showing close coincidence between conditions.

The preregistered decision for both cohorts was inconclusive. The confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results do not support the hypothesis that the intervention yields higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator with a mean contrast exceeding the margin.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This study tested whether cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Across 43 primary and 43 replication seeds, the intervention produced small, statistically nonsignificant accuracy differences (primary: 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]; replication: 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence suggests that standard training is sufficient for this architecture and dataset, as the consistency loss adds complexity without verified gain. To settle the question next, future work should test deeper architectures or alternative consistency targets, such as attention maps, to determine if the null result is specific to weight alignment in shallow networks.
Discussion: The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency did not yield statistically significant improvements in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort. The mean differences were small (0.000773 and 0.00196) and the confidence intervals included zero in both cases. This suggests that, in this specific regime of a 2-block PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI HAR dataset, stabilizing query weights across depth does not enhance subject-disjoint generalization.

This result is consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. If cross-layer consistency improved generalization, we would expect the proposed condition to outperform the baseline with a confidence interval excluding zero and exceeding the worthwhile margin. The fact that the intervals include zero indicates that the data are compatible with no effect or a negligible effect. The replication cohort adds weight to this conclusion by showing that the null result is stable under fresh sampling. The effect size (Cohen's dz=0.06 in primary, 0.15 in replication) is small, suggesting that even if a true effect exists, it is likely too small to be practically important under the registered margin.

A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that the attention query weights in a shallow network (2 blocks) do not benefit from explicit alignment. The first block may not yet have learned stable enough features to serve as a reliable target for the second block. Alternatively, the detachment of the reference weights prevents the first block from adapting to support the consistency constraint, potentially limiting the regularization's effectiveness. An alternative explanation is that the consistency coefficient (0.01) was too small to influence the optimization trajectory meaningfully, though the negative control matched this compute and also showed no gain.

These findings stand against specific cited papers in nuanced ways. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* found gains from consistency on encoder/decoder outputs [11], but our weight-based consistency on a single encoder stack did not replicate this benefit. *CDAC* imposes attention map consistency across domains [12], which differs from our within-domain weight consistency; the domain gap may be a necessary condition for consistency regularization to show benefits. *Global Evolutionary Steering* applies cross-layer consistency to activation steering [20], a different intervention target than training weights. The null result here does not contradict those works but clarifies the boundary conditions for weight-based consistency in time-series classification.

The independent replication cohort on disjoint seeds confirms that the inconclusive decision is not an artifact of a specific seed set. However, this design does not establish that cross-layer consistency is ineffective in all time-series settings. It establishes only that it does not exceed the worthwhile margin in this specific testbed. Future work should test whether deeper networks or different consistency targets (e.g., attention maps rather than weights) yield different outcomes.
Limitations: This study is limited to a single testbed (UCI HAR) and a specific architecture (2-block PreNormTransformerEncoder). The results do not support claims about cross-dataset or cross-model scale generalization. The subject-disjoint split supports a claim about unseen subjects within the UCI HAR distribution, but not about out-of-distribution generalization to different sensors or activities. The consistency coefficient was fixed at 0.01; a different coefficient might yield different results, though the negative control suggests the penalty magnitude alone is not the driver. The detachment of reference weights prevents joint optimization of both blocks for consistency, which may limit the potential benefit. Finally, the power calculation targets a specific margin; smaller effects may exist but are not detected as practically significant under this framework.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet the architectural inductive biases that enable subject-disjoint generalization remain unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line, suggesting simple linear models may outperform complex architectures in some forecasting tasks [4, 22]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation and representing multivariate series as graphs [9, 13]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [15]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including generalization challenges and data shift issues [18].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data and proposes constraining encoder and decoder outputs [11]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention and imposes consistency between predictions from cross-domain attention and self-attention modules [12]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [10], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering, grounded in the geometric stability of the network's representation evolution [20]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [16]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it, and its conclusions may not be relied on [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [6]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [19]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [21]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio, though specific vision surveys limit their scope to computer vision tasks [7, 14, 23]. *Point Transformer* and *Transformer Tracking* explicitly focus on computer vision applications, investigating self-attention for point cloud processing and feature fusion in tracking, respectively [5, 8]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [17].

This study positions itself against these themes by isolating cross-layer query consistency in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. Unlike vision surveys that document broad application [7, 14], we focus on the mechanistic impact of weight regularization on generalization. Unlike domain adaptation works that align attention maps across domains [12], we regularize weights within a single domain to test stability. We extend the inquiry into consistency regularization [11] by testing a specific weight-based loss in a time-series transformer, distinct from output-level consistency.
Method: The core of this experiment is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces similarity between the query projection weights of the first and second attention blocks. The hypothesis is that stabilizing attention query patterns across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization by reducing layer-specific overfitting. The operator is applied during the loss computation of every optimization step, adding a regularization term to the classification objective.

The operator retrieves the reference weights from the first block's query projection (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight) and detaches them from the gradient graph. This detachment ensures that the regularization penalty does not induce gradients in the first block, isolating the effect to the target parameters in the second block (blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight). The operator computes the element-wise difference between the target weights and the detached reference weights, squares these differences, and sums them to form a raw loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01 and added to the training objective. The coefficient was chosen to prevent the consistency term from dominating the classification objective while remaining large enough to influence optimization.

The comparator for this intervention is the baseline condition, which executes the identical training code path but returns a zero loss term for the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, ensuring that dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. This pairing controls for variance arising from initialization and data sampling, allowing the contrast to isolate the effect of the loss term. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, recording operator activity to verify that the control arm leaves the target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged.

A first negative control is included to distinguish the effect of meaningful cross-layer relationship from mere compute matching. This condition penalizes the difference between the second block's weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as the first block's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the computational cost of the proposed condition. If the proposed condition outperforms this negative control, it suggests that the specific alignment to the first block's weights, rather than just the presence of a penalty, drives any observed effect.

The operator specification is fixed before any compute was spent. The reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients from this term. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds. This design ensures that any difference in outcome is attributable to the gradient signal imposed on the second block's query weights, not to changes in the first block or optimization dynamics unrelated to the penalty.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Experimental setup: The experimental design prioritizes a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization to unseen individuals. A random split would allow data from the same subject to appear in both training and testing sets, inflating accuracy estimates by leveraging subject-specific idiosyncrasies rather than generalizable temporal features. The subject-disjoint split ensures that the held-out evaluation measures performance on people who appear nowhere in training, supporting a claim about unseen subjects. This design choice is critical for assessing the utility of the intervention in real-world deployment where new users will not be represented in the training data.

Pairing conditions by seed is a key design feature to reduce variance. By deriving the dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters once and reusing them for both the proposed condition and the baseline, we isolate the effect of the intervention from the stochasticity of training. This pairing increases the statistical power to detect small effects, as the contrast is computed on paired differences rather than independent samples. The seed budget consists of 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. This budget was determined by a registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targeting 90% power to reject a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin.

The negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any regularization penalty, regardless of its target, might improve generalization by simply adding noise or constraining the optimization trajectory. By comparing the proposed condition to a negative control that penalizes against a random matrix, we test whether the specific cross-layer relationship is necessary. If the proposed condition does not outperform the negative control, it suggests that the meaningful alignment is not the active ingredient. The observed contrast supports or refutes the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency specifically, rather than regularization generally, drives improvement.

The analysis plan distinguishes between the primary cohort and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort. Results are reported separately for each, and they are never pooled. A result is only considered replicated if both cohorts show a statistically significant effect exceeding the worthwhile margin. This strict criterion prevents false positives arising from random variation in a single cohort. The power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; detecting a non-zero effect does not guarantee the effect is large enough to be practically important.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Registered conditions.
- Proposed condition: Server-bound target blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight has stored tensor shape (64, 64). Add loss term that applies Frobenius norm consistency regularization to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Baseline: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. Recorded activity — primary: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Negative control 1: Add loss term penalizing difference between blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
Results: We report the held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition, the baseline, and the first negative control across both cohorts. Figure 1 illustrates the methodology flow, showing the dataset, model, registered conditions, intervention application at the loss term, and subject-disjoint evaluation. The results are presented quantitatively, stating the effect, its confidence interval, and whether it is significant.

In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for all three conditions in the primary cohort. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The first negative control achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). The confidence interval for the difference includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. Figure 3 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098. The lower confidence bound does not exceed this threshold. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps, where the curves for all conditions coincide closely, distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern.

In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 5 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for all three conditions in the replication cohort. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), while the baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). The first negative control achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]). Figure 6 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The confidence interval includes zero and does not exceed the worthwhile margin. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the replication cohort, again showing close coincidence between conditions.

The preregistered decision for both cohorts was inconclusive. The confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results do not support the hypothesis that the intervention yields higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator with a mean contrast exceeding the margin.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This study tested whether cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Across 43 primary and 43 replication seeds, the intervention produced small, statistically nonsignificant accuracy differences (primary: 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]; replication: 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence suggests that standard training is sufficient for this architecture and dataset, as the consistency loss adds complexity without verified gain. To settle the question next, future work should test deeper architectures or alternative consistency targets, such as attention maps, to determine if the null result is specific to weight alignment in shallow networks.
Discussion: The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency did not yield statistically significant improvements in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort. The mean differences were small (0.000773 and 0.00196) and the confidence intervals included zero in both cases. This suggests that, in this specific regime of a 2-block PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI HAR dataset, stabilizing query weights across depth does not enhance subject-disjoint generalization.

This result is consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. If cross-layer consistency improved generalization, we would expect the proposed condition to outperform the baseline with a confidence interval excluding zero and exceeding the worthwhile margin. The fact that the intervals include zero indicates that the data are compatible with no effect or a negligible effect. The replication cohort adds weight to this conclusion by showing that the null result is stable under fresh sampling. The effect size (Cohen's dz=0.06 in primary, 0.15 in replication) is small, suggesting that even if a true effect exists, it is likely too small to be practically important under the registered margin.

A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that the attention query weights in a shallow network (2 blocks) do not benefit from explicit alignment. The first block may not yet have learned stable enough features to serve as a reliable target for the second block. Alternatively, the detachment of the reference weights prevents the first block from adapting to support the consistency constraint, potentially limiting the regularization's effectiveness. An alternative explanation is that the consistency coefficient (0.01) was too small to influence the optimization trajectory meaningfully, though the negative control matched this compute and also showed no gain.

These findings stand against specific cited papers in nuanced ways. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* found gains from consistency on encoder/decoder outputs [11], but our weight-based consistency on a single encoder stack did not replicate this benefit. *CDAC* imposes attention map consistency across domains [12], which differs from our within-domain weight consistency; the domain gap may be a necessary condition for consistency regularization to show benefits. *Global Evolutionary Steering* applies cross-layer consistency to activation steering [20], a different intervention target than training weights. The null result here does not contradict those works but clarifies the boundary conditions for weight-based consistency in time-series classification.

The independent replication cohort on disjoint seeds confirms that the inconclusive decision is not an artifact of a specific seed set. However, this design does not establish that cross-layer consistency is ineffective in all time-series settings. It establishes only that it does not exceed the worthwhile margin in this specific testbed. Future work should test whether deeper networks or different consistency targets (e.g., attention maps rather than weights) yield different outcomes.
Limitations: This study is limited to a single testbed (UCI HAR) and a specific architecture (2-block PreNormTransformerEncoder). The results do not support claims about cross-dataset or cross-model scale generalization. The subject-disjoint split supports a claim about unseen subjects within the UCI HAR distribution, but not about out-of-distribution generalization to different sensors or activities. The consistency coefficient was fixed at 0.01; a different coefficient might yield different results, though the negative control suggests the penalty magnitude alone is not the driver. The detachment of reference weights prevents joint optimization of both blocks for consistency, which may limit the potential benefit. Finally, the power calculation targets a specific margin; smaller effects may exist but are not detected as practically significant under this framework.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

We introduce Depth-Attention, which performs this selection inside the attention module itself: before a layer attends over the sequence, its query attends over the keys of earlier layers at the same token position and mixes their values into the value that self-attention then reads. These embeddings allow a transformer to learn the mapping across different views without ever explicitly modeling it geometrically. You are writing a rigorous, honest research paper (IMRaD) about an experiment that has ALREADY been run; the REAL results — including means, 95% confidence intervals, significance, and effect sizes — are given to you. Be faithful to those numbers and do NOT invent results, references, or findings. Write clear, precise academic prose. CITE numbered references in square brackets (e.g. [1] or [2, 3]); the Introduction and Related Work MUST cite them inline. An automated auditor checks each cited sentence against its abstract: say what a paper actually establishes, not merely its topic. You are NOT required to cite every reference; unused references are removed. NEVER cite a paper as evidence for something it does NOT discuss, including a gap in a different setting. State a gap WITHOUT a marker, use the reviewed gap statement, or cite an abstract that identifies that gap itself. Never attribute the opposite of what an abstract says. Stay INSIDE the abstract's own wording: use its terms, do not generalise them or add an unstated mechanism, domain or consequence. Plausible extensions are unsupported claims too; if in doubt, write less about the paper. Refer to figures and tables by number (e.g. 'Figure 1', 'Table 1'). Report results quantitatively (state the effect, its confidence interval, and whether it is significant). When the analysis contains primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts, report BOTH separately, state each preregistered decision, and never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. Distinguish training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations.
EVIDENCE AND INTERPRETATION. The registered condition descriptions and executed activation records below are authoritative: a baseline/no-op and an active negative control are different conditions. Do not infer inactivity from a small or nonsignificant outcome contrast. Describe only what the control manipulates; its outcome cannot prove that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: name the directly recorded outcomes, and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. If a reference tensor is detached inside a penalty, this stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient. Use the registered CI classifications without equating nonsignificance with equality. If a CI crosses zero but lies below the worthwhile margin, preserve its registered label and separately explain that it excludes gains of that target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model. The supplied power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; do not claim the former guarantees the latter. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

LENGTH. Write a full paper, not an extended abstract. Aim for roughly: introduction 600-800 words; related work 600-900; method 500-800 (BEFORE the operator specification that is appended for you); experimental setup 300-500; results 500-800; discussion 500-800; limitations 200-300; conclusion 150-250; abstract 150-250. A section that is three sentences long has not done its job. Depth means argument and detail, never padding or repetition.
INTRODUCTION. Open with the problem and why it matters, say what is missing in the current literature, then state what this paper does. End it with an explicit contributions list ('- We ...') of two to four items, then state the preregistered prediction.
RELATED WORK — 600-900 words. Synthesise by theme: what papers establish together, where they disagree, and what remains unsettled. The failure this section keeps producing looks like this: 'X studies uncertainty [1]. Y studies approximations [2].' — a list with citations attached. Write instead: 'Uncertainty motivates Bayesian methods [1], but their tractable approximations lose guarantees [2], motivating our boundary test.' Use that argumentative structure only when the abstracts support it. End by positioning this study against the themes; omit irrelevant references and quoted or italicised paper titles. Each reference in a grouped citation must independently support the WHOLE sentence. If papers support different halves, use separate sentences and markers.
RESULTS. Walk the reader through the evidence: discuss each figure and each table where it is relevant to the point being made, rather than listing them at the end.
DO NOT RESTATE THE CONFIGURATION. The dataset, split, architecture, training budget and outcome definition are written for you into the Experimental Setup and the appendix. State them nowhere else — not in the Method, not a second time in the setup.
WHAT THE SETUP SECTION IS FOR is DESIGN justification (300-500 words): why a subject-disjoint split answers the question and a random split would not; benefits and costs of pairing conditions by seed; each negative control's intended alternative explanation and what its observed contrast supports; the seed budget and analysis. These arguments are not supplied by the configuration block.
The METHOD is about the OPERATOR — what it does, why that is the right expression of the hypothesis, and what its comparator neutralises.
The CONCLUSION (150-250 words) states what was found, what it changes for someone choosing between these methods, and what would settle the question next. Not a one-paragraph restatement of the abstract.
NAME THE ARMS AS THE TABLES DO: 'the proposed condition', 'the baseline', 'the first negative control', 'the second negative control'. Do not invent a parallel name such as 'Intervention' — the reader has to match your prose to the tables.

[claim-language] Claim what the evidence carries, and no more. Keep four registers apart and make it obvious which one a sentence is in: a RESULT states a measured quantity; an INTERPRETATION says what it may mean and is marked as such ('suggests', 'is consistent with'); a LIMITATION says what this design cannot tell anyone; FUTURE WORK proposes what would settle the question, and is the only register in which a wider setting may appear. Be exact about who was held out: evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen SUBJECTS — name that population — and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution, so do not call it out-of-distribution or domain generalisation. Cover, in whatever order the argument wants: the principal finding; what it means; what this design does and does NOT establish; a mechanism that would produce the observed result and at least one alternative that would too; what the independent replication cohort adds or fails to add; and how the finding stands against specific cited papers [n] — agreeing, conflicting, extending, or not comparable because the intervention, task, data regime or evaluation differ. Break at the argument's own joints — never split one argument to hit a shape, and never add a heading a section has not earned. Paragraphs of 60-150 words read well; one past 200 is doing more than one job and should be split where it turns.
