Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4, 20]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Time Series Attention Transformer* [7, 11]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including generalization challenges and data shift issues [16].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [8, 18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it, indicating that implementation fidelity is critical for such claims [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [6, 12, 21]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15].

This study positions itself against these themes by isolating cross-layer query consistency as a specific inductive bias. Unlike domain adaptation methods that align features across domains [10], or spectral regularization that constrains weight geometry [3], this intervention directly penalizes divergence between query projection weights across layers. The use of a subject-disjoint split distinguishes this work from studies that evaluate on random splits, which may overestimate generalization [4]. By employing a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, we address the reproducibility concerns raised in recent literature regarding Transformer modifications [1, 2].
Method: The core hypothesis of this experiment is that enforcing consistency between attention query projections across transformer blocks will improve subject-disjoint generalization. The intervention implements a CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator that adds a regularization term to the training objective. This term computes the squared Frobenius norm of the difference between the query projection weights of the first attention block and the second attention block. The rationale is that if attention mechanisms should be stable across depth for robust temporal feature extraction, penalizing divergence between these weights will encourage the model to learn more generalizable representations.

The operator is applied during the loss computation of every optimization step. The reference weights from the first block are detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients from flowing backward to the earlier layer through this specific loss term. This ensures that the consistency penalty only updates the target parameters in the deeper block. The loss term is differentiable with respect to the target parameters only, and the coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds to maintain a consistent regularization strength relative to the classification objective.

The comparator condition is a baseline control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, ensuring that dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters are identical. The control arm executes the identical code path but returns a zero loss term for the intervention. This design isolates the effect of the consistency loss from any other implementation details or seed-specific variance. A negative control condition is also included, which penalizes the difference between the second block's weights and a fixed random matrix. This control destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the computational cost, allowing us to distinguish the effect of cross-layer consistency from generic regularization or compute overhead.

The operator specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Experimental setup: The experiment uses the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset, which contains raw inertial signals from 30 subjects performing six activities. We use the official subject-disjoint split, with 7,352 training windows and 2,947 held-out test windows from unseen subjects. This split is critical because it tests generalization to new individuals, which is the relevant deployment scenario for activity recognition, rather than generalization to new time windows from the same individuals. A random split would confound subject-specific style with activity patterns, potentially inflating accuracy estimates.

The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder with two blocks, 64 hidden dimensions, and 4-head attention. Training runs for 12 epochs with a batch size of 128 using SGD. We employ 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. Pairing conditions by seed controls for initialization and data ordering variance, allowing us to detect small effects with higher power than independent sampling. The seed budget was chosen to achieve 90% planning target power for detecting the registered margin, though this power applies to rejecting a zero-effect null, not necessarily to exceeding the margin with the lower confidence bound.

The negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. This condition tests whether any improvement in the proposed condition is due to the specific cross-layer relationship or merely the addition of a regularization term with similar compute. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, it suggests the cross-layer structure matters. If both regularized conditions perform similarly, the benefit may be generic regularization. The observed contrast supports or refutes the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency specifically, rather than regularization generally, drives any accuracy changes. We report 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for all accuracy estimates to quantify uncertainty without assuming normality.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Results: We report results for the primary and confirmatory replication cohorts separately. In the primary cohort, across 43 seeds, the proposed condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 2 visualizes these means with error bars. The paired mean difference between the proposed and baseline conditions was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). As shown in Figure 3, the confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. The registered decision for the primary cohort is inconclusive.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This study tested whether cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series Transformers. Across 43 primary and 43 replication seeds, the intervention produced small, statistically nonsignificant accuracy differences (primary: 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]; replication: 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. For practitioners choosing between these methods on similar tasks, the evidence suggests that standard training is sufficient, and cross-layer query consistency adds complexity without robust accuracy gains. Future work should explore whether other forms of cross-layer alignment or different architectural inductive biases better support subject-disjoint generalization in time-series domains.
Discussion: The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not yield a statistically significant or practically worthwhile improvement in subject-disjoint generalization on the UCI HAR dataset. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohorts produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals spanning zero and failing to exceed the registered margin. This outcome suggests that, in this specific architecture and data regime, layer-specific adaptation of query projections may be more beneficial than enforcing consistency across depth.

This result stands in contrast to hypotheses derived from cross-layer consistency literature in other domains. For instance, *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention* found that strengthening layer interactions improved image classification accuracy [8]. Similarly, *Global Evolutionary Steering* reported that cross-layer consistency refined activation steering in language models [18]. However, those studies operated on different tasks (vision, language) and often evaluated on in-distribution or random splits. The subject-disjoint split used here imposes a stricter generalization requirement, which may explain the divergence. Our findings align more closely with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found inconclusive results for weight regularization in this time-series setting [3].

One mechanism that would produce the observed null result is that attention queries need to specialize at each layer to capture hierarchical temporal features. Enforcing consistency might constrain this specialization, preventing the deeper layer from refining the representations formed by the shallower layer. An alternative explanation is that the regularization coefficient (0.01) was too small to influence the optimization trajectory meaningfully, though the negative control condition, which used the same coefficient, also showed no significant deviation from baseline. This suggests the issue is not merely the magnitude of the penalty but the nature of the constraint itself.

The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds confirms that the inconclusive decision is not an artifact of a specific seed set. The consistency of the null result across 86 total seeds increases confidence that the effect, if it exists, is smaller than the worthwhile margin. However, this design does not establish that the effect is zero; it only excludes gains of the target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model. The negative control condition helps rule out generic regularization effects, as it performed similarly to the baseline. This implies that the compute overhead of the loss term itself does not drive accuracy changes.

Compared to *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which reported BLEU score increases in machine translation [9], our study highlights that consistency benefits may not transfer to time-series classification with subject shifts. The domain gap in activity recognition involves movement style and sensor noise, which may require flexible, layer-specific attention rather than stable, consistent attention. Future work should investigate whether consistency losses applied to values or keys, rather than queries, or applied across time rather than depth, might yield different outcomes.
Limitations: This study is limited to a single dataset (UCI HAR) and a specific Transformer architecture (2-block PreNormEncoder). While the subject-disjoint split supports claims about unseen subjects, the results do not generalize to other time-series domains, sensor modalities, or sequence lengths without further verification. The registered margin was derived from calibration noise, which reflects measurement precision but does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance for all deployment scenarios. Additionally, the power calculation targeted rejecting a zero-effect null, not necessarily detecting effects smaller than the margin. The study does not measure attention maps directly, so claims about attention stability are inferred from accuracy contrasts rather than observed mechanism.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformer architectures have become prominent in time-series analysis due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [38]. However, their effectiveness in settings requiring generalization across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds remains uncertain [5]. While standard Transformers excel in within-subject or random-split evaluations, it is unclear whether their depth encodes progressively refined representations or consistently stable attention patterns that benefit out-of-distribution (OOD) time-series tasks. Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for OOD time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

Existing studies often report accuracy improvements without rigorous controls for seed variance or without testing against a preregistered margin of practical significance [3, 17]. Furthermore, some claims regarding Transformer efficacy in time series have been questioned due to potential temporal information loss in permutation-invariant self-attention mechanisms [5]. This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. Specifically, we investigate whether regularizing deeper layer query weights toward shallower layer weights enhances generalization to unseen subjects.

This paper presents a preregistered replication study evaluating the CrossLayerQueryConsistency intervention. We contribute:
- A rigorous test of cross-layer query consistency loss on subject-disjoint generalization using 43 primary and 43 replication seeds.
- An analysis of whether attention stability across depth improves accuracy beyond standard regularization, evaluated against a fixed worthwhile margin.
- Transparent reporting of inconclusive outcomes where confidence intervals include zero and fail to exceed the registered threshold.

The preregistered prediction stated: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [38], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line due to temporal information loss [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [11], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [21], and *A survey of transformers* [41] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by isolating cross-layer weight consistency as a specific inductive bias for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, distinct from domain adaptation or activation steering.

=== method ===
The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear projection (9 to 64 channels), learned positional embedding (128 timesteps, 64 dimensions), and two transformer blocks. Each block contains LayerNorm, 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with query/key/value/output Linear projections (64 to 64), residual connections, and a feed-forward network (64 to 128 to 64). The final layer applies LayerNorm, mean-pooling over time, and a Linear projection to 6 classes. Training proceeds for 12 epochs with batch size 128 using SGD (lr=0.05, momentum=0.9).

The intervention, CrossLayerQueryConsistency, enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight → blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight) during training. The operator adds a loss term (coefficient=0.01) computed as the squared element-wise difference, detached from block 0 to prevent gradient flow to the reference weights. This design tests whether aligning deeper query projections to shallower ones stabilizes attention patterns across depth. The control arm executes identical code but returns zero loss term, leaving target parameters and optimizer momentum unchanged. The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix (same shape/norm as block 0), destroying meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This control isolates whether any accuracy change stems from regularization generally or cross-layer consistency specifically.

All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. The harness records operator activity at each lifecycle point; results are rejected if the control arm records non-zero activity. Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on test windows from unseen subjects. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. The operator specification ensures reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients, while the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification.** We use the official subject-disjoint split, with 1.03e+04 training windows and 2,947 held-out test windows from unseen subjects. A subject-disjoint split answers the question of generalization to new individuals, whereas a random split would allow information leakage from training subjects to test windows, overestimating performance. This design targets the open problem of architectural inductive biases for OOD time-series tasks where movement styles and sensor characteristics vary.

**Pairing and Controls.** Pairing conditions by seed controls for initialization and data ordering variance, allowing us to attribute differences to the intervention rather than seed noise. Each negative control's intended alternative explanation is tested via observed contrast: the first negative control matches compute but destroys the cross-layer relationship, testing if regularization *per se* drives changes. The seed budget (43 primary, 43 replication) supports detection of effects exceeding the registered margin with planned power. The analysis distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects; here, replication uses disjoint seeds on the same subject-disjoint test set to verify stability of the primary finding.

**Outcome and Decision.** The primary outcome is held-out classification accuracy. The registered decision rule classifies results as supported only if the lower confidence bound exceeds the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort.** Across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 2 displays the mean accuracy for the proposed, baseline, and negative control 1 conditions, with error bars showing 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimate for the proposed condition is 0.9062, compared to 0.9054 for the baseline. Figure 3 plots the paired mean difference, where the confidence interval includes zero. The green dash-dot marker in Figure 3 shows the registered worthwhile threshold; support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

**Replication Cohort.** Across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 5 shows the mean accuracy in the replication cohort, with the proposed condition at 0.9055 and baseline at 0.9035. Figure 6 plots the paired mean difference, where the confidence interval again includes zero and fails to exceed the margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Table 1 and Table 2 summarize the condition means and confidence intervals for primary and replication cohorts respectively.

**Training Dynamics.** Figure 4 and Figure 7 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the primary and replication cohorts. The curves for the proposed, baseline, and negative control 1 conditions overlap closely, indicating similar convergence behavior. Series encoding distinguishes conditions by marker shape and dash pattern. No condition demonstrates a clear separation in accuracy during training. The observed contrast supports the registered decision that the outcome is inconclusive; it does not refute the hypothesis definitively but fails to support it under the stated uncertainty model.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency did not yield statistically significant or practically worthwhile accuracy gains in either the primary or replication cohorts. The confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither lower bound exceeded the preregistered margin of 0.0125098. This outcome is inconclusive regarding the hypothesis that attention stability across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization.

**Interpretation.** These results suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. One mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class, meaning forcing deeper layers to match shallower ones constrains necessary refinement. An alternative explanation is that the consistency coefficient (0.01) was too small to influence optimization meaningfully, though the negative control matched compute without showing gains either. The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is stable across seeds; it fails to add evidence for the hypothesis.

**Comparison to Literature.** This finding stands in contrast to works suggesting cross-layer mechanisms enhance representation power [15, 34]. However, those studies often operate on hidden states or activation steering rather than weight regularization during training [37]. Our result aligns with *Spectral Entropy Minimization* [3], which also found inconclusive results for weight-geometry regularization in this setting. It differs from *Double Consistency Regularization* [17], which reported gains on machine translation tasks, suggesting the benefit may be task-dependent. The result is not comparable to *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers* [32] as we did not fine-tune on target domains.

**Mechanistic Claims.** Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. We did not measure attention maps directly; thus, we cannot claim attention stability from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. The observed contrast supports the registered decision that the outcome is inconclusive; it does not prove the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency benefits other time-series benchmarks or architectures. The study is limited to the UCI HAR dataset with a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder configuration. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. We did not measure attention maps directly, so claims about attention stability are unsupported. The study evaluates on people who appear nowhere in training, supporting a claim about unseen subjects, but is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. Future work should test whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks with direct attention measurements.

=== conclusion ===
We found that cross-layer query consistency loss did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers under the tested conditions. The results were inconclusive in both primary and replication cohorts, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This changes practice by indicating that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class, and practitioners should not expect robust gains from this specific regularization without further evidence. To settle the question next, future work should evaluate cross-layer consistency on diverse time-series benchmarks with direct measurements of attention stability and larger effect sizes.

REGISTERED OPERATOR (including gradient handling; do not infer that detaching one loss term freezes ordinary task-loss learning):
Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention. === abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformer architectures have become prominent in time-series analysis due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [38]. However, their effectiveness in settings requiring generalization across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds remains uncertain [5]. While standard Transformers excel in within-subject or random-split evaluations, it is unclear whether their depth encodes progressively refined representations or consistently stable attention patterns that benefit out-of-distribution (OOD) time-series tasks. Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for OOD time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

Existing studies often report accuracy improvements without rigorous controls for seed variance or without testing against a preregistered margin of practical significance [3, 17]. Furthermore, some claims regarding Transformer efficacy in time series have been questioned due to potential temporal information loss in permutation-invariant self-attention mechanisms [5]. This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. Specifically, we investigate whether regularizing deeper layer query weights toward shallower layer weights enhances generalization to unseen subjects.

This paper presents a preregistered replication study evaluating the CrossLayerQueryConsistency intervention. We contribute:
- A rigorous test of cross-layer query consistency loss on subject-disjoint generalization using 43 primary and 43 replication seeds.
- An analysis of whether attention stability across depth improves accuracy beyond standard regularization, evaluated against a fixed worthwhile margin.
- Transparent reporting of inconclusive outcomes where confidence intervals include zero and fail to exceed the registered threshold.

The preregistered prediction stated: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [38], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line due to temporal information loss [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [11], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [21], and *A survey of transformers* [41] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by isolating cross-layer weight consistency as a specific inductive bias for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, distinct from domain adaptation or activation steering.

=== method ===
The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear projection (9 to 64 channels), learned positional embedding (128 timesteps, 64 dimensions), and two transformer blocks. Each block contains LayerNorm, 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with query/key/value/output Linear projections (64 to 64), residual connections, and a feed-forward network (64 to 128 to 64). The final layer applies LayerNorm, mean-pooling over time, and a Linear projection to 6 classes. Training proceeds for 12 epochs with batch size 128 using SGD (lr=0.05, momentum=0.9).

The intervention, CrossLayerQueryConsistency, enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight → blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight) during training. The operator adds a loss term (coefficient=0.01) computed as the squared element-wise difference, detached from block 0 to prevent gradient flow to the reference weights. This design tests whether aligning deeper query projections to shallower ones stabilizes attention patterns across depth. The control arm executes identical code but returns zero loss term, leaving target parameters and optimizer momentum unchanged. The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix (same shape/norm as block 0), destroying meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This control isolates whether any accuracy change stems from regularization generally or cross-layer consistency specifically.

All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. The harness records operator activity at each lifecycle point; results are rejected if the control arm records non-zero activity. Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on test windows from unseen subjects. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. The operator specification ensures reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients, while the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification.** We use the official subject-disjoint split, with 1.03e+04 training windows and 2,947 held-out test windows from unseen subjects. A subject-disjoint split answers the question of generalization to new individuals, whereas a random split would allow information leakage from training subjects to test windows, overestimating performance. This design targets the open problem of architectural inductive biases for OOD time-series tasks where movement styles and sensor characteristics vary.

**Pairing and Controls.** Pairing conditions by seed controls for initialization and data ordering variance, allowing us to attribute differences to the intervention rather than seed noise. Each negative control's intended alternative explanation is tested via observed contrast: the first negative control matches compute but destroys the cross-layer relationship, testing if regularization *per se* drives changes. The seed budget (43 primary, 43 replication) supports detection of effects exceeding the registered margin with planned power. The analysis distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects; here, replication uses disjoint seeds on the same subject-disjoint test set to verify stability of the primary finding.

**Outcome and Decision.** The primary outcome is held-out classification accuracy. The registered decision rule classifies results as supported only if the lower confidence bound exceeds the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort.** Across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 2 displays the mean accuracy for the proposed, baseline, and negative control 1 conditions, with error bars showing 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimate for the proposed condition is 0.9062, compared to 0.9054 for the baseline. Figure 3 plots the paired mean difference, where the confidence interval includes zero. The green dash-dot marker in Figure 3 shows the registered worthwhile threshold; support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

**Replication Cohort.** Across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 5 shows the mean accuracy in the replication cohort, with the proposed condition at 0.9055 and baseline at 0.9035. Figure 6 plots the paired mean difference, where the confidence interval again includes zero and fails to exceed the margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Table 1 and Table 2 summarize the condition means and confidence intervals for primary and replication cohorts respectively.

**Training Dynamics.** Figure 4 and Figure 7 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the primary and replication cohorts. The curves for the proposed, baseline, and negative control 1 conditions overlap closely, indicating similar convergence behavior. Series encoding distinguishes conditions by marker shape and dash pattern. No condition demonstrates a clear separation in accuracy during training. The observed contrast supports the registered decision that the outcome is inconclusive; it does not refute the hypothesis definitively but fails to support it under the stated uncertainty model.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency did not yield statistically significant or practically worthwhile accuracy gains in either the primary or replication cohorts. The confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither lower bound exceeded the preregistered margin of 0.0125098. This outcome is inconclusive regarding the hypothesis that attention stability across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization.

**Interpretation.** These results suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. One mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class, meaning forcing deeper layers to match shallower ones constrains necessary refinement. An alternative explanation is that the consistency coefficient (0.01) was too small to influence optimization meaningfully, though the negative control matched compute without showing gains either. The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is stable across seeds; it fails to add evidence for the hypothesis.

**Comparison to Literature.** This finding stands in contrast to works suggesting cross-layer mechanisms enhance representation power [15, 34]. However, those studies often operate on hidden states or activation steering rather than weight regularization during training [37]. Our result aligns with *Spectral Entropy Minimization* [3], which also found inconclusive results for weight-geometry regularization in this setting. It differs from *Double Consistency Regularization* [17], which reported gains on machine translation tasks, suggesting the benefit may be task-dependent. The result is not comparable to *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers* [32] as we did not fine-tune on target domains.

**Mechanistic Claims.** Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. We did not measure attention maps directly; thus, we cannot claim attention stability from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. The observed contrast supports the registered decision that the outcome is inconclusive; it does not prove the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency benefits other time-series benchmarks or architectures. The study is limited to the UCI HAR dataset with a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder configuration. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. We did not measure attention maps directly, so claims about attention stability are unsupported. The study evaluates on people who appear nowhere in training, supporting a claim about unseen subjects, but is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. Future work should test whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks with direct attention measurements.

=== conclusion ===
We found that cross-layer query consistency loss did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers under the tested conditions. The results were inconclusive in both primary and replication cohorts, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This changes practice by indicating that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class, and practitioners should not expect robust gains from this specific regularization without further evidence. To settle the question next, future work should evaluate cross-layer consistency on diverse time-series benchmarks with direct measurements of attention stability and larger effect sizes.

Related-work section:
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [20], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line due to temporal information loss [4]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [8], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3].
