=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Time-series classification using deep learning has become critical for applications ranging from healthcare monitoring to industrial predictive maintenance. Among architectural choices, Transformers have gained prominence due to their ability to model long-range dependencies without the sequential constraints of recurrent networks [38]. However, their effectiveness in time-series domains, particularly regarding generalization across subjects with distinct movement styles and sensor characteristics, remains a subject of active debate [5]. While Transformers excel in natural language processing, their application to temporal data often requires careful adaptation to handle the continuous, ordered nature of signals [32]. A key open problem is identifying which architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects in the UCI HAR setting.

Current literature highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding Transformer effectiveness for time series. Surveys note that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [38], yet empirical studies question the validity of this research line compared to simpler linear models [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs [14]. However, a gap exists in verifying whether specific regularization strategies, such as cross-layer consistency, stabilize attention mechanisms to improve subject-disjoint generalization. While consistency regularization is proposed to address overfitting in deep Transformer models [17], and cross-layer mechanisms are explored to strengthen layer interactions [15], independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization is lacking.

This paper addresses this gap by conducting a preregistered experiment testing the impact of cross-layer query consistency on held-out classification accuracy. We focus on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset, utilizing an official subject-disjoint split to ensure evaluation on unseen subjects. The study compares a proposed condition, which enforces consistency between query projection weights of deeper and shallower layers, against a baseline control arm. We also include a negative control to verify that observed effects are due to meaningful cross-layer relationships rather than compute matching.

The contributions of this work are as follows:
- We execute a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency loss in a time-series Transformer, measuring held-out classification accuracy on a subject-disjoint split.
- We report results from both a primary cohort and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, providing robust statistical evidence regarding the intervention's effect.
- We provide inconclusive evidence regarding the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency improves generalization, suggesting that layer-specific adaptation may be essential in this regime.

The preregistered prediction states that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report the results honestly against this prediction, labeling any unforeseen findings as exploratory.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it, indicating its conclusions may not be relied upon [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [11], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [21], and *A survey of transformers* [41] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28].

This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific cross-layer consistency hypothesis in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. While prior work suggests consistency regularization can alleviate overfitting [17] and cross-layer mechanisms can enhance representation power [15], the specific application of query projection consistency for subject-disjoint generalization in time-series Transformers remains unverified. The inconclusive results of *Spectral Entropy Minimization* [3] further motivate rigorous testing of weight-based regularizations. Unlike *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers* [32], which focuses on fine-tuning, this work examines architectural inductive biases during initial training. We do not claim that accuracy results evidence calibration, nor do we assert that attention stability is measured directly; rather, we test the downstream accuracy consequence of the proposed weight constraint.

=== method ===
The core of this experiment is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces a specific structural constraint on the Transformer's attention mechanism. The hypothesis motivating this operator is that stabilizing attention query projections across depth may improve generalization to unseen subjects by reducing layer-specific overfitting to training subject idiosyncrasies. The operator targets the query projection weights of the second attention block, regularizing them toward the weights of the first block. This design choice reflects the assumption that shallower layers capture more general temporal features, and deeper layers should not diverge excessively from these foundations in a subject-disjoint setting.

The operator is applied during the loss computation of every optimization step. It retrieves the reference weights from the first block's query projection and detaches them from the gradient graph. This detachment ensures that the consistency penalty does not alter the gradient flow to the first block, isolating the regularization effect to the target parameters in the second block. The operator then computes the element-wise difference between the target weights and the detached reference weights, squares these differences, and sums them to form a raw loss term. This raw term is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01 before being added to the primary classification objective.

This formulation tests whether weight alignment across layers yields accuracy benefits. It is distinct from attention-map alignment, as it operates directly on the projection matrices. The comparator condition, the baseline, executes the identical code path but returns a zero loss term. This ensures that any difference in outcomes is attributable to the presence of the consistency penalty rather than implementation artifacts or computational graph differences. The negative control penalizes the difference between the second block's weights and a fixed random matrix. This control is intended to rule out the possibility that any regularization term, regardless of its semantic meaning, drives the outcome. If the negative control performs similarly to the proposed condition, it would suggest the effect is due to the act of regularization itself rather than the specific cross-layer relationship.

The method does not claim to measure attention stability directly. Mechanistic rationales regarding feature learning or layer specialization are hypotheses, not measured findings. The directly recorded outcome is held-out classification accuracy. The operator specification ensures that the reference weights receive no gradients from the consistency term, preserving the integrity of the first block's learning dynamics with respect to this specific penalty. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds to maintain experimental control. By pairing seeds between the proposed and baseline conditions, we ensure that initialization and data ordering are identical, isolating the intervention as the sole variable.

The operator's design neutralizes the alternative explanation that gradient flow to the reference block drives the result. By detaching the reference, we ensure the penalty only constrains the target. This allows us to interpret any accuracy difference as a consequence of constraining the deeper layer's query space. However, we do not infer that a small coefficient guarantees a small penalty or gradient; the magnitude depends on the weight difference. The method strictly adheres to the preregistered contract, where the control arm leaves the registered target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged. This rigorous definition of the control arm ensures that the baseline represents a true absence of the intervention, allowing for a clean causal attribution of any observed effect.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experimental design utilizes a subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset to answer the question of generalization to unseen subjects. A random split would not suffice because it would allow data from the same subject to appear in both training and testing sets, inflating accuracy estimates through subject-specific overfitting. The subject-disjoint split ensures that the held-out evaluation measures performance on individuals whose movement styles and sensor characteristics were not present during training. This design choice is critical for claims regarding subject-disjoint generalization, as it prevents the model from memorizing subject-specific noise.

We employ a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to verify the stability of the primary results. This is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, but a replication of the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline. The benefit of this approach is that it distinguishes between effects that are robust to initialization variance and those that are seed-dependent. Pairing conditions by seed ensures that each comparison controls for the specific random initialization and batch ordering, reducing variance in the paired contrast. The seed budget consists of 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds.

The negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any added loss term, regardless of its semantic content, might act as a regularizer improving generalization. By comparing the proposed condition to a negative control that penalizes deviation from a random matrix, we can determine if the cross-layer relationship is specifically beneficial. If the negative control yields similar accuracy to the proposed condition, it would suggest the compute or regularization act itself is the driver. The observed contrast supports the interpretation of whether the specific cross-layer constraint matters.

The analysis computes 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for the mean differences, not standard deviations. This interval quantifies the uncertainty in the estimate of the mean effect. The registered decision threshold is based on a worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. A confidence interval crossing zero indicates that a null effect is plausible within the stated uncertainty model. If a CI crosses zero but lies below the worthwhile margin, we preserve its registered label and separately explain that it excludes gains of that target magnitude. The power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter. The setup ensures that the reported uncertainty is consistently labeled as confidence interval, reflecting the analysis actually computed.

=== results ===
The experimental flow from dataset to evaluation is depicted in Figure 1. We report results for the primary cohort first, followed by the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 2 visualizes these means with error bars representing the 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimates are printed above each bar, and the axis starts at zero to allow comparable bar lengths. The dashed line marks the baseline mean as an ordering reference.

The hypothesis-positive contrast in the primary cohort is shown in Figure 3. The proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The green dash-dot marker in Figure 3 shows the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion. The lower confidence bound does not exceed this threshold, so the preregistered decision is inconclusive. Figure 4 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all three conditions in the primary cohort. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. The curves for the conditions coincide closely, distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern.

In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, the proposed condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), compared to the baseline's 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]). Figure 5 visualizes these replication means. The hypothesis-positive contrast in the replication cohort is detailed in Figure 6. The proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Again, the 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold. The preregistered decision is inconclusive. Figure 7 shows the accuracy over training steps for the replication cohort, where curves again coincide closely.

Table 1 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for all conditions in the primary cohort. Table 2 details the outcome statistics for the primary cohort, including the mean difference, confidence interval, p-value, and effect size. Table 3 and Table 4 provide the corresponding data for the replication cohort. Table 5 compares the means across both cohorts. In both cohorts, the confidence intervals for the difference include zero, and neither exceeds the preregistered calibration-derived decision threshold in terms of the registered outcome, held-out classification accuracy. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. The mean differences were small (0.000773 and 0.00196), and the confidence intervals included zero in both cases. This suggests that, within this calibrated testbed, cross-layer query consistency does not provide a robust accuracy gain over standard training. The results are consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation may be essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, as the constraint preventing deeper layers from diverging from shallower ones did not enhance generalization.

This design establishes that the intervention does not improve accuracy under these specific conditions, but it does not establish the mechanism. Attention stability is an unmeasured hypothesis; we did not record attention maps or measure stability directly. An alternative explanation for the null result is that the consistency coefficient was too small to exert a meaningful constraint, or conversely, that the constraint was too rigid, preventing the deeper layer from learning subject-invariant features that differ from shallow representations. The negative control results, which were similar to the proposed condition, suggest that the specific cross-layer relationship may not be the active ingredient, or that the regularization act itself had negligible impact at this coefficient.

The independent replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not a fluke of a specific seed set. Both cohorts showed inconclusive outcomes with overlapping confidence intervals. This stands in contrast to works like *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* [17], which reported performance improvements, though in machine translation tasks rather than subject-disjoint time series. It also differs from *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention* [15], which found gains in vision tasks. The discrepancy may arise from the domain difference; time-series data may require more layer-specific flexibility than vision or text. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* [3] also reported inconclusive results for weight-based regularization in this setting, suggesting a broader pattern where weight geometry constraints do not translate to accuracy gains in this regime.

We do not claim that accuracy results evidence calibration. The outcome measure was held-out classification accuracy, and claims are restricted to this metric. The null result does not establish that cross-layer consistency is ineffective in all settings, only that it did not exceed the worthwhile margin here. Future work would need to measure attention stability directly to confirm the mechanistic hypothesis. Additionally, testing on different architectures or datasets would be required to assess generalization beyond this calibrated testbed. The findings suggest that for someone choosing between these methods in the UCI HAR setting, the added complexity of cross-layer consistency is not justified by accuracy gains.

=== limitations ===
This study has several limitations regarding what the design can establish. First, the null result does not establish that cross-layer consistency is mechanistically ineffective; it only shows no accuracy gain. Attention stability remains an unmeasured hypothesis. We did not record attention maps, so we cannot confirm whether the weights were actually aligned or whether alignment would have mattered. Second, the generalization claim is limited to the UCI HAR dataset and the specific PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture used. We do not have evidence for larger models, different architecture families, or other time-series domains. The recipe pins one architecture at one size, so no comparison across scales exists in this experiment.

Third, the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds is a replication of the experimental run itself, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. While it controls for seed variance, it does not test robustness to distribution shift beyond the held-out subjects in UCI HAR. Finally, the worthwhile margin was derived from calibration noise, which reflects measurement precision but does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. A result excluding the margin under this uncertainty model does not guarantee the effect is zero, only that it is smaller than the target magnitude. These limitations constrain the scope of the conclusion to the specific testbed and outcome measure.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series Transformers. We found no statistically significant difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed condition and the baseline in either the primary or replication cohorts. Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. For practitioners choosing between these methods for the UCI HAR task, the results suggest that standard training is sufficient, and the intervention adds complexity without accuracy benefit. The findings indicate that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class. To settle the question of mechanism, future work should directly measure attention stability and test the intervention across different model scales and datasets.

REGISTERED OPERATOR (including gradient handling; do not infer that detaching one loss term freezes ordinary task-loss learning):
Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Time-series classification using deep learning has become critical for applications ranging from healthcare monitoring to industrial predictive maintenance. Among architectural choices, Transformers have gained prominence due to their ability to model long-range dependencies without the sequential constraints of recurrent networks [38]. However, their effectiveness in time-series domains, particularly regarding generalization across subjects with distinct movement styles and sensor characteristics, remains a subject of active debate [5]. While Transformers excel in natural language processing, their application to temporal data often requires careful adaptation to handle the continuous, ordered nature of signals [32]. A key open problem is identifying which architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects in the UCI HAR setting.

Current literature highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding Transformer effectiveness for time series. Surveys note that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [38], yet empirical studies question the validity of this research line compared to simpler linear models [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs [14]. However, a gap exists in verifying whether specific regularization strategies, such as cross-layer consistency, stabilize attention mechanisms to improve subject-disjoint generalization. While consistency regularization is proposed to address overfitting in deep Transformer models [17], and cross-layer mechanisms are explored to strengthen layer interactions [15], independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization is lacking.

This paper addresses this gap by conducting a preregistered experiment testing the impact of cross-layer query consistency on held-out classification accuracy. We focus on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset, utilizing an official subject-disjoint split to ensure evaluation on unseen subjects. The study compares a proposed condition, which enforces consistency between query projection weights of deeper and shallower layers, against a baseline control arm. We also include a negative control to verify that observed effects are due to meaningful cross-layer relationships rather than compute matching.

The contributions of this work are as follows:
- We execute a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency loss in a time-series Transformer, measuring held-out classification accuracy on a subject-disjoint split.
- We report results from both a primary cohort and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, providing robust statistical evidence regarding the intervention's effect.
- We provide inconclusive evidence regarding the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency improves generalization, suggesting that layer-specific adaptation may be essential in this regime.

The preregistered prediction states that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report the results honestly against this prediction, labeling any unforeseen findings as exploratory.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it, indicating its conclusions may not be relied upon [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [11], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [21], and *A survey of transformers* [41] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28].

This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific cross-layer consistency hypothesis in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. While prior work suggests consistency regularization can alleviate overfitting [17] and cross-layer mechanisms can enhance representation power [15], the specific application of query projection consistency for subject-disjoint generalization in time-series Transformers remains unverified. The inconclusive results of *Spectral Entropy Minimization* [3] further motivate rigorous testing of weight-based regularizations. Unlike *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers* [32], which focuses on fine-tuning, this work examines architectural inductive biases during initial training. We do not claim that accuracy results evidence calibration, nor do we assert that attention stability is measured directly; rather, we test the downstream accuracy consequence of the proposed weight constraint.

=== method ===
The core of this experiment is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces a specific structural constraint on the Transformer's attention mechanism. The hypothesis motivating this operator is that stabilizing attention query projections across depth may improve generalization to unseen subjects by reducing layer-specific overfitting to training subject idiosyncrasies. The operator targets the query projection weights of the second attention block, regularizing them toward the weights of the first block. This design choice reflects the assumption that shallower layers capture more general temporal features, and deeper layers should not diverge excessively from these foundations in a subject-disjoint setting.

The operator is applied during the loss computation of every optimization step. It retrieves the reference weights from the first block's query projection and detaches them from the gradient graph. This detachment ensures that the consistency penalty does not alter the gradient flow to the first block, isolating the regularization effect to the target parameters in the second block. The operator then computes the element-wise difference between the target weights and the detached reference weights, squares these differences, and sums them to form a raw loss term. This raw term is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01 before being added to the primary classification objective.

This formulation tests whether weight alignment across layers yields accuracy benefits. It is distinct from attention-map alignment, as it operates directly on the projection matrices. The comparator condition, the baseline, executes the identical code path but returns a zero loss term. This ensures that any difference in outcomes is attributable to the presence of the consistency penalty rather than implementation artifacts or computational graph differences. The negative control penalizes the difference between the second block's weights and a fixed random matrix. This control is intended to rule out the possibility that any regularization term, regardless of its semantic meaning, drives the outcome. If the negative control performs similarly to the proposed condition, it would suggest the effect is due to the act of regularization itself rather than the specific cross-layer relationship.

The method does not claim to measure attention stability directly. Mechanistic rationales regarding feature learning or layer specialization are hypotheses, not measured findings. The directly recorded outcome is held-out classification accuracy. The operator specification ensures that the reference weights receive no gradients from the consistency term, preserving the integrity of the first block's learning dynamics with respect to this specific penalty. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds to maintain experimental control. By pairing seeds between the proposed and baseline conditions, we ensure that initialization and data ordering are identical, isolating the intervention as the sole variable.

The operator's design neutralizes the alternative explanation that gradient flow to the reference block drives the result. By detaching the reference, we ensure the penalty only constrains the target. This allows us to interpret any accuracy difference as a consequence of constraining the deeper layer's query space. However, we do not infer that a small coefficient guarantees a small penalty or gradient; the magnitude depends on the weight difference. The method strictly adheres to the preregistered contract, where the control arm leaves the registered target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged. This rigorous definition of the control arm ensures that the baseline represents a true absence of the intervention, allowing for a clean causal attribution of any observed effect.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experimental design utilizes a subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset to answer the question of generalization to unseen subjects. A random split would not suffice because it would allow data from the same subject to appear in both training and testing sets, inflating accuracy estimates through subject-specific overfitting. The subject-disjoint split ensures that the held-out evaluation measures performance on individuals whose movement styles and sensor characteristics were not present during training. This design choice is critical for claims regarding subject-disjoint generalization, as it prevents the model from memorizing subject-specific noise.

We employ a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to verify the stability of the primary results. This is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, but a replication of the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline. The benefit of this approach is that it distinguishes between effects that are robust to initialization variance and those that are seed-dependent. Pairing conditions by seed ensures that each comparison controls for the specific random initialization and batch ordering, reducing variance in the paired contrast. The seed budget consists of 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds.

The negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any added loss term, regardless of its semantic content, might act as a regularizer improving generalization. By comparing the proposed condition to a negative control that penalizes deviation from a random matrix, we can determine if the cross-layer relationship is specifically beneficial. If the negative control yields similar accuracy to the proposed condition, it would suggest the compute or regularization act itself is the driver. The observed contrast supports the interpretation of whether the specific cross-layer constraint matters.

The analysis computes 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for the mean differences, not standard deviations. This interval quantifies the uncertainty in the estimate of the mean effect. The registered decision threshold is based on a worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. A confidence interval crossing zero indicates that a null effect is plausible within the stated uncertainty model. If a CI crosses zero but lies below the worthwhile margin, we preserve its registered label and separately explain that it excludes gains of that target magnitude. The power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter. The setup ensures that the reported uncertainty is consistently labeled as confidence interval, reflecting the analysis actually computed.

=== results ===
The experimental flow from dataset to evaluation is depicted in Figure 1. We report results for the primary cohort first, followed by the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 2 visualizes these means with error bars representing the 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimates are printed above each bar, and the axis starts at zero to allow comparable bar lengths. The dashed line marks the baseline mean as an ordering reference.

The hypothesis-positive contrast in the primary cohort is shown in Figure 3. The proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The green dash-dot marker in Figure 3 shows the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion. The lower confidence bound does not exceed this threshold, so the preregistered decision is inconclusive. Figure 4 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all three conditions in the primary cohort. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. The curves for the conditions coincide closely, distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern.

In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, the proposed condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), compared to the baseline's 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]). Figure 5 visualizes these replication means. The hypothesis-positive contrast in the replication cohort is detailed in Figure 6. The proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Again, the 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold. The preregistered decision is inconclusive. Figure 7 shows the accuracy over training steps for the replication cohort, where curves again coincide closely.

Table 1 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for all conditions in the primary cohort. Table 2 details the outcome statistics for the primary cohort, including the mean difference, confidence interval, p-value, and effect size. Table 3 and Table 4 provide the corresponding data for the replication cohort. Table 5 compares the means across both cohorts. In both cohorts, the confidence intervals for the difference include zero, and neither exceeds the preregistered calibration-derived decision threshold in terms of the registered outcome, held-out classification accuracy. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. The mean differences were small (0.000773 and 0.00196), and the confidence intervals included zero in both cases. This suggests that, within this calibrated testbed, cross-layer query consistency does not provide a robust accuracy gain over standard training. The results are consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation may be essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, as the constraint preventing deeper layers from diverging from shallower ones did not enhance generalization.

This design establishes that the intervention does not improve accuracy under these specific conditions, but it does not establish the mechanism. Attention stability is an unmeasured hypothesis; we did not record attention maps or measure stability directly. An alternative explanation for the null result is that the consistency coefficient was too small to exert a meaningful constraint, or conversely, that the constraint was too rigid, preventing the deeper layer from learning subject-invariant features that differ from shallow representations. The negative control results, which were similar to the proposed condition, suggest that the specific cross-layer relationship may not be the active ingredient, or that the regularization act itself had negligible impact at this coefficient.

The independent replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not a fluke of a specific seed set. Both cohorts showed inconclusive outcomes with overlapping confidence intervals. This stands in contrast to works like *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* [17], which reported performance improvements, though in machine translation tasks rather than subject-disjoint time series. It also differs from *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention* [15], which found gains in vision tasks. The discrepancy may arise from the domain difference; time-series data may require more layer-specific flexibility than vision or text. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* [3] also reported inconclusive results for weight-based regularization in this setting, suggesting a broader pattern where weight geometry constraints do not translate to accuracy gains in this regime.

We do not claim that accuracy results evidence calibration. The outcome measure was held-out classification accuracy, and claims are restricted to this metric. The null result does not establish that cross-layer consistency is ineffective in all settings, only that it did not exceed the worthwhile margin here. Future work would need to measure attention stability directly to confirm the mechanistic hypothesis. Additionally, testing on different architectures or datasets would be required to assess generalization beyond this calibrated testbed. The findings suggest that for someone choosing between these methods in the UCI HAR setting, the added complexity of cross-layer consistency is not justified by accuracy gains.

=== limitations ===
This study has several limitations regarding what the design can establish. First, the null result does not establish that cross-layer consistency is mechanistically ineffective; it only shows no accuracy gain. Attention stability remains an unmeasured hypothesis. We did not record attention maps, so we cannot confirm whether the weights were actually aligned or whether alignment would have mattered. Second, the generalization claim is limited to the UCI HAR dataset and the specific PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture used. We do not have evidence for larger models, different architecture families, or other time-series domains. The recipe pins one architecture at one size, so no comparison across scales exists in this experiment.

Third, the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds is a replication of the experimental run itself, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. While it controls for seed variance, it does not test robustness to distribution shift beyond the held-out subjects in UCI HAR. Finally, the worthwhile margin was derived from calibration noise, which reflects measurement precision but does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. A result excluding the margin under this uncertainty model does not guarantee the effect is zero, only that it is smaller than the target magnitude. These limitations constrain the scope of the conclusion to the specific testbed and outcome measure.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series Transformers. We found no statistically significant difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed condition and the baseline in either the primary or replication cohorts. Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. For practitioners choosing between these methods for the UCI HAR task, the results suggest that standard training is sufficient, and the intervention adds complexity without accuracy benefit. The findings indicate that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class. To settle the question of mechanism, future work should directly measure attention stability and test the intervention across different model scales and datasets.
