Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [3]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN* [10] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Time Series Attention Transformer* [6]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [12]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [15].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [8]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [9]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [7], and *Global Evolutionary Steering* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [17]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [13]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [2]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it, indicating its conclusions may not be relied upon [1].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [4]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [16]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [18]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [5], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [11], and *A survey of transformers* [20] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [14].

This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific cross-layer consistency hypothesis in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. While prior work suggests consistency regularization can alleviate overfitting [8] and cross-layer mechanisms can enhance representation power [7], the specific application of query projection consistency for subject-disjoint generalization in time-series Transformers remains unverified. The inconclusive results of *Spectral Entropy Minimization* [2] further motivate rigorous testing of weight-based regularizations. Unlike *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers* [15], which focuses on fine-tuning, this work examines architectural inductive biases during initial training. We do not claim that accuracy results evidence calibration, nor do we assert that attention stability is measured directly; rather, we test the downstream accuracy consequence of the proposed weight constraint.
Method: The core of this experiment is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces a specific structural constraint on the Transformer's attention mechanism. The hypothesis motivating this operator is that stabilizing attention query projections across depth may improve generalization to unseen subjects by reducing layer-specific overfitting to training subject idiosyncrasies. The operator targets the query projection weights of the second attention block, regularizing them toward the weights of the first block. This design choice reflects the assumption that shallower layers capture more general temporal features, and deeper layers should not diverge excessively from these foundations in a subject-disjoint setting.

The operator is applied during the loss computation of every optimization step. It retrieves the reference weights from the first block's query projection and detaches them from the gradient graph. This detachment ensures that the consistency penalty does not alter the gradient flow to the first block, isolating the regularization effect to the target parameters in the second block. The operator then computes the element-wise difference between the target weights and the detached reference weights, squares these differences, and sums them to form a raw loss term. This raw term is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01 before being added to the primary classification objective.

This formulation tests whether weight alignment across layers yields accuracy benefits. It is distinct from attention-map alignment, as it operates directly on the projection matrices. The comparator condition, the baseline, executes the identical code path but returns a zero loss term. This ensures that any difference in outcomes is attributable to the presence of the consistency penalty rather than implementation artifacts or computational graph differences. The negative control penalizes the difference between the second block's weights and a fixed random matrix. This control is intended to rule out the possibility that any regularization term, regardless of its semantic meaning, drives the outcome. If the negative control performs similarly to the proposed condition, it would suggest the effect is. This experiment did not test whether this was due to the act of regularization itself rather than the specific cross-layer relationship.

The method does not claim to measure attention stability directly. Mechanistic rationales regarding feature learning or layer specialization are hypotheses, not measured findings. The directly recorded outcome is held-out classification accuracy. The operator specification ensures that the reference weights receive no gradients from the consistency term, preserving the integrity of the first block's learning dynamics with respect to this specific penalty. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds to maintain experimental control. By pairing seeds between the proposed and baseline conditions, we ensure that initialization and data ordering are identical, isolating the intervention as the sole variable.

The operator's design neutralizes the alternative explanation that gradient flow to the reference block drives the result. By detaching the reference, we ensure the penalty only constrains the target. This allows us to interpret any accuracy difference as a consequence of constraining the deeper layer's query space. However, we do not infer that a small coefficient guarantees a small penalty or gradient; the magnitude depends on the weight difference. The method strictly adheres to the preregistered contract, where the control arm leaves the registered target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged. This rigorous definition of the control arm ensures that the baseline represents a true absence of the intervention, allowing for a clean causal attribution of any observed effect.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Experimental setup: The experimental design utilizes a subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset to answer the question of generalization to unseen subjects. A random split would not suffice because it would allow data from the same subject to appear in both training and testing sets, inflating accuracy estimates through subject-specific overfitting. The subject-disjoint split ensures that the held-out evaluation measures performance on individuals whose movement styles and sensor characteristics were not present during training. This design choice is critical for claims regarding subject-disjoint generalization, as it prevents the model from memorizing subject-specific noise.

We employ a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to verify the stability of the primary results. This is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, but a replication of the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline. The benefit of this approach is that it distinguishes between effects that are robust to initialization variance and those that are seed-dependent. Pairing conditions by seed ensures that each comparison controls for the specific random initialization and batch ordering, reducing variance in the paired contrast. The seed budget consists of 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds.

The negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any added loss term, regardless of its semantic content, might act as a regularizer improving generalization. By comparing the proposed condition to a negative control that penalizes deviation from a random matrix, we can determine if the cross-layer relationship is specifically beneficial. If the negative control yields similar accuracy to the proposed condition, it would suggest the compute or regularization act itself is the driver. The observed contrast supports the interpretation of whether the specific cross-layer constraint matters.

The analysis computes 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for the mean differences, not standard deviations. This interval quantifies the uncertainty in the estimate of the mean effect. The registered decision threshold is based on a worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. A confidence interval crossing zero indicates that a null effect is plausible within the stated uncertainty model. If a CI crosses zero but lies below the worthwhile margin, we preserve its registered label and separately explain that it excludes gains of that target magnitude. The power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter. The setup ensures that the reported uncertainty is consistently labeled as confidence interval, reflecting the analysis actually computed.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Results: The experimental flow from dataset to evaluation is depicted in Figure 1. We report results for the primary cohort first, followed by the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 2 visualizes these means with error bars representing the 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimates are printed above each bar, and the axis starts at zero to allow comparable bar lengths. The dashed line marks the baseline mean as an ordering reference.

The contrast in the hypothesised direction in the primary cohort is shown in Figure 3. The proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The green dash-dot marker in Figure 3 shows the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion. The lower confidence bound does not exceed this threshold, so the preregistered decision is inconclusive. Figure 4 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all three conditions in the primary cohort. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. The curves for the conditions coincide closely, distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern.

In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, the proposed condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), compared to the baseline's 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]). Figure 5 visualizes these replication means. The contrast in the hypothesised direction in the replication cohort is detailed in Figure 6. The proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Again, the 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold. The preregistered decision is inconclusive. Figure 7 shows the accuracy over training steps for the replication cohort, where curves again coincide closely.

Table 1 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for all conditions in the primary cohort. Table 2 details the outcome statistics for the primary cohort, including the mean difference, confidence interval, p-value, and effect size. Table 3 and Table 4 provide the corresponding data for the replication cohort. Table 5 compares the means across both cohorts. In both cohorts, the confidence intervals for the difference include zero, and neither exceeds the preregistered calibration-derived decision threshold in terms of the registered outcome, held-out classification accuracy. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This study tested whether cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series Transformers. We found no statistically significant difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed condition and the baseline in either the primary or replication cohorts. Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. For practitioners choosing between these methods for the UCI HAR task, the results suggest that standard training is sufficient, and the intervention adds complexity without accuracy benefit. One possibility, which this experiment did not test, is that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class. To settle the question of mechanism, future work should directly measure attention stability and test the intervention across different model scales and datasets.
Discussion: The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. The mean differences were small (0.000773 and 0.00196), and the confidence intervals included zero in both cases. This suggests that, within this calibrated testbed, cross-layer query consistency does not provide a robust accuracy gain over standard training. The results are consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation may be essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, as the constraint preventing deeper layers from diverging from shallower ones did not enhance generalization.

This design establishes that the intervention does not improve accuracy under these specific conditions, but it does not establish the mechanism. Attention stability is an unmeasured hypothesis; we did not record attention maps or measure stability directly. An alternative explanation for the null result is that the consistency coefficient was too small to exert a meaningful constraint, or conversely, that the constraint was too rigid, preventing the deeper layer from learning subject-invariant features that differ from shallow representations. The negative control results, which were similar to the proposed condition, suggest that the specific cross-layer relationship may not be the active ingredient, or that the regularization act itself had negligible impact at this coefficient.

The independent replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not a fluke of a specific seed set. Both cohorts showed inconclusive outcomes with overlapping confidence intervals. This stands in contrast to works like *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* [8], which reported performance improvements, though in machine translation tasks rather than subject-disjoint time series. It also differs from *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention* [7], which found gains in vision tasks. The discrepancy may arise from the domain difference; time-series data may require more layer-specific flexibility than vision or text. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* [2] also reported inconclusive results for weight-based regularization in this setting, suggesting a broader pattern where weight geometry constraints do not translate to accuracy gains in this regime.

We do not claim that accuracy results evidence calibration. The outcome measure was held-out classification accuracy, and claims are restricted to this metric. The null result does not establish that cross-layer consistency is ineffective in all settings, only that it did not exceed the worthwhile margin here. Future work would need to measure attention stability directly to confirm the mechanistic hypothesis. Additionally, testing on different architectures or datasets would be required to assess generalization beyond this calibrated testbed. The findings suggest that for someone choosing between these methods in the UCI HAR setting, the added complexity of cross-layer consistency is not justified by accuracy gains.
Limitations: This study has several limitations regarding what the design can establish. First, the null result does not establish that cross-layer consistency is mechanistically ineffective; it only shows no accuracy gain. Attention stability remains an unmeasured hypothesis. We did not record attention maps, so we cannot confirm whether the weights were actually aligned or whether alignment would have mattered. Second, the generalization claim is limited to the UCI HAR dataset and the specific PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture used. We do not have evidence for larger models, different architecture families, or other time-series domains. The recipe pins one architecture at one size, so no comparison across scales exists in this experiment.

Third, the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds is a replication of the experimental run itself, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. While it controls for seed variance, it does not test robustness to distribution shift beyond the held-out subjects in UCI HAR. Finally, the worthwhile margin was derived from calibration noise, which reflects measurement precision but does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. A result excluding the margin under this uncertainty model does not guarantee the effect is zero, only that it is smaller than the target magnitude. These limitations constrain the scope of the conclusion to the specific testbed and outcome measure.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

Thinking Process:

1.  **Analyze the Request:**
    *   **Role:** Critical but fair peer reviewer of an AI-generated research paper.
    *   **Task:** Judge publishability as a small, honest study (Registered Report).
    *   **Decision Options:** ACCEPT, REVISE, REVISE-EXPERIMENT.
    *   **Key Constraints:**
        *   Check manuscript arm descriptions against registered conditions and measured activity.
        *   A randomized active negative control is not an inactive baseline; its outcome cannot establish that the harness is unbiased.
        *   Distinguish proposed mechanism from directly measured (parameter regularization != attention-map stability).
        *   Detaching a tensor in a penalty blocks that gradient only, not ordinary task-loss learning.
        *   Check power claims against supplied zero-null versus margin-success qualification.
        *   Preserve registered decisions (inconclusive is publishable).
        *   Never reject/downgrade because result is negative/null/small.
        *   Post-results review demands accurate reporting, citations, limitations, calibrated claims.
        *   Do not reopen approved design or create outcome-selected rerun.
        *   **Format:** EXACTLY `DECISION: <accept | revise | revise-experiment>` followed by `FEEDBACK: <one short paragraph of specific, actionable feedback>`.

    *   **Title/Abstract:** Tests cross-layer query consistency loss on UCI HAR (subject-disjoint). Results: Inconclusive (null effect).

From the perspective of network structure, we summarize the adaptations and modifications that have been made to Transformers in order to accommodate the challenges in time series analysis. From the perspective of applications, we categorize time series Transformers based on common tasks including forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification. Empirically, we perform robust analysis, model size analysis, and seasonal-trend decomposition analysis to study how Transformers perform in time series. Finally, we discuss and suggest future directions to provide useful research guidance. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first work to comprehensively and systematically summarize the recent advances of Transformers for modeling time series data. We hope this survey will ignite further research interests in time series Transformers.
[39] Brady Zhou, Philipp Krähenbühl. Cross-view Transformers for real-time Map-view Semantic Segmentation (2022).
    Abstract: We present cross-view transformers, an efficient attention-based model for map-view semantic segmentation from multiple cameras. Our architecture implicitly learns a mapping from individual camera views into a canonical map-view representation using a camera-aware cross-view attention mechanism. Each camera uses positional embeddings that depend on its intrinsic and extrinsic calibration. These embeddings allow a transformer to learn the mapping across different views without ever explicitly modeling it geometrically. The architecture consists of a convolutional image encoder for each view and cross-view transformer layers to infer a map-view semantic segmentation. Our model is simple, easily parallelizable, and runs in real-time. The presented architecture performs at state-of-the-art on the nuScenes dataset, with 4x faster inference speeds. Code is available at https://github.com/bradyz/cross_view_transformers.
[40] Liangrui Pan, Wenjuan Liu et al. CVFC: Attention-Based Cross-View Feature Consistency for Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation of Pathology Images (2023).
    Abstract: Histopathology image segmentation is the gold standard for diagnosing cancer, and can indicate cancer prognosis. However, histopathology image segmentation requires high-quality masks, so many studies now use image-level labels to achieve pixel-level segmentation to reduce the need for fine-grained annotation. To solve this problem, we propose an attention-based cross-view feature consistency end-to-end pseudo-mask generation framework named CVFC based on the attention mechanism. Specifically, CVFC is a three-branch joint framework composed of two Resnet38 and one Resnet50, and the independent branch multi-scale integrated feature map to generate a class activation map (CAM); in each branch, through down-sampling and The expansion method adjusts the size of the CAM; the middle branch projects the feature matrix to the query and key feature spaces, and generates a feature space perception matrix through the connection layer and inner product to adjust and refine the CAM of each branch; finally, through the feature consistency loss and feature cross loss to optimize the parameters of CVFC in co-training mode. After a large number of experiments, An IoU of 0.7122 and a fwIoU of 0.7018 are obtained on the WSSS4LUAD dataset, which outperforms HistoSegNet, SEAM, C-CAM, WSSS-Tissue, and OEEM, respectively.
[41] Tianyang Lin, Yuxin Wang et al. A survey of transformers (2022).
    Abstract: Transformers have achieved great success in many artificial intelligence fields, such as natural language processing, computer vision, and audio processing. Therefore, it is natural to attract lots of interest from academic and industry researchers. Up to the present, a great variety of Transformer variants (a.k.a. X-formers) have been proposed, however, a systematic and comprehensive literature review on these Transformer variants is still missing. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive review of various X-formers. We first briefly introduce the vanilla Transformer and then propose a new taxonomy of X-formers. Next, we introduce the various X-formers from three perspectives: architectural modification, pre-training, and applications. Finally, we outline some potential directions for future research.
[42] Joohyung Lee, Kwanhyung Lee et al. Structure-Aware Set Transformers: Temporal and Variable-Type Attention Biases for Asynchronous Clinical Time Series (2026).
    Abstract: Electronic health records (EHR) are irregular, asynchronous multivariate time series. As time-series foundation models increasingly tokenize events rather than discretizing time, the input layout becomes a key design choice. Grids expose time$\times$variable structure but require imputation or missingness masks, risking error or sampling-policy shortcuts. Point-set tokenization avoids discretization but loses within-variable trajectories and time-local cross-variable context (Fig.1). We restore these priors in STructure-AwaRe (STAR) Set Transformer by adding parameter-efficient soft attention biases: a temporal locality penalty $-|Δt|/τ$ with learnable timescales and a variable-type affinity $B_{s_i,s_j}$ from a learned feature-compatibility matrix. We benchmark 10 depth-wise fusion schedules (Fig.2). On three ICU prediction tasks, STAR-Set achieves AUC/APR of 0.7158/0.0026 (CPR), 0.9164/0.2033 (mortality), and 0.8373/0.1258 (vasopressor use), outperforming regular-grid, event-time grid, and prior set baselines. Learned $τ$ and $B$ provide interpretable summaries of temporal context and variable interactions, offering a practical plug-in for context-informed time-series models.

CITE numbered references in square brackets (e.g. [1] or [2, 3]); the Introduction and Related Work MUST cite them inline. You are NOT required to cite every reference; unused references are removed. NEVER cite a paper as evidence for something it does NOT discuss, including a gap in a different setting. State a gap WITHOUT a marker, use the reviewed gap statement, or cite an abstract that identifies that gap itself. Never attribute the opposite of what an abstract says. Stay INSIDE the abstract's own wording: use its terms, do not generalise them or add an unstated mechanism, domain or consequence. When the analysis contains primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts, report BOTH separately, state each preregistered decision, and never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. === abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% bootstrap confidence interval [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% bootstrap confidence interval [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [38]. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications [38]. However, the validity of this research line for time series forecasting and classification remains questioned, with simple linear models sometimes outperforming sophisticated Transformer-based solutions [5]. Recent breakthroughs have drawn significant attention to the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies, yet Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [32]. Specifically, tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones, and domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [22, 18].

The open problem this work addresses is what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. Despite proposed mechanisms, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. This work addresses this gap by testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling.

This paper reports a rigorous experiment testing the hypothesis that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization. We contribute the following:
- We execute a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency loss on a subject-disjoint time-series benchmark using a calibrated testbed.
- We report results from both a primary cohort and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, ensuring robustness against seed-specific variance.
- We provide inconclusive null results that clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra and consistency in finite-width networks under subject-disjoint evaluation.

The preregistered prediction states that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report honestly against this prediction, labeling any unforeseen finding as exploratory.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [38, 5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [20, 14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15]. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific cross-layer consistency loss in a subject-disjoint time-series setting, distinguishing training-seed replication from replication on new subjects or datasets.

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights during training. The hypothesis posits that stabilizing attention query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization. The operator adds a loss term computed as the squared element-wise difference between the target weights (block 1) and reference weights (block 0), scaled by a fixed coefficient. This expression directly tests whether aligning deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights yields accuracy gains over standard training.

The comparator neutralizes the intervention by executing the identical code path but returning a zero loss term. This control arm ensures that any observed contrast arises from the loss term itself rather than implementation artifacts or computational differences. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them.

The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. The operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients, ensuring the penalty flows only to the target parameters. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective. Mechanistic rationales regarding attention stability are hypotheses; the measured outcome is held-out classification accuracy.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

=== experimental_setup ===
The design employs a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization to unseen subjects, which a random split would not address. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance by ensuring both arms share identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters, isolating the effect of the loss term. This pairing allows for paired statistical tests rather than independent samples tests, increasing power to detect small effects.

The analysis includes a negative control that penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. This control's intended alternative explanation is that any compute-matching penalty might yield gains regardless of meaningful cross-layer relationship. Its observed contrast supports whether the specific cross-layer alignment matters versus generic regularization. The seed budget comprises 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. This budget supports the registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targeting rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin.

This is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, but a replication of the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline. We call it the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. The analysis computes 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for the mean differences. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance. The registered condition descriptions and executed activation records are authoritative: a baseline/no-op and an active negative control are different conditions. We describe only what the control manipulates; its outcome cannot prove that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct.

=== results ===
Figure 1 depicts the experimental flow from UCI HAR data through PreNormTransformerEncoder training with CrossLayerQueryConsistency at the loss term to subject-disjoint evaluation. It illustrates how the intervention modifies the training objective while evaluation remains on held-out windows from unseen subjects. In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% bootstrap confidence interval [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Table 1 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed (0.9062), baseline (0.9054), and negative control 1 (0.9051) conditions. Figure 2 visualizes these means with error bars representing the 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimate is printed above each bar; the axis starts at zero, so the bar lengths are comparable.

Figure 3 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. Points are the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Zero marks no directional effect. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold (0.0125098 proportion); support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it. The 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the preregistered decision was inconclusive. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% bootstrap confidence interval [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Table 3 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed (0.9055), baseline (0.9035), and negative control 1 (0.9043) conditions. Figure 5 visualizes these means for the replication cohort. Figure 6 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the preregistered decision was inconclusive. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin. Figure 4 and Figure 7 show the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. Conditions whose curves coincide are distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern as well as by colour.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. The results are inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. This suggests that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. The observed contrast supports that the specific cross-layer alignment does not matter versus generic regularization in this setting, as the negative control also showed no significant gain.

This design establishes that the intervention does not exceed the worthwhile margin under the stated uncertainty model. It does not establish that the effect is zero, only that the confidence intervals include zero. A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that attention patterns need to diverge across depth to capture hierarchical temporal features. An alternative is that the coefficient was too small to influence optimization meaningfully, though the registered coefficient was chosen to prevent dominating the classification objective. The independent replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not a fluke of a specific seed set; we call it the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds.

The finding stands against specific cited papers. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting and reported BLEU score increases [17], but that study focused on machine translation, not subject-disjoint time-series classification. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* also found inconclusive results in a subject-disjoint time-series setting [3], agreeing with our null finding. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34], but that work targets large language models and activation steering, not training-time weight regularization for time-series. *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32], which is consistent with our finding that architectural tweaks alone may not overcome generalization challenges.

What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks or whether larger models exhibit different behavior. However, claim about model scale or architecture family is untestable on this calibrated testbed: the recipe pins one arch. Future work should investigate whether attention stability is beneficial in domains with different temporal dynamics or sensor modalities.

=== limitations ===
Third, the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds is a replication of the experimental run itself, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. The study is limited to one architecture (PreNormTransformerEncoder) and one dataset (UCI HAR). Claim about model scale or architecture family ('larger models') is untestable on this calibrated testbed: the recipe pins one arch. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. The margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. Conformance and activation counts describe execution; they do not establish the mechanism or prove the absence of implementation bias.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The results were inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin, and confidence intervals included zero. For someone choosing between these methods, the findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. Future work should investigate whether attention stability is beneficial in domains with different temporal dynamics or sensor modalities to settle the question.

7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation

=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% bootstrap confidence interval [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% bootstrap confidence interval [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [38]. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications [38]. However, the validity of this research line for time series forecasting and classification remains questioned, with simple linear models sometimes outperforming sophisticated Transformer-based solutions [5]. Recent breakthroughs have drawn significant attention to the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies, yet Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [32]. Specifically, tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones, and domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [22, 18].

The open problem this work addresses is what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. Despite proposed mechanisms, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. This work addresses this gap by testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling.

This paper reports a rigorous experiment testing the hypothesis that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization. We contribute the following:
- We execute a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency loss on a subject-disjoint time-series benchmark using a calibrated testbed.
- We report results from both a primary cohort and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, ensuring robustness against seed-specific variance.
- We provide inconclusive null results that clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra and consistency in finite-width networks under subject-disjoint evaluation.

The preregistered prediction states that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report honestly against this prediction, labeling any unforeseen finding as exploratory.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [38, 5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [20, 14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15]. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific cross-layer consistency loss in a subject-disjoint time-series setting, distinguishing training-seed replication from replication on new subjects or datasets.

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights during training. The hypothesis posits that stabilizing attention query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization. The operator adds a loss term computed as the squared element-wise difference between the target weights (block 1) and reference weights (block 0), scaled by a fixed coefficient. This expression directly tests whether aligning deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights yields accuracy gains over standard training.

The comparator neutralizes the intervention by executing the identical code path but returning a zero loss term. This control arm ensures that any observed contrast arises from the loss term itself rather than implementation artifacts or computational differences. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them.

The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. The operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients, ensuring the penalty flows only to the target parameters. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective. Mechanistic rationales regarding attention stability are hypotheses; the measured outcome is held-out classification accuracy.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

=== experimental_setup ===
The design employs a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization to unseen subjects, which a random split would not address. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance by ensuring both arms share identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters, isolating the effect of the loss term. This pairing allows for paired statistical tests rather than independent samples tests, increasing power to detect small effects.

The analysis includes a negative control that penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. This control's intended alternative explanation is that any compute-matching penalty might yield gains regardless of meaningful cross-layer relationship. Its observed contrast supports whether the specific cross-layer alignment matters versus generic regularization. The seed budget comprises 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. This budget supports the registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targeting rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin.

This is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, but a replication of the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline. We call it the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. The analysis computes 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for the mean differences. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance. The registered condition descriptions and executed activation records are authoritative: a baseline/no-op and an active negative control are different conditions. We describe only what the control manipulates; its outcome cannot prove that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct.

=== results ===
Figure 1 depicts the experimental flow from UCI HAR data through PreNormTransformerEncoder training with CrossLayerQueryConsistency at the loss term to subject-disjoint evaluation. It illustrates how the intervention modifies the training objective while evaluation remains on held-out windows from unseen subjects. In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% bootstrap confidence interval [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Table 1 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed (0.9062), baseline (0.9054), and negative control 1 (0.9051) conditions. Figure 2 visualizes these means with error bars representing the 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimate is printed above each bar; the axis starts at zero, so the bar lengths are comparable.

Figure 3 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. Points are the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Zero marks no directional effect. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold (0.0125098 proportion); support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it. The 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the preregistered decision was inconclusive. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% bootstrap confidence interval [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Table 3 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed (0.9055), baseline (0.9035), and negative control 1 (0.9043) conditions. Figure 5 visualizes these means for the replication cohort. Figure 6 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the preregistered decision was inconclusive. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin. Figure 4 and Figure 7 show the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. Conditions whose curves coincide are distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern as well as by colour.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. The results are inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. This suggests that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. The observed contrast supports that the specific cross-layer alignment does not matter versus generic regularization in this setting, as the negative control also showed no significant gain.

This design establishes that the intervention does not exceed the worthwhile margin under the stated uncertainty model. It does not establish that the effect is zero, only that the confidence intervals include zero. A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that attention patterns need to diverge across depth to capture hierarchical temporal features. An alternative is that the coefficient was too small to influence optimization meaningfully, though the registered coefficient was chosen to prevent dominating the classification objective. The independent replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not a fluke of a specific seed set; we call it the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds.

The finding stands against specific cited papers. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting and reported BLEU score increases [17], but that study focused on machine translation, not subject-disjoint time-series classification. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* also found inconclusive results in a subject-disjoint time-series setting [3], agreeing with our null finding. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34], but that work targets large language models and activation steering, not training-time weight regularization for time-series. *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32], which is consistent with our finding that architectural tweaks alone may not overcome generalization challenges.

What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks or whether larger models exhibit different behavior. However, claim about model scale or architecture family is untestable on this calibrated testbed: the recipe pins one arch. Future work should investigate whether attention stability is beneficial in domains with different temporal dynamics or sensor modalities.

=== limitations ===
Third, the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds is a replication of the experimental run itself, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. The study is limited to one architecture (PreNormTransformerEncoder) and one dataset (UCI HAR). Claim about model scale or architecture family ('larger models') is untestable on this calibrated testbed: the recipe pins one arch. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. The margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. Conformance and activation counts describe execution; they do not establish the mechanism or prove the absence of implementation bias.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The results were inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin, and confidence intervals included zero. For someone choosing between these methods, the findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. Future work should investigate whether attention stability is beneficial in domains with different temporal dynamics or sensor modalities to settle the question.
