=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0007734 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.001957 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
**The Problem of Subject-Disjoint Generalization.** Time-series classification in biomedical and wearable contexts often requires models to generalize across individuals with distinct movement styles, sensor placements, and execution speeds. Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [38]. However, their effectiveness in subject-disjoint settings remains uncertain [5]. Standard architectures assume that attention mechanisms learned from one set of subjects transfer effectively to unseen subjects, yet this assumption lacks rigorous verification regarding the stability of attention patterns across network depth. If deeper layers refine attention patterns significantly differently from shallower layers, the model may overfit to subject-specific noise rather than learning invariant temporal features.

**Gap in Current Literature.** Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs [14]. To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. However, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. Existing studies often test on random splits or single seeds, leaving the robustness of such architectural biases unsettled [1].

**This Study.** This paper reports a preregistered experiment testing whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. We address the lack of verification by running a calibrated testbed with paired seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. We test if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling.

**Contributions.**
- We execute a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency loss on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset using an official subject-disjoint split.
- We report results from both a primary cohort (43 seeds) and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds (43 seeds), ensuring robustness against seed-specific variance.
- We provide inconclusive evidence regarding the efficacy of cross-layer consistency for subject-disjoint generalization in this regime, clarifying the boundary conditions for this architectural bias.

**Preregistered Prediction.** The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
**Transformers in Time-Series Analysis.** Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14, 20]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32]. These works establish that while Transformers are widely applied, their generalization mechanisms in time-series domains are not fully understood.

**Consistency Regularization and Cross-Layer Mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15]. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering, grounded in the geometric stability of the network's representation evolution [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it, highlighting the risk of implementation errors in such studies [2].

**Attention Mechanisms and Architectures.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* and *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* document the application of Transformers specifically in computer vision [11, 21]. *A survey of transformers* documents the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific cross-layer consistency intervention in a subject-disjoint time-series setting, distinct from the vision or language domains where many of these mechanisms were originally validated.

=== method ===
**Operator Specification.** The core intervention is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator applied to the query projection weights of the second attention block (`blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight`). The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent. The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step; the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated. The scope is the full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space. The ordering is element-wise subtraction then sum, which is order-invariant due to commutativity of addition. There is no normalization; the raw Frobenius norm squared is scaled by a fixed coefficient. Numerical safeguards include a coefficient of 0.01 to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective.

**Hypothesis Expression.** The hypothesis is that enforcing consistency between the query projection weights of the first and second attention blocks will stabilize attention patterns across depth, thereby improving generalization to unseen subjects. This is expressed as a regularization term added to the training objective. The reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients, ensuring the penalty only affects the target parameters in block 1. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds. This design isolates the effect of weight alignment from other training dynamics.

**Comparator and Controls.** The baseline condition is a control arm defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. This ensures any observed difference is attributable to the loss term itself.

**Negative Control.** A negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix (same shape/norm as block 0), destroying meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This control tests whether the mere presence of a regularization term, regardless of its semantic content, drives any observed effects. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, it suggests the specific cross-layer relationship matters. If both perform similarly, the effect may be due to regularization generally.

**Algorithm 1.**
1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

=== experimental_setup ===
**Subject-Disjoint Split Justification.** The experiment uses the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset with an official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. A subject-disjoint split answers the question of generalization to unseen individuals, whereas a random split would allow the model to memorize subject-specific features. This design choice is critical because the research question targets architectural inductive biases that enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution.

**Seed Pairing and Replication.** All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. We used 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance due to initialization and data ordering, increasing the power to detect small effects. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds replicates the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline. This is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, but a replication of the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline. This distinction is crucial: it tests the stability of the result under fresh sampling within the same domain, not generalization to new domains.

**Negative Control Purpose.** The first negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any regularization term, regardless of its semantic content, might improve generalization by simply constraining the weights. Its observed contrast supports or refutes the claim that the specific cross-layer relationship is necessary. If the proposed condition does not outperform the negative control, the specific alignment of query weights is not the active ingredient. The seed budget and analysis were planned to achieve 90% power to detect an effect equal to the registered margin, though the registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin, not the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort Accuracy.** Figure 1 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Bars are means over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]). The baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The negative control 1 achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 3 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for these conditions, where curves coincide and are distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern.

**Primary Cohort Contrast.** Figure 2 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. Points are the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The green dash-dot marker in Figure 2 shows the registered worthwhile threshold (0.0125098 proportion); support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it. The lower bound (-0.00271) does not exceed the threshold. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

**Replication Cohort Accuracy.** Figure 4 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.909]). The baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.907]). The negative control 1 achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.908]). Figure 6 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for these conditions in the replication cohort.

**Replication Cohort Contrast.** Figure 5 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). The 95% CI includes zero. The lower bound (-0.00196) does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Table 1 summarizes the primary cohort means and CIs. Table 2 summarizes the primary cohort outcome contrasts. Table 3 summarizes the replication cohort means and CIs. Table 4 summarizes the replication cohort outcome contrasts. Table 5 compares the means across both cohorts.

**Summary of Findings.** In both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, the proposed condition did not yield a statistically significant improvement over the baseline. The confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive regarding the hypothesis that cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in this regime.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not yield robust accuracy gains in the UCI HAR subject-disjoint setting. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This suggests that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class in this domain. The intervention did not harm performance, but it did not provide the predicted benefit.

**Interpretation of Mechanism.** Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings. The hypothesis was that stabilizing attention patterns across depth would improve generalization. The observed null result is consistent with the alternative that deeper layers need to learn distinct attention patterns to capture progressively refined temporal features. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment; the intervention regularized weights, not the resulting attention distributions. It is possible that weight consistency does not translate to functional consistency in the attention maps, or that the regularization coefficient (0.01) was insufficient to enforce meaningful alignment without degrading task performance. The negative control results (0.9051 in primary, 0.9043 in replication) were similar to the baseline, suggesting that the mere presence of a regularization term did not drive effects.

**Comparison to Literature.** These findings stand in contrast to works that report benefits from consistency regularization in other domains. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data, but our results suggest this may not apply to subject-disjoint time-series tasks with this specific intervention [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, but our subject-disjoint gap may differ from the domain gaps in vision segmentation [18]. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering, but our weight-based intervention may not capture the same geometric stability [34]. Surveys such as *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio, but our results highlight that mechanisms successful in those domains do not automatically transfer to subject-disjoint time-series classification [41].

**Replication Cohort Contribution.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not a fluke of a specific seed set. However, we clarify this is the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. The consistency of the inconclusive result across both cohorts strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if it exists, is smaller than the registered margin.

**Future Directions.** What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks or whether a different formulation (e.g., attention-map consistency rather than weight consistency) yields benefits. Additionally, testing with larger models or different regularization coefficients might reveal boundary conditions where this bias becomes useful.

=== limitations ===
**Design Constraints.** This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency would work in a different data regime, such as with more training data or a larger model architecture. The fixed testbed scope (2-block transformer, 64 hidden) limits generalizability to deeper or wider networks. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds replicates the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. Therefore, we cannot claim the result holds for other time-series domains or sensor modalities.

**Measurement Precision.** A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient. We preserved the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

**Mechanistic Inference.** We did not directly measure attention stability or feature learning; we inferred these from accuracy contrasts. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. Conformance and activation counts describe execution; they do not establish the mechanism or prove the absence of implementation bias.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. We found inconclusive evidence in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. The proposed condition did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin, and confidence intervals included zero. For someone choosing between these methods, the results suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential. Future work should test whether attention-map consistency or different regularization strengths settle the question in broader settings.

=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0007734 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.001957 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
**The Problem of Subject-Disjoint Generalization.** Time-series classification in biomedical and wearable contexts often requires models to generalize across individuals with distinct movement styles, sensor placements, and execution speeds. Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [38]. However, their effectiveness in subject-disjoint settings remains uncertain [5]. Standard architectures assume that attention mechanisms learned from one set of subjects transfer effectively to unseen subjects, yet this assumption lacks rigorous verification regarding the stability of attention patterns across network depth. If deeper layers refine attention patterns significantly differently from shallower layers, the model may overfit to subject-specific noise rather than learning invariant temporal features.

**Gap in Current Literature.** Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs [14]. To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. However, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. Existing studies often test on random splits or single seeds, leaving the robustness of such architectural biases unsettled [1].

**This Study.** This paper reports a preregistered experiment testing whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. We address the lack of verification by running a calibrated testbed with paired seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. We test if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling.

**Contributions.**
- We execute a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency loss on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset using an official subject-disjoint split.
- We report results from both a primary cohort (43 seeds) and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds (43 seeds), ensuring robustness against seed-specific variance.
- We provide inconclusive evidence regarding the efficacy of cross-layer consistency for subject-disjoint generalization in this regime, clarifying the boundary conditions for this architectural bias.

**Preregistered Prediction.** The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
**Transformers in Time-Series Analysis.** Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14, 20]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32]. These works establish that while Transformers are widely applied, their generalization mechanisms in time-series domains are not fully understood.

**Consistency Regularization and Cross-Layer Mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15]. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering, grounded in the geometric stability of the network's representation evolution [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it, highlighting the risk of implementation errors in such studies [2].

**Attention Mechanisms and Architectures.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* and *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* document the application of Transformers specifically in computer vision [11, 21]. *A survey of transformers* documents the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific cross-layer consistency intervention in a subject-disjoint time-series setting, distinct from the vision or language domains where many of these mechanisms were originally validated.

=== method ===
**Operator Specification.** The core intervention is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator applied to the query projection weights of the second attention block (`blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight`). The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent. The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step; the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated. The scope is the full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space. The ordering is element-wise subtraction then sum, which is order-invariant due to commutativity of addition. There is no normalization; the raw Frobenius norm squared is scaled by a fixed coefficient. Numerical safeguards include a coefficient of 0.01 to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective.

**Hypothesis Expression.** The hypothesis is that enforcing consistency between the query projection weights of the first and second attention blocks will stabilize attention patterns across depth, thereby improving generalization to unseen subjects. This is expressed as a regularization term added to the training objective. The reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients, ensuring the penalty only affects the target parameters in block 1. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds. This design isolates the effect of weight alignment from other training dynamics.

**Comparator and Controls.** The baseline condition is a control arm defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. This ensures any observed difference is attributable to the loss term itself.

**Negative Control.** A negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix (same shape/norm as block 0), destroying meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This control tests whether the mere presence of a regularization term, regardless of its semantic content, drives any observed effects. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, it suggests the specific cross-layer relationship matters. If both perform similarly, the effect may be due to regularization generally.

**Algorithm 1.**
1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

=== experimental_setup ===
**Subject-Disjoint Split Justification.** The experiment uses the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset with an official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. A subject-disjoint split answers the question of generalization to unseen individuals, whereas a random split would allow the model to memorize subject-specific features. This design choice is critical because the research question targets architectural inductive biases that enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution.

**Seed Pairing and Replication.** All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. We used 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance due to initialization and data ordering, increasing the power to detect small effects. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds replicates the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline. This is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, but a replication of the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline. This distinction is crucial: it tests the stability of the result under fresh sampling within the same domain, not generalization to new domains.

**Negative Control Purpose.** The first negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any regularization term, regardless of its semantic content, might improve generalization by simply constraining the weights. Its observed contrast supports or refutes the claim that the specific cross-layer relationship is necessary. If the proposed condition does not outperform the negative control, the specific alignment of query weights is not the active ingredient. The seed budget and analysis were planned to achieve 90% power to detect an effect equal to the registered margin, though the registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin, not the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort Accuracy.** Figure 1 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Bars are means over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]). The baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The negative control 1 achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 3 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for these conditions, where curves coincide and are distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern.

**Primary Cohort Contrast.** Figure 2 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. Points are the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The green dash-dot marker in Figure 2 shows the registered worthwhile threshold (0.0125098 proportion); support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it. The lower bound (-0.00271) does not exceed the threshold. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

**Replication Cohort Accuracy.** Figure 4 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.909]). The baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.907]). The negative control 1 achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.908]). Figure 6 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for these conditions in the replication cohort.

**Replication Cohort Contrast.** Figure 5 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). The 95% CI includes zero. The lower bound (-0.00196) does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Table 1 summarizes the primary cohort means and CIs. Table 2 summarizes the primary cohort outcome contrasts. Table 3 summarizes the replication cohort means and CIs. Table 4 summarizes the replication cohort outcome contrasts. Table 5 compares the means across both cohorts.

**Summary of Findings.** In both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, the proposed condition did not yield a statistically significant improvement over the baseline. The confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive regarding the hypothesis that cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in this regime.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not yield robust accuracy gains in the UCI HAR subject-disjoint setting. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This suggests that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class in this domain. The intervention did not harm performance, but it did not provide the predicted benefit.

**Interpretation of Mechanism.** Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings. The hypothesis was that stabilizing attention patterns across depth would improve generalization. The observed null result is consistent with the alternative that deeper layers need to learn distinct attention patterns to capture progressively refined temporal features. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment; the intervention regularized weights, not the resulting attention distributions. It is possible that weight consistency does not translate to functional consistency in the attention maps, or that the regularization coefficient (0.01) was insufficient to enforce meaningful alignment without degrading task performance. The negative control results (0.9051 in primary, 0.9043 in replication) were similar to the baseline, suggesting that the mere presence of a regularization term did not drive effects.

**Comparison to Literature.** These findings stand in contrast to works that report benefits from consistency regularization in other domains. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data, but our results suggest this may not apply to subject-disjoint time-series tasks with this specific intervention [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, but our subject-disjoint gap may differ from the domain gaps in vision segmentation [18]. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering, but our weight-based intervention may not capture the same geometric stability [34]. Surveys such as *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio, but our results highlight that mechanisms successful in those domains do not automatically transfer to subject-disjoint time-series classification [41].

**Replication Cohort Contribution.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not a fluke of a specific seed set. However, we clarify this is the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. The consistency of the inconclusive result across both cohorts strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if it exists, is smaller than the registered margin.

**Future Directions.** What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks or whether a different formulation (e.g., attention-map consistency rather than weight consistency) yields benefits. Additionally, testing with larger models or different regularization coefficients might reveal boundary conditions where this bias becomes useful.

=== limitations ===
**Design Constraints.** This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency would work in a different data regime, such as with more training data or a larger model architecture. The fixed testbed scope (2-block transformer, 64 hidden) limits generalizability to deeper or wider networks. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds replicates the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. Therefore, we cannot claim the result holds for other time-series domains or sensor modalities.

**Measurement Precision.** A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient. We preserved the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

**Mechanistic Inference.** We did not directly measure attention stability or feature learning; we inferred these from accuracy contrasts. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. Conformance and activation counts describe execution; they do not establish the mechanism or prove the absence of implementation bias.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. We found inconclusive evidence in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. The proposed condition did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin, and confidence intervals included zero. For someone choosing between these methods, the results suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential. Future work should test whether attention-map consistency or different regularization strengths settle the question in broader settings.

Related-work section:
**Transformers in Time-Series Analysis.** Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14, 20]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32]. These works establish that while Transformers are widely applied, their generalization mechanisms in time-series domains are not fully understood.

**Consistency Regularization and Cross-Layer Mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15]. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering, grounded in the geometric stability of the network's representation evolution [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it, highlighting the risk of implementation errors in such studies [2].

**Attention Mechanisms and Architectures.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* and *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* document the application of Transformers specifically in computer vision [11, 21]. *A survey of transformers* documents the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific cross-layer consistency intervention in a subject-disjoint time-series setting, distinct from the vision or language domains where many of these mechanisms were originally validated.

In this work, we propose a double consistency regularization (DOCR) method for the end-to-end model structure, which separately constrains the output of the encoder and decoder during the training process to alleviate the above problems. Specifically, on the basis of the cross-entropy loss function, we build the mean model by integrating the model parameters of the previous rounds and measure the consistency between the models by calculating the KL divergence between the features of the encoder output and the probability distribution of the decoder output of the mean model and the base model so as to impose regularization constraints on the solution space of the model. We conducted extensive experiments on machine translation tasks, and the results show that the BLEU score increased by 2.60 on average, demonstrating the effectiveness of DOCR in improving model performance and its complementary impacts with other regularization techniques.

Specifically, we impose consistency between predictions from cross-domain attention and self-attention modules to encourage similar distributions across domains in both the attention and output of the model, i.e., attention-level and output-level alignment. We also enforce consistency in attention maps between different augmented views to further strengthen the attention-based alignment. Combining these two components, CDAC mitigates the discrepancy in attention maps across domains and further boosts the performance of the transformer under unsupervised domain adaptation settings. Our method is evaluated on various widely used benchmarks and outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines, including GTAV-to-Cityscapes by 1.3 and 1.5 percent point (pp) and Synthia-to-Cityscapes by 0.6 pp and 2.9 pp when combining with two competitive Transformer-based backbones, respectively. We evaluate ABN on several image recognition tasks such as image classification, fine-grained recognition, and multiple facial attribute recognition. Experimental results indicate that ABN outperforms the baseline models on these image recognition tasks while generating an attention map for visual explanation. Our code is available.

This enables LPTM to perform similar to or better than domain-specific state-of-art model when fine-tuned to different downstream time-series analysis tasks and under zero-shot settings. LPTM achieves superior forecasting and time-series classification results taking up to 40% less data and 50% less training time compared to state-of-art baselines.

To overcome the above limitations, this paper proposes a novel end-to-end learning model, called cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network (CLFETNet), for remote sensing scene classification. Firstly, we utilize the FPN to extract multi-scale features and design a fine feature aggregation module (RFA) to integrate complementary information from different layers to obtain more reliable and accurate features. Second, the efficient frequency transformer (EFT) is proposed to deeply mine global information, local spatial features, and edge detail information. Finally, the graph-aware fusion (GAF) module is proposed to model the relationships among […abstract truncated here]

Abstract: Analyzing inter-individual variability of physiological functions is particularly appealing in medical and biological contexts to describe or quantify health conditions. Once the deformations and the reference time series are learned, the vector representations of individual time series are given by the parametrization of their corresponding deformation. At the crossroads between URL for time series and shape analysis, the proposed algorithm handles irregularly sampled multivariate time series of variable lengths and provides shape-based representations of temporal data.In this work, we establish a representation theorem for the graph of a time series and derive its consequences on the LDDMM framework. By constraining features from the same location to be closer than those from different ones, it implicitly ensures the result to take content from the source. However, previous work uses the features from random locations to impose the constraint, which may not be appropriate since some locations contain less information of source domain. Moreover, the feature itself does not reflect the relation with others. This paper deals with these problems by intentionally selecting significant anchor points for contrastive learning. We design a query-selected attention (QS-Attn) module, which compares feature distances in the source domain, giving an attention matrix with a probability distribution in each row. Then we select queries according to their measurement of significance, computed from the distribution. The selected ones are regarded as anchors for contrastive loss. At the same time, the reduced attention matrix is employed to route features in both domains, so that source relations maintain in the synthesis. Abstract: The discovery of knowledge by analyzing time series is an important field of research. In this paper we investigate multiple multivariate time series, because we assume a higher information value than regarding only one time series at a time. There are several approaches which make use of the granger causality or the cross correlation in order to analyze the influence of time series on each other. In this paper we extend the idea of mutual influence and present FCSETS (Fuzzy Clustering Stability Evaluation of Time Series), a new approach which makes use of the membership degree produced by the fuzzy c-means (FCM) algorithm. We first cluster time series per timestamp and then compare the relative assignment agreement (introduced by Eyke Hüllermeier and Maria Rifqi) of all subsequences. This leads us to a stability score for every time series which itself can be used to evaluate single time series in the data set. It is then used to rate the stability of the entire clustering. The stability score of a time series is higher the more the time series sticks to its peers over time. This not only reveals a new idea of mutual time series impact but also enables the identification of an optimal amount of clusters per timestamp. We applied our model on different data, such as financial, country related economy and generated data, and present the results.

Conducted on a variety of applications, the study yields significant findings about spatial attention in deep networks, some of which run counter to conventional understanding. For example, we find that the query and key content comparison in Transformer attention is negligible for self-attention, but vital for encoder-decoder attention. A proper combination of deformable convolution with key content only saliency achieves the best accuracy-efficiency tradeoff in self-attention. Our results suggest that there exists much room for improvement in the design of attention mechanisms.

The second improves the eﬃciency of cross-encoders by deactivating the attention between various sub-sequences, such as between query and document tokens. The third improves the eﬀectiveness of cross-encoders by allowing multiple documents to attend to one another via an additional interaction token. Our analyses show that our attention adaptations lead to substantial eﬀectiveness and eﬃciency improvements. In addition, we introduce two resources that simplify ﬁne-tuning and evaluating bi-encoders and cross-encoders. The ﬁrst is LightningIR, a framework that uniﬁes the implementation of various model variants, and the second is Rank-DistiLLM, a set of high-quality distillation datasets for ﬁne-tuning. Abstract: The computational burden of attention in long-context language models has motivated two largely independent lines of work: sparse attention mechanisms that reduce complexity by attending to selected tokens, and gated attention variants that improve training sta-bility while mitigating the attention sink phenomenon. GSA incorporates a gated lightning indexer with sigmoid activations that produce bounded, interpretable selection scores, an adaptive sparsity controller that modulates the number of attended tokens based on local uncertainty, and dual gating at the value and output stages. We establish theoretical foundations for the approach, including complexity analysis, expressiveness results, and convergence guarantees. In experiments with 1.7B parameter models trained on 400B tokens, GSA matches the efficiency of sparse-only baselines (12-16x speedup at 128K context) while achieving the quality gains associated with gated attention: perplexity improves from 6.03 to 5.70, RULER scores at 128K context nearly double, and attention to the first token, a proxy for attention sinks, drops from 47% to under 4%. Training stability improves markedly, with loss spikes reduced by 98%.

[31] Time-Series Forecasting
Abstract: From the author of the bestselling "Analysis of Time Series," Time-Series Forecasting offers a comprehensive, up-to-date review of forecasting methods. It provides a summary of time-series modelling procedures, followed by a brief catalogue of many different time-series forecasting methods, ranging from ad-hoc methods through ARIMA and state-space

[32] Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning
Abstract: The recent breakthrough of Transformers in deep learning has drawn significant attention of the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies. However, like other deep learning models, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding, generalization challenges, and data shift issues for the domains with limited data. Additionally, addressing the issue of catastrophic forgetting, where models forget previously learned information when exposed to new data, is another critical aspect that requires attention in enhancing the robustness of Transformers for time series tasks. To address these limitations, in this paper, we pre-train the time series Transformer model on a source domain with sufficient data and fine-tune it on the target domain with limited data. We introduce the \emph{One-step fine-tuning} approach, adding some percentage of source domain data to the target domains, providing the model with diverse time series instances. We then fine-tune the pre-trained model using a gradual unfreezing technique. This helps enhance the model's performance in time series prediction for domains with limited data. Extensive experimental results on two real-world datasets show that our approach improves over the state-of-the-art baselines by 4.35% and 11.54% for indoor temperature and wind power prediction, respectively.

Abstract: Attention mechanisms, especially self-attention, have played an increasingly important role in deep feature representation for visual tasks. Self-attention updates the feature at each position by computing a weighted sum of features using pair-wise affinities across all positions to capture the long-range dependency within a single sample. However, self-attention has quadratic complexity and ignores potential correlation between different samples. This article proposes a novel attention mechanism which we call external attention, based on two external, small, learnable, shared memories, which can be implemented easily by simply using two cascaded linear layers and two normalization layers; it conveniently replaces self-attention in existing popular architectures. External attention has linear complexity and implicitly considers the correlations between all data samples. We further incorporate the multi-head mechanism into external attention to provide an all-MLP architecture, external attention MLP (EAMLP), for image classification. Extensive experiments on image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, image generation, and point cloud analysis reveal that our method provides results comparable or superior to the self-attention mechanism and some of its variants, with much lower computational and memory costs.

[34] Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency
Abstract: Activation engineering enables precise control over Large Language Models (LLMs) without the computational cost of fine-tuning. However, existing methods deriving vectors from static activation differences are susceptible to high-dimensional noise and layer-wise semantic drift, often capturing spurious correlations rather than the target intent. To address this, we propose Global Evolutionary Refined Steering (GER-steer), a training-free framework that grounded in the geometric stability of the network's representation evolution. GER-steer exploits this global signal to rectify raw steering vectors, effectively decoupling robust semantic intent from orthogonal artifacts. Extensive evaluations confirm that GER-steer consistently outperforms baselines, delivering superior efficacy and generalization without layer-specific tuning, establishing a universal solution for reliable model alignment.

Abstract: The Probabilistic Transformer (PT) establishes that the Transformer's self-attention plus its feed-forward block is mathematically equivalent to Mean-Field Variational Inference (MFVI) on a Conditional Random Field (CRF). We first lift PT into the Spatial-Temporal Probabilistic Transformer (ST-PT) to repair PT's missing channel axis and weak per-step semantics, and adopt ST-PT as a shared cornerstone backbone. We then identify three distinct properties that PT/ST-PT offers as a factor-graph model and derive three Research Questions, one per property, that probe how each property can be exploited in time series: RQ1. The graph topology and potentials are direct programmable primitives. Can this be used to inject symbolic time-series priors into ST-PT through structural graph modifications, especially under data scarcity and noise? RQ2. The CRF's factor matrices are the operator's potentials. Can an external condition program these factor matrices on a per-sample basis, so that conditional generation becomes structural rather than feature-level modulation of a fixed one? RQ3. [36] Research on sentiment analysis model improved based on Transformer attention mechanism
Abstract: In response to the limitations of traditional sentiment analysis models, this paper proposes an improved sentiment analysis model based on Transformer attention mechanism. This model enhances contextual semantic modeling capability by optimizing self attention and multi head attention mechanisms; Increase the number of multi head attention heads in the BERT architecture from 12 to 16 to capture multi-level emotional features; Introducing dynamic position encoding to enhance modeling of long-distance dependencies. At the same time, adjusting the learning rate to 3e-5 and combining it with data augmentation can improve the stability and generalization ability of the model. The experiment on the 33396 McDonald's review dataset showed that the accuracy, recall, and F1 score of the improved model on the test set were 78%, 75%, and 76.5%, respectively; Improved to 85%, 82%, and 83.5%. This model effectively handles multidimensional emotional expression and domain specific language. Although its interpretability needs improvement, it provides a new path for the field of sentiment analysis and has important value in scenarios such as public opinion monitoring.

We introduce Depth-Attention, which performs this selection inside the attention module itself: before a layer attends over the sequence, its query attends over the keys of earlier layers at the same token position and mixes their values into the value that self-attention then reads. Because Depth-Attention reuses the standard attention queries, keys, and value-cache slots, storing depth-mixed values in place of the original values, it adds no parameters and introduces no persistent inference state beyond the standard key-value cache--the same cache size as a vanilla decoder and less than hidden-state-based cross-layer methods. On Qwen3-style decoders at 1.5B and 3B parameters, Depth-Attention attains the lowest perplexity and the highest average downstream accuracy, improving over the vanilla Transformer by up to 2.3 accuracy points and surpassing strong cross-layer baselines in perplexity and average accuracy, while adding under 0.01% extra arithmetic FLOPs and no additional persistent inference state. [38] Transformers in Time Series: A Survey
Abstract: Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications. In this paper, we systematically review Transformer schemes for time series modeling by highlighting their strengths as well as limitations. In particular, we examine the development of time series Transformers in two perspectives. From the perspective of network structure, we summarize the adaptations and modifications that have been made to Transformers in order to accommodate the challenges in time series analysis. From the perspective of applications, we categorize time series Transformers based on common tasks including forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification. Empirically, we perform robust analysis, model size analysis, and seasonal-trend decomposition analysis to study how Transformers perform in time series. Finally, we discuss and suggest future directions to provide useful research guidance. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first work to comprehensively and systematically summarize the recent advances of Transformers for modeling time series data. We hope this survey will ignite further research interests in time series Transformers.

[39] Cross-view Transformers for real-time Map-view Semantic Segmentation
Abstract: We present cross-view transformers, an efficient attention-based model for map-view semantic segmentation from multiple cameras. Our architecture implicitly learns a mapping from individual camera views into a canonical map-view representation using a camera-aware cross-view attention mechanism. Each camera uses positional embeddings that depend on its intrinsic and extrinsic calibration. These embeddings allow a transformer to learn the mapping across different views without ever explicitly modeling it geometrically. The architecture consists of a convolutional image encoder for each view and cross-view transformer layers to infer a map-view semantic segmentation. Our model is simple, easily parallelizable, and runs in real-time. The presented architecture performs at state-of-the-art on the nuScenes dataset, with 4x faster inference speeds. Code is available at https://github.com/bradyz/cross_view_transformers.

[41] A survey of transformers
Abstract: Transformers have achieved great success in many artificial intelligence fields, such as natural language processing, computer vision, and audio processing. Therefore, it is natural to attract lots of interest from academic and industry researchers. Up to the present, a great variety of Transformer variants (a.k.a. X-formers) have been proposed, however, a systematic and comprehensive literature review on these Transformer variants is still missing. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive review of various X-formers. We first briefly introduce the vanilla Transformer and then propose a new taxonomy of X-formers. Next, we introduce the various X-formers from three perspectives: architectural modification, pre-training, and applications. Finally, we outline some potential directions for future research.

We restore these priors in STructure-AwaRe (STAR) Set Transformer by adding parameter-efficient soft attention biases: a temporal locality penalty $-|Δt|/τ$ with learnable timescales and a variable-type affinity $B_{s_i,s_j}$ from a learned feature-compatibility matrix. We benchmark 10 depth-wise fusion schedules (Fig.2). On three ICU prediction tasks, STAR-Set achieves AUC/APR of 0.7158/0.0026 (CPR), 0.9164/0.2033 (mortality), and 0.8373/0.1258 (vasopressor use), outperforming regular-grid, event-time grid, and prior set baselines. Learned $τ$ and $B$ provide interpretable summaries of temporal context and variable interactions, offering a practical plug-in for context-informed time-series models.

Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0007734 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.001957 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.
