=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Deep learning models for time-series analysis face a persistent challenge: learning representations that generalize across subjects with distinct movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Transformers have become prominent in this domain due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [38]. However, their effectiveness in subject-disjoint settings remains uncertain, with some evidence suggesting simpler linear models may outperform complex attention mechanisms on certain forecasting tasks [5]. The core open problem is identifying which architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that transfer to unseen subjects. Specifically, it is unclear whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined attention patterns or consistently stable ones to support generalization.

This uncertainty matters because answering it clarifies the design space for out-of-distribution time-series tasks. If cross-layer consistency improves generalization, it would justify testing whether this bias transfers to other subject-disjoint benchmarks. Conversely, if layer-specific adaptation is essential, efforts to enforce stability across depth may hinder performance. Current literature lacks independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. While consistency regularization has been explored in other contexts [17], its application to cross-layer query projections in time-series transformers remains untested under rigorous subject-disjoint conditions.

This paper addresses this gap by executing a preregistered experiment testing the hypothesis that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization. We implement a CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator that regularizes deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights. We compare this intervention against a baseline control and a negative control that destroys meaningful cross-layer relationships. The study utilizes the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split to ensure evaluation on unseen subjects.

Our contributions are as follows:
- We execute a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency loss in a time-series transformer, reporting both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts.
- We provide exact quantitative estimates of the effect on held-out classification accuracy, including confidence intervals and effect sizes, rather than binary significance claims.
- We distinguish between training-seed replication on the same held-out split and replication on new subjects, clarifying the scope of the generalization claim.

The preregistered prediction states that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report the results honestly against this prediction, labeling any unforeseen finding as exploratory.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [38], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [11], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [21], and *A survey of transformers* [41] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28].

This study positions itself against these themes by isolating the specific effect of cross-layer query weight consistency on subject-disjoint generalization. Unlike works that focus on domain adaptation [18] or activation steering [34], we test a weight-space regularization during training. Unlike surveys that catalog architectures [11, 21, 41], we provide empirical evidence on a specific inductive bias. The unsettled question is whether weight alignment across layers aids generalization in time-series transformers, a gap this experiment addresses directly.

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces similarity between query projection weights across transformer blocks. The hypothesis is that stabilizing attention patterns across depth improves generalization to unseen subjects. The operator targets the query projection weight matrix of the second attention block, regularizing it toward the corresponding weights of the first block. This expression of the hypothesis assumes that consistent query projections facilitate more robust temporal feature extraction across varying subject dynamics.

The operator is applied during the loss computation of every optimization step. Its term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, ensuring the combined objective is differentiated. The scope is the full weight matrix of dimensions 64 by 64 treated as flat parameter space. The operation computes the element-wise subtraction between the target weights and the reference weights, squares the differences, and sums them to produce a raw loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed coefficient of 0.01 before being added to the training objective. Reference weights from the first block are detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients from flowing to them, ensuring the regularization is one-directional.

The comparator neutralizes the intervention's specific effect while maintaining the computational path. The baseline control arm executes identical code but returns a zero loss term. This ensures that any difference in outcome is attributable to the regularization term itself, not to implementation artifacts or computational overhead. The harness records operator activity for every seed and condition, refusing results where the control arm acted at any registered point. This guarantees the control's recorded activity is zero.

A negative control condition penalizes the difference between the second block's weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as the first block's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the compute and regularization magnitude. If the proposed condition outperforms this negative control, it suggests the specific cross-layer relationship matters, not just the presence of a penalty. Both conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. The intervention implementation serves every arm; the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch.

Algorithm 1 details the operator contract. It retrieves reference weights, detaches them, computes the difference, squares elements, sums them, scales by the coefficient, and stores the term. The invariants hold that reference weights receive no gradients, the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only, and the coefficient is fixed. The control arm adds no term to the training objective and leaves the target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification.** The experimental design employs a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization to unseen individuals. A random split would leak subject-specific information into training, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to test the core hypothesis about subject-disjoint generalization. The UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset provides an official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows, ensuring evaluation on people who appear nowhere in training. This supports a claim about unseen subjects, not a different corpus or sensor distribution.

**Seed Pairing and Variation.** We use 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. Pairing conditions by seed controls for initialization and data ordering variance, isolating the effect of the intervention. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them, not to subjects, as the subject split is fixed. This seed budget allows for precise estimation of the paired contrast. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds replicates the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline. This is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, but a verification of the experimental run's stability under fresh sampling.

**Negative Control Purpose.** The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. Its intended alternative explanation is that any regularization, regardless of target, might improve generalization by reducing overfitting. If the proposed condition outperforms this control, it supports the specific cross-layer consistency hypothesis. If not, it suggests the penalty structure itself is insufficient or harmful. The baseline control ensures the harness is unbiased; its outcome cannot prove the implementation correct, but its zero activity confirms the intervention is the only difference.

**Analysis Plan.** We report held-out classification accuracy for each condition. The primary analysis compares the proposed condition against the baseline using paired differences. The registered decision rule requires the lower confidence bound of the mean difference to exceed the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report results for both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds separately, without pooling them. This distinguishes training-seed replication from replication on new subjects or datasets.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort.** In the primary cohort, we evaluated the proposed condition against the baseline and negative control 1 across 43 seeds. Figure 1 illustrates the methodology flow from data to evaluation. Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for each condition. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The negative control 1 achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]).

Figure 3 plots the mean difference in accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 4 shows the accuracy over training steps, where curves for all conditions coincide closely, indicating no divergence in learning dynamics.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort.** In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, we repeated the evaluation with a fresh set of 43 seeds. Figure 5 displays the mean accuracy for this cohort. The proposed condition achieved 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), and the baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). Figure 6 plots the paired mean difference. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Again, the confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the margin. The decision was inconclusive. Figure 7 shows training curves similar to the primary cohort.

**Summary of Outcomes.** Table 1 summarizes the primary cohort metrics, and Table 2 summarizes the replication cohort metrics. Table 3 compares means across both cohorts. In both cohorts, the proposed condition showed a small positive point estimate relative to the baseline, but the uncertainty intervals were wide enough to include zero and exclude the target margin. The negative control performed similarly to the baseline, suggesting the specific cross-layer target did not drive a measurable gain over generic regularization in this setting. The results are inconclusive regarding the preregistered hypothesis.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency did not yield a statistically significant or practically worthwhile improvement in subject-disjoint generalization. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds produced inconclusive outcomes under the registered decision rule. The point estimates were positive but small (0.000773 and 0.00196), and the confidence intervals excluded the preregistered margin of 0.0125098. This suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime.

**Interpretation and Mechanism.** These results are consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation is essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. If attention patterns need to refine progressively across depth to capture complex temporal hierarchies, forcing them to be similar may constrain the model's representational capacity. An alternative mechanism is that the regularization coefficient was too small to influence the optimization trajectory meaningfully, though the negative control suggests the penalty structure itself was not the driver. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses; attention-map stability was not directly measured, so we cannot claim the intervention stabilized attention. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment.

**Comparison to Literature.** These findings contrast with works suggesting consistency regularization improves performance in other domains [17, 18]. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* found gains in machine translation [17], but that task involves sequence generation rather than classification of fixed windows. *CDAC* found attention consistency helpful for domain adaptation [18], but that work aligned attention maps across domains, not weights across layers within a single domain. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* also found inconclusive results for weight-space regularization in this setting [3], supporting the view that weight geometry constraints may not translate to accuracy gains in finite-width time-series transformers.

**Replication Cohort Value.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not a fluke of a specific seed set. The replication effect size (dz=0.15) was slightly larger than the primary (dz=0.06), but the conclusion remained the same. This is a replication of the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. It confirms the instability of the effect across seeds rather than generalizing to new populations.

**Future Directions.** To settle the question, future work should measure attention-map stability directly to verify if the weight regularization achieved its mechanistic goal. Testing on larger datasets or with different regularization coefficients might reveal a regime where the bias is beneficial. However, given the inconclusive outcome here, practitioners should not assume cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency helps in other time-series domains or with different architectures. The UCI HAR dataset is specific to human activity recognition with inertial sensors; results may not transfer to medical or financial time series. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds replicates the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. Therefore, we cannot claim the finding holds for new populations or sensor types.

The study adheres to its preregistered design and correctly reports the inconclusive outcome. A limitation is that we did not measure attention maps directly, so we cannot confirm the intervention stabilized attention as hypothesized. The variation observed is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. We preserve the registered labels and report the exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The results were inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin, and confidence intervals included zero. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence does not support adopting cross-layer query consistency for this task. Layer-specific adaptation may remain essential. Future work should measure attention stability directly and test larger coefficients or datasets to settle the question.

payload.title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers

payload.user:
Related-work section:
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [20], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [11] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [7]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [16].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [8], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [6], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [12], and *A survey of transformers* [21] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15].

This study positions itself against these themes by isolating the specific effect of cross-layer query weight consistency on subject-disjoint generalization. Unlike works that focus on domain adaptation [10] or activation steering [18], we test a weight-space regularization during training. Unlike surveys that catalog architectures [6, 12, 21], we provide empirical evidence on a specific inductive bias. The unsettled question is whether weight alignment across layers aids generalization in time-series transformers, a gap this experiment addresses directly.

Cited papers and their abstracts:
[1] Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00133 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by -0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

[2] Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness
Abstract: [EDITORIAL NOTICE — RETRACTED: this paper carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it. Stated reason: The numerical outputs reported in this paper remain computationally reproducible: an independent re-run from the archived reproducibility bundle reproduced all eight aggregate metrics within tolerance. A post-publication audit of the artifact source found that the executed intervention did not implement the preregistered intervention. The preregistration committed to a multiplicative weight perturbation applied BEFORE the forward pass, an entropy term added to the training OBJECTIVE, and a noise scale learned by BACKPROPAGATION, with held-out evaluation on the clean weights. The experiment har. Its conclusions may not be relied on; cite it only with its status stated.] Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic training often fails to provide calibrated confidence under distribution shift. This study investigates whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We preregistered a hypothesis that entropy maximization would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the baseline, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the intervention across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results refuted the preregistered hypothesis in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by 0.04805 proportion (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002) relative to the baseline. The replication cohort confirmed this degradation with a contrast of -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Negative controls involving entropy minimization and fixed noise performed comparably to the deterministic baseline. These findings indicate that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over explicit entropy maximization for robustness tasks in this regime.

[3] Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning
Abstract: Regularization design for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. This study tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy compared to standard weight decay in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would exceed a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion in accuracy gain. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset, we evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and two negative controls across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results were inconclusive: the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0004419 (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], p=0.75) in the primary cohort and 0.002549 (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], p=0.106) in the replication cohort. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. These findings suggest that spectral entropy minimization of input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks.

[4] Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?
Abstract: Recently, there has been a surge of Transformer-based solutions for the long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) task. Despite the growing performance over the past few years, we question the validity of this line of research in this work. Specifically, Transformers is arguably the most successful solution to extract the semantic correlations among the elements in a long sequence. However, in time series modeling, we are to extract the temporal relations in an ordered set of continuous points. While employing positional encoding and using tokens to embed sub-series in Transformers facilitate preserving some ordering information, the nature of the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss. To validate our claim, we introduce a set of embarrassingly simple one-layer linear models named LTSF-Linear for comparison. Experimental results on nine real-life datasets show that LTSF-Linear surprisingly outperforms existing sophisticated Transformer-based LTSF models in all cases, and often by a large margin. Moreover, we conduct comprehensive empirical studies to explore the impacts of various design elements of LTSF models on their temporal relation extraction capability. We hope this surprising finding opens up new research directions for the LTSF task. We also advocate revisiting the validity of Transformer-based solutions for other time series analysis tasks (e.g., anomaly detection) in the future.

[5] Selective Attention Improves Transformer
Abstract: Unneeded elements in the attention’s context degrade performance. We introduce Selective Attention, a simple parameter-free change to the standard attention mechanism which reduces attention to unneeded elements. Selective attention consistently improves language modeling and downstream task performance in a variety of model sizes and context lengths. For example, transformers trained with the language modeling objective on C4 with selective attention perform language modeling equivalently to standard transformers with ~2X more heads and parameters in their attention modules. Selective attention also allows decreasing the size of the attention’s context buffer, leading to meaningful reductions in the memory and compute requirements during inference. For example, transformers trained on C4 with context sizes of 512, 1,024, and 2,048 need 16X, 25X, and 47X less memory for their attention module, respectively, when equipped with selective attention, as those without selective attention, with the same validation perplexity.

[6] A Survey on Vision Transformer
Abstract: Transformer, first applied to the field of natural language processing, is a type of deep neural network mainly based on the self-attention mechanism. Thanks to its strong representation capabilities, researchers are looking at ways to apply transformer to computer vision tasks. In a variety of visual benchmarks, transformer-based models perform similar to or better than other types of networks such as convolutional and recurrent neural networks. Given its high performance and less need for vision-specific inductive bias, transformer is receiving more and more attention from the computer vision community. In this paper, we review these vision transformer models by categorizing them in different tasks and analyzing their advantages and disadvantages. The main categories we explore include the backbone network, high/mid-level vision, low-level vision, and video processing. We also include efficient transformer methods for pushing transformer into real device-based applications. Furthermore, we also take a brief look at the self-attention mechanism in computer vision, as it is the base component in transformer. Toward the end of this paper, we discuss the challenges and provide several further research directions for vision transformers.

[7] Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer
Abstract: A reliable and efficient representation of multivariate time series is crucial in various downstream machine learning tasks. In multivariate time series forecasting, each variable depends on its historical values and there are inter-dependencies among variables as well. Models have to be designed to capture both intra- and inter-relationships among the time series. To move towards this goal, we propose the Time Series Attention Transformer (TSAT) for multivariate time series representation learning. Using TSAT, we represent both temporal information and inter-dependencies of multivariate time series in terms of edge-enhanced dynamic graphs. The intra-series correlations are represented by nodes in a dynamic graph; a self-attention mechanism is modified to capture the inter-series correlations by using the super-empirical mode decomposition (SMD) module. We applied the embedded dynamic graphs to times series forecasting problems, including two real-world datasets and two benchmark datasets. Extensive experiments show that TSAT clearly outerperforms six state-of-the-art baseline methods in various forecasting horizons. We further visualize the embedded dynamic graphs to illustrate the graph representation power of TSAT. We share our code at https://github.com/RadiantResearch/TSAT.

[8] Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention
Abstract: More and more evidence has shown that strengthening layer interactions can enhance the representation power of a deep neural network, while self-attention excels at learning interdependencies by retrieving query-activated information. Motivated by this, we devise a cross-layer attention mechanism, called multi-head recurrent layer attention (MRLA), that sends a query representation of the current layer to all previous layers to retrieve query-related information from different levels of receptive fields. A light-weighted version of MRLA is also proposed to reduce the quadratic computation cost. The proposed layer attention mechanism can enrich the representation power of many state-of-the-art vision networks, including CNNs and vision transformers. Its effectiveness has been extensively evaluated in image classification, object detection and instance segmentation tasks, where improvements can be consistently observed. For example, our MRLA can improve 1.6% Top-1 accuracy on ResNet-50, while only introducing 0.16M parameters and 0.07B FLOPs. Surprisingly, it can boost the performances by a large margin of 3-4% box AP and mask AP in dense prediction tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/joyfang1106/MRLA.

[9] Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks
Abstract: The large-scale and deep-layer deep neural network based on the Transformer model is very powerful in sequence tasks, but it is prone to overfitting for small-scale training data. Moreover, the prediction result of the model with a small disturbance input is significantly lower than that without disturbance. In this work, we propose a double consistency regularization (DOCR) method for the end-to-end model structure, which separately constrains the output of the encoder and decoder during the training process to alleviate the above problems. Specifically, on the basis of the cross-entropy loss function, we build the mean model by integrating the model parameters of the previous rounds and measure the consistency between the models by calculating the KL divergence between the features of the encoder output and the probability distribution of the decoder output of the mean model and the base model so as to impose regularization constraints on the solution space of the model. We conducted extensive experiments on machine translation tasks, and the results show that the BLEU score increased by 2.60 on average, demonstrating the effectiveness of DOCR in improving model performance and its complementary impacts with other regularization techniques.

[10] CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation
Abstract: While transformers have greatly boosted performance in semantic segmentation, domain adaptive transformers are not yet well explored. We identify that the domain gap can cause discrepancies in self-attention. Due to this gap, the transformer attends to spurious regions or pixels, which deteriorates accuracy on the target domain. We propose Cross-Domain Attention Consistency (CDAC), to perform adaptation on attention maps using cross-domain attention layers that share features between source and target domains. Specifically, we impose consistency between predictions from cross-domain attention and self-attention modules to encourage similar distributions across domains in both the attention and output of the model, i.e., attention-level and output-level alignment. We also enforce consistency in attention maps between different augmented views to further strengthen the attention-based alignment. Combining these two components, CDAC mitigates the discrepancy in attention maps across domains and further boosts the performance of the transformer under unsupervised domain adaptation settings. Our method is evaluated on various widely used benchmarks and outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines, including GTAV-to-Cityscapes by 1.3 and 1.5 percent point (pp) and Synthia-to-Cityscapes by 0.6 pp and 2.9 pp when combining with two competitive Transformer-based backbones, respectively. Our code will be publicly available at https://github.com/wangkaihong/CDAC.

[11] TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation
Abstract: Signal measurement appearing in the form of time series is one of the most common types of data used in medical machine learning applications. Such datasets are often small in size, expensive to collect and annotate, and might involve privacy issues, which hinders our ability to train large, state-of-the-art deep learning models for biomedical applications. For time-series data, the suite of data augmentation strategies we can use to expand the size of the dataset is limited by the need to maintain the basic properties of the signal. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) can be utilized as another data augmentation tool. In this paper, we present TTS-CGAN, a transformer-based conditional GAN model that can be trained on existing multi-class datasets and generate class-specific synthetic time-series sequences of arbitrary length. We elaborate on the model architecture and design strategies. Synthetic sequences generated by our model are indistinguishable from real ones, and can be used to complement or replace real signals of the same type, thus achieving the goal of data augmentation. To evaluate the quality of the generated data, we modify the wavelet coherence metric to be able to compare the similarity between two sets of signals, and also conduct a case study where a mix of synthetic and real data are used to train a deep learning model for sequence classification. Together with other visualization techniques and qualitative evaluation approaches, we demonstrate that TTS-CGAN generated synthetic data are similar to real data, and that our model performs better than the other state-of-the-art GAN models built for time-series data generation.

[12] Transformers in Vision: A Survey
Abstract: Astounding results from Transformer models on natural language tasks have intrigued the vision community to study their application to computer vision problems. Among their salient benefits, Transformers enable modeling long dependencies between input sequence elements and support parallel processing of sequence as compared to recurrent networks, e.g., Long short-term memory. Different from convolutional networks, Transformers require minimal inductive biases for their design and are naturally suited as set-functions. Furthermore, the straightforward design of Transformers allows processing multiple modalities (e.g., images, videos, text, and speech) using similar processing blocks and demonstrates excellent scalability to very large capacity networks and huge datasets. These strengths have led to exciting progress on a number of vision tasks using Transformer networks. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the Transformer models in the computer vision discipline. We start with an introduction to fundamental concepts behind the success of Transformers, i.e., self-attention, large-scale pre-training, and bidirectional feature encoding. We then cover extensive applications of transformers in vision including popular recognition tasks (e.g., image classification, object detection, action recognition, and segmentation), generative modeling, multi-modal tasks (e.g., visual-question answering, visual reasoning, and visual grounding), video processing (e.g., activity recognition, video forecasting), low-level vision (e.g., image super-resolution, image enhancement, and colorization), and three-dimensional analysis (e.g., point cloud classification and segmentation). We compare the respective advantages and limitations of popular techniques both in terms of architectural design and their experimental value. Finally, we provide an analysis on open research directions and possible future works. We hope this effort will ignite further interest in the community to solve current challenges toward the application of transformer models in computer vision.

[13] Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks
Abstract: Large pre-trained models have been vital in recent advancements in domains like language and vision, making model training for individual downstream tasks more efficient and provide superior performance. However, tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model from scratch leveraging training data and domain expertise specific to the task. We tackle a significant challenge for pre-training a foundational time-series model from multi-domain time-series datasets: extracting semantically useful tokenized inputs to the model across heterogeneous time-series from different domains. We propose Large Pre-trained Time-series Models (LPTM) that introduces a novel method of adaptive segmentation that automatically identifies optimal dataset-specific segmentation strategy during pre-training. This enables LPTM to perform similar to or better than domain-specific state-of-art model when fine-tuned to different downstream time-series analysis tasks and under zero-shot settings. LPTM achieves superior forecasting and time-series classification results taking up to 40% less data and 50% less training time compared to state-of-art baselines.

[14] Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification
Abstract: Abstract The rapid development of deep learning, especially the application of CNN and Transformer, brings a new direction for remote sensing scene classification. CNN is challenging to capture multi-scale features due to the limitation of the receptive field. Although the feature pyramid network (FPN) is a multi-scale structure, its fusion mechanism inherently limits the extraction of fine-grained information. The Transformer architecture excels at capturing long-range dependencies through its self-attention mechanism. While the multihead self-attention mechanism allows it to concentrate on both global and local patterns, there is still room for improvement in explicitly enhancing the extraction of local spatial features and edge detail information. To overcome the above limitations, this paper proposes a novel end-to-end learning model, called cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network (CLFETNet), for remote sensing scene classification. The innovative contribution of this paper is to embed three novel modules into the traditional CNN model. Firstly, we utilize the FPN to extract multi-scale features and design a fine feature aggregation module (RFA) to integrate complementary information from different layers to obtain more reliable and accurate features. Second, the efficient frequency transformer (EFT) is proposed to deeply mine global information, local spatial features, and edge detail information. Finally, the graph-aware fusion (GAF) module is proposed to model the relationships among regions in the feature graph by graph convolutional network (GCN), which enhances the intra-class feature consistency. A wide range of experiments have been carried out on three publicly accessible RS scene datasets. Positive results show that our CLFETNet framework outperforms many existing methods, has high robustness and superiority in remote sensing scene classification tasks, and can effectively handle complex scenes and meet multi-scale feature challenges.

[15] An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks
Abstract: Attention mechanisms have become a popular component in deep neural networks, yet there has been little examination of how different influencing factors and methods for computing attention from these factors affect performance. Related-work section:
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [20], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [11] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [7]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [16].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [8], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [6], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [12], and *A survey of transformers* [21] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15].

This study positions itself against these themes by isolating the specific effect of cross-layer query weight consistency on subject-disjoint generalization. Unlike works that focus on domain adaptation [10] or activation steering [18], we test a weight-space regularization during training. Unlike surveys that catalog architectures [6, 12, 21], we provide empirical evidence on a specific inductive bias. The unsettled question is whether weight alignment across layers aids generalization in time-series transformers, a gap this experiment addresses directly.

However, existing methods deriving vectors from static activation differences are susceptible to high-dimensional noise and layer-wise semantic drift, often capturing spurious correlations rather than the target intent. To address this, we propose Global Evolutionary Refined Steering (GER-steer), a training-free framework that grounded in the geometric stability of the network's representation evolution. GER-steer exploits this global signal to rectify raw steering vectors, effectively decoupling robust semantic intent from orthogonal artifacts. Extensive evaluations confirm that GER-steer consistently outperforms baselines, delivering superior efficacy and generalization without layer-specific tuning, establishing a universal solution for reliable model alignment.

[19] Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models
Abstract: Self-attention selects information freely across the sequence, but across depth, Transformers merely add each layer's output to the residual stream, so later layers cannot selectively reuse earlier-layer representations. Recent cross-layer methods improve this flow but operate on hidden states outside attention, adding state beyond the key-value cache at inference--a cost that becomes increasingly salient as modern LLMs compress the cache with grouped-query and multi-head latent attention. We introduce Depth-Attention, which performs this selection inside the attention module itself: before a layer attends over the sequence, its query attends over the keys of earlier layers at the same token position and mixes their values into the value that self-attention then reads. Because Depth-Attention reuses the standard attention queries, keys, and value-cache slots, storing depth-mixed values in place of the original values, it adds no parameters and introduces no persistent inference state beyond the standard key-value cache--the same cache size as a vanilla decoder and less than hidden-state-based cross-layer methods. On Qwen3-style decoders at 1.5B and 3B parameters, Depth-Attention attains the lowest perplexity and the highest average downstream accuracy, improving over the vanilla Transformer by up to 2.3 accuracy points and surpassing strong cross-layer baselines in perplexity and average accuracy, while adding under 0.01% extra arithmetic FLOPs and no additional persistent inference state. The gains hold from 360M to 3B parameters and extend to looped Transformers.

[20] Transformers in Time Series: A Survey
Abstract: Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications. In this paper, we systematically review Transformer schemes for time series modeling by highlighting their strengths as well as limitations. In particular, we examine the development of time series Transformers in two perspectives. From the perspective of network structure, we summarize the adaptations and modifications that have been made to Transformers in order to accommodate the challenges in time series analysis. From the perspective of applications, we categorize time series Transformers based on common tasks including forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification. Empirically, we perform robust analysis, model size analysis, and seasonal-trend decomposition analysis to study how Transformers perform in time series. Finally, we discuss and suggest future directions to provide useful research guidance. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first work to comprehensively and systematically summarize the recent advances of Transformers for modeling time series data. We hope this survey will ignite further research interests in time series Transformers.

[21] A survey of transformers
Abstract: Transformers have achieved great success in many artificial intelligence fields, such as natural language processing, computer vision, and audio processing. Therefore, it is natural to attract lots of interest from academic and industry researchers. Up to the present, a great variety of Transformer variants (a.k.a. X-formers) have been proposed, however, a systematic and comprehensive literature review on these Transformer variants is still missing. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive review of various X-formers. We first briefly introduce the vanilla Transformer and then propose a new taxonomy of X-formers. Next, we introduce the various X-formers from three perspectives: architectural modification, pre-training, and applications. Finally, we outline some potential directions for future research.

Introduction: Deep learning models for time-series analysis face a persistent challenge: learning representations that generalize across subjects with distinct movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. The core open problem is identifying which architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that transfer to unseen subjects. Specifically, it is unclear whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined attention patterns or consistently stable ones to support generalization.

This uncertainty matters because answering it clarifies the design space for out-of-distribution time-series tasks. If cross-layer consistency improves generalization, it would justify testing whether this bias transfers to other subject-disjoint benchmarks. Conversely, if layer-specific adaptation is essential, efforts to enforce stability across depth may hinder performance. Current literature lacks independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. While consistency regularization has been explored in other contexts [9], its application to cross-layer query projections in time-series transformers remains untested under rigorous subject-disjoint conditions.

- We execute a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency loss in a time-series transformer, reporting both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts.
- We provide exact quantitative estimates of the effect on held-out classification accuracy, including confidence intervals and effect sizes, rather than binary significance claims.

The results were inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin, and confidence intervals included zero. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence does not support adopting cross-layer query consistency for this task. Layer-specific adaptation may remain essential. Future work should measure attention stability directly and test larger coefficients or datasets to settle the question.
