Judge whether it is publishable as a small, honest study, paying particular attention to whether the results are interpreted in light of the cited literature and whether claims are properly supported by citations. Decide ACCEPT or REVISE. If the EXPERIMENT ITSELF is fundamentally flawed (wrong setup, not just wording), say REVISE-EXPERIMENT. Check the manuscript's arm descriptions against the supplied registered conditions and measured activity. A randomized active negative control is not an inactive baseline; its outcome cannot establish that the harness is unbiased. Distinguish a proposed mechanism from one directly measured: parameter regularization and accuracy alone do not measure attention-map stability. Detaching a tensor in a penalty blocks that gradient only, not ordinary task-loss learning. Check power claims against the supplied zero-null versus margin-success qualification, and preserve the registered decisions. Be concise. This is a REGISTERED REPORT whose protocol was approved and anchored before compute. A valid worthwhile, refuted, null, mixed, or inconclusive outcome is equally publishable. Never reject, downgrade, or request a new experiment because the result is negative, null, small, surprising, or inconclusive. Post-results review may demand accurate reporting, citations, limitations, and calibrated claims, but it must not reopen the approved design or create an outcome-selected rerun.

Respond in EXACTLY this format:
DECISION: <accept | revise | revise-experiment>
FEEDBACK: <one short paragraph of specific, actionable feedback>

Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [20], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [11] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [7]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [16].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [8], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [6], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [12], and *A survey of transformers* [21] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15].

This study positions itself against these themes by isolating the specific effect of cross-layer query weight consistency on subject-disjoint generalization. Unlike works that focus on domain adaptation [10] or activation steering [18], we test a weight-space regularization during training. Unlike surveys that catalog architectures [6, 12, 21], we provide empirical evidence on a specific inductive bias. The unsettled question is whether weight alignment across layers aids generalization in time-series transformers, a gap this experiment addresses directly.
Method: The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces similarity between query projection weights across transformer blocks. The hypothesis is that stabilizing attention patterns across depth improves generalization to unseen subjects. The operator targets the query projection weight matrix of the second attention block, regularizing it toward the corresponding weights of the first block. This expression of the hypothesis assumes that consistent query projections facilitate more robust temporal feature extraction across varying subject dynamics.

The operator is applied during the loss computation of every optimization step. Its term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, ensuring the combined objective is differentiated. The scope is the full weight matrix of dimensions 64 by 64 treated as flat parameter space. The operation computes the element-wise subtraction between the target weights and the reference weights, squares the differences, and sums them to produce a raw loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed coefficient of 0.01 before being added to the training objective. Reference weights from the first block are detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients from flowing to them, ensuring the regularization is one-directional.

The comparator neutralizes the intervention's specific effect while maintaining the computational path. The baseline control arm executes identical code but returns a zero loss term. This ensures that any difference in outcome is attributable to the regularization term itself, not to implementation artifacts or computational overhead. The harness records operator activity for every seed and condition, refusing results where the control arm acted at any registered point. This guarantees the control's recorded activity is zero.

A negative control condition penalizes the difference between the second block's weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as the first block's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the compute and regularization magnitude. If the proposed condition outperforms this negative control, it suggests the specific cross-layer relationship matters, not just the presence of a penalty. Both conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. The intervention implementation serves every arm; the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch.

Algorithm 1 details the operator contract. It retrieves reference weights, detaches them, computes the difference, squares elements, sums them, scales by the coefficient, and stores the term. The invariants hold that reference weights receive no gradients, the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only, and the coefficient is fixed. The control arm adds no term to the training objective and leaves the target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Experimental setup: **Design Justification.** The experimental design employs a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization to unseen individuals. A random split would leak subject-specific information into training, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to test the core hypothesis about subject-disjoint generalization. The UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset provides an official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows, ensuring evaluation on people who appear nowhere in training. This supports a claim about unseen subjects, not a different corpus or sensor distribution.

**Seed Pairing and Variation.** We use 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. Pairing conditions by seed controls for initialization and data ordering variance, isolating the effect of the intervention. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them, not to subjects, as the subject split is fixed. This seed budget allows for precise estimation of the paired contrast. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds replicates the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline. This is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, but a verification of the experimental run's stability under fresh sampling.

**Negative Control Purpose.** The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. Its intended alternative explanation is that any regularization, regardless of target, might improve generalization by reducing overfitting. If the proposed condition outperforms this control, it supports the specific cross-layer consistency hypothesis. If not, it suggests the penalty structure itself is insufficient or harmful. The baseline control ensures the harness is unbiased; its outcome cannot prove the implementation correct, but its zero activity confirms the intervention is the only difference.

**Analysis Plan.** We report held-out classification accuracy for each condition. The primary analysis compares the proposed condition against the baseline using paired differences. The registered decision rule requires the lower confidence bound of the mean difference to exceed the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report results for both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds separately, without pooling them. This distinguishes training-seed replication from replication on new subjects or datasets.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Registered conditions.
- Proposed condition: Server-bound target blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight has stored tensor shape (64, 64). Add loss term that applies Frobenius norm consistency regularization to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Baseline: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. Recorded activity — primary: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Negative control 1: Add loss term penalizing difference between blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
Results: **Primary Cohort.** In the primary cohort, we evaluated the proposed condition against the baseline and negative control 1 across 43 seeds. Figure 1 illustrates the methodology flow from data to evaluation. Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for each condition. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The negative control 1 achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]).

Figure 3 plots the mean difference in accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 4 shows the accuracy over training steps, where curves for all conditions coincide closely, indicating no divergence in learning dynamics.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort.** In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, we repeated the evaluation with a fresh set of 43 seeds. Figure 5 displays the mean accuracy for this cohort. The proposed condition achieved 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), and the baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). Figure 6 plots the paired mean difference. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Again, the confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the margin. The decision was inconclusive. Figure 7 shows training curves similar to the primary cohort.

**Summary of Outcomes.** Table 1 summarizes the primary cohort metrics, and Table 2 summarizes the replication cohort metrics. Table 3 compares means across both cohorts. In both cohorts, the proposed condition showed a small positive point estimate relative to the baseline, but the uncertainty intervals were wide enough to include zero and exclude the target margin. The negative control performed similarly to the baseline, suggesting the specific cross-layer target did not drive a measurable gain over generic regularization in this setting. The results are inconclusive regarding the preregistered hypothesis.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This study tested whether cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The results were inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin, and confidence intervals included zero. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence does not support adopting cross-layer query consistency for this task. Layer-specific adaptation may remain essential. Future work should measure attention stability directly and test larger coefficients or datasets to settle the question.
Discussion: **Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency did not yield a statistically significant or practically worthwhile improvement in subject-disjoint generalization. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds produced inconclusive outcomes under the registered decision rule. The point estimates were positive but small (0.000773 and 0.00196), and the confidence intervals excluded the preregistered margin of 0.0125098. This suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime.

**Interpretation and Mechanism.** These results are consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation is essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. If attention patterns need to refine progressively across depth to capture complex temporal hierarchies, forcing them to be similar may constrain the model's representational capacity. An alternative mechanism is that the regularization coefficient was too small to influence the optimization trajectory meaningfully, though the negative control suggests the penalty structure itself was not the driver. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses; attention-map stability was not directly measured, so we cannot claim the intervention stabilized attention. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment.

**Comparison to Literature.** These findings contrast with works suggesting consistency regularization improves performance in other domains [9, 10]. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* found gains in machine translation [9], but that task involves sequence generation rather than classification of fixed windows. *CDAC* found attention consistency helpful for domain adaptation [10], but that work aligned attention maps across domains, not weights across layers within a single domain. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* also found inconclusive results for weight-space regularization in this setting [3], supporting the view that weight geometry constraints may not translate to accuracy gains in finite-width time-series transformers.

**Replication Cohort Value.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not a fluke of a specific seed set. The replication effect size (dz=0.15) was slightly larger than the primary (dz=0.06), but the conclusion remained the same. This is a replication of the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. It confirms the instability of the effect across seeds rather than generalizing to new populations.

**Future Directions.** To settle the question, future work should measure attention-map stability directly to verify if the weight regularization achieved its mechanistic goal. Testing on larger datasets or with different regularization coefficients might reveal a regime where the bias is beneficial. However, given the inconclusive outcome here, practitioners should not assume cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers.
Limitations: This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency helps in other time-series domains or with different architectures. The UCI HAR dataset is specific to human activity recognition with inertial sensors; results may not transfer to medical or financial time series. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds replicates the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. Therefore, we cannot claim the finding holds for new populations or sensor types.

The study adheres to its preregistered design and correctly reports the inconclusive outcome. A limitation is that we did not measure attention maps directly, so we cannot confirm the intervention stabilized attention as hypothesized. The variation observed is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. We preserve the registered labels and report the exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

Thinking Process:

1.  **Analyze the Request:**
    *   **Role:** Critical but fair peer reviewer of an AI-generated research paper.
    *   **Task:** Judge whether it is publishable as a small, honest study (Registered Report).
    *   **Focus:** Results interpreted in light of cited literature, claims supported by citations, experimental design fidelity (registered conditions vs. described), power claims, mechanism vs. measurement distinctions.
    *   **Constraints:**
        *   Respond in EXACTLY this format: `DECISION: <accept | revise | revise-experiment>` followed by `FEEDBACK: <one short paragraph of specific, actionable feedback>`.
        *   Do not reject/downgrade due to negative/null results.
        *   Check arm descriptions against registered conditions.
        *   Check power claims against zero-null vs. margin-success.
        *   Check mechanism claims (parameter regularization != attention-map stability).
        *   Check control arm definitions (randomized active negative control is not an inactive baseline).
        *   Check citation accuracy.
        *   Check presentation claims (independent replication vs. seed replication).
    *   **Input:** A paper titled "Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers" along with audit logs (citation errors, text overlap, preregistration check, claim-evidence check).

2.  **Evaluate the Paper against Criteria:**

    *   **Registered Report Status:** The paper claims to be a Registered Report. The audit log confirms: "The paper is faithful to its preregistration." Registered decisions were `primary=inconclusive; replication=inconclusive`. The paper reports these correctly in the Results and Conclusion sections mostly, but there are flagged issues in the Claim-Evidence check.
    *   **Experimental Design:**
        *   *Conditions:* Proposed (consistency loss), Baseline (control arm, zero loss), Negative Control 1 (random matrix penalty).

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. === abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0007734 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.001957 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Time-series classification using deep learning has become critical for applications ranging from healthcare monitoring to industrial predictive maintenance. Among architectural choices, Transformers have gained prominence due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies without the sequential constraints of recurrent networks [38]. However, their effectiveness in time-series domains, particularly regarding generalization to unseen subjects, remains a subject of active debate [5]. While Transformers excel in natural language processing, time-series data presents distinct challenges, including varying execution speeds, sensor characteristics, and movement styles across individuals. Consequently, identifying architectural inductive biases that facilitate robust subject-disjoint generalization is a pressing open problem.

Current literature highlights both the potential and uncertainty surrounding Transformer applications in time series. Surveys indicate that while Transformers capture long-range interactions effectively, their performance gains over simpler baselines are not guaranteed across all tasks [38, 5]. Specific modifications, such as consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms, have been proposed to enhance stability and generalization [17, 18]. For instance, cross-layer interactions have been explored to strengthen layer dependencies in vision tasks [15], and consistency losses have been applied to domain adaptation [18]. However, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Existing studies often focus on forecasting or domain adaptation rather than subject-disjoint classification, leaving a gap in understanding how depth-wise weight regularization affects generalization to new individuals.

This paper addresses this gap by rigorously testing the hypothesis that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization. We replicate and extend previous investigations by employing a preregistered design with a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. Our study utilizes the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, ensuring that evaluation reflects generalization to unseen subjects rather than memorization of subject-specific patterns.

The contributions of this work are as follows:
- We provide exact quantitative estimates of the effect on held-out classification accuracy, including confidence intervals and effect sizes, rather than binary significance claims.
- We execute a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to verify the stability of the experimental run under fresh sampling.
- We evaluate the proposed condition against a baseline and a negative control to isolate the effect of meaningful cross-layer relationships from computational artifacts.

The preregistered prediction states that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report the results honestly against this hypothesis, labeling any unforeseen findings as exploratory.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [20, 14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [15, 34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28].

This study positions itself against these themes by focusing specifically on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers, distinguishing our work from forecasting tasks [5] and domain adaptation settings [18]. While cross-layer mechanisms have shown promise in vision and language [15, 37], their efficacy in subject-disjoint time-series classification remains unsettled. We build upon the verified findings of [1] by conducting a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to assess stability, addressing the lack of independent verification noted in the literature. Unlike works that propose new architectures [14, 23], we test a specific regularization operator within a fixed architecture to isolate the effect of cross-layer query consistency.

=== method ===
The core of this experiment is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces weight alignment between attention query projections across transformer blocks. The hypothesis motivating this operator is that stabilizing attention patterns across depth may improve generalization to unseen subjects by reducing overfitting to subject-specific temporal features. The operator applies a Frobenius norm consistency regularization between the query projection weights of block 0 and block 1. Specifically, the loss term is computed as the squared element-wise difference between the target weights (block 1) and the reference weights (block 0), scaled by a fixed coefficient.

**Operator Design and Hypothesis**
The intervention adds a loss term during training that penalizes divergence between deeper and shallower query projections. This design choice reflects the hypothesis that consistent attention mechanisms across layers provide a more robust inductive bias for time-series data, where temporal dependencies may be captured effectively without layer-specific specialization. The reference weights from block 0 are detached from the gradient graph, ensuring that the consistency penalty only updates the target parameters in block 1. This prevents the regularization from altering the shallower layer's task-loss gradients, isolating the effect to the deeper layer's adaptation toward the shallower representation.

The comparator neutralizes this intervention by executing the identical code path but returning a zero loss term. This control arm ensures that any observed difference in accuracy is attributable to the consistency loss itself rather than implementation artifacts or computational overhead. Both conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters, ensuring that variance due to random initialization is controlled.

**Negative Control**
To verify that the observed effect (or lack thereof) is due to the meaningful cross-layer relationship rather than the mere presence of a regularization term, we include a negative control. This condition penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the computational cost and gradient flow of the proposed condition. If the proposed condition outperforms this negative control, it suggests that the specific alignment to block 0 is beneficial; if not, the regularization itself may be inert or detrimental.

**Gradient Handling**
A critical aspect of the operator specification is the handling of gradients. Detaching the reference tensor inside the penalty stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. This distinction is vital for interpreting the results: the shallower layer continues to learn from the classification objective, while the deeper layer is constrained to remain close to it. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient, so we rely on the registered coefficient of 0.01 to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective.

**Decision Rule**
The registered decision rule requires the lower confidence bound of the paired contrast to exceed the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This strict criterion ensures that we do not claim a positive effect unless the uncertainty model excludes gains smaller than the target magnitude. The analysis distinguishes between detecting a non-zero effect and exceeding the margin; a confidence interval crossing zero indicates an inconclusive result regarding the direction of the effect, regardless of the margin.

**Algorithm Specification**
The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. The combined objective is differentiated, and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The algorithm retrieves reference weights, detaches them, computes the element-wise difference, squares the elements, sums them, and scales by the coefficient. This process is repeated for every seed and condition, with the harness recording operator activity to ensure compliance with the preregistration.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Subject-Disjoint Split Justification**
The experimental design employs an official subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset. This choice is critical because the research question concerns generalization to unseen subjects, not merely held-out windows from the same individuals. A random split would allow the model to learn subject-specific movement styles or sensor characteristics, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to answer the open problem. By holding out entire subjects, we ensure that the evaluation reflects the model's ability to generalize across different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. This design supports a claim about unseen subjects but is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task, or deployment distribution.

**Seed Pairing and Variance Control**
We pair conditions by seed, meaning the proposed condition and the baseline are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. This pairing reduces variance due to random initialization and data ordering, increasing the power to detect small effects. The analysis uses 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. This seed budget allows us to estimate the stability of the result under fresh sampling without conflating seed variance with subject variance.

**Negative Control Purpose**
The first negative control penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. This condition is intended to test the alternative explanation that any regularization term, regardless of its target, improves generalization by simply adding noise or constraint. If the proposed condition performs similarly to this negative control, it suggests that the specific cross-layer alignment is not the active ingredient. The observed contrast between the proposed condition and this negative control supports or refutes the hypothesis that meaningful cross-layer relationships are necessary for any benefit.

**Replication Cohort Design**
The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds serves as a verification of the experimental run's stability under fresh sampling. This is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, but a verification that the primary result is not an artifact of the specific seed set used. By running the same pipeline on a disjoint set of seeds, we assess whether the inconclusive primary result holds under repeated sampling. This design distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations.

**Measurement and Power**
The outcome measure is held-out classification accuracy, defined as the number of correct activity predictions divided by 2,947 windows in the official subject-disjoint test split. The planning target power was 90% with a planning SD of 0.0250196. The registered margin of 0.0125098 proportion was derived from calibration noise, reflecting measurement precision rather than practical importance. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance, but it provides a consistent decision rule for the study.

=== results ===
We report the results for the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohorts separately, adhering to the preregistered decision rules. The analysis focuses on held-out classification accuracy, with all estimates accompanied by bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.

**Primary Cohort**
In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). As shown in Figure 2, the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), compared to 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]) for the baseline. The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 3 displays the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions, with the 95% confidence interval clearly including zero. The green dash-dot marker in Figure 3 indicates the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion; the lower confidence bound does not exceed this threshold. Consequently, the preregistered decision for the primary cohort is inconclusive.

**Replication Cohort**
In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), compared to 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]) for the baseline. The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]). Figure 6 illustrates the mean difference, with the 95% confidence interval again including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. The preregistered decision for the replication cohort is also inconclusive.

**Training Dynamics**
Figure 4 and Figure 7 depict the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. The curves for the proposed, baseline, and negative control 1 conditions coincide closely throughout training, with no condition demonstrating a clear divergence in learning speed or final performance. This visual evidence aligns with the statistical findings, suggesting that the consistency loss does not substantially alter the optimization trajectory in this regime.

**Summary of Findings**
Table 1 and Table 2 summarize the condition means and confidence intervals for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Table 3 and Table 4 present the outcome differences and registered decisions. In both cohorts, the confidence intervals include zero, and neither estimate exceeds the preregistered margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency in attention projections does not yield robust accuracy gains in subject-disjoint time-series classification. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This suggests that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class, contrary to the hypothesis that weight alignment across depth improves generalization.

**Interpretation of Null Result**
The inconclusive outcome indicates that the intervention did not achieve the predicted effect size. It is consistent with the possibility that the consistency loss is too weak to influence the learned representations meaningfully, or that the hypothesis itself is incorrect for this task. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment; regularizing weights does not guarantee that the resulting attention patterns are more stable or generalizable. The negative control results, which were similar to the baseline, suggest that the computational cost of the regularization term itself does not drive performance changes. This design does not establish the mechanism or prove the absence of implementation bias, but the recorded activity confirms the operator executed as specified.

**Mechanism and Alternatives**
A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that time-series data requires layer-specific specialization to capture multi-scale temporal features, making cross-layer consistency detrimental or neutral. An alternative explanation is that the coefficient of 0.01 was insufficient to overcome the classification objective's gradient, resulting in negligible regularization. However, the registered coefficient was chosen to prevent dominance, and increasing it might destabilize training. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds replicates the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. This confirms that the null result is stable under seed variation, but it does not generalize to other datasets or architectures.

**Relation to Cited Work**
These findings stand in contrast to works that report gains from cross-layer mechanisms in vision and language [15, 34]. However, those studies often operate in different data regimes or tasks, making direct comparison difficult. Our results align with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found inconclusive results for weight-based regularization in this setting [3]. They also support the caution raised in *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* regarding the validity of Transformer modifications for time series [5]. Unlike *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which reported improvements on machine translation [17], we find no evidence of benefit for subject-disjoint classification. This discrepancy may arise from the difference between sequence-to-sequence tasks and classification, or the nature of the consistency constraint.

**Implications for Practice**
For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence suggests that adding cross-layer query consistency loss is not justified by accuracy gains in this regime. The computational cost of the operator, while small, yields no measurable return. Future work should investigate whether stronger regularization or different alignment targets (e.g., attention maps rather than weights) produce different outcomes. Direct measurement of attention stability would be required to test the mechanistic hypothesis that weight alignment stabilizes attention.

=== limitations ===
This study has several limitations that constrain the interpretation of the results. First, the evaluation is limited to the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with a subject-disjoint split. While this supports a claim about unseen subjects within this corpus, it is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task, or deployment distribution. We do not call this out-of-distribution or domain generalisation in the broader sense. Second, we measure weight alignment, not attention-map stability. The hypothesis that weight regularization stabilizes attention is unmeasured; accuracy contrasts alone cannot prove attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization. Third, the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds replicates the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. This limits our ability to claim robustness across data distributions. Finally, the registered margin was derived from calibration noise, which reflects measurement precision but does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The results were inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This finding suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. For practitioners, this implies that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, and adding this regularization is not supported by the evidence. To settle the question next, future work should measure attention-map stability directly and test stronger regularization coefficients or alternative alignment targets on diverse subject-disjoint benchmarks.

Topic: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Research question: Does enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections, where deeper layer weights are regularized toward shallower layer weights, improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers?
Hypothesis: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.
Open problem this targets: What architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds?
Why it matters (impact): Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for OOD time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

REGISTERED OPERATOR (including gradient handling; do not infer that detaching one loss term freezes ordinary task-loss learning):
Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer*. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it.

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance.
