=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0007734 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.001957 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Time-series classification using deep learning has become critical for applications ranging from healthcare monitoring to industrial predictive maintenance. Among architectural choices, Transformers have gained prominence due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies without the sequential constraints of recurrent networks [38]. However, their effectiveness in time-series domains, particularly regarding generalization to unseen subjects, remains a subject of active debate [5]. While Transformers excel in natural language processing, time-series data presents distinct challenges, including varying execution speeds, sensor characteristics, and movement styles across individuals. Consequently, identifying architectural inductive biases that facilitate robust subject-disjoint generalization is a pressing open problem.

Current literature highlights both the potential and uncertainty surrounding Transformer applications in time series. Surveys indicate that while Transformers capture long-range interactions effectively, their performance gains over simpler baselines are not guaranteed across all tasks [38, 5]. Specific modifications, such as consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms, have been proposed to enhance stability and generalization [17, 18]. For instance, cross-layer interactions have been explored to strengthen layer dependencies in vision tasks [15], and consistency losses have been applied to domain adaptation [18]. However, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Existing studies often focus on forecasting or domain adaptation rather than subject-disjoint classification, leaving a gap in understanding how depth-wise weight regularization affects generalization to new individuals.

This paper addresses this gap by rigorously testing the hypothesis that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization. We replicate and extend previous investigations by employing a preregistered design with a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. Our study utilizes the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, ensuring that evaluation reflects generalization to unseen subjects rather than memorization of subject-specific patterns.

The contributions of this work are as follows:
- We provide exact quantitative estimates of the effect on held-out classification accuracy, including confidence intervals and effect sizes, rather than binary significance claims.
- We execute a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to verify the stability of the experimental run under fresh sampling.
- We evaluate the proposed condition against a baseline and a negative control to isolate the effect of meaningful cross-layer relationships from computational artifacts.

The preregistered prediction states that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report the results honestly against this hypothesis, labeling any unforeseen findings as exploratory.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [20, 14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [15, 34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28].

This study positions itself against these themes by focusing specifically on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers, distinguishing our work from forecasting tasks [5] and domain adaptation settings [18]. While cross-layer mechanisms have shown promise in vision and language [15, 37], their efficacy in subject-disjoint time-series classification remains unsettled. We build upon the verified findings of [1] by conducting a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to assess stability, addressing the lack of independent verification noted in the literature. Unlike works that propose new architectures [14, 23], we test a specific regularization operator within a fixed architecture to isolate the effect of cross-layer query consistency.

=== method ===
The core of this experiment is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces weight alignment between attention query projections across transformer blocks. The hypothesis motivating this operator is that stabilizing attention patterns across depth may improve generalization to unseen subjects by reducing overfitting to subject-specific temporal features. The operator applies a Frobenius norm consistency regularization between the query projection weights of block 0 and block 1. Specifically, the loss term is computed as the squared element-wise difference between the target weights (block 1) and the reference weights (block 0), scaled by a fixed coefficient.

**Operator Design and Hypothesis**
The intervention adds a loss term during training that penalizes divergence between deeper and shallower query projections. This design choice reflects the hypothesis that consistent attention mechanisms across layers provide a more robust inductive bias for time-series data, where temporal dependencies may be captured effectively without layer-specific specialization. The reference weights from block 0 are detached from the gradient graph, ensuring that the consistency penalty only updates the target parameters in block 1. This prevents the regularization from altering the shallower layer's task-loss gradients, isolating the effect to the deeper layer's adaptation toward the shallower representation.

The comparator neutralizes this intervention by executing the identical code path but returning a zero loss term. This control arm ensures that any observed difference in accuracy is attributable to the consistency loss itself rather than implementation artifacts or computational overhead. Both conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters, ensuring that variance due to random initialization is controlled.

**Negative Control**
To verify that the observed effect (or lack thereof) is due to the meaningful cross-layer relationship rather than the mere presence of a regularization term, we include a negative control. This condition penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the computational cost and gradient flow of the proposed condition. If the proposed condition outperforms this negative control, it suggests that the specific alignment to block 0 is beneficial; if not, the regularization itself may be inert or detrimental.

**Gradient Handling**
A critical aspect of the operator specification is the handling of gradients. Detaching the reference tensor inside the penalty stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. This distinction is vital for interpreting the results: the shallower layer continues to learn from the classification objective, while the deeper layer is constrained to remain close to it. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient, so we rely on the registered coefficient of 0.01 to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective.

**Decision Rule**
The registered decision rule requires the lower confidence bound of the paired contrast to exceed the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This strict criterion ensures that we do not claim a positive effect unless the uncertainty model excludes gains smaller than the target magnitude. The analysis distinguishes between detecting a non-zero effect and exceeding the margin; a confidence interval crossing zero indicates an inconclusive result regarding the direction of the effect, regardless of the margin.

**Algorithm Specification**
The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. The combined objective is differentiated, and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The algorithm retrieves reference weights, detaches them, computes the element-wise difference, squares the elements, sums them, and scales by the coefficient. This process is repeated for every seed and condition, with the harness recording operator activity to ensure compliance with the preregistration.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Subject-Disjoint Split Justification**
The experimental design employs an official subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset. This choice is critical because the research question concerns generalization to unseen subjects, not merely held-out windows from the same individuals. A random split would allow the model to learn subject-specific movement styles or sensor characteristics, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to answer the open problem. By holding out entire subjects, we ensure that the evaluation reflects the model's ability to generalize across different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. This design supports a claim about unseen subjects but is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task, or deployment distribution.

**Seed Pairing and Variance Control**
We pair conditions by seed, meaning the proposed condition and the baseline are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. This pairing reduces variance due to random initialization and data ordering, increasing the power to detect small effects. The analysis uses 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. This seed budget allows us to estimate the stability of the result under fresh sampling without conflating seed variance with subject variance.

**Negative Control Purpose**
The first negative control penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. This condition is intended to test the alternative explanation that any regularization term, regardless of its target, improves generalization by simply adding noise or constraint. If the proposed condition performs similarly to this negative control, it suggests that the specific cross-layer alignment is not the active ingredient. The observed contrast between the proposed condition and this negative control supports or refutes the hypothesis that meaningful cross-layer relationships are necessary for any benefit.

**Replication Cohort Design**
The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds serves as a verification of the experimental run's stability under fresh sampling. This is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, but a verification that the primary result is not an artifact of the specific seed set used. By running the same pipeline on a disjoint set of seeds, we assess whether the inconclusive primary result holds under repeated sampling. This design distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations.

**Measurement and Power**
The outcome measure is held-out classification accuracy, defined as the number of correct activity predictions divided by 2,947 windows in the official subject-disjoint test split. The planning target power was 90% with a planning SD of 0.0250196. The registered margin of 0.0125098 proportion was derived from calibration noise, reflecting measurement precision rather than practical importance. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance, but it provides a consistent decision rule for the study.

=== results ===
We report the results for the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohorts separately, adhering to the preregistered decision rules. The analysis focuses on held-out classification accuracy, with all estimates accompanied by bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.

**Primary Cohort**
In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). As shown in Figure 2, the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), compared to 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]) for the baseline. The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 3 displays the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions, with the 95% confidence interval clearly including zero. The green dash-dot marker in Figure 3 indicates the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion; the lower confidence bound does not exceed this threshold. Consequently, the preregistered decision for the primary cohort is inconclusive.

**Replication Cohort**
In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), compared to 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]) for the baseline. The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]). Figure 6 illustrates the mean difference, with the 95% confidence interval again including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. The preregistered decision for the replication cohort is also inconclusive.

**Training Dynamics**
Figure 4 and Figure 7 depict the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. The curves for the proposed, baseline, and negative control 1 conditions coincide closely throughout training, with no condition demonstrating a clear divergence in learning speed or final performance. This visual evidence aligns with the statistical findings, suggesting that the consistency loss does not substantially alter the optimization trajectory in this regime.

**Summary of Findings**
Table 1 and Table 2 summarize the condition means and confidence intervals for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Table 3 and Table 4 present the outcome differences and registered decisions. In both cohorts, the confidence intervals include zero, and neither estimate exceeds the preregistered margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency in attention projections does not yield robust accuracy gains in subject-disjoint time-series classification. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This suggests that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class, contrary to the hypothesis that weight alignment across depth improves generalization.

**Interpretation of Null Result**
The inconclusive outcome indicates that the intervention did not achieve the predicted effect size. It is consistent with the possibility that the consistency loss is too weak to influence the learned representations meaningfully, or that the hypothesis itself is incorrect for this task. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment; regularizing weights does not guarantee that the resulting attention patterns are more stable or generalizable. The negative control results, which were similar to the baseline, suggest that the computational cost of the regularization term itself does not drive performance changes. This design does not establish the mechanism or prove the absence of implementation bias, but the recorded activity confirms the operator executed as specified.

**Mechanism and Alternatives**
A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that time-series data requires layer-specific specialization to capture multi-scale temporal features, making cross-layer consistency detrimental or neutral. An alternative explanation is that the coefficient of 0.01 was insufficient to overcome the classification objective's gradient, resulting in negligible regularization. However, the registered coefficient was chosen to prevent dominance, and increasing it might destabilize training. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds replicates the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. This confirms that the null result is stable under seed variation, but it does not generalize to other datasets or architectures.

**Relation to Cited Work**
These findings stand in contrast to works that report gains from cross-layer mechanisms in vision and language [15, 34]. However, those studies often operate in different data regimes or tasks, making direct comparison difficult. Our results align with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found inconclusive results for weight-based regularization in this setting [3]. They also support the caution raised in *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* regarding the validity of Transformer modifications for time series [5]. Unlike *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which reported improvements on machine translation [17], we find no evidence of benefit for subject-disjoint classification. This discrepancy may arise from the difference between sequence-to-sequence tasks and classification, or the nature of the consistency constraint.

**Implications for Practice**
For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence suggests that adding cross-layer query consistency loss is not justified by accuracy gains in this regime. The computational cost of the operator, while small, yields no measurable return. Future work should investigate whether stronger regularization or different alignment targets (e.g., attention maps rather than weights) produce different outcomes. Direct measurement of attention stability would be required to test the mechanistic hypothesis that weight alignment stabilizes attention.

=== limitations ===
This study has several limitations that constrain the interpretation of the results. First, the evaluation is limited to the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with a subject-disjoint split. While this supports a claim about unseen subjects within this corpus, it is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task, or deployment distribution. We do not call this out-of-distribution or domain generalisation in the broader sense. Second, we measure weight alignment, not attention-map stability. The hypothesis that weight regularization stabilizes attention is unmeasured; accuracy contrasts alone cannot prove attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization. Third, the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds replicates the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. This limits our ability to claim robustness across data distributions. Finally, the registered margin was derived from calibration noise, which reflects measurement precision but does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The results were inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This finding suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. For practitioners, this implies that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, and adding this regularization is not supported by the evidence. To settle the question next, future work should measure attention-map stability directly and test stronger regularization coefficients or alternative alignment targets on diverse subject-disjoint benchmarks.

payload.title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers

payload.user:
Related-work section:
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4, 20]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [11, 7]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [16].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [8, 18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [6, 12, 21]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15].

This study positions itself against these themes by focusing specifically on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers, distinguishing our work from forecasting tasks [4] and domain adaptation settings [10]. While cross-layer mechanisms have shown promise in vision and language [8, 19], their efficacy in subject-disjoint time-series classification remains unsettled. We build upon the verified findings of [1] by conducting a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to assess stability, addressing the lack of independent verification noted in the literature. Unlike works that propose new architectures [7, 14], we test a specific regularization operator within a fixed architecture to isolate the effect of cross-layer query consistency.

Cited papers and their abstracts:
[1] Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00133 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by -0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

[2] Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness
Abstract: [EDITORIAL NOTICE — RETRACTED: this paper carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it. Stated reason: The numerical outputs reported in this paper remain computationally reproducible: an independent re-run from the archived reproducibility bundle reproduced all eight aggregate metrics within tolerance. A post-publication audit of the artifact source found that the executed intervention did not implement the preregistered intervention. The preregistration committed to a multiplicative weight perturbation applied BEFORE the forward pass, an entropy term added to the training OBJECTIVE, and a noise scale learned by BACKPROPAGATION, with held-out evaluation on the clean weights. The experiment har. Its conclusions may not be relied on; cite it only with its status stated.] Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic training often fails to provide calibrated confidence under distribution shift. This study investigates whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We preregistered a hypothesis that entropy maximization would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the baseline, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the intervention across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results refuted the preregistered hypothesis in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by 0.04805 proportion (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002) relative to the baseline. The replication cohort confirmed this degradation with a contrast of -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Negative controls involving entropy minimization and fixed noise performed comparably to the deterministic baseline. These findings indicate that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over explicit entropy maximization for robustness tasks in this regime.

[3] Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning
Abstract: Regularization design for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. This study tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy compared to standard weight decay in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would exceed a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion in accuracy gain. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset, we evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and two negative controls across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results were inconclusive: the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0004419 (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], p=0.75) in the primary cohort and 0.002549 (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], p=0.106) in the replication cohort. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. These findings suggest that spectral entropy minimization of input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks.

[4] Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?
Abstract: Recently, there has been a surge of Transformer-based solutions for the long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) task. Despite the growing performance over the past few years, we question the validity of this line of research in this work. Specifically, Transformers is arguably the most successful solution to extract the semantic correlations among the elements in a long sequence. However, in time series modeling, we are to extract the temporal relations in an ordered set of continuous points. While employing positional encoding and using tokens to embed sub-series in Transformers facilitate preserving some ordering information, the nature of the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss. To validate our claim, we introduce a set of embarrassingly simple one-layer linear models named LTSF-Linear for comparison. Experimental results on nine real-life datasets show that LTSF-Linear surprisingly outperforms existing sophisticated Transformer-based LTSF models in all cases, and often by a large margin. Moreover, we conduct comprehensive empirical studies to explore the impacts of various design elements of LTSF models on their temporal relation extraction capability. We hope this surprising finding opens up new research directions for the LTSF task. We also advocate revisiting the validity of Transformer-based solutions for other time series analysis tasks (e.g., anomaly detection) in the future.

[5] Selective Attention Improves Transformer
Abstract: Unneeded elements in the attention’s context degrade performance. We introduce Selective Attention, a simple parameter-free change to the standard attention mechanism which reduces attention to unneeded elements. Selective attention consistently improves language modeling and downstream task performance in a variety of model sizes and context lengths. For example, transformers trained with the language modeling objective on C4 with selective attention perform language modeling equivalently to standard transformers with ~2X more heads and parameters in their attention modules. Selective attention also allows decreasing the size of the attention’s context buffer, leading to meaningful reductions in the memory and compute requirements during inference. For example, transformers trained on C4 with context sizes of 512, 1,024, and 2,048 need 16X, 25X, and 47X less memory for their attention module, respectively, when equipped with selective attention, as those without selective attention, with the same validation perplexity.

[6] A Survey on Vision Transformer
Abstract: Transformer, first applied to the field of natural language processing, is a type of deep neural network mainly based on the self-attention mechanism. Thanks to its strong representation capabilities, researchers are looking at ways to apply transformer to computer vision tasks. In a variety of visual benchmarks, transformer-based models perform similar to or better than other types of networks such as convolutional and recurrent neural networks. Given its high performance and less need for vision-specific inductive bias, transformer is receiving more and more attention from the computer vision community. In this paper, we review these vision transformer models by categorizing them in different tasks and analyzing their advantages and disadvantages. The main categories we explore include the backbone network, high/mid-level vision, low-level vision, and video processing. We also include efficient transformer methods for pushing transformer into real device-based applications. Furthermore, we also take a brief look at the self-attention mechanism in computer vision, as it is the base component in transformer. Toward the end of this paper, we discuss the challenges and provide several further research directions for vision transformers.

[7] Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer
Abstract: A reliable and efficient representation of multivariate time series is crucial in various downstream machine learning tasks. In multivariate time series forecasting, each variable depends on its historical values and there are inter-dependencies among variables as well. Models have to be designed to capture both intra- and inter-relationships among the time series. To move towards this goal, we propose the Time Series Attention Transformer (TSAT) for multivariate time series representation learning. Using TSAT, we represent both temporal information and inter-dependencies of multivariate time series in terms of edge-enhanced dynamic graphs. The intra-series correlations are represented by nodes in a dynamic graph; a self-attention mechanism is modified to capture the inter-series correlations by using the super-empirical mode decomposition (SMD) module. We applied the embedded dynamic graphs to times series forecasting problems, including two real-world datasets and two benchmark datasets. Extensive experiments show that TSAT clearly outerperforms six state-of-the-art baseline methods in various forecasting horizons. We further visualize the embedded dynamic graphs to illustrate the graph representation power of TSAT. We share our code at https://github.com/RadiantResearch/TSAT.

[8] Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention
Abstract: More and more evidence has shown that strengthening layer interactions can enhance the representation power of a deep neural network, while self-attention excels at learning interdependencies by retrieving query-activated information. Motivated by this, we devise a cross-layer attention mechanism, called multi-head recurrent layer attention (MRLA), that sends a query representation of the current layer to all previous layers to retrieve query-related information from different levels of receptive fields. A light-weighted version of MRLA is also proposed to reduce the quadratic computation cost. The proposed layer attention mechanism can enrich the representation power of many state-of-the-art vision networks, including CNNs and vision transformers. Its effectiveness has been extensively evaluated in image classification, object detection and instance segmentation tasks, where improvements can be consistently observed. For example, our MRLA can improve 1.6% Top-1 accuracy on ResNet-50, while only introducing 0.16M parameters and 0.07B FLOPs. Surprisingly, it can boost the performances by a large margin of 3-4% box AP and mask AP in dense prediction tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/joyfang1106/MRLA.

[9] Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks
Abstract: The large-scale and deep-layer deep neural network based on the Transformer model is very powerful in sequence tasks, but it is prone to overfitting for small-scale training data. Moreover, the prediction result of the model with a small disturbance input is significantly lower than that without disturbance. In this work, we propose a double consistency regularization (DOCR) method for the end-to-end model structure, which separately constrains the output of the encoder and decoder during the training process to alleviate the above problems. Specifically, on the basis of the cross-entropy loss function, we build the mean model by integrating the model parameters of the previous rounds and measure the consistency between the models by calculating the KL divergence between the features of the encoder output and the probability distribution of the decoder output of the mean model and the base model so as to impose regularization constraints on the solution space of the model. We conducted extensive experiments on machine translation tasks, and the results show that the BLEU score increased by 2.60 on average, demonstrating the effectiveness of DOCR in improving model performance and its complementary impacts with other regularization techniques.

[10] CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation
Abstract: While transformers have greatly boosted performance in semantic segmentation, domain adaptive transformers are not yet well explored. We identify that the domain gap can cause discrepancies in self-attention. Due to this gap, the transformer attends to spurious regions or pixels, which deteriorates accuracy on the target domain. We propose Cross-Domain Attention Consistency (CDAC), to perform adaptation on attention maps using cross-domain attention layers that share features between source and target domains. Specifically, we impose consistency between predictions from cross-domain attention and self-attention modules to encourage similar distributions across domains in both the attention and output of the model, i.e., attention-level and output-level alignment. We also enforce consistency in attention maps between different augmented views to further strengthen the attention-based alignment. Combining these two components, CDAC mitigates the discrepancy in attention maps across domains and further boosts the performance of the transformer under unsupervised domain adaptation settings. Our method is evaluated on various widely used benchmarks and outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines, including GTAV-to-Cityscapes by 1.3 and 1.5 percent point (pp) and Synthia-to-Cityscapes by 0.6 pp and 2.9 pp when combining with two competitive Transformer-based backbones, respectively. Our code will be publicly available at https://github.com/wangkaihong/CDAC.

[11] TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation
Abstract: Signal measurement appearing in the form of time series is one of the most common types of data used in medical machine learning applications. Such datasets are often small in size, expensive to collect and annotate, and might involve privacy issues, which hinders our ability to train large, state-of-the-art deep learning models for biomedical applications. For time-series data, the suite of data augmentation strategies we can use to expand the size of the dataset is limited by the need to maintain the basic properties of the signal. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) can be utilized as another data augmentation tool. In this paper, we present TTS-CGAN, a transformer-based conditional GAN model that can be trained on existing multi-class datasets and generate class-specific synthetic time-series sequences of arbitrary length. We elaborate on the model architecture and design strategies. Synthetic sequences generated by our model are indistinguishable from real ones, and can be used to complement or replace real signals of the same type, thus achieving the goal of data augmentation. To evaluate the quality of the generated data, we modify the wavelet coherence metric to be able to compare the similarity between two sets of signals, and also conduct a case study where a mix of synthetic and real data are used to train a deep learning model for sequence classification. Together with other visualization techniques and qualitative evaluation approaches, we demonstrate that TTS-CGAN generated synthetic data are similar to real data, and that our model performs better than the other state-of-the-art GAN models built for time-series data generation.

[12] Transformers in Vision: A Survey
Abstract: Astounding results from Transformer models on natural language tasks have intrigued the vision community to study their application to computer vision problems. Among their salient benefits, Transformers enable modeling long dependencies between input sequence elements and support parallel processing of sequence as compared to recurrent networks, e.g., Long short-term memory. Different from convolutional networks, Transformers require minimal inductive biases for their design and are naturally suited as set-functions. Furthermore, the straightforward design of Transformers allows processing multiple modalities (e.g., images, videos, text, and speech) using similar processing blocks and demonstrates excellent scalability to very large capacity networks and huge datasets. These strengths have led to exciting progress on a number of vision tasks using Transformer networks. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the Transformer models in the computer vision discipline. We start with an introduction to fundamental concepts behind the success of Transformers, i.e., self-attention, large-scale pre-training, and bidirectional feature encoding. We then cover extensive applications of transformers in vision including popular recognition tasks (e.g., image classification, object detection, action recognition, and segmentation), generative modeling, multi-modal tasks (e.g., visual-question answering, visual reasoning, and visual grounding), video processing (e.g., activity recognition, video forecasting), low-level vision (e.g., image super-resolution, image enhancement, and colorization), and three-dimensional analysis (e.g., point cloud classification and segmentation). We compare the respective advantages and limitations of popular techniques both in terms of architectural design and their experimental value. Finally, we provide an analysis on open research directions and possible future works. We hope this effort will ignite further interest in the community to solve current challenges toward the application of transformer models in computer vision.

[13] Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks
Abstract: Large pre-trained models have been vital in recent advancements in domains like language and vision, making model training for individual downstream tasks more efficient and provide superior performance. However, tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model from scratch leveraging training data and domain expertise specific to the task. We tackle a significant challenge for pre-training a foundational time-series model from multi-domain time-series datasets: extracting semantically useful tokenized inputs to the model across heterogeneous time-series from different domains. We propose Large Pre-trained Time-series Models (LPTM) that introduces a novel method of adaptive segmentation that automatically identifies optimal dataset-specific segmentation strategy during pre-training. This enables LPTM to perform similar to or better than domain-specific state-of-art model when fine-tuned to different downstream time-series analysis tasks and under zero-shot settings. LPTM achieves superior forecasting and time-series classification results taking up to 40% less data and 50% less training time compared to state-of-art baselines.

[14] Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification
Abstract: Abstract The rapid development of deep learning, especially the application of CNN and Transformer, brings a new direction for remote sensing scene classification. CNN is challenging to capture multi-scale features due to the limitation of the receptive field. Although the feature pyramid network (FPN) is a multi-scale structure, its fusion mechanism inherently limits the extraction of fine-grained information. The Transformer architecture excels at capturing long-range dependencies through its self-attention mechanism. While the multihead self-attention mechanism allows it to concentrate on both global and local patterns, there is still room for improvement in explicitly enhancing the extraction of local spatial features and edge detail information. To overcome the above limitations, this paper proposes a novel end-to-end learning model, called cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network (CLFETNet), for remote sensing scene classification. The innovative contribution of this paper is to embed three novel modules into the traditional CNN model. Firstly, we utilize the FPN to extract multi-scale features and design a fine feature aggregation module (RFA) to integrate complementary information from different layers to obtain more reliable and accurate features. Second, the efficient frequency transformer (EFT) is proposed to deeply mine global information, local spatial features, and edge detail information. Finally, the graph-aware fusion (GAF) module is proposed to model the relationships among regions in the feature graph by graph convolutional network (GCN), which enhances the intra-class feature consistency. A wide range of experiments have been carried out on three publicly accessible RS scene datasets. Positive results show that our CLFETNet framework outperforms many existing methods, has high robustness and superiority in remote sensing scene classification tasks, and can effectively handle complex scenes and meet multi-scale feature challenges.

[15] An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks
Abstract: Attention mechanisms have become a popular component in deep neural networks, yet there has been little examination of how different influencing factors and methods for computing attention from these factors affect performance. Toward a better general understanding of attention mechanisms, we present an empirical study that ablates various spatial attention elements within a generalized attention formulation, encompassing the dominant Transformer attention as well as the prevalent deformable convolution and dynamic convolution modules. Conducted on a variety of applications, the study yields significant findings about spatial attention in deep networks, some of which run counter to conventional understanding. For example, we find that the query and key content comparison in Transformer attention is negligible for self-attention, but vital for encoder-decoder attention. A proper combination of deformable convolution with key content only saliency achieves the best accuracy-efficiency tradeoff in self-attention. Our results suggest that there exists much room for improvement in the design of attention mechanisms.

[16] Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning
Abstract: The recent breakthrough of Transformers in deep learning has drawn significant attention of the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies. However, like other deep learning models, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding, generalization challenges, and data shift issues for the domains with limited data. Additionally, addressing the issue of catastrophic forgetting, where models forget previously learned information when exposed to new data, is another critical aspect that requires attention in enhancing the robustness of Transformers for time series tasks. To address these limitations, in this paper, we pre-train the time series Transformer model on a source domain with sufficient data and fine-tune it on the target domain with limited data. We introduce the \emph{One-step fine-tuning} approach, adding some percentage of source domain data to the target domains, providing the model with diverse time series instances. We then fine-tune the pre-trained model using a gradual unfreezing technique. This helps enhance the model's performance in time series prediction for domains with limited data. Extensive experimental results on two real-world datasets show that our approach improves over the state-of-the-art baselines by 4.35% and 11.54% for indoor temperature and wind power prediction, respectively.

[17] Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks
Abstract: Attention mechanisms, especially self-attention, have played an increasingly important role in deep feature representation for visual tasks. Self-attention updates the feature at each position by computing a weighted sum of features using pair-wise affinities across all positions to capture the long-range dependency within a single sample. However, self-attention has quadratic complexity and ignores potential correlation between different samples. This article proposes a novel attention mechanism which we call external attention, based on two external, small, learnable, shared memories, which can be implemented easily by simply using two cascaded linear layers and two normalization layers; it conveniently replaces self-attention in existing popular architectures. External attention has linear complexity and implicitly considers the correlations between all data samples. We further incorporate the multi-head mechanism into external attention to provide an all-MLP architecture, external attention MLP (EAMLP), for image classification. Extensive experiments on image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, image generation, and point cloud analysis reveal that our method provides results comparable or superior to the self-attention mechanism and some of its variants, with much lower computational and memory costs.

[18] Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency
Abstract: Activation engineering enables precise control over Large Language Models (LLMs) without the computational cost of fine-tuning. However, existing methods deriving vectors from static activation differences are susceptible to high-dimensional noise and layer-wise semantic drift, often capturing spurious correlations rather than the target intent. To address this, we propose Global Evolutionary Refined Steering (GER-steer), a training-free framework that grounded in the geometric stability of the network's representation evolution. GER-steer exploits this global signal to rectify raw steering vectors, effectively decoupling robust semantic intent from orthogonal artifacts. Extensive evaluations confirm that GER-steer consistently outperforms baselines, delivering superior efficacy and generalization without layer-specific tuning, establishing a universal solution for reliable model alignment.

[19] Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models
Abstract: Self-attention selects information freely across the sequence, but across depth, Transformers merely add each layer's output to the residual stream, so later layers cannot selectively reuse earlier-layer representations. Recent cross-layer methods improve this flow but operate on hidden states outside attention, adding state beyond the key-value cache at inference--a cost that becomes increasingly salient as modern LLMs compress the cache with grouped-query and multi-head latent attention. We introduce Depth-Attention, which performs this selection inside the attention module itself: before a layer attends over the sequence, its query attends over the keys of earlier layers at the same token position and mixes their values into the value that self-attention then reads. Because Depth-Attention reuses the standard attention queries, keys, and value-cache slots, storing depth-mixed values in place of the original values, it adds no parameters and introduces no persistent inference state beyond the standard key-value cache--the same cache size as a vanilla decoder and less than hidden-state-based cross-layer methods. On Qwen3-style decoders at 1.5B and 3B parameters, Depth-Attention attains the lowest perplexity and the highest average downstream accuracy, improving over the vanilla Transformer by up to 2.3 accuracy points and surpassing strong cross-layer baselines in perplexity and average accuracy, while adding under 0.01% extra arithmetic FLOPs and no additional persistent inference state. The gains hold from 360M to 3B parameters and extend to looped Transformers.

[20] Transformers in Time Series: A Survey
Abstract: Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications. In this paper, we systematically review Transformer schemes for time series modeling by highlighting their strengths as well as limitations. In particular, we examine the development of time series Transformers in two perspectives. From the perspective of network structure, we summarize the adaptations and modifications that have been made to Transformers in order to accommodate the challenges in time series analysis. From the perspective of applications, we categorize time series Transformers based on common tasks including forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification. Empirically, we perform robust analysis, model size analysis, and seasonal-trend decomposition analysis to study how Transformers perform in time series. Finally, we discuss and suggest future directions to provide useful research guidance. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first work to comprehensively and systematically summarize the recent advances of Transformers for modeling time series data. We hope this survey will ignite further research interests in time series Transformers.

[21] A survey of transformers

Related-work section:
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4, 20]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [11, 7]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [16].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [8, 18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [6, 12, 21]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15].

This study positions itself against these themes by focusing specifically on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers, distinguishing our work from forecasting tasks [4] and domain adaptation settings [10]. While cross-layer mechanisms have shown promise in vision and language [8, 19], their efficacy in subject-disjoint time-series classification remains unsettled. We build upon the verified findings of [1] by conducting a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to assess stability, addressing the lack of independent verification noted in the literature. Unlike works that propose new architectures [7, 14], we test a specific regularization operator within a fixed architecture to isolate the effect of cross-layer query consistency.

[1] Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00133 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by -0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

Abstract: Recently, there has been a surge of Transformer-based solutions for the long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) task. Despite the growing performance over the past few years, we question the validity of this line of research in this work. Specifically, Transformers is arguably the most successful solution to extract the semantic correlations among the elements in a long sequence. However, in time series modeling, we are to extract the temporal relations in an ordered set of continuous points. While employing positional encoding and using tokens to embed sub-series in Transformers facilitate preserving some ordering information, the nature of the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss. To validate our claim, we introduce a set of embarrassingly simple one-layer linear models named LTSF-Linear for comparison. Experimental results on nine real-life datasets show that LTSF-Linear surprisingly outperforms existing sophisticated Transformer-based LTSF models in all cases, and often by a large margin. Moreover, we conduct comprehensive empirical studies to explore the impacts of various design elements of LTSF models on their temporal relation extraction capability. We hope this surprising finding opens up new research directions for the LTSF task. We also advocate revisiting the validity of Transformer-based solutions for other time series analysis tasks (e.g., anomaly detection) in the future.

Abstract: Unneeded elements in the attention’s context degrade performance. We introduce Selective Attention, a simple parameter-free change to the standard attention mechanism which reduces attention to unneeded elements. Selective attention consistently improves language modeling and downstream task performance in a variety of model sizes and context lengths. For example, transformers trained with the language modeling objective on C4 with selective attention perform language modeling equivalently to standard transformers with ~2X more heads and parameters in their attention modules. Selective attention also allows decreasing the size of the attention’s context buffer, leading to meaningful reductions in the memory and compute requirements during inference. For example, transformers trained on C4 with context sizes of 512, 1,024, and 2,048 need 16X, 25X, and 47X less memory for their attention module, respectively, when equipped with selective attention, as those without selective attention, with the same validation perplexity.

Abstract: A reliable and efficient representation of multivariate time series is crucial in various downstream machine learning tasks. The intra-series correlations are represented by nodes in a dynamic graph; a self-attention mechanism is modified to capture the inter-series correlations by using the super-empirical mode decomposition (SMD) module. We applied the embedded dynamic graphs to times series forecasting problems, including two real-world datasets and two benchmark datasets. Extensive experiments show that TSAT clearly outerperforms six state-of-the-art baseline methods in various forecasting horizons. Specifically, on the basis of the cross-entropy loss function, we build the mean model by integrating the model parameters of the previous rounds and measure the consistency between the models by calculating the KL divergence between the features of the encoder output and the probability distribution of the decoder output of the mean model and the base model so as to impose regularization constraints on the solution space of the model. Specifically, we impose consistency between predictions from cross-domain attention and self-attention modules to encourage similar distributions across domains in both the attention and output of the model, i.e., attention-level and output-level alignment. We also enforce consistency in attention maps between different augmented views to further strengthen the attention-based alignment. Combining these two components, CDAC mitigates the discrepancy in attention maps across domains and further boosts the performance of the transformer under unsupervised domain adaptation settings. Our method is evaluated on various widely used benchmarks and outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines, including GTAV-to-Cityscapes by 1.3 and 1.5 percent point (pp) and Synthia-to-Cityscapes by 0.6 pp and 2.9 pp when combining with two competitive Transformer-based backbones, respectively. Abstract: Signal measurement appearing in the form of time series is one of the most common types of data used in medical machine learning applications. We elaborate on the model architecture and design strategies. Synthetic sequences generated by our model are indistinguishable from real ones, and can be used to complement or replace real signals of the same type, thus achieving the goal of data augmentation. Together with other visualization techniques and qualitative evaluation approaches, we demonstrate that TTS-CGAN generated synthetic data are similar to real data, and that our model performs better than the other state-of-the-art GAN models built for time-series data generation.

[12] Transformers in Vision: A Survey
Abstract: Astounding results from Transformer models on natural language tasks have intrigued the vision community to study their application to computer vision problems. Among their salient benefits, Transformers enable modeling long dependencies between input sequence elements and support parallel processing of sequence as compared to recurrent networks, e.g., Long short-term memory. Different from convolutional networks, Transformers require minimal inductive biases for their design and are naturally suited as set-functions. Furthermore, the straightforward design of Transformers allows processing multiple modalities (e.g., images, videos, text, and speech) using similar processing blocks and demonstrates excellent scalability to very large capacity networks and huge datasets. These strengths have led to exciting progress on a number of vision tasks using Transformer networks. We start with an introduction to fundamental concepts behind the success of Transformers, i.e., self-attention, large-scale pre-training, and bidirectional feature encoding. We then cover extensive applications of transformers in vision including popular recognition tasks (e.g., image classification, object detection, action recognition, and segmentation), generative modeling, multi-modal tasks (e.g., visual-question answering, visual reasoning, and visual grounding), video processing (e.g., activity recognition, video forecasting), low-level vision (e.g., image super-resolution, image enhancement, and colorization), and three-dimensional analysis (e.g., point cloud classification and segmentation). We compare the respective advantages and limitations of popular techniques both in terms of architectural design and their experimental value. Finally, we provide an analysis on open research directions and possible future works. We hope this effort will ignite further interest in the community to solve current challenges toward the application of transformer models in computer vision.

Abstract: Large pre-trained models have been vital in recent advancements in domains like language and vision, making model training for individual downstream tasks more efficient and provide superior performance. This enables LPTM to perform similar to or better than domain-specific state-of-art model when fine-tuned to different downstream time-series analysis tasks and under zero-shot settings. LPTM achieves superior forecasting and time-series classification results taking up to 40% less data and 50% less training time compared to state-of-art baselines.

Abstract: Abstract The rapid development of deep learning, especially the application of CNN and Transformer, brings a new direction for remote sensing scene classification. CNN is challenging to capture multi-scale features due to the limitation of the receptive field. Although the feature pyramid network (FPN) is a multi-scale structure, its fusion mechanism inherently limits the extraction of fine-grained information. The Transformer architecture excels at capturing long-range dependencies through its self-attention mechanism. While the multihead self-attention mechanism allows it to concentrate on both global and local patterns, there is still room for improvement in explicitly enhancing the extraction of local spatial features and edge detail information. To overcome the above limitations, this paper proposes a novel end-to-end learning model, called cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network (CLFETNet), for remote sensing scene classification. The innovative contribution of this paper is to embed three novel modules into the traditional CNN model. Firstly, we utilize the FPN to extract multi-scale features and design a fine feature aggregation module (RFA) to integrate complementary information from different layers to obtain more reliable and accurate features. Second, the efficient frequency transformer (EFT) is proposed to deeply mine global information, local spatial features, and edge detail information. Finally, the graph-aware fusion (GAF) module is proposed to model the relationships among regions in the feature graph by graph convolutional network (GCN), which enhances the intra-class feature consistency. A wide range of experiments have been carried out on three publicly accessible RS scene datasets. Positive results show that our CLFETNet framework outperforms many existing methods, has high robustness and superiority in remote sensing scene classification tasks, and can effectively handle complex scenes and meet multi-scale feature challenges.

Abstract: Attention mechanisms have become a popular component in deep neural networks, yet there has been little examination of how different influencing factors and methods for computing attention from these factors affect performance.
