Conducted on a variety of applications, the study yields significant findings about spatial attention in deep networks, some of which run counter to conventional understanding. For example, we find that the query and key content comparison in Transformer attention is negligible for self-attention, but vital for encoder-decoder attention. A proper combination of deformable convolution with key content only saliency achieves the best accuracy-efficiency tradeoff in self-attention. Our results suggest that there exists much room for improvement in the design of attention mechanisms.

[16] Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning
Abstract: The recent breakthrough of Transformers in deep learning has drawn significant attention of the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies. However, like other deep learning models, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding, generalization challenges, and data shift issues for the domains with limited data. Additionally, addressing the issue of catastrophic forgetting, where models forget previously learned information when exposed to new data, is another critical aspect that requires attention in enhancing the robustness of Transformers for time series tasks. To address these limitations, in this paper, we pre-train the time series Transformer model on a source domain with sufficient data and fine-tune it on the target domain with limited data. We introduce the \emph{One-step fine-tuning} approach, adding some percentage of source domain data to the target domains, providing the model with diverse time series instances. We then fine-tune the pre-trained model using a gradual unfreezing technique. This helps enhance the model's performance in time series prediction for domains with limited data. Extensive experimental results on two real-world datasets show that our approach improves over the state-of-the-art baselines by 4.35% and 11.54% for indoor temperature and wind power prediction, respectively.

[17] Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks
Abstract: Attention mechanisms, especially self-attention, have played an increasingly important role in deep feature representation for visual tasks. Self-attention updates the feature at each position by computing a weighted sum of features using pair-wise affinities across all positions to capture the long-range dependency within a single sample. However, self-attention has quadratic complexity and ignores potential correlation between different samples. This article proposes a novel attention mechanism which we call external attention, based on two external, small, learnable, shared memories, which can be implemented easily by simply using two cascaded linear layers and two normalization layers; it conveniently replaces self-attention in existing popular architectures. External attention has linear complexity and implicitly considers the correlations between all data samples. We further incorporate the multi-head mechanism into external attention to provide an all-MLP architecture, external attention MLP (EAMLP), for image classification. Extensive experiments on image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, image generation, and point cloud analysis reveal that our method provides results comparable or superior to the self-attention mechanism and some of its variants, with much lower computational and memory costs.

[18] Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency
Abstract: Activation engineering enables precise control over Large Language Models (LLMs) without the computational cost of fine-tuning. However, existing methods deriving vectors from static activation differences are susceptible to high-dimensional noise and layer-wise semantic drift, often capturing spurious correlations rather than the target intent. To address this, we propose Global Evolutionary Refined Steering (GER-steer), a training-free framework that grounded in the geometric stability of the network's representation evolution. GER-steer exploits this global signal to rectify raw steering vectors, effectively decoupling robust semantic intent from orthogonal artifacts. Extensive evaluations confirm that GER-steer consistently outperforms baselines, delivering superior efficacy and generalization without layer-specific tuning, establishing a universal solution for reliable model alignment.

Abstract: Self-attention selects information freely across the sequence, but across depth, Transformers merely add each layer's output to the residual stream, so later layers cannot selectively reuse earlier-layer representations. Recent cross-layer methods improve this flow but operate on hidden states outside attention, adding state beyond the key-value cache at inference--a cost that becomes increasingly salient as modern LLMs compress the cache with grouped-query and multi-head latent attention. We introduce Depth-Attention, which performs this selection inside the attention module itself: before a layer attends over the sequence, its query attends over the keys of earlier layers at the same token position and mixes their values into the value that self-attention then reads. Because Depth-Attention reuses the standard attention queries, keys, and value-cache slots, storing depth-mixed values in place of the original values, it adds no parameters and introduces no persistent inference state beyond the standard key-value cache--the same cache size as a vanilla decoder and less than hidden-state-based cross-layer methods. On Qwen3-style decoders at 1.5B and 3B parameters, Depth-Attention attains the lowest perplexity and the highest average downstream accuracy, improving over the vanilla Transformer by up to 2.3 accuracy points and surpassing strong cross-layer baselines in perplexity and average accuracy, while adding under 0.01% extra arithmetic FLOPs and no additional persistent inference state. [20] Transformers in Time Series: A Survey
Abstract: Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications. In this paper, we systematically review Transformer schemes for time series modeling by highlighting their strengths as well as limitations. In particular, we examine the development of time series Transformers in two perspectives. From the perspective of network structure, we summarize the adaptations and modifications that have been made to Transformers in order to accommodate the challenges in time series analysis. From the perspective of applications, we categorize time series Transformers based on common tasks including forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification. Empirically, we perform robust analysis, model size analysis, and seasonal-trend decomposition analysis to study how Transformers perform in time series. Finally, we discuss and suggest future directions to provide useful research guidance. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first work to comprehensively and systematically summarize the recent advances of Transformers for modeling time series data. We hope this survey will ignite further research interests in time series Transformers.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [8, 18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [6, 12, 21]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15].

This study positions itself against these themes by focusing specifically on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers, distinguishing our work from forecasting tasks [4] and domain adaptation settings [10]. While cross-layer mechanisms have shown promise in vision and language [8, 19], their efficacy in subject-disjoint time-series classification remains unsettled. We build upon the verified findings of [1] by conducting a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to assess stability, addressing the lack of independent verification noted in the literature. Unlike works that propose new architectures [7, 14], we test a specific regularization operator within a fixed architecture to isolate the effect of cross-layer query consistency.
Method: The core of this experiment is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces weight alignment between attention query projections across transformer blocks. The hypothesis motivating this operator is that stabilizing attention patterns across depth may improve generalization to unseen subjects by reducing overfitting to subject-specific temporal features. The operator applies a Frobenius norm consistency regularization between the query projection weights of block 0 and block 1. Specifically, the loss term is computed as the squared element-wise difference between the target weights (block 1) and the reference weights (block 0), scaled by a fixed coefficient.

**Operator Design and Hypothesis**
The intervention adds a loss term during training that penalizes divergence between deeper and shallower query projections. This design choice reflects the hypothesis that consistent attention mechanisms across layers provide a more robust inductive bias for time-series data, where temporal dependencies may be captured effectively without layer-specific specialization. The reference weights from block 0 are detached from the gradient graph, ensuring that the consistency penalty only updates the target parameters in block 1. This prevents the regularization from altering the shallower layer's task-loss gradients, isolating the effect to the deeper layer's adaptation toward the shallower representation.

The comparator neutralizes this intervention by executing the identical code path but returning a zero loss term. This control arm ensures that any observed difference in accuracy is attributable to the consistency loss itself rather than implementation artifacts or computational overhead. Both conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters, ensuring that variance due to random initialization is controlled.

**Negative Control**
To verify that the observed effect (or lack thereof) is. This experiment did not test whether this was due to the meaningful cross-layer relationship rather than the mere presence of a regularization term, we include a negative control. This condition penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the computational cost and gradient flow of the proposed condition. If the proposed condition outperforms this negative control, it suggests that the specific alignment to block 0 is beneficial; if not, the regularization itself may be inert or detrimental.

**Gradient Handling**
A critical aspect of the operator specification is the handling of gradients. Detaching the reference tensor inside the penalty stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. This distinction is vital for interpreting the results: the shallower layer continues to learn from the classification objective, while the deeper layer is constrained to remain close to it. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient, so we rely on the registered coefficient of 0.01 to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective.

**Decision Rule**
The registered decision rule requires the lower confidence bound of the paired contrast to exceed the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This strict criterion ensures that we do not claim a positive effect unless the uncertainty model excludes gains smaller than the target magnitude. The analysis distinguishes between detecting a non-zero effect and exceeding the margin; a confidence interval crossing zero indicates an inconclusive result regarding the direction of the effect, regardless of the margin.

**Algorithm Specification**
The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. The combined objective is differentiated, and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The algorithm retrieves reference weights, detaches them, computes the element-wise difference, squares the elements, sums them, and scales by the coefficient. This process is repeated for every seed and condition, with the harness recording operator activity to ensure compliance with the preregistration.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. This choice is critical because the research question concerns generalization to unseen subjects, not merely held-out windows from the same individuals. A random split would allow the model to learn subject-specific movement styles or sensor characteristics, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to answer the open problem. By holding out entire subjects, we ensure that the evaluation reflects the model's ability to generalize across different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. This design supports a claim about unseen subjects but is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task, or deployment distribution.

**Seed Pairing and Variance Control**
We pair conditions by seed, meaning the proposed condition and the baseline are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. This pairing reduces variance. This experiment did not test whether this was due to random initialization and data ordering, increasing the power to detect small effects. The analysis uses 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. This seed budget allows us to estimate the stability of the result under fresh sampling without conflating seed variance with subject variance.

**Negative Control Purpose**
The first negative control penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. This condition is intended to test the alternative explanation that any regularization term, regardless of its target, improves generalization by simply adding noise or constraint. If the proposed condition performs similarly to this negative control, it suggests that the specific cross-layer alignment is not the active ingredient. The observed contrast between the proposed condition and this negative control supports or refutes the hypothesis that meaningful cross-layer relationships are necessary for any benefit.

**Replication Cohort Design**
The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds serves as a verification of the experimental run's stability under fresh sampling. This is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, but a verification that the primary result is not an artifact of the specific seed set used. By running the same pipeline on a disjoint set of seeds, we assess whether the inconclusive primary result holds under repeated sampling. This design distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations.

**Measurement and Power**
The outcome measure is held-out classification accuracy, defined as the number of correct activity predictions divided by 2,947 windows in the official subject-disjoint test split. The planning target power was 90% with a planning SD of 0.0250196. The registered margin of 0.0125098 proportion was derived from calibration noise, reflecting measurement precision rather than practical importance. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance, but it provides a consistent decision rule for the study.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Results: We report the results for the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohorts separately, adhering to the preregistered decision rules. The analysis focuses on held-out classification accuracy, with all estimates accompanied by bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.

**Primary Cohort**
In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). As shown in Figure 2, the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), compared to 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]) for the baseline. The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 3 displays the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions, with the 95% confidence interval clearly including zero. The green dash-dot marker in Figure 3 indicates the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion; the lower confidence bound does not exceed this threshold. Consequently, the preregistered decision for the primary cohort is inconclusive.

**Replication Cohort**
In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), compared to 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]) for the baseline. The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]). Figure 6 illustrates the mean difference, with the 95% confidence interval again including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. The preregistered decision for the replication cohort is also inconclusive.

**Training Dynamics**
Figure 4 and Figure 7 depict the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. The curves for the proposed, baseline, and negative control 1 conditions coincide closely throughout training, with no condition demonstrating a clear divergence in learning speed or final performance. This visual evidence aligns with the statistical findings, suggesting that the consistency loss does not substantially alter the optimization trajectory in this regime.

**Summary of Findings**
Table 1 and Table 2 summarize the condition means and confidence intervals for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Table 3 and Table 4 present the outcome differences and registered decisions. In both cohorts, the confidence intervals include zero, and neither estimate exceeds the preregistered margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This study tested whether cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The results were inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This finding suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. For practitioners, this implies that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, and adding this regularization is not supported by the evidence. To settle the question next, future work should measure attention-map stability directly and test stronger regularization coefficients or alternative alignment targets on diverse subject-disjoint benchmarks.
Discussion: The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency in attention projections does not yield robust accuracy gains in subject-disjoint time-series classification. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This suggests that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class, contrary to the hypothesis that weight alignment across depth improves generalization.

**Interpretation of Null Result**
The inconclusive outcome indicates that the intervention did not achieve the predicted effect size. It is consistent with the possibility that the consistency loss is too weak to influence the learned representations meaningfully, or that the hypothesis itself is incorrect for this task. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment; regularizing weights does not guarantee that the resulting attention patterns are more stable or generalizable. The negative control results, which were similar to the baseline, suggest that the computational cost of the regularization term itself does not drive performance changes. This design does not establish the mechanism or prove the absence of implementation bias, but the recorded activity confirms the operator executed as specified.

**Mechanism and Alternatives**
A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that time-series data requires layer-specific specialization to capture multi-scale temporal features, making cross-layer consistency detrimental or neutral. An alternative explanation is that the coefficient of 0.01 was insufficient to overcome the classification objective's gradient, resulting in negligible regularization. However, the registered coefficient was chosen to prevent dominance, and increasing it might destabilize training. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds replicates the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. This confirms that the null result is stable under seed variation, but it does not generalize to other datasets or architectures.

**Relation to Cited Work**
These findings stand in contrast to works that report gains from cross-layer mechanisms in vision and language [8, 18]. However, those studies often operate in different data regimes or tasks, making direct comparison difficult. Our results align with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found inconclusive results for weight-based regularization in this setting [3]. They also support the caution raised in *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* regarding the validity of Transformer modifications for time series [4]. Unlike *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which reported improvements on machine translation [9], we find no evidence of benefit for subject-disjoint classification. This discrepancy may arise from the difference between sequence-to-sequence tasks and classification, or the nature of the consistency constraint.

**Implications for Practice**
For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence suggests that adding cross-layer query consistency loss is not justified by accuracy gains in this regime. The computational cost of the operator, while small, yields no measurable return. Future work should investigate whether stronger regularization or different alignment targets (e.g., attention maps rather than weights) produce different outcomes. Direct measurement of attention stability would be required to test the mechanistic hypothesis that weight alignment stabilizes attention.
Limitations: This study has several limitations that constrain the interpretation of the results. First, the evaluation is limited to the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with a subject-disjoint split. While this supports a claim about unseen subjects within this corpus, it is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task, or deployment distribution. We do not call this out-of-distribution or domain generalisation in the broader sense. Second, we measure weight alignment, not attention-map stability. The hypothesis that weight regularization stabilizes attention is unmeasured; accuracy contrasts alone cannot prove attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization. Third, the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds replicates the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. This limits our ability to claim robustness across data distributions. Finally, the registered margin was derived from calibration noise, which reflects measurement precision but does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0007734 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.001957 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4, 20]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [11, 7]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [16].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [8, 18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [6, 12, 21]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15].

This study positions itself against these themes by focusing specifically on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers, distinguishing our work from forecasting tasks [4] and domain adaptation settings [10]. While cross-layer mechanisms have shown promise in vision and language [8, 19], their efficacy in subject-disjoint time-series classification remains unsettled. We build upon the verified findings of [1] by conducting a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to assess stability, addressing the lack of independent verification noted in the literature. Unlike works that propose new architectures [7, 14], we test a specific regularization operator within a fixed architecture to isolate the effect of cross-layer query consistency.
Method: The core of this experiment is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces weight alignment between attention query projections across transformer blocks. The hypothesis motivating this operator is that stabilizing attention patterns across depth may improve generalization to unseen subjects by reducing overfitting to subject-specific temporal features. The operator applies a Frobenius norm consistency regularization between the query projection weights of block 0 and block 1. Specifically, the loss term is computed as the squared element-wise difference between the target weights (block 1) and the reference weights (block 0), scaled by a fixed coefficient.

**Operator Design and Hypothesis**
The intervention adds a loss term during training that penalizes divergence between deeper and shallower query projections. This design choice reflects the hypothesis that consistent attention mechanisms across layers provide a more robust inductive bias for time-series data, where temporal dependencies may be captured effectively without layer-specific specialization. The reference weights from block 0 are detached from the gradient graph, ensuring that the consistency penalty only updates the target parameters in block 1. This prevents the regularization from altering the shallower layer's task-loss gradients, isolating the effect to the deeper layer's adaptation toward the shallower representation.

The comparator neutralizes this intervention by executing the identical code path but returning a zero loss term. This control arm ensures that any observed difference in accuracy is attributable to the consistency loss itself rather than implementation artifacts or computational overhead. Both conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters, ensuring that variance due to random initialization is controlled.

**Negative Control**
To verify that the observed effect (or lack thereof) is. This experiment did not test whether this was due to the meaningful cross-layer relationship rather than the mere presence of a regularization term, we include a negative control. This condition penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the computational cost and gradient flow of the proposed condition. If the proposed condition outperforms this negative control, it suggests that the specific alignment to block 0 is beneficial; if not, the regularization itself may be inert or detrimental.

**Gradient Handling**
A critical aspect of the operator specification is the handling of gradients. Detaching the reference tensor inside the penalty stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. This distinction is vital for interpreting the results: the shallower layer continues to learn from the classification objective, while the deeper layer is constrained to remain close to it. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient, so we rely on the registered coefficient of 0.01 to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective.

**Decision Rule**
The registered decision rule requires the lower confidence bound of the paired contrast to exceed the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This strict criterion ensures that we do not claim a positive effect unless the uncertainty model excludes gains smaller than the target magnitude. The analysis distinguishes between detecting a non-zero effect and exceeding the margin; a confidence interval crossing zero indicates an inconclusive result regarding the direction of the effect, regardless of the margin.

**Algorithm Specification**
The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. The combined objective is differentiated, and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The algorithm retrieves reference weights, detaches them, computes the element-wise difference, squares the elements, sums them, and scales by the coefficient. This process is repeated for every seed and condition, with the harness recording operator activity to ensure compliance with the preregistration.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Experimental setup: **Subject-Disjoint Split Justification**
The experimental design employs an official subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset. This choice is critical because the research question concerns generalization to unseen subjects, not merely held-out windows from the same individuals. A random split would allow the model to learn subject-specific movement styles or sensor characteristics, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to answer the open problem. By holding out entire subjects, we ensure that the evaluation reflects the model's ability to generalize across different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. This design supports a claim about unseen subjects but is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task, or deployment distribution.

**Seed Pairing and Variance Control**
We pair conditions by seed, meaning the proposed condition and the baseline are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. This pairing reduces variance. This experiment did not test whether this was due to random initialization and data ordering, increasing the power to detect small effects. The analysis uses 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. This seed budget allows us to estimate the stability of the result under fresh sampling without conflating seed variance with subject variance.

**Negative Control Purpose**
The first negative control penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. This condition is intended to test the alternative explanation that any regularization term, regardless of its target, improves generalization by simply adding noise or constraint. If the proposed condition performs similarly to this negative control, it suggests that the specific cross-layer alignment is not the active ingredient. The observed contrast between the proposed condition and this negative control supports or refutes the hypothesis that meaningful cross-layer relationships are necessary for any benefit.

**Replication Cohort Design**
The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds serves as a verification of the experimental run's stability under fresh sampling. This is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, but a verification that the primary result is not an artifact of the specific seed set used. By running the same pipeline on a disjoint set of seeds, we assess whether the inconclusive primary result holds under repeated sampling. This design distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations.

**Measurement and Power**
The outcome measure is held-out classification accuracy, defined as the number of correct activity predictions divided by 2,947 windows in the official subject-disjoint test split. The planning target power was 90% with a planning SD of 0.0250196. The registered margin of 0.0125098 proportion was derived from calibration noise, reflecting measurement precision rather than practical importance. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance, but it provides a consistent decision rule for the study.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Registered conditions.
- Proposed condition: Server-bound target blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight has stored tensor shape (64, 64). Add loss term that applies Frobenius norm consistency regularization to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Baseline: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. Recorded activity — primary: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity.

Results: We report the results for the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohorts separately, adhering to the preregistered decision rules. The analysis focuses on held-out classification accuracy, with all estimates accompanied by bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.

**Primary Cohort**
In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). As shown in Figure 2, the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), compared to 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]) for the baseline. The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 3 displays the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions, with the 95% confidence interval clearly including zero. The green dash-dot marker in Figure 3 indicates the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion; the lower confidence bound does not exceed this threshold. Consequently, the preregistered decision for the primary cohort is inconclusive.

**Replication Cohort**
In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), compared to 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]) for the baseline. The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]). Figure 6 illustrates the mean difference, with the 95% confidence interval again including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. The preregistered decision for the replication cohort is also inconclusive.

**Training Dynamics**
Figure 4 and Figure 7 depict the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. The curves for the proposed, baseline, and negative control 1 conditions coincide closely throughout training, with no condition demonstrating a clear divergence in learning speed or final performance. This visual evidence aligns with the statistical findings, suggesting that the consistency loss does not substantially alter the optimization trajectory in this regime.

**Summary of Findings**
Table 1 and Table 2 summarize the condition means and confidence intervals for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Table 3 and Table 4 present the outcome differences and registered decisions. In both cohorts, the confidence intervals include zero, and neither estimate exceeds the preregistered margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This study tested whether cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The results were inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This finding suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. For practitioners, this implies that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, and adding this regularization is not supported by the evidence. To settle the question next, future work should measure attention-map stability directly and test stronger regularization coefficients or alternative alignment targets on diverse subject-disjoint benchmarks.
Discussion: The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency in attention projections does not yield robust accuracy gains in subject-disjoint time-series classification. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This suggests that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class, contrary to the hypothesis that weight alignment across depth improves generalization.

**Interpretation of Null Result**
The inconclusive outcome indicates that the intervention did not achieve the predicted effect size. It is consistent with the possibility that the consistency loss is too weak to influence the learned representations meaningfully, or that the hypothesis itself is incorrect for this task. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment; regularizing weights does not guarantee that the resulting attention patterns are more stable or generalizable. The negative control results, which were similar to the baseline, suggest that the computational cost of the regularization term itself does not drive performance changes. This design does not establish the mechanism or prove the absence of implementation bias, but the recorded activity confirms the operator executed as specified.

**Mechanism and Alternatives**
A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that time-series data requires layer-specific specialization to capture multi-scale temporal features, making cross-layer consistency detrimental or neutral. An alternative explanation is that the coefficient of 0.01 was insufficient to overcome the classification objective's gradient, resulting in negligible regularization. However, the registered coefficient was chosen to prevent dominance, and increasing it might destabilize training. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds replicates the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. This confirms that the null result is stable under seed variation, but it does not generalize to other datasets or architectures.

**Relation to Cited Work**
These findings stand in contrast to works that report gains from cross-layer mechanisms in vision and language [8, 18]. However, those studies often operate in different data regimes or tasks, making direct comparison difficult. Our results align with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found inconclusive results for weight-based regularization in this setting [3]. They also support the caution raised in *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* regarding the validity of Transformer modifications for time series [4]. Unlike *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which reported improvements on machine translation [9], we find no evidence of benefit for subject-disjoint classification. This discrepancy may arise from the difference between sequence-to-sequence tasks and classification, or the nature of the consistency constraint.

**Implications for Practice**
For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence suggests that adding cross-layer query consistency loss is not justified by accuracy gains in this regime. The computational cost of the operator, while small, yields no measurable return. Future work should investigate whether stronger regularization or different alignment targets (e.g., attention maps rather than weights) produce different outcomes. Direct measurement of attention stability would be required to test the mechanistic hypothesis that weight alignment stabilizes attention.
Limitations: This study has several limitations that constrain the interpretation of the results. First, the evaluation is limited to the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with a subject-disjoint split. While this supports a claim about unseen subjects within this corpus, it is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task, or deployment distribution. We do not call this out-of-distribution or domain generalisation in the broader sense. Second, we measure weight alignment, not attention-map stability. The hypothesis that weight regularization stabilizes attention is unmeasured; accuracy contrasts alone cannot prove attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization. Third, the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds replicates the experimental run itself using a fresh set of random seeds through the same pipeline, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets. This limits our ability to claim robustness across data distributions. Finally, the registered margin was derived from calibration noise, which reflects measurement precision but does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

You are writing a rigorous, honest research paper (IMRaD) about an experiment that has ALREADY been run; the REAL results — including means, 95% confidence intervals, significance, and effect sizes — are given to you. Be faithful to those numbers and do NOT invent results, references, or findings. Write clear, precise academic prose. CITE numbered references in square brackets (e.g. [1] or [2, 3]); the Introduction and Related Work MUST cite them inline. An automated auditor checks each cited sentence against its abstract: say what a paper actually establishes, not merely its topic. You are NOT required to cite every reference; unused references are removed. NEVER cite a paper as evidence for something it does NOT discuss, including a gap in a different setting. State a gap WITHOUT a marker, use the reviewed gap statement, or cite an abstract that identifies that gap itself. Never attribute the opposite of what an abstract says. Stay INSIDE the abstract's own wording: use its terms, do not generalise them or add an unstated mechanism, domain or consequence. Plausible extensions are unsupported claims too; if in doubt, write less about the paper. Refer to figures and tables by number (e.g. 'Figure 1', 'Table 1'). Report results quantitatively (state the effect, its confidence interval, and whether it is significant). When the analysis contains primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts, report BOTH separately, state each preregistered decision, and never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. Distinguish training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations.
EVIDENCE AND INTERPRETATION. The registered condition descriptions and executed activation records below are authoritative: a baseline/no-op and an active negative control are different conditions. Do not infer inactivity from a small or nonsignificant outcome contrast. Describe only what the control manipulates; its outcome cannot prove that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: name the directly recorded outcomes, and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. If a reference tensor is detached inside a penalty, this stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient. Use the registered CI classifications without equating nonsignificance with equality. If a CI crosses zero but lies below the worthwhile margin, preserve its registered label and separately explain that it excludes gains of that target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model. The supplied power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; do not claim the former guarantees the latter. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

LENGTH. Write a full paper, not an extended abstract. Aim for roughly: introduction 600-800 words; related work 600-900; method 500-800 (BEFORE the operator specification that is appended for you); experimental setup 300-500; results 500-800; discussion 500-800; limitations 200-300; conclusion 150-250; abstract 150-250. A section that is three sentences long has not done its job. Depth means argument and detail, never padding or repetition.

The failure this section keeps producing looks like this: 'X studies uncertainty [1]. Y studies approximations [2].' — a list with citations attached. Use that argumentative structure only when the abstracts support it. End by positioning this study against the themes; omit irrelevant references and quoted or italicised paper titles.
