Specifically, it is unclear whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined attention patterns or consistently stable attention patterns across layers to support out-of-distribution time-series tasks.

This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. While consistency regularization has shown promise in other domains [9], and cross-layer mechanisms have been explored to strengthen layer interactions [8], their impact on subject-disjoint time-series generalization lacks empirical validation. Prior work has questioned the validity of transformer-based solutions for time series tasks when compared to simpler linear models [4], suggesting that architectural complexity may not always yield generalization benefits. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [6, 12, 21]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing whether cross-layer weight consistency, rather than activation steering or fusion, improves subject-disjoint generalization in a controlled time-series setting.
Method: The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights during training. The hypothesis is that stabilizing attention query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization. The operator is applied to `blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight` with `blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight` serving as the reference. The reference weights are detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0, ensuring the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The loss term is computed as the squared element-wise difference scaled by a fixed coefficient of 0.01. This coefficient prevents the loss term from dominating the classification objective. The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step, added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph.

The proposed condition adds this loss term. The baseline is a control arm defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them.

The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This condition tests whether any penalty term yields benefits, or if the specific cross-layer relationship is required. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. Training uses PreNormTransformerEncoder (2 blocks, 64 hidden, 4-head attention, 128 timesteps, 9 channels) on UCI HAR subject-disjoint split. Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects. The operator specification is appended below.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Experimental setup: **Design Justification.** The experimental design employs a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization across individuals. In a random split, windows from the same individual appear in both training and testing, allowing the model to exploit idiosyncratic sensor noise or movement styles unique to that person. The held-out cohort is subject-disjoint, ensuring that evaluation measures generalization to unseen subjects rather than memorization of subject-specific artifacts. This design choice is critical for claims about subject-disjoint generalization.

**Pairing and Controls.** Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance. This experiment did not test whether this was attributable to initialization and data ordering, increasing power to detect small effects. Each negative control's intended alternative explanation is tested via observed contrast. The first negative control matches compute but destroys the semantic cross-layer relationship; if it performs similarly to the proposed condition, the benefit may derive from regularization generally rather than consistency specifically. The seed budget comprises 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. This budget supports detection of effects exceeding the registered margin with planned power.

**Margin and Decision.** The registered margin of 0.0125098 proportion is a calibration-derived decision threshold. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. Preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign. The analysis distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations. This study uses disjoint seeds through the same pipeline, constituting a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Results: **Primary Cohort.** In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). No statistically significant difference was observed as the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Bars are means over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The proposed condition mean was 0.9062 (CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), baseline was 0.9054 (CI [0.9019, 0.9088]), and negative control 1 was 0.9051 (CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 3 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold; support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it. Figure 4 plots mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the primary cohort.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort.** In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). No statistically significant difference was observed as the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 5 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. The proposed condition mean was 0.9055 (CI [0.9016, 0.909]), baseline was 0.9035 (CI [0.9000, 0.907]), and negative control 1 was 0.9043 (CI [0.9003, 0.908]). Figure 6 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The 43 individual paired differences are plotted behind the interval at their exact values. Figure 7 plots mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the replication cohort. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero in both cohorts.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This study found inconclusive evidence that cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Neither the primary nor the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. For someone choosing between these methods, the results indicate that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class. Future work should test deeper architectures and directly measure attention stability to settle the question.
Discussion: **Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohorts produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the calibration-derived decision threshold. This suggests that enforcing weight alignment between query projections in shallow and deep layers does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this specific architecture and dataset.

**Interpretation and Mechanism.** These findings suggest that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. While consistency regularization has shown benefits in other domains [9], the time-series setting with subject-disjoint splits may require layers to specialize in different temporal features rather than maintaining consistent attention patterns. An alternative explanation is that the coefficient of 0.01 was too small to influence optimization meaningfully, though the negative control matched compute without semantic relationship. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: name the directly recorded outcomes, and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment.

**Comparison to Literature.** This result conflicts with works suggesting cross-layer mechanisms strengthen representation power [8, 18]. However, it aligns with *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* which questions the validity of transformer-based solutions for time series tasks [4]. The inconclusive outcome also resonates with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which found null results for spectral regularization in this regime [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy, and this execution reports the outcome [1].

**Replication Value.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds robustness to the null finding. Had only the primary cohort been reported, the small positive point estimate (0.0007734) might have been misinterpreted as a trend. The replication cohort's similar inconclusive outcome (0.001957) reinforces that the effect is not robust. This is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, but it verifies stability across the optimization landscape within the same pipeline.

**Future Work.** What would settle the question next is testing on deeper architectures or different time-series benchmarks where long-range dependencies are more critical. Additionally, directly measuring attention map stability rather than inferring it from accuracy would clarify the mechanism.
Limitations: This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency benefits deeper transformers or different time-series domains. The UCI HAR dataset, while standard, may not capture the complexity of tasks where long-range dependencies are paramount. The margin was derived from calibration noise, reflecting measurement precision rather than practical importance; a larger effect might be required for scientific significance. The study used 2 blocks; deeper networks might exhibit different consistency dynamics. Finally, the negative control destroyed the cross-layer relationship but did not test other forms of regularization, leaving open whether general regularization rather than specific consistency drives any potential benefits.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0007734 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.001957 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4, 20]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [7, 11]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [16].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [8], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [6, 12, 21]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing whether cross-layer weight consistency, rather than activation steering or fusion, improves subject-disjoint generalization in a controlled time-series setting.
Method: The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights during training. The hypothesis is that stabilizing attention query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization. The operator is applied to `blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight` with `blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight` serving as the reference. The reference weights are detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0, ensuring the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The loss term is computed as the squared element-wise difference scaled by a fixed coefficient of 0.01. This coefficient prevents the loss term from dominating the classification objective. The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step, added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph.

The proposed condition adds this loss term. The baseline is a control arm defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them.

The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This condition tests whether any penalty term yields benefits, or if the specific cross-layer relationship is required. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. Training uses PreNormTransformerEncoder (2 blocks, 64 hidden, 4-head attention, 128 timesteps, 9 channels) on UCI HAR subject-disjoint split. Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects. The operator specification is appended below.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Experimental setup: **Design Justification.** The experimental design employs a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization across individuals. In a random split, windows from the same individual appear in both training and testing, allowing the model to exploit idiosyncratic sensor noise or movement styles unique to that person. The held-out cohort is subject-disjoint, ensuring that evaluation measures generalization to unseen subjects rather than memorization of subject-specific artifacts. This design choice is critical for claims about subject-disjoint generalization.

**Pairing and Controls.** Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance. This experiment did not test whether this was attributable to initialization and data ordering, increasing power to detect small effects. Each negative control's intended alternative explanation is tested via observed contrast. The first negative control matches compute but destroys the semantic cross-layer relationship; if it performs similarly to the proposed condition, the benefit may derive from regularization generally rather than consistency specifically. The seed budget comprises 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. This budget supports detection of effects exceeding the registered margin with planned power.

**Margin and Decision.** The registered margin of 0.0125098 proportion is a calibration-derived decision threshold. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. Preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign. The analysis distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations. This study uses disjoint seeds through the same pipeline, constituting a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Registered conditions.

Add loss term that applies Frobenius norm consistency regularization to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Baseline: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. Recorded activity — primary: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Negative control 1: Add loss term penalizing difference between blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
Results: **Primary Cohort.** In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). No statistically significant difference was observed as the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Bars are means over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The proposed condition mean was 0.9062 (CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), baseline was 0.9054 (CI [0.9019, 0.9088]), and negative control 1 was 0.9051 (CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 3 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold; support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it. Figure 4 plots mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the primary cohort.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort.** In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). No statistically significant difference was observed as the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 5 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. The proposed condition mean was 0.9055 (CI [0.9016, 0.909]), baseline was 0.9035 (CI [0.9000, 0.907]), and negative control 1 was 0.9043 (CI [0.9003, 0.908]). Figure 6 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The 43 individual paired differences are plotted behind the interval at their exact values. Figure 7 plots mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the replication cohort. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero in both cohorts.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This study found inconclusive evidence that cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Neither the primary nor the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. For someone choosing between these methods, the results indicate that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class. Future work should test deeper architectures and directly measure attention stability to settle the question.
Discussion: **Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohorts produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the calibration-derived decision threshold. This suggests that enforcing weight alignment between query projections in shallow and deep layers does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this specific architecture and dataset.

**Interpretation and Mechanism.** These findings suggest that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. While consistency regularization has shown benefits in other domains [9], the time-series setting with subject-disjoint splits may require layers to specialize in different temporal features rather than maintaining consistent attention patterns. An alternative explanation is that the coefficient of 0.01 was too small to influence optimization meaningfully, though the negative control matched compute without semantic relationship. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: name the directly recorded outcomes, and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment.

**Comparison to Literature.** This result conflicts with works suggesting cross-layer mechanisms strengthen representation power [8, 18]. However, it aligns with *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* which questions the validity of transformer-based solutions for time series tasks [4]. The inconclusive outcome also resonates with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which found null results for spectral regularization in this regime [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy, and this execution reports the outcome [1].

**Replication Value.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds robustness to the null finding. Had only the primary cohort been reported, the small positive point estimate (0.0007734) might have been misinterpreted as a trend. The replication cohort's similar inconclusive outcome (0.001957) reinforces that the effect is not robust. This is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets, but it verifies stability across the optimization landscape within the same pipeline.

**Future Work.** What would settle the question next is testing on deeper architectures or different time-series benchmarks where long-range dependencies are more critical. Additionally, directly measuring attention map stability rather than inferring it from accuracy would clarify the mechanism.
Limitations: This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency benefits deeper transformers or different time-series domains. The UCI HAR dataset, while standard, may not capture the complexity of tasks where long-range dependencies are paramount. The margin was derived from calibration noise, reflecting measurement precision rather than practical importance; a larger effect might be required for scientific significance. The study used 2 blocks; deeper networks might exhibit different consistency dynamics. Finally, the negative control destroyed the cross-layer relationship but did not test other forms of regularization, leaving open whether general regularization rather than specific consistency drives any potential benefits.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly used for time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The registered decision was inconclusive in both cohorts. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Time-series classification using deep learning often relies on the assumption that learned temporal representations generalize across individuals. In domains such as human activity recognition, models must perform reliably on data from subjects who did not contribute to the training set. This subject-disjoint generalization is critical for deployment, as models that exploit idiosyncratic sensor noise or movement styles unique to training subjects will fail in production. Transformers have become prominent in this space due to their ability to model long-range dependencies, yet it remains unsettled whether their depth should encode progressively refined features or consistently stable attention patterns to support this generalization.

Current literature offers conflicting guidance on architectural inductive biases for time-series transformers. Some works suggest that consistency regularization stabilizes training and improves robustness, while others question the validity of transformer-based approaches for time-series tasks compared to simpler linear models. Specifically, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. Existing studies often evaluate on random splits or do not isolate the cross-layer mechanism from other regularization effects. This gap leaves practitioners without clear evidence on whether to enforce weight alignment between attention blocks when generalization to unseen subjects is the primary goal.

This paper reports the honest outcome of a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency, recorded as inconclusive against the preregistered margin. We executed a calibrated testbed using the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The experiment compared a proposed condition, which added a consistency loss term between attention blocks, against a baseline control arm and a negative control. We adhered strictly to the preregistered analysis plan, including a confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to verify stability.

The contributions of this work are:
- We preregistered a test of cross-layer query consistency loss on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers.
- We executed the test with a confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to distinguish optimization stability from sampling variance.
- We report the measured contrasts and registered decisions without upgrading inconclusive outcomes to positive findings.

The preregistered prediction stated: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We evaluate this prediction against the observed data in both primary and replication cohorts.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [38], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32]. These works collectively motivate a rigorous test of architectural modifications intended to improve generalization.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by isolating the cross-layer query consistency mechanism in a subject-disjoint setting, distinct from domain adaptation or visual tasks, to determine if weight alignment translates to accuracy gains in time-series classification.

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator applied to the query projection weights of the second attention block. The hypothesis posits that stabilizing attention patterns across depth improves generalization by preventing deeper layers from diverging too sharply from shallower representations. The operator computes a loss term based on the squared element-wise difference between the target weights (block 1) and reference weights (block 0). The reference weights are detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0, ensuring the penalty acts only on the deeper layer's alignment to the shallower one. This design isolates the effect of forcing consistency without altering the shallower layer's task-loss gradient.

The control arm executes the identical code path but returns a zero loss term, leaving the target parameter and optimizer state unchanged. This ensures any observed difference arises from the loss term itself, not implementation variance. The harness records operator activity for every seed and condition, refusing results where the control arm acted at any registered lifecycle point. The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This tests whether any regularization effect drives results rather than the specific cross-layer alignment.

The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step, adding its term to the classification objective inside the autograd graph. The combined objective is differentiated, and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The coefficient is fixed at 0.01 across all steps and seeds to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective. This specification ensures that the intervention is a pure addition to the training objective, with no evaluation-time lifecycle points. The comparator neutralizes the intervention by taking the control branch of the same implementation, guaranteeing that the only difference between arms is the presence of the consistency loss term.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experimental design prioritizes validity in estimating subject-disjoint generalization. A subject-disjoint split is used rather than a random split. In a random split, windows from the same individual appear in both training and testing, allowing the model to exploit idiosyncratic sensor noise or movement styles unique to that person. The held-out cohort consists of windows from unseen subjects, ensuring the metric reflects generalization to new individuals. This design choice answers the question of cross-subject robustness, which a random split would not address.

Conditions are paired by seed, meaning both the proposed condition and the baseline share identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters for each seed. This pairing reduces variance in the contrast estimate attributable to stochastic training factors, increasing the power to detect small effects. The seed budget includes 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The confirmatory cohort allows verification of stability across the optimization landscape within the same pipeline, distinct from independent replication on new subjects or datasets. This pre-specified replication cohort tests whether the primary result holds under fresh sampling of the optimization process.

The negative controls serve to isolate the mechanism. The first negative control matches the compute cost and regularization form but removes the semantic link between layers. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, it suggests the cross-layer relationship matters; if both match the baseline, the penalty itself may be inert or harmful. The analysis plan distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations. We report both cohorts separately and never pool them. The registered margin of 0.0125098 proportion was derived from calibration noise, reflecting measurement precision rather than practical importance alone.

=== results ===
Figure 1 illustrates the methodology flow, showing UCI HAR data entering the PreNormTransformerEncoder, where CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied at the loss_term across registered conditions. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved held-out classification accuracy by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 2 displays the mean accuracy for all conditions, and Figure 3 shows the paired mean difference. The 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. The registered decision was inconclusive.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 5 and Figure 6 present these replication results. Again, the confidence interval includes zero, and the registered decision was inconclusive. Figure 4 and Figure 7 show the accuracy over training steps, indicating no divergence in learning dynamics between conditions. The negative control condition performed similarly to the baseline in both cohorts (Table 1 and Table 2). In the primary cohort, the negative control mean accuracy was 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). In the replication cohort, the negative control mean accuracy was 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]).

These results indicate that the cross-layer consistency loss did not produce a measurable accuracy gain exceeding the noise threshold in this setting. The point estimates are positive but small, and the confidence intervals exclude the target margin. The replication cohort confirms that the primary result was not a sampling artifact of the initial seeds. We report these outcomes as measured, without upgrading the inconclusive decision to a positive finding. The data do not support the hypothesis that the mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeds the fixed worthwhile margin.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency loss did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. Both primary and replication cohorts yielded inconclusive decisions against the preregistered margin. This suggests that enforcing weight alignment between attention blocks does not translate to accuracy gains on the UCI HAR task. One interpretation is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class, allowing deeper layers to refine features differently from shallower ones. An alternative explanation is that the penalty coefficient was too small to influence optimization, though the negative control suggests the compute path itself was not the driver.

This design does not establish attention-map stability, as accuracy results do not directly measure attention patterns. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings. Compared to *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* [17], which found gains on machine translation, this result highlights a potential domain difference between language and sensor time-series. Similarly, *Spectral Entropy Minimization...* [3] found inconclusive results for input projection regularization, suggesting weight geometry constraints may not robustly improve generalization in this setting. The confirmatory replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is stable across seeds, not a sampling artifact.

The inconclusive outcome owes the reader an explanation of what would settle the question next. Future work should measure attention maps directly to verify if consistency was achieved without accuracy gain. Additionally, testing on datasets with larger domain shifts or different sensor modalities would clarify whether the finding generalizes beyond UCI HAR. The registered margin reflects measurement precision; a different margin might yield a different decision, but the data do not support gains of the target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model. This study clarifies that cross-layer query consistency is not a robust accuracy booster in this specific regime, guiding practitioners away from adopting it for this purpose without further evidence.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to the UCI HAR dataset and a specific transformer architecture with two attention blocks. The results do not establish whether cross-layer consistency improves attention-map stability, as this was not directly measured. Accuracy contrasts alone cannot confirm mechanistic hypotheses about feature learning or layer specialization. The findings apply to subject-disjoint generalization within this sensor modality and do not guarantee performance on other time-series domains or architectures with more layers. The inconclusive decision reflects the registered margin and uncertainty model; it does not prove the effect is zero, only that gains of the target magnitude were not detected. We cannot claim out-of-distribution generalization beyond the subject-disjoint split defined in the setup.

=== conclusion ===
This study found inconclusive evidence that cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The measured contrasts in both primary and replication cohorts failed to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. For practitioners choosing between these methods, the results do not support adopting cross-layer consistency loss for accuracy gains in this setting. Layer-specific adaptation may remain preferable. To settle the question, future work should directly measure attention stability and test on datasets with larger distribution shifts. The honest reporting of inconclusive outcomes prevents the field from pursuing ineffective architectural biases.

This paper reports the honest outcome of a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency, recorded as inconclusive against the preregistered margin. We executed a calibrated testbed using the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The data do not support the hypothesis that the mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeds the fixed worthwhile margin.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency loss did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. Both primary and replication cohorts yielded inconclusive decisions against the preregistered margin. This suggests that enforcing weight alignment between attention blocks does not translate to accuracy gains on the UCI HAR task. One interpretation is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class, allowing deeper layers to refine features differently from shallower ones. An alternative explanation is that the penalty coefficient was too small to influence optimization, though the negative control suggests the compute path itself was not the driver.

This design does not establish attention-map stability, as accuracy results do not directly measure attention patterns. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings. Compared to *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* [17], which found gains on machine translation, this result highlights a potential domain difference between language and sensor time-series. Similarly, *Spectral Entropy Minimization...* [3] found inconclusive results for input projection regularization, suggesting weight geometry constraints may not robustly improve generalization in this setting. The confirmatory replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is stable across seeds, not a sampling artifact.

The inconclusive outcome owes the reader an explanation of what would settle the question next. Future work should measure attention maps directly to verify if consistency was achieved without accuracy gain. Additionally, testing on datasets with larger domain shifts or different sensor modalities would clarify whether the finding generalizes beyond UCI HAR. The registered margin reflects measurement precision; a different margin might yield a different decision, but the data do not support gains of the target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model. This study clarifies that cross-layer query consistency is not a robust accuracy booster in this specific regime, guiding practitioners away from adopting it for this purpose without further evidence.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to the UCI HAR dataset and a specific transformer architecture with two attention blocks. The results do not establish whether cross-layer consistency improves attention-map stability, as this was not directly measured. Accuracy contrasts alone cannot confirm mechanistic hypotheses about feature learning or layer specialization. The findings apply to subject-disjoint generalization within this sensor modality and do not guarantee performance on other time-series domains or architectures with more layers. The inconclusive decision reflects the registered margin and uncertainty model; it does not prove the effect is zero, only that gains of the target magnitude were not detected. We cannot claim out-of-distribution generalization beyond the subject-disjoint split defined in the setup.

=== conclusion ===
This study found inconclusive evidence that cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The measured contrasts in both primary and replication cohorts failed to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. For practitioners choosing between these methods, the results do not support adopting cross-layer consistency loss for accuracy gains in this setting. Layer-specific adaptation may remain preferable. To settle the question, future work should directly measure attention stability and test on datasets with larger distribution shifts. The honest reporting of inconclusive outcomes prevents the field from pursuing ineffective architectural biases.

payload.title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
