Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [20], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [11] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [7]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [16].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [8], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [6, 12, 21]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15].

This study positions itself against these themes by isolating the effect of weight consistency from activation consistency. While [8] and [18] suggest cross-layer mechanisms can improve representation, [3] and [1] test specific regularization forms with inconclusive results in subject-disjoint settings. The disagreement lies in whether consistency should apply to weights or activations, and whether it aids generalization or restricts necessary layer-specific adaptation. This work tests the weight consistency hypothesis directly, contributing evidence to this unsettled question.
Method: The method centers on the `CrossLayerQueryConsistency` operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency between query projection weights of adjacent transformer blocks. The hypothesis posits that stabilizing attention patterns across depth improves generalization to unseen subjects. The operator targets `blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight` (the deeper layer) and regularizes it toward `blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight` (the shallower layer). This expression of the hypothesis assumes that consistent query projections reduce overfitting to subject-specific noise by constraining the representational capacity of deeper layers to align with earlier, potentially more robust features.

The comparator neutralizes this intervention through two distinct control conditions. The baseline is an inactive control arm. It executes the identical code path and lifecycle machinery as the proposed condition but returns a zero loss term. The harness guarantees that the baseline leaves the registered target parameter and its optimizer momentum buffer unchanged. Recorded activity for the baseline is zero across all seeds, confirming it acts as a no-op regarding the intervention logic. This establishes the counterfactual: what accuracy would be without the consistency penalty.

The first negative control is an active control. It adds a loss term penalizing the difference between `blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight` and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as the reference weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the compute and gradient flow of the proposed condition. Recorded activity for the negative control shows operator activity on all seeds. This condition tests whether any loss term addition, regardless of semantic content, drives the outcome. If the negative control performs similarly to the proposed condition, the specific cross-layer alignment is not the active ingredient. If it performs worse, the alignment may matter. However, the outcome of a negative control cannot prove that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct; it only isolates the semantic content of the regularization.

The operator specification is fixed. It retrieves reference weights from block 0, detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0, computes the element-wise squared difference, sums these elements, and scales by a fixed coefficient of 0.01. This coefficient prevents the loss term from dominating the classification objective. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The control arm takes the same code path but branches to return zero loss and make no parameter modifications. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Conclusion: This study found inconclusive evidence that cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Neither the primary nor the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Adding this consistency penalty does not justify the computational cost given the lack of accuracy gain. Future work should settle the question by measuring attention stability directly and testing on datasets with stronger distribution shifts to determine if a regime exists where this inductive bias is beneficial.
Discussion: The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency did not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohorts on disjoint seeds produced inconclusive outcomes, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this specific architecture and dataset setting.

What this means for the hypothesis is that the mechanistic rationale—stabilizing attention across depth to improve generalization—is not supported by the accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment, and the accuracy metric does not measure attention stability directly. An alternative explanation is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. Transformers may require deeper layers to diverge from shallower layers to capture subject-specific nuances that a consistency penalty suppresses. This aligns with findings that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting, but consistency regularization may not be the correct remedy for subject-disjoint shifts [9].

The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not a sampling artifact of the primary seeds. The effect size increased slightly in replication (dz=0.15 vs 0.06), but the uncertainty remained too high to support the hypothesis. This consistency in inconclusiveness across cohorts strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if it exists, is smaller than the worthwhile margin.

Comparing this finding to specific cited papers, the result agrees with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found inconclusive evidence for weight regularization in this setting [3]. It conflicts with the implication in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention* that strengthening layer interactions enhances representation power [8], suggesting that interaction mechanisms operating on hidden states may differ fundamentally from weight consistency penalties. It is not comparable to *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* because that work addresses domain adaptation in vision with attention-map consistency, not weight consistency in time-series classification [10].

The negative control results suggest that adding a loss term alone does not drive accuracy changes, as the negative control performed similarly to the baseline and proposed condition. However, the outcome of a negative control cannot prove that the harness is unbiased. The baseline's zero recorded activity confirms the control arm was inactive, distinguishing it from the active negative control.

What would settle the question next is direct measurement of attention stability. If attention maps diverge significantly between layers in the baseline but converge in the proposed condition without accuracy gains, it would confirm that stability is achievable but not beneficial for this task. Alternatively, testing on a dataset with stronger subject-shift characteristics might reveal a regime where consistency aids generalization.
Limitations: This design cannot tell us whether cross-layer consistency aids generalization on different corpora, sensors, or tasks. The claim is scoped to the single calibrated testbed used (UCI HAR). A cross-dataset claim is untestable by construction in this registered report. The power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; the sample size targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin, but does not guarantee power for the stricter support rule. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. We did not measure attention maps or feature geometry, so claims about attention stability are interpretations, not measured findings.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
**The Problem of Generalization in Time-Series Transformers.** Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [38]. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling [38]. However, like other deep learning models, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding, generalization challenges, and data shift issues for the domains with limited data [32]. Specifically, what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds remains an open question. Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting.

**The Gap in Current Literature.** Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. While *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs [14]. However, this work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. Existing works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms to address stability and generalization [17], but independent verification in subject-disjoint time-series settings is missing.

**This Study's Contribution.** This paper reports a preregistered experiment testing the effect of cross-layer query consistency on subject-disjoint generalization. We contribute:
- A rigorous test of cross-layer consistency loss in a subject-disjoint time-series classification setting using a calibrated testbed.
- Independent verification of the intervention's effect across primary and confirmatory-replication seed cohorts.
- Quantitative evidence regarding the magnitude of accuracy gains relative to a preregistered worthwhile margin.

**Preregistered Prediction.** The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Specifically, we predict the intervention will exceed this margin in held-out classification accuracy.

=== related_work ===
**Transformers in Time-Series Analysis.** Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear [1]. Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [38]. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling [38]. However, recent breakthroughs have drawn significant attention of the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies, yet Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding, generalization challenges, and data shift issues [32]. Specifically, *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line, noting that the nature of the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss [5]. This uncertainty motivates rigorous testing of specific architectural modifications like consistency losses.

**Consistency Regularization and Cross-Layer Mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15]. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it, indicating conclusions may not be relied on [2].

**Attention Mechanisms and Architectures.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. These works establish that attention modifications are common, but their effect on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers requires specific verification [1].

**Positioning This Study.** This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific cross-layer consistency loss in a subject-disjoint setting. Unlike *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning*, which addresses limitations via fine-tuning [32], we test architectural regularization during initial training. Unlike *Extending Momentum Contrast With Cross Similarity Consistency Regularization*, which applies cross consistency to negative pairs in contrastive learning [13], we apply it to query weights in supervised classification. The failure of prior works to verify this specific mechanism in this specific setting motivates our boundary test.

=== method ===
**The Operator.** The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent. The scope is the full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space. The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The ordering is element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition. There is no normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient. Numerical safeguards include coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

**Operator Specification.**
1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout: Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients; Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only; Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

**The Comparator.** The baseline is a control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

**Hypothesis Expression.** This operator expresses the hypothesis that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy. === experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification.** The setup ensures that the registered condition descriptions and executed activation records are authoritative, distinguishing a baseline/no-op from an active negative control. The baseline recorded 0/43 seeds operator activity, confirming it was inactive. The first negative control recorded 43/43 seeds operator activity, confirming it was an active condition penalizing difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. This distinction allows us to verify that the harness correctly invoked the intervention logic. The setup uses a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization across subjects; a random split would not isolate subject-specific variation. Pairing conditions by seed controls for initialization and data ordering variance, ensuring differences are attributed to the intervention rather than seed noise.

**Seed Budget and Analysis.** The experiment uses 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. This budget supports the registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targeting rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin, and is not an exact power calculation for the percentile bootstrap. The margin is derived from calibration noise, reflecting measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance.

**Dataset and Model.** The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1: UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows), model PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)), 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9), evaluated as number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort Outcomes.** In the primary cohort, across 3 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition achieved 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), the baseline 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]), and negative control 1 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 3 plots the paired mean difference with the registered worthwhile threshold. The 95% CI includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps, where conditions whose curves coincide are distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern.

**Replication Cohort Outcomes.** In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition achieved 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.909]), the baseline 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.907]), and negative control 1 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.908]). Figure 5 displays these means. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 7 shows the training curves for the replication cohort.

In both cohorts, the confidence intervals included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Both the primary and replication cohorts returned inconclusive decisions, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this specific architecture and dataset setting.

**Mechanism and Alternatives.** The mechanistic rationale hypothesized that stabilizing attention across depth would improve generalization. However, an alternative explanation is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. The negative control, which actively penalized weights against a random matrix, recorded 43/43 seeds operator activity, confirming the harness correctly executed active loss terms. The baseline recorded 0/43 seeds operator activity, confirming it was inactive. The fact that the proposed condition did not outperform the baseline despite active regularization suggests the specific consistency constraint may not align with the inductive biases needed for this task. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment; the operator regularized weights, not attention distributions, which may explain the lack of effect.

**Replication Value.** The replication cohort adds confidence in the inconclusive status. The effect size increased slightly in replication (dz=0.15 vs 0.06), but the uncertainty remained too high to support the hypothesis, and the registered decision label was inconclusive. This consistency across disjoint seeds indicates the null result is not an artifact of a specific seed selection. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them, not subjects, as the subject split was held constant.

**Relation to Cited Works.** These findings align with *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?*, which questions the validity of Transformer-based solutions for time series analysis tasks [5]. They also extend *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which found inconclusive results for spectral entropy minimization in this regime [3]. Unlike *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which noted deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17], our results suggest consistency regularization alone does not resolve generalization challenges in subject-disjoint settings. *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32], which is consistent with our finding that architectural tweaks alone may not overcome these limitations.

**Future Directions.** What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks or whether different consistency targets (e.g., attention maps rather than weights) yield different outcomes.

=== limitations ===
**Scope of Claims.** This study measures ONE calibrated testbed, so a cross-dataset claim is untestable by construction. The claims are scoped to the UCI HAR testbed. We do not claim out-of-distribution or domain generalisation beyond unseen subjects in this corpus. The margin is derived from calibration noise, reflecting measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance.

**Design Limits.** The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings; we did not directly measure attention stability.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. The results were inconclusive in both primary and replication cohorts, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence does not support adopting cross-layer query consistency loss for subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. These findings suggest that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. Future work should test whether different consistency targets or benchmarks yield robust gains.

=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
**The Problem of Generalization in Time-Series Transformers.** Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [38]. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling [38]. However, like other deep learning models, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding, generalization challenges, and data shift issues for the domains with limited data [32]. Specifically, what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds remains an open question. Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting.

**The Gap in Current Literature.** Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. While *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs [14]. However, this work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. Existing works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms to address stability and generalization [17], but independent verification in subject-disjoint time-series settings is missing.

**This Study's Contribution.** This paper reports a preregistered experiment testing the effect of cross-layer query consistency on subject-disjoint generalization. We contribute:
- A rigorous test of cross-layer consistency loss in a subject-disjoint time-series classification setting using a calibrated testbed.
- Independent verification of the intervention's effect across primary and confirmatory-replication seed cohorts.
- Quantitative evidence regarding the magnitude of accuracy gains relative to a preregistered worthwhile margin.

**Preregistered Prediction.** The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Specifically, we predict the intervention will exceed this margin in held-out classification accuracy.

=== related_work ===
**Transformers in Time-Series Analysis.** Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear [1]. Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [38]. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling [38]. However, recent breakthroughs have drawn significant attention of the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies, yet Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding, generalization challenges, and data shift issues [32]. Specifically, *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line, noting that the nature of the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss [5]. This uncertainty motivates rigorous testing of specific architectural modifications like consistency losses.

**Consistency Regularization and Cross-Layer Mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15]. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it, indicating conclusions may not be relied on [2].

**Attention Mechanisms and Architectures.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. These works establish that attention modifications are common, but their effect on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers requires specific verification [1].

**Positioning This Study.** This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific cross-layer consistency loss in a subject-disjoint setting. Unlike *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning*, which addresses limitations via fine-tuning [32], we test architectural regularization during initial training. Unlike *Extending Momentum Contrast With Cross Similarity Consistency Regularization*, which applies cross consistency to negative pairs in contrastive learning [13], we apply it to query weights in supervised classification. The failure of prior works to verify this specific mechanism in this specific setting motivates our boundary test.

=== method ===
**The Operator.** The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent. The scope is the full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space. The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The ordering is element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition. There is no normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient. Numerical safeguards include coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

**Operator Specification.**
1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout: Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients; Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only; Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

**The Comparator.** The baseline is a control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

**Hypothesis Expression.** This operator expresses the hypothesis that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy. The comparator neutralizes the loss term addition, isolating the effect of the consistency penalty from the training procedure itself.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification.** The setup ensures that the registered condition descriptions and executed activation records are authoritative, distinguishing a baseline/no-op from an active negative control. The baseline recorded 0/43 seeds operator activity, confirming it was inactive. The first negative control recorded 43/43 seeds operator activity, confirming it was an active condition penalizing difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. This distinction allows us to verify that the harness correctly invoked the intervention logic. The setup uses a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization across subjects; a random split would not isolate subject-specific variation. Pairing conditions by seed controls for initialization and data ordering variance, ensuring differences are attributed to the intervention rather than seed noise.

**Seed Budget and Analysis.** The experiment uses 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. This budget supports the registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targeting rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin, and is not an exact power calculation for the percentile bootstrap. The margin is derived from calibration noise, reflecting measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance.

**Dataset and Model.** The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1: UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows), model PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)), 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9), evaluated as number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort Outcomes.** In the primary cohort, across 3 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition achieved 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), the baseline 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]), and negative control 1 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 2 displays these means with error bars. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 3 plots the paired mean difference with the registered worthwhile threshold. The 95% CI includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps, where conditions whose curves coincide are distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern.

**Replication Cohort Outcomes.** In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition achieved 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.909]), the baseline 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.907]), and negative control 1 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.908]). Figure 5 displays these means. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 6 plots the paired mean difference. The 95% CI includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 7 shows the training curves for the replication cohort.

**Decision Summary.** Table 1 summarizes the primary cohort outcomes. Table 2 summarizes the replication cohort outcomes. Table 3 compares means across cohorts. In both cohorts, the confidence intervals included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Both the primary and replication cohorts returned inconclusive decisions, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this specific architecture and dataset setting.

**Mechanism and Alternatives.** The mechanistic rationale hypothesized that stabilizing attention across depth would improve generalization. However, an alternative explanation is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. The negative control, which actively penalized weights against a random matrix, recorded 43/43 seeds operator activity, confirming the harness correctly executed active loss terms. The baseline recorded 0/43 seeds operator activity, confirming it was inactive. The fact that the proposed condition did not outperform the baseline despite active regularization suggests the specific consistency constraint may not align with the inductive biases needed for this task. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment; the operator regularized weights, not attention distributions, which may explain the lack of effect.

**Replication Value.** The replication cohort adds confidence in the inconclusive status. The effect size increased slightly in replication (dz=0.15 vs 0.06), but the uncertainty remained too high to support the hypothesis, and the registered decision label was inconclusive. This consistency across disjoint seeds indicates the null result is not an artifact of a specific seed selection. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them, not subjects, as the subject split was held constant.

**Relation to Cited Works.** These findings align with *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?*, which questions the validity of Transformer-based solutions for time series analysis tasks [5]. They also extend *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which found inconclusive results for spectral entropy minimization in this regime [3]. Unlike *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which noted deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17], our results suggest consistency regularization alone does not resolve generalization challenges in subject-disjoint settings. *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32], which is consistent with our finding that architectural tweaks alone may not overcome these limitations.

**Future Directions.** What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks or whether different consistency targets (e.g., attention maps rather than weights) yield different outcomes.

=== limitations ===
**Scope of Claims.** This study measures ONE calibrated testbed, so a cross-dataset claim is untestable by construction. The claims are scoped to the UCI HAR testbed. We do not claim out-of-distribution or domain generalisation beyond unseen subjects in this corpus. The margin is derived from calibration noise, reflecting measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance.

**Design Limits.** The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings; we did not directly measure attention stability.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. The results were inconclusive in both primary and replication cohorts, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence does not support adopting cross-layer query consistency loss for subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. These findings suggest that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. Future work should test whether different consistency targets or benchmarks yield robust gains.

Related-work section:
**Transformers in Time-Series Analysis.** Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear [1]. Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [38]. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling [38]. However, recent breakthroughs have drawn significant attention of the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies, yet Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding, generalization challenges, and data shift issues [32]. Specifically, *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line, noting that the nature of the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss [5]. This uncertainty motivates rigorous testing of specific architectural modifications like consistency losses.

**Consistency Regularization and Cross-Layer Mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15]. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it, indicating conclusions may not be relied on [2].

**Attention Mechanisms and Architectures.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. These works establish that attention modifications are common, but their effect on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers requires specific verification [1].

**Positioning This Study.** This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific cross-layer consistency loss in a subject-disjoint setting. Unlike *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning*, which addresses limitations via fine-tuning [32], we test architectural regularization during initial training. Unlike *Extending Momentum Contrast With Cross Similarity Consistency Regularization*, which applies cross consistency to negative pairs in contrastive learning [13], we apply it to query weights in supervised classification. The failure of prior works to verify this specific mechanism in this specific setting motivates our boundary test.

Abstract: The recent breakthrough of Transformers in deep learning has drawn significant attention of the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies. Additionally, addressing the issue of catastrophic forgetting, where models forget previously learned information when exposed to new data, is another critical aspect that requires attention in enhancing the robustness of Transformers for time series tasks. To address these limitations, in this paper, we pre-train the time series Transformer model on a source domain with sufficient data and fine-tune it on the target domain with limited data. We introduce the \emph{One-step fine-tuning} approach, adding some percentage of source domain data to the target domains, providing the model with diverse time series instances. We then fine-tune the pre-trained model using a gradual unfreezing technique. This helps enhance the model's performance in time series prediction for domains with limited data. Extensive experimental results on two real-world datasets show that our approach improves over the state-of-the-art baselines by 4.35% and 11.54% for indoor temperature and wind power prediction, respectively.

This article proposes a novel attention mechanism which we call external attention, based on two external, small, learnable, shared memories, which can be implemented easily by simply using two cascaded linear layers and two normalization layers; it conveniently replaces self-attention in existing popular architectures. External attention has linear complexity and implicitly considers the correlations between all data samples. We further incorporate the multi-head mechanism into external attention to provide an all-MLP architecture, external attention MLP (EAMLP), for image classification. Extensive experiments on image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, image generation, and point cloud analysis reveal that our method provides results comparable or superior to the self-attention mechanism and some of its variants, with much lower computational and memory costs.

GER-steer exploits this global signal to rectify raw steering vectors, effectively decoupling robust semantic intent from orthogonal artifacts. Extensive evaluations confirm that GER-steer consistently outperforms baselines, delivering superior efficacy and generalization without layer-specific tuning, establishing a universal solution for reliable model alignment.

Our model is simple, easily parallelizable, and runs in real-time. The presented architecture performs at state-of-the-art on the nuScenes dataset, with 4x faster inference speeds. Introduction: **The Problem of Generalization in Time-Series Transformers.** Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [38]. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling [38]. However, like other deep learning models, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding, generalization challenges, and data shift issues for the domains with limited data [32]. Specifically, what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds remains an open question. Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting.

**The Gap in Current Literature.** Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. While *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs [14]. However, this work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. Existing works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms to address stability and generalization [17], but independent verification in subject-disjoint time-series settings is missing.

- A rigorous test of cross-layer consistency loss in a subject-disjoint time-series classification setting using a calibrated testbed.

Both the primary and replication cohorts returned inconclusive decisions, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. However, an alternative explanation is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. The negative control, which actively penalized weights against a random matrix, recorded 43/43 seeds operator activity, confirming the harness correctly executed active loss terms. Unlike *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which noted deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17], our results suggest consistency regularization alone does not resolve generalization challenges in subject-disjoint settings. *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32], which is consistent with our finding that architectural tweaks alone may not overcome these limitations.

The results were inconclusive in both primary and replication cohorts, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence does not support adopting cross-layer query consistency loss for subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. These findings suggest that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. Future work should test whether different consistency targets or benchmarks yield robust gains.

    *   Primary Metric: Held-out classification accuracy.

    *   **Abstract:** States the study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency improves accuracy.     *   **Discussion:** States principal finding is that it did not yield robust accuracy gains. Both cohorts inconclusive. CIs include zero, failed to exceed margin. Suggests consistency does not improve generalization in this setting.
    *   **Conclusion:** Results inconclusive. Evidence does not support adopting the loss.

4.  **Compare Pre-Registration vs. Paper:**
    *   *Hypothesis/Prediction:* The paper explicitly restates the preregistered prediction in the Introduction ("Preregistered Prediction" subsection) exactly as it was registered (Intervention > Comparator, exceeding margin 0.0125098).
    *   *Results:* The results (0.000773 and 0.00196 improvements) are far below the margin (0.0125098) and CIs include zero.

    *   *HARKing Check:* Did the authors change the hypothesis to match the null result?

They explicitly state the results are inconclusive regarding the primary hypothesis.
    *   *Faithfulness:* The paper honestly reports the null/negative result against the registered hypothesis. It does not claim the hypothesis was supported when it wasn't. It does not change the margin or the direction post-hoc to claim success.

    *   The paper faithfully reports the results (null/inconclusive).
    *   The paper does not claim the hypothesis was confirmed.

The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Related work: **Transformers in Time-Series Analysis.** Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear [1]. Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [38]. Specifically, *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line, noting that the nature of the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss [5]. This uncertainty motivates rigorous testing of specific architectural modifications like consistency losses.

**Consistency Regularization and Cross-Layer Mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15]. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it, indicating conclusions may not be relied on [2].

**Attention Mechanisms and Architectures.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. These works establish that attention modifications are common, but their effect on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers requires specific verification [1].

**Positioning This Study.** This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific cross-layer consistency loss in a subject-disjoint setting. Unlike *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning*, which addresses limitations via fine-tuning [32], we test architectural regularization during initial training. Unlike *Extending Momentum Contrast With Cross Similarity Consistency Regularization*, which applies cross consistency to negative pairs in contrastive learning [13], we apply it to query weights in supervised classification. The failure of prior works to verify this specific mechanism in this specific setting motivates our boundary test.

The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent. The scope is the full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space. The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The ordering is element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition. There is no normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient. Numerical safeguards include coefficient 0.01 prevents in the training objective from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

**Operator Specification.**
1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute in the training objective = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store in the training objective in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return in the training objective to harness for addition to training objective

Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

**Hypothesis Expression.** This operator expresses the hypothesis that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy. The comparator neutralizes the loss term addition, isolating the effect of the consistency penalty from the training procedure itself.

This distinction allows us to verify that the harness correctly invoked the intervention logic. The setup uses a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization across subjects; a random split would not isolate subject-specific variation. Pairing conditions by seed controls for initialization and data ordering variance, ensuring differences are attributed to the intervention rather than seed noise.
