Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00077 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [19], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line due to potential temporal information loss [3]. Specific applications include representing multivariate series as graphs for forecasting [6] and biosignal data augmentation using generative models [10]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [12]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including generalization challenges [15].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data and proposes constraining encoder and decoder outputs [8]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention and proposes attention-level alignment [9]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions by retrieving query-related information from previous layers [7]. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering to rectify steering vectors [17]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [13]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy, reporting inconclusive results in a similar subject-disjoint setting [2]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it and its conclusions may not be relied on [1].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [4]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks to reduce complexity [16]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow and proposes mixing values inside the attention module [18]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [5, 11, 20]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [14]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight-level consistency intervention in a subject-disjoint time-series regime, distinguishing measured accuracy from hypothesized attention stability.
Method: The core intervention is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, applied to the query projection weights of the second attention block (blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight). The hypothesis posits that regularizing deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights stabilizes attention patterns across depth, thereby improving generalization to unseen subjects. The operator adds a loss term to the classification objective during every optimization step. This term is computed as the squared Frobenius norm of the element-wise difference between the target weights (block 1) and reference weights (block 0), scaled by a fixed coefficient of 0.01.

The reference weights from block 0 are detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients from flowing to the shallower layer. This ensures the penalty acts only on the target parameters, encouraging them to align with the frozen reference state at each step without altering the reference layer's task-loss learning. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only, and the coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds. This design isolates the effect of cross-layer weight alignment from other training dynamics.

The comparator is the baseline condition, defined by the harness guarantees rather than a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, ensuring identical dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step—the same forward pass, classification objective, backward pass, and optimizer update. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm, the intervention leaves the registered target parameter unchanged, leaves that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and adds nothing to the training objective. This ensures any observed contrast is. This experiment did not test whether this was attributable to the loss term addition rather than implementation artifacts.

A negative control condition penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute, testing whether the observed effect (if any) stems from the specific alignment to block 0 or merely the addition of a weight penalty. The operator specification is fixed before any compute was spent, and the invariants hold throughout: reference weights receive no gradients, and the loss term is added to the training objective. Mechanistic rationales regarding attention stability are hypotheses; the measured outcome is held-out classification accuracy.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Experimental setup: **Design Justification for Subject-Disjoint Split.** The experiment uses the official subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset. A random split would allow data from the same subject to appear in both training and testing, inflating accuracy estimates by capturing subject-specific idiosyncrasies rather than generalizable movement patterns. The subject-disjoint split answers the question of whether the intervention improves generalization to unseen subjects, which is the relevant population for deployment in this domain. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task, or deployment distribution.

**Paired Seeds and Variance Control.** All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. This pairing reduces variance in the contrast estimate by controlling for random initialization effects, which are known to influence Transformer training outcomes. The seed budget consists of 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. The confirmatory cohort is a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, not an independent replication in terms of data source or implementation. It provides a test of stability under fresh sampling within the same pipeline.

**Negative Control Rationale.** The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. Its intended alternative explanation is that any accuracy change might result from the mere presence of a weight regularization term rather than the specific cross-layer relationship. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, it supports the specific alignment hypothesis. If both differ from baseline similarly, the effect may be. This experiment did not test whether this was due to generic regularization. The observed contrast supports interpretation only within the bounds of the recorded outcomes; conformance and activation counts describe execution but do not establish the mechanism.

**Analysis Plan.** The registered decision rule requires the lower confidence bound of the mean difference to exceed the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The planning target power was 90% for rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. This does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Registered conditions.
- Proposed condition: Server-bound target blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight has stored tensor shape (64, 64). Add loss term that applies Frobenius norm consistency regularization to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Baseline: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. Recorded activity — primary: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Negative control 1: Add loss term penalizing difference between blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. Results: **Primary Cohort Accuracy.** Figure 1 illustrates the experimental pipeline mapping the UCI HAR dataset through the PreNormTransformerEncoder, applying CrossLayerQueryConsistency at the loss term under registered conditions, and measuring accuracy on the subject-disjoint test split. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), compared to 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]) for the baseline. The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 2 displays these means with error bars, showing the proposed condition against the baseline. The point estimate is printed above each bar.

**Primary Cohort Contrast.** Figure 3 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00077 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The 43 individual paired differences are plotted behind the interval at their exact values. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps, where conditions whose curves coincide are distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern.

**Replication Cohort Accuracy.** In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, the proposed condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), compared to 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]) for the baseline. The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]). Figure 5 displays these means with error bars. The dashed line marks the baseline mean as an ordering reference only.

**Replication Cohort Contrast.** Figure 6 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the replication cohort. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive in both cohorts.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This study tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The results were inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence does not support adopting cross-layer query consistency loss for accuracy gains in this regime. Layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. Future work should measure attention stability directly and test on diverse benchmarks to settle the question.
Discussion: **Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency loss did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. The confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. This outcome is inconclusive regarding the hypothesis that cross-layer weight alignment improves subject-disjoint generalization in this regime.

**Mechanism and Interpretation.** We measured accuracy, not attention map stability or feature learning dynamics directly. The mechanistic rationale that weight alignment stabilizes attention is a hypothesis consistent with the intervention design but not verified by these outcomes. An alternative explanation is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, and constraining deeper layers to match shallower layers restricts the model's capacity to refine representations for subject variability. This aligns with findings that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction regarding generalization challenges [15]. The inconclusive result suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard training in this setting.

**Replication and Stability.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds ensures the outcome is not an artifact of a specific random initialization batch. The consistency of the inconclusive decision across both cohorts strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if any, is below the worthwhile margin. This distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations. The disjoint seeds provide a pre-specified test of stability under fresh sampling within the same pipeline.

**Relation to Cited Work.** These findings contrast with works proposing consistency regularization to alleviate overfitting [8], suggesting that weight-level consistency may not translate to accuracy gains in subject-disjoint time-series tasks. They are consistent with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which reported inconclusive results for spectral regularization on the same testbed [2]. The results do not support the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks without further evidence.

We measured accuracy, not attention map stability or feature learning dynamics directly, so mechanistic claims remain hypothetical. The confirmatory cohort is a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, not an independent replication in terms of data source or implementation. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. === abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00077 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
**The Problem of Subject-Disjoint Generalization.** Time-series classification tasks, such as human activity recognition, often require models to generalize across individuals with distinct movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Transformers have emerged as a powerful architecture for modeling sequential data due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [38]. However, their effectiveness in time-series forecasting and classification remains a subject of debate, with some evidence suggesting that simpler linear models can outperform sophisticated Transformer-based solutions in certain regimes [5]. A critical open question is what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects. Specifically, it is unclear whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined attention patterns or consistently stable attention patterns to support out-of-distribution performance in subject-disjoint settings.

**The Gap in Current Literature.** While consistency regularization has been proposed to improve Transformer stability and generalization [17], there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. Existing works explore cross-layer interactions to strengthen representation power [15] or apply cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34], but these mechanisms have not been rigorously tested for subject-disjoint time-series generalization using preregistered confirmatory replication. The literature identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18], motivating the hypothesis that enforcing consistency across layers might mitigate such discrepancies. However, without controlled experimentation, it remains unknown whether this specific inductive bias yields measurable accuracy gains over standard training.

**This Study.** This paper reports a calibrated test of the cross-layer query consistency hypothesis. We implement a Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights in a PreNormTransformerEncoder. We compare this intervention against a baseline control arm that executes the identical training pipeline without the loss term. To ensure robustness, we employ a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, allowing us to distinguish sampling variation from true effects. We report quantitative evidence on held-out classification accuracy, including effect sizes, confidence intervals, and significance tests for both cohorts.

**Contributions.**
- We implement and evaluate a cross-layer query consistency loss designed to stabilize attention projections across transformer depth in a time-series classification task.
- We provide a preregistered comparison against a baseline and a negative control, using a subject-disjoint split to assess generalization to unseen subjects.
- We report inconclusive results in both primary and replication cohorts, suggesting that layer-specific adaptation may be preferable to cross-layer consistency in this setting.

**Preregistered Prediction.** The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
**Transformers in Time-Series Analysis.** Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [38]. However, *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line, demonstrating that simple linear models can outperform Transformer-based solutions in long-term forecasting tasks [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [32]. These works collectively motivate the search for architectural modifications that enhance robustness in subject-disjoint settings.

**Consistency Regularization and Cross-Layer Mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data and proposes constraining encoder and decoder outputs [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, proposing attention-level alignment to mitigate this [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions by retrieving query-related information from previous layers [15]. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering to rectify steering vectors [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it, indicating that not all proposed regularization strategies hold under audit [2].

**Attention Mechanisms and Architectures.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements, improving efficiency and performance [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks, offering linear complexity [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow, proposing a method to mix values inside the attention module [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* and *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* document the application of Transformers across vision and other modalities [11, 21]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance, finding that query and key content comparison is negligible for self-attention in some contexts [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing whether cross-layer query consistency specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers, a gap not settled by the cited literature.

=== method ===
**The CrossLayerQueryConsistency Operator.** The core intervention is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, applied to the query projection weights of the second attention block (blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight). This operator enforces a Frobenius norm consistency regularization between the query weights of the first block (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight) and the second block. The hypothesis is that aligning these weights stabilizes attention patterns across depth, potentially improving generalization to unseen subjects. The operator is invoked during the loss computation of every optimization step, adding its term to the classification objective inside the autograd graph.

**Operator Specification.** The operator retrieves reference weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients from flowing to the first block. It then computes the element-wise difference between the target weights (block 1) and the reference weights. The squared elements are summed to produce a raw loss, which is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01. This loss term is differentiable with respect to the target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds to prevent the consistency term from dominating the classification objective. The reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients from this term, ensuring that the regularization only constrains the deeper layer to match the shallower one.

**Control and Negative Control Arms.** The baseline condition is a control arm defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step—the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass, and the same optimizer update. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm, the intervention leaves the registered target parameter unchanged, leaves that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and adds nothing to the training objective. This ensures that any observed difference in outcomes is attributable to the loss term itself rather than implementation artifacts.

A negative control condition penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the computational cost of the proposed condition. This arm tests whether the observed effect (if any) is due to the specific cross-layer relationship or merely the addition of a regularization term. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. Training uses a PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks, 64 hidden units, 4-head attention, 128 timesteps, and 9 channels. Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on the official subject-disjoint test split.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Subject-Disjoint Split Justification.** The experiment uses the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. This design choice is critical because the research question concerns generalization to unseen subjects, not merely unseen data points from the same subjects. A random split would allow the model to learn subject-specific features that do not transfer, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to answer the open problem. By holding out entire subjects, we ensure that the evaluation metric reflects the model's ability to generalize across different movement styles and sensor characteristics. This aligns with the goal of determining whether architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects.

**Pairing Conditions by Seed.** We pair the proposed condition and the baseline by seed, deriving the dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters once and reusing them for both arms. This pairing reduces variance in the contrast estimate by controlling for stochastic factors inherent in training deep networks. Each seed produces a paired difference, which is the unit of analysis for the hypothesis test. This design increases the power to detect small effects compared to an unpaired design, given the same computational budget. The seed budget consists of 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix.

**Negative Control Purpose.** The first negative control penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. This condition is intended to rule out the alternative explanation that any regularization term, regardless of its structure, improves accuracy. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, it suggests that the specific cross-layer relationship is beneficial. If both perform similarly, the effect may be due to general regularization rather than cross-layer consistency. The observed contrast between the proposed condition and the negative control supports or refutes the specific mechanistic hypothesis.

**Analysis Plan.** We report mean held-out classification accuracy with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for each condition. The primary decision rule compares the mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast against a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The confirmatory cohort is a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, not an independent replication in terms of data source or implementation. This distinction is important because the replication uses the same pipeline and dataset, testing the stability of the result under fresh sampling rather than generalization to new domains. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort Outcomes.** In the primary cohort, we evaluated the proposed condition against the baseline across 43 seeds. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline, and negative control 1 conditions, with error bars showing the 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimates are printed above each bar. Figure 3 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions, with the registered worthwhile threshold marked by a green dash-dot line. The lower confidence bound does not exceed the threshold. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions, with curves distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern.

**Replication Cohort Outcomes.** In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, we evaluated the same conditions across 43 fresh seeds. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 5 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the replication cohort, mirroring the structure of Figure 2. Figure 6 plots the mean difference for the replication cohort, again showing that the lower confidence bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the replication cohort.

**Summary of Metrics.** Table 1 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for each condition in the primary cohort, while Table 2 summarizes the outcome contrasts. Table 3 and Table 4 provide the corresponding data for the replication cohort. Table 5 compares the means across both cohorts. In all cases, the confidence intervals overlap substantially, and the effect sizes are small (Cohen's dz=0.06 in primary, 0.15 in replication). The negative control 1 condition performed similarly to the baseline in both cohorts (Primary: 0.9051 vs 0.9054; Replication: 0.9043 vs 0.9035), suggesting that the addition of a regularization term alone did not drive accuracy changes. The results are inconclusive in both cohorts, as neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency in attention projections did not yield robust accuracy gains in a subject-disjoint time-series classification task. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. This suggests that, in this regime, layer-specific adaptation may be more effective than enforcing consistency across depth. The small effect sizes (Cohen's dz < 0.2) indicate that even if a true effect exists, it is likely too small to be of practical importance for this task.

**Mechanistic Interpretation.** The hypothesis motivating this intervention was that stabilizing attention patterns across depth would improve generalization to unseen subjects. However, we measured accuracy, not attention map stability or feature learning dynamics directly. Attention stability was a hypothesis not directly measured. It is possible that the consistency loss successfully aligned the weights without impacting the functional behavior of the attention maps, or that the alignment was too weak to influence the final representation. Alternatively, the model may benefit from layer-specific specialization, where deeper layers refine features in ways that are incompatible with shallow layer weights. This interpretation is consistent with findings in *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which notes that deep Transformers are prone to overfitting, but our results suggest that this specific form of consistency does not mitigate that risk in the subject-disjoint setting [17].

**Comparison with Related Work.** Our findings contrast with works that report positive effects for cross-layer mechanisms in other domains. *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention* reports improvements in image classification and detection by strengthening layer interactions [15]. *Global Evolutionary Steering* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering with positive results [34]. However, these studies operate in different settings (vision, language steering) and may not transfer to subject-disjoint time-series data. *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of Transformer-based solutions for time series, suggesting that architectural complexity may not always yield benefits [5]. Our results support the view that not all architectural inductive biases improve generalization in this domain. The inconclusive outcome aligns with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found null results for a weight-based regularization in a similar setting [3].

**Replication and Stability.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds provides evidence about the stability of the result under fresh sampling. The fact that both cohorts were inconclusive strengthens the conclusion that the effect is not robust. However, this is not an independent replication in terms of data source or implementation; it uses the same pipeline and dataset. Therefore, it does not establish generalization to other time-series benchmarks. The variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them, as the confidence intervals overlap substantially between cohorts. Future work should test whether this finding holds on different datasets or with different Transformer depths.

=== limitations ===
**Mechanism and Measurement.** A key limitation is that we measured accuracy, not attention map stability or feature learning dynamics directly. Mechanistic claims remain hypothetical. We cannot confirm whether the consistency loss actually stabilized attention patterns or whether it merely constrained the weights without functional impact. Direct measurement of attention maps or intermediate representations would be required to settle this question. Additionally, the detachment of reference weights from the gradient graph stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. This design choice was preregistered but limits our ability to attribute effects solely to the consistency term.

**Generalization and Scope.** The experiment uses a single dataset (UCI HAR) and a specific Transformer architecture (2 blocks, 64 hidden). The findings may not generalize to deeper models, different time-series domains, or other subject-disjoint benchmarks. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds tests stability under fresh sampling but does not establish out-of-distribution generalization to new sensors or tasks. The registered margin reflects measurement precision and does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

**Statistical Power.** The study was powered to detect an effect equal to the registered margin. The observed effect sizes were smaller than the margin, and the confidence intervals included zero. This does not prove the null hypothesis; it indicates that the data are compatible with no effect or a small effect. The power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter. Further sampling would be required to narrow the confidence intervals sufficiently to rule out small effects.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. We found inconclusive evidence in both primary and replication cohorts, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. These results suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. For practitioners choosing between these methods, the findings indicate that standard training may be preferable to this specific consistency regularization, as it adds computational cost without clear benefit. To settle the question next, future work should measure attention stability directly and test the intervention on deeper architectures and diverse time-series benchmarks.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00077 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
**The Problem of Subject-Disjoint Generalization.** Time-series classification tasks, such as human activity recognition, often require models to generalize across individuals with distinct movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Transformers have emerged as a powerful architecture for modeling sequential data due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [38]. However, their effectiveness in time-series forecasting and classification remains a subject of debate, with some evidence suggesting that simpler linear models can outperform sophisticated Transformer-based solutions in certain regimes [5]. A critical open question is what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects. Specifically, it is unclear whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined attention patterns or consistently stable attention patterns to support out-of-distribution performance in subject-disjoint settings.

**The Gap in Current Literature.** While consistency regularization has been proposed to improve Transformer stability and generalization [17], there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. Existing works explore cross-layer interactions to strengthen representation power [15] or apply cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34], but these mechanisms have not been rigorously tested for subject-disjoint time-series generalization using preregistered confirmatory replication. The literature identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18], motivating the hypothesis that enforcing consistency across layers might mitigate such discrepancies. However, without controlled experimentation, it remains unknown whether this specific inductive bias yields measurable accuracy gains over standard training.

**This Study.** This paper reports a calibrated test of the cross-layer query consistency hypothesis. We implement a Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights in a PreNormTransformerEncoder. We compare this intervention against a baseline control arm that executes the identical training pipeline without the loss term. To ensure robustness, we employ a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, allowing us to distinguish sampling variation from true effects. We report quantitative evidence on held-out classification accuracy, including effect sizes, confidence intervals, and significance tests for both cohorts.

**Contributions.**
- We implement and evaluate a cross-layer query consistency loss designed to stabilize attention projections across transformer depth in a time-series classification task.
- We provide a preregistered comparison against a baseline and a negative control, using a subject-disjoint split to assess generalization to unseen subjects.
- We report inconclusive results in both primary and replication cohorts, suggesting that layer-specific adaptation may be preferable to cross-layer consistency in this setting.

**Preregistered Prediction.** The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
**Transformers in Time-Series Analysis.** Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [38]. However, *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line, demonstrating that simple linear models can outperform Transformer-based solutions in long-term forecasting tasks [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [32]. These works collectively motivate the search for architectural modifications that enhance robustness in subject-disjoint settings.

**Consistency Regularization and Cross-Layer Mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data and proposes constraining encoder and decoder outputs [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, proposing attention-level alignment to mitigate this [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions by retrieving query-related information from previous layers [15]. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering to rectify steering vectors [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it, indicating that not all proposed regularization strategies hold under audit [2].

**Attention Mechanisms and Architectures.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements, improving efficiency and performance [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks, offering linear complexity [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow, proposing a method to mix values inside the attention module [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* and *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* document the application of Transformers across vision and other modalities [11, 21]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance, finding that query and key content comparison is negligible for self-attention in some contexts [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing whether cross-layer query consistency specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers, a gap not settled by the cited literature.

=== method ===
**The CrossLayerQueryConsistency Operator.** The core intervention is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, applied to the query projection weights of the second attention block (blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight). This operator enforces a Frobenius norm consistency regularization between the query weights of the first block (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight) and the second block. The hypothesis is that aligning these weights stabilizes attention patterns across depth, potentially improving generalization to unseen subjects. The operator is invoked during the loss computation of every optimization step, adding its term to the classification objective inside the autograd graph.

**Operator Specification.** The operator retrieves reference weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients from flowing to the first block. It then computes the element-wise difference between the target weights (block 1) and the reference weights. The squared elements are summed to produce a raw loss, which is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01. This loss term is differentiable with respect to the target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds to prevent the consistency term from dominating the classification objective. The reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients from this term, ensuring that the regularization only constrains the deeper layer to match the shallower one.

**Control and Negative Control Arms.** The baseline condition is a control arm defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step—the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass, and the same optimizer update. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm, the intervention leaves the registered target parameter unchanged, leaves that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and adds nothing to the training objective. This ensures that any observed difference in outcomes is attributable to the loss term itself rather than implementation artifacts.

A negative control condition penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the computational cost of the proposed condition. This arm tests whether the observed effect (if any) is due to the specific cross-layer relationship or merely the addition of a regularization term. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. Training uses a PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks, 64 hidden units, 4-head attention, 128 timesteps, and 9 channels. Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on the official subject-disjoint test split.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Subject-Disjoint Split Justification.** The experiment uses the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. This design choice is critical because the research question concerns generalization to unseen subjects, not merely unseen data points from the same subjects. A random split would allow the model to learn subject-specific features that do not transfer, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to answer the open problem. By holding out entire subjects, we ensure that the evaluation metric reflects the model's ability to generalize across different movement styles and sensor characteristics. This aligns with the goal of determining whether architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects.

**Pairing Conditions by Seed.** We pair the proposed condition and the baseline by seed, deriving the dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters once and reusing them for both arms. This pairing reduces variance in the contrast estimate by controlling for stochastic factors inherent in training deep networks. Each seed produces a paired difference, which is the unit of analysis for the hypothesis test. This design increases the power to detect small effects compared to an unpaired design, given the same computational budget. The seed budget consists of 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix.

**Negative Control Purpose.** The first negative control penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. This condition is intended to rule out the alternative explanation that any regularization term, regardless of its structure, improves accuracy. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, it suggests that the specific cross-layer relationship is beneficial. If both perform similarly, the effect may be due to general regularization rather than cross-layer consistency. The observed contrast between the proposed condition and the negative control supports or refutes the specific mechanistic hypothesis.

**Analysis Plan.** We report mean held-out classification accuracy with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for each condition. The primary decision rule compares the mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast against a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The confirmatory cohort is a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, not an independent replication in terms of data source or implementation. This distinction is important because the replication uses the same pipeline and dataset, testing the stability of the result under fresh sampling rather than generalization to new domains. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort Outcomes.** In the primary cohort, we evaluated the proposed condition against the baseline across 43 seeds. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline, and negative control 1 conditions, with error bars showing the 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimates are printed above each bar. Figure 3 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions, with the registered worthwhile threshold marked by a green dash-dot line. The lower confidence bound does not exceed the threshold. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions, with curves distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern.

**Replication Cohort Outcomes.** In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, we evaluated the same conditions across 43 fresh seeds. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 5 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the replication cohort, mirroring the structure of Figure 2. Figure 6 plots the mean difference for the replication cohort, again showing that the lower confidence bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the replication cohort.

**Summary of Metrics.** Table 1 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for each condition in the primary cohort, while Table 2 summarizes the outcome contrasts. Table 3 and Table 4 provide the corresponding data for the replication cohort. Table 5 compares the means across both cohorts. In all cases, the confidence intervals overlap substantially, and the effect sizes are small (Cohen's dz=0.06 in primary, 0.15 in replication). The negative control 1 condition performed similarly to the baseline in both cohorts (Primary: 0.9051 vs 0.9054; Replication: 0.9043 vs 0.9035), suggesting that the addition of a regularization term alone did not drive accuracy changes. The results are inconclusive in both cohorts, as neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency in attention projections did not yield robust accuracy gains in a subject-disjoint time-series classification task. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. This suggests that, in this regime, layer-specific adaptation may be more effective than enforcing consistency across depth. The small effect sizes (Cohen's dz < 0.2) indicate that even if a true effect exists, it is likely too small to be of practical importance for this task.

**Mechanistic Interpretation.** The hypothesis motivating this intervention was that stabilizing attention patterns across depth would improve generalization to unseen subjects. However, we measured accuracy, not attention map stability or feature learning dynamics directly. Attention stability was a hypothesis not directly measured. It is possible that the consistency loss successfully aligned the weights without impacting the functional behavior of the attention maps, or that the alignment was too weak to influence the final representation. Alternatively, the model may benefit from layer-specific specialization, where deeper layers refine features in ways that are incompatible with shallow layer weights. This interpretation is consistent with findings in *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which notes that deep Transformers are prone to overfitting, but our results suggest that this specific form of consistency does not mitigate that risk in the subject-disjoint setting [17].

**Comparison with Related Work.** Our findings contrast with works that report positive effects for cross-layer mechanisms in other domains. *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention* reports improvements in image classification and detection by strengthening layer interactions [15]. *Global Evolutionary Steering* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering with positive results [34]. However, these studies operate in different settings (vision, language steering) and may not transfer to subject-disjoint time-series data. *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of Transformer-based solutions for time series, suggesting that architectural complexity may not always yield benefits [5]. Our results support the view that not all architectural inductive biases improve generalization in this domain. The inconclusive outcome aligns with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found null results for a weight-based regularization in a similar setting [3].

**Replication and Stability.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds provides evidence about the stability of the result under fresh sampling. The fact that both cohorts were inconclusive strengthens the conclusion that the effect is not robust. However, this is not an independent replication in terms of data source or implementation; it uses the same pipeline and dataset. Therefore, it does not establish generalization to other time-series benchmarks. The variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them, as the confidence intervals overlap substantially between cohorts. Future work should test whether this finding holds on different datasets or with different Transformer depths.

=== limitations ===
**Mechanism and Measurement.** A key limitation is that we measured accuracy, not attention map stability or feature learning dynamics directly. Mechanistic claims remain hypothetical. We cannot confirm whether the consistency loss actually stabilized attention patterns or whether it merely constrained the weights without functional impact. Direct measurement of attention maps or intermediate representations would be required to settle this question. Additionally, the detachment of reference weights from the gradient graph stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. This design choice was preregistered but limits our ability to attribute effects solely to the consistency term.

**Generalization and Scope.** The experiment uses a single dataset (UCI HAR) and a specific Transformer architecture (2 blocks, 64 hidden). The findings may not generalize to deeper models, different time-series domains, or other subject-disjoint benchmarks. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds tests stability under fresh sampling but does not establish out-of-distribution generalization to new sensors or tasks. The registered margin reflects measurement precision and does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

**Statistical Power.** The study was powered to detect an effect equal to the registered margin. The observed effect sizes were smaller than the margin, and the confidence intervals included zero. This does not prove the null hypothesis; it indicates that the data are compatible with no effect or a small effect. The power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter. Further sampling would be required to narrow the confidence intervals sufficiently to rule out small effects.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. We found inconclusive evidence in both primary and replication cohorts, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. These results suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. For practitioners choosing between these methods, the findings indicate that standard training may be preferable to this specific consistency regularization, as it adds computational cost without clear benefit. To settle the question next, future work should measure attention stability directly and test the intervention on deeper architectures and diverse time-series benchmarks.
