Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00077 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: **Transformers in Time-Series Analysis.** Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [19]. However, *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line, demonstrating that simple linear models can outperform Transformer-based solutions in long-term forecasting tasks [3]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [10] and representing multivariate series as graphs [6]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [12]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [15]. These works collectively motivate the search for architectural modifications that enhance robustness in subject-disjoint settings.

**Consistency Regularization and Cross-Layer Mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data and proposes constraining encoder and decoder outputs [8]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, proposing attention-level alignment to mitigate this [9]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions by retrieving query-related information from previous layers [7]. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering to rectify steering vectors [17]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [13]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it, indicating that not all proposed regularization strategies hold under audit [1].

**Attention Mechanisms and Architectures.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements, improving efficiency and performance [4]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks, offering linear complexity [16]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow, proposing a method to mix values inside the attention module [18]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* and *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* document the application of Transformers across vision and other modalities [5, 11]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance, finding that query and key content comparison is negligible for self-attention in some contexts [14]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing whether cross-layer query consistency specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers, a gap not settled by the cited literature.
Method: **The CrossLayerQueryConsistency Operator.** The core intervention is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, applied to the query projection weights of the second attention block (blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight). This operator enforces a Frobenius norm consistency regularization between the query weights of the first block (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight) and the second block. The hypothesis is that aligning these weights stabilizes attention patterns across depth, potentially improving generalization to unseen subjects. The operator is invoked during the loss computation of every optimization step, adding its term to the classification objective inside the autograd graph.

**Operator Specification.** The operator retrieves reference weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients from flowing to the first block. It then computes the element-wise difference between the target weights (block 1) and the reference weights. The squared elements are summed to produce a raw loss, which is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01. This loss term is differentiable with respect to the target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds to prevent the consistency term from dominating the classification objective. The reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients from this term, ensuring that the regularization only constrains the deeper layer to match the shallower one.

**Control and Negative Control Arms.** The baseline condition is a control arm defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step—the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass, and the same optimizer update. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm, the intervention leaves the registered target parameter unchanged, leaves that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and adds nothing to the training objective. This ensures that any observed difference in outcomes is attributable to the loss term itself rather than implementation artifacts.

A negative control condition penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the computational cost of the proposed condition. This arm tests whether the observed effect (if any) is due to the specific cross-layer relationship or merely the addition of a regularization term. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. Training uses a PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks, 64 hidden units, 4-head attention, 128 timesteps, and 9 channels. Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on the official subject-disjoint test split.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Experimental setup: **Subject-Disjoint Split Justification.** The experiment uses the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. This design choice is critical because the research question concerns generalization to unseen subjects, not merely unseen data points from the same subjects. A random split would allow the model to learn subject-specific features that do not transfer, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to answer the open problem. By holding out entire subjects, we ensure that the evaluation metric reflects the model's ability to generalize across different movement styles and sensor characteristics. This aligns with the goal of determining whether architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects.

**Pairing Conditions by Seed.** We pair the proposed condition and the baseline by seed, deriving the dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters once and reusing them for both arms. This pairing reduces variance in the contrast estimate by controlling for stochastic factors inherent in training deep networks. Each seed produces a paired difference, which is the unit of analysis for the hypothesis test. This design increases the power to detect small effects compared to an unpaired design, given the same computational budget. The seed budget consists of 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix.

**Negative Control Purpose.** The first negative control penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. This condition is intended to rule out the alternative explanation that any regularization term, regardless of its structure, improves accuracy. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, it suggests that the specific cross-layer relationship is beneficial. If both perform similarly, the effect may be due to general regularization rather than cross-layer consistency. The observed contrast between the proposed condition and the negative control supports or refutes the specific mechanistic hypothesis.

**Analysis Plan.** We report mean held-out classification accuracy with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for each condition. The primary decision rule compares the mean paired contrast in the hypothesised direction against a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The confirmatory cohort is a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, not an independent replication in terms of data source or implementation. This distinction is important. This experiment did not test whether this was because the replication uses the same pipeline and dataset, testing the stability of the result under fresh sampling rather than generalization to new domains. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Add loss term that applies Frobenius norm consistency regularization to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Baseline: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline, and negative control 1 conditions, with error bars showing the 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimates are printed above each bar. Figure 3 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions, with the registered worthwhile threshold marked by a green dash-dot line. The lower confidence bound does not exceed the threshold. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions, with curves distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern.

**Replication Cohort Outcomes.** In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, we evaluated the same conditions across 43 fresh seeds. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 5 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the replication cohort, mirroring the structure of Figure 2. Figure 6 plots the mean difference for the replication cohort, again showing that the lower confidence bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the replication cohort.

**Summary of Metrics.** Table 1 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for each condition in the primary cohort, while Table 2 summarizes the outcome contrasts. Table 3 and Table 4 provide the corresponding data for the replication cohort. Table 5 compares the means across both cohorts. In all cases, the confidence intervals overlap substantially, and the effect sizes are small (Cohen's dz=0.06 in primary, 0.15 in replication). The negative control 1 condition performed similarly to the baseline in both cohorts (Primary: 0.9051 vs 0.9054; Replication: 0.9043 vs 0.9035), suggesting that the addition of a regularization term alone did not drive accuracy changes. The results are inconclusive in both cohorts, as neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This study tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. We found inconclusive evidence in both primary and replication cohorts, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. These results suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. For practitioners choosing between these methods, the findings indicate that standard training may be preferable to this specific consistency regularization, as it adds computational cost without clear benefit. To settle the question next, future work should measure attention stability directly and test the intervention on deeper architectures and diverse time-series benchmarks.
Discussion: **Principal Finding.** The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency in attention projections did not yield robust accuracy gains in a subject-disjoint time-series classification task. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. This suggests that, in this regime, layer-specific adaptation may be more effective than enforcing consistency across depth. The small effect sizes (Cohen's dz < 0.2) indicate that even if a true effect exists, it is likely too small to be of practical importance for this task.

**Mechanistic Interpretation.** The hypothesis motivating this intervention was that stabilizing attention patterns across depth would improve generalization to unseen subjects. However, we measured accuracy, not attention map stability or feature learning dynamics directly. Attention stability was a hypothesis not directly measured. It is possible that the consistency loss successfully aligned the weights without impacting the functional behavior of the attention maps, or that the alignment was too weak to influence the final representation. Alternatively, the model may benefit from layer-specific specialization, where deeper layers refine features in ways that are incompatible with shallow layer weights. This interpretation is consistent with findings in *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which notes that deep Transformers are prone to overfitting, but our results suggest that this specific form of consistency does not mitigate that risk in the subject-disjoint setting [8].

**Comparison with Related Work.** Our findings contrast with works that report positive effects for cross-layer mechanisms in other domains. *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention* reports improvements in image classification and detection by strengthening layer interactions [7]. *Global Evolutionary Steering* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering with positive results [17]. However, these studies operate in different settings (vision, language steering) and may not transfer to subject-disjoint time-series data. *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of Transformer-based solutions for time series, suggesting that architectural complexity may not always yield benefits [3]. Our results support the view that not all architectural inductive biases improve generalization in this domain. The inconclusive outcome aligns with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found null results for a weight-based regularization in a similar setting [2].

**Replication and Stability.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds provides evidence about the stability of the result under fresh sampling. The fact that both cohorts were inconclusive strengthens the conclusion that the effect is not robust. However, this is not an independent replication in terms of data source or implementation; it uses the same pipeline and dataset. Therefore, it does not establish generalization to other time-series benchmarks. The variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them, as the confidence intervals overlap substantially between cohorts. Future work should test whether this finding holds on different datasets or with different Transformer depths.
Limitations: **Mechanism and Measurement.** A key limitation is that we measured accuracy, not attention map stability or feature learning dynamics directly. Mechanistic claims remain hypothetical. We cannot confirm whether the consistency loss actually stabilized attention patterns or whether it merely constrained the weights without functional impact. Direct measurement of attention maps or intermediate representations would be required to settle this question. Additionally, the detachment of reference weights from the gradient graph stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. This design choice was preregistered but limits our ability to attribute effects solely to the consistency term.

**Generalization and Scope.** The experiment uses a single dataset (UCI HAR) and a specific Transformer architecture (2 blocks, 64 hidden). The findings may not generalize to deeper models, different time-series domains, or other subject-disjoint benchmarks. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds tests stability under fresh sampling but does not establish out-of-distribution generalization to new sensors or tasks. The registered margin reflects measurement precision and does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

**Statistical Power.** The study was powered to detect an effect equal to the registered margin. The observed effect sizes were smaller than the margin, and the confidence intervals included zero. This does not prove the null hypothesis; it indicates that the data are compatible with no effect or a small effect. The power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter. Further sampling would be required to narrow the confidence intervals sufficiently to rule out small effects.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

We establish theoretical foundations for the approach, including complexity analysis, expressiveness results, and convergence guarantees. In experiments with 1.7B parameter models trained on 400B tokens, GSA matches the efficiency of sparse-only baselines (12-16x speedup at 128K context) while achieving the quality gains associated with gated attention: perplexity improves from 6.03 to 5.70, RULER scores at 128K context nearly double, and attention to the first token, a proxy for attention sinks, drops from 47% to under 4%. Training stability improves markedly, with loss spikes reduced by 98%.

However, like other deep learning models, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding, generalization challenges, and data shift issues for the domains with limited data. Additionally, addressing the issue of catastrophic forgetting, where models forget previously learned information when exposed to new data, is another critical aspect that requires attention in enhancing the robustness of Transformers for time series tasks. To address these limitations, in this paper, we pre-train the time series Transformer model on a source domain with sufficient data and fine-tune it on the target domain with limited data. We introduce the \emph{One-step fine-tuning} approach, adding some percentage of source domain data to the target domains, providing the model with diverse time series instances. We then fine-tune the pre-trained model using a gradual unfreezing technique. This helps enhance the model's performance in time series prediction for domains with limited data. We introduce Depth-Attention, which performs this selection inside the attention module itself: before a layer attends over the sequence, its query attends over the keys of earlier layers at the same token position and mixes their values into the value that self-attention then reads. In particular, we examine the development of time series Transformers in two perspectives. From the perspective of network structure, we summarize the adaptations and modifications that have been made to Transformers in order to accommodate the challenges in time series analysis. From the perspective of applications, we categorize time series Transformers based on common tasks including forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification. Empirically, we perform robust analysis, model size analysis, and seasonal-trend decomposition analysis to study how Transformers perform in time series. Finally, we discuss and suggest future directions to provide useful research guidance. These embeddings allow a transformer to learn the mapping across different views without ever explicitly modeling it geometrically. CITE numbered references in square brackets (e.g. [1] or [2, 3]); the Introduction and Related Work MUST cite them inline. You are NOT required to cite every reference; unused references are removed. NEVER cite a paper as evidence for something it does NOT discuss, including a gap in a different setting. State a gap WITHOUT a marker, use the reviewed gap statement, or cite an abstract that identifies that gap itself. Never attribute the opposite of what an abstract says. Stay INSIDE the abstract's own wording: use its terms, do not generalise them or add an unstated mechanism, domain or consequence. Plausible extensions are unsupported claims too; if in doubt, write less about the paper. Refer to figures and tables by number (e.g. 'Figure 1', 'Table 1'). Report results quantitatively (state the effect, its confidence interval, and whether it is significant). When the analysis contains primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts, report BOTH separately, state each preregistered decision, and never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. EVIDENCE AND INTERPRETATION. The registered condition descriptions and executed activation records below are authoritative: a baseline/no-op and an active negative control are different conditions. Do not infer inactivity from a small or nonsignificant outcome contrast. Describe only what the control manipulates; its outcome cannot prove that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: name the directly recorded outcomes, and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. If a reference tensor is detached inside a penalty, this stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient. Use the registered CI classifications without equating nonsignificance with equality. If a CI crosses zero but lies below the worthwhile margin, preserve its registered label and separately explain that it excludes gains of that target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model. The supplied power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; do not claim the former guarantees the latter. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

LENGTH. Write a full paper, not an extended abstract. Aim for roughly: introduction 600-800 words; related work 600-900; method 500-800 (BEFORE the operator specification that is appended for you); experimental setup 300-500; results 500-800; discussion 500-800; limitations 200-300; conclusion 150-250; abstract 150-250. A section that is three sentences long has not done its job. Depth means argument and detail, never padding or repetition.

=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [38]. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications [38]. However, recent work questions the validity of this research line, noting that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [5, 32]. Specifically, the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss compared to models designed for ordered sequences [5]. This uncertainty motivates a rigorous examination of the architectural inductive biases that enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds.

Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. Despite proposals for consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. This work addresses this gap by testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling.

This paper reports quantitative evidence on held-out classification accuracy, including effect sizes, confidence intervals, and significance tests for both cohorts. We adhere to a preregistered protocol to ensure the validity of the experimental design and inconclusive outcome. The study contributes the following:
- We implement a cross-layer query consistency loss enforcing Frobenius norm alignment between deeper and shallower attention query projections.
- We evaluate this intervention against a baseline and negative control on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset using an official subject-disjoint split.
- We report results from both a primary cohort and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, distinguishing training-seed replication from independent replication.
- We provide an honest assessment of the evidence, labeling unforeseen findings as exploratory and adhering to registered decision thresholds.

The preregistered prediction states that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report the results against this prediction without silently changing the hypothesis to fit the outcomes.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation and representing multivariate series as graphs [14, 20]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32]. These works establish that while Transformers are widely applied, their generalization capabilities in time-series domains remain unsettled.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy, finding inconclusive results in a subject-disjoint setting [3]. These studies suggest that regularization strategies are common, but their efficacy varies by context.

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing cross-layer consistency specifically for subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers, where evidence remains lacking.

=== method ===
The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear input projection, learned positional embedding, and two transformer blocks. Each block consists of LayerNorm, 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear projections, residual connections, and a feed-forward network. The final layer involves LayerNorm, mean-pooling over time, and a Linear classification head. The intervention enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights during training.

The CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator is applied to the target parameter blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The operator retrieves reference weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. It computes the element-wise difference between the target and reference weights, squares the elements, sums them to obtain the raw loss, and scales by a fixed coefficient of 0.01. This loss term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is differentiated. The reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients, ensuring the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

The control arm executes identical code path but returns zero loss term. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation.

This design isolates the effect of the consistency loss from other training dynamics. The comparator neutralizes the computational path without applying the regularization, ensuring any observed contrast is attributable to the loss term itself. The hypothesis is that enforcing consistency will stabilize attention patterns across depth, leading to improved generalization on unseen subjects.

=== experimental_setup ===
The dataset is the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones, comprising raw inertial signals in 128-timestep windows over 9 channels. We use the official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. This split ensures that evaluation is performed on people who appear nowhere in training, supporting a claim about unseen subjects. A random split would not answer the question of subject-disjoint generalization, as it would allow subject-specific features to leak into the training set. The subject-disjoint split is therefore necessary to test the hypothesis regarding generalization across different movement styles and sensor characteristics.

We use 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them, not to subjects, as the subject split is fixed. Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance by ensuring both arms see the same initialization and data ordering, allowing for paired statistical tests. The seed budget supports the registered power qualification, distinguishing zero-null detection from exceeding the margin.

The negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. Its observed contrast supports the interpretation that any effect in the proposed condition is due to the specific cross-layer relationship rather than the mere presence of a regularization term. The baseline control arm ensures the harness is unbiased and the implementation correct, though its outcome cannot prove this definitively.

The confirmatory cohort is a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, not an independent replication in terms of data source or implementation. This distinction is critical: it replicates the pipeline on fresh stochasticity rather than new data. Figure 1 and Figure 4 visualize the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Figure 2 and Figure 5 show the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions. Figure 3 and Figure 6 display the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps.

=== results ===
In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 1 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions, with error bars representing 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimate is printed above each bar. Figure 2 plots the paired mean difference over 43 seeds, with the green dash-dot marker showing the registered worthwhile threshold. The lower confidence bound does not exceed the threshold.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the replication cohort, and Figure 5 shows the mean difference. The individual paired differences are plotted behind the interval at their exact values.

Figure 3 and Figure 6 show the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. Conditions whose curves coincide are distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern as well as by colour. The curves for the proposed and baseline conditions track closely throughout training, consistent with the small mean differences observed at convergence. The negative control 1 condition also tracks closely, suggesting the regularization term magnitude itself does not disrupt optimization.

Table 1 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for each condition in the primary cohort. The proposed condition achieved 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). Table 2 summarizes the outcome statistics for the primary cohort, confirming the inconclusive decision. Table 3 and Table 4 provide the corresponding data for the replication cohort. The proposed condition achieved 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), and the baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). The consistency between cohorts reinforces the inconclusive finding.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds produced confidence intervals that included zero. This suggests that enforcing Frobenius norm alignment between query projections across depth does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this specific architecture and dataset. The results are consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

We measured accuracy, not attention map stability or feature learning dynamics directly. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings. While the intervention was designed to stabilize attention across depth, the observed accuracy contrast alone cannot prove attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. The detached reference tensor in the penalty stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. Thus, the null result does not prove the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct, though the control arm recorded zero activity.

This design establishes the effect on held-out accuracy but does not establish the mechanism. An alternative explanation is that the consistency constraint is too weak to influence the learned representations meaningfully, or that the optimal solution for subject-disjoint generalization requires divergent query projections at different depths. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not a fluke of a specific seed set, but it is not an independent replication in terms of data source or implementation.

These findings agree with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which found inconclusive results for spectral entropy minimization in a subject-disjoint setting [3]. They conflict with *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which noted improvements on machine translation tasks, suggesting consistency benefits may be task-dependent [17]. They are not comparable to *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation*, which addresses domain gaps in vision rather than subject-disjoint generalization in time series [18]. *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of Transformer-based solutions, which aligns with our finding that architectural modifications do not automatically yield gains [5].

What would settle the question next is direct measurement of attention maps across layers during training and evaluation. Future work should test whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks with larger models or different modalities.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether attention stability was achieved, as only accuracy was recorded. Claiming attention stability from an accuracy contrast is unsupported. The study is limited to the UCI HAR dataset and a two-block transformer architecture; results may not generalize to deeper models or other time-series domains. The registered margin reflects measurement precision and does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient. The power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter. The calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

=== conclusion ===
We found inconclusive evidence that cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Both primary and replication cohorts showed confidence intervals including zero. This changes the choice for someone choosing between these methods by indicating that cross-layer consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Layer-specific adaptation may remain essential. Future work should settle the question by directly measuring attention stability and testing on diverse benchmarks.

=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [38]. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications [38]. However, recent work questions the validity of this research line, noting that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [5, 32]. Specifically, the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss compared to models designed for ordered sequences [5]. This uncertainty motivates a rigorous examination of the architectural inductive biases that enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds.

Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. Despite proposals for consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. This work addresses this gap by testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling.

This paper reports quantitative evidence on held-out classification accuracy, including effect sizes, confidence intervals, and significance tests for both cohorts. We adhere to a preregistered protocol to ensure the validity of the experimental design and inconclusive outcome. The study contributes the following:
- We implement a cross-layer query consistency loss enforcing Frobenius norm alignment between deeper and shallower attention query projections.
- We evaluate this intervention against a baseline and negative control on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset using an official subject-disjoint split.
- We report results from both a primary cohort and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, distinguishing training-seed replication from independent replication.
- We provide an honest assessment of the evidence, labeling unforeseen findings as exploratory and adhering to registered decision thresholds.

The preregistered prediction states that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report the results against this prediction without silently changing the hypothesis to fit the outcomes.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation and representing multivariate series as graphs [14, 20]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32]. These works establish that while Transformers are widely applied, their generalization capabilities in time-series domains remain unsettled.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy, finding inconclusive results in a subject-disjoint setting [3]. These studies suggest that regularization strategies are common, but their efficacy varies by context.

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing cross-layer consistency specifically for subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers, where evidence remains lacking.

=== method ===
The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear input projection, learned positional embedding, and two transformer blocks. Each block consists of LayerNorm, 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear projections, residual connections, and a feed-forward network. The final layer involves LayerNorm, mean-pooling over time, and a Linear classification head. The intervention enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights during training.

The CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator is applied to the target parameter blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The operator retrieves reference weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. It computes the element-wise difference between the target and reference weights, squares the elements, sums them to obtain the raw loss, and scales by a fixed coefficient of 0.01. This loss term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is differentiated. The reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients, ensuring the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

The control arm executes identical code path but returns zero loss term. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation.

This design isolates the effect of the consistency loss from other training dynamics. The comparator neutralizes the computational path without applying the regularization, ensuring any observed contrast is attributable to the loss term itself. The hypothesis is that enforcing consistency will stabilize attention patterns across depth, leading to improved generalization on unseen subjects.

=== experimental_setup ===
The dataset is the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones, comprising raw inertial signals in 128-timestep windows over 9 channels. We use the official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. This split ensures that evaluation is performed on people who appear nowhere in training, supporting a claim about unseen subjects. A random split would not answer the question of subject-disjoint generalization, as it would allow subject-specific features to leak into the training set. The subject-disjoint split is therefore necessary to test the hypothesis regarding generalization across different movement styles and sensor characteristics.

We use 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them, not to subjects, as the subject split is fixed. Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance by ensuring both arms see the same initialization and data ordering, allowing for paired statistical tests. The seed budget supports the registered power qualification, distinguishing zero-null detection from exceeding the margin.

The negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. Its observed contrast supports the interpretation that any effect in the proposed condition is due to the specific cross-layer relationship rather than the mere presence of a regularization term. The baseline control arm ensures the harness is unbiased and the implementation correct, though its outcome cannot prove this definitively.

The confirmatory cohort is a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, not an independent replication in terms of data source or implementation. This distinction is critical: it replicates the pipeline on fresh stochasticity rather than new data. Figure 1 and Figure 4 visualize the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Figure 2 and Figure 5 show the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions. Figure 3 and Figure 6 display the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps.

=== results ===
In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 1 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions, with error bars representing 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimate is printed above each bar. Figure 2 plots the paired mean difference over 43 seeds, with the green dash-dot marker showing the registered worthwhile threshold. The lower confidence bound does not exceed the threshold.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the replication cohort, and Figure 5 shows the mean difference. The individual paired differences are plotted behind the interval at their exact values.

Figure 3 and Figure 6 show the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. Conditions whose curves coincide are distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern as well as by colour. The curves for the proposed and baseline conditions track closely throughout training, consistent with the small mean differences observed at convergence. The negative control 1 condition also tracks closely, suggesting the regularization term magnitude itself does not disrupt optimization.

Table 1 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for each condition in the primary cohort. The proposed condition achieved 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). Table 2 summarizes the outcome statistics for the primary cohort, confirming the inconclusive decision. Table 3 and Table 4 provide the corresponding data for the replication cohort. The proposed condition achieved 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), and the baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). The consistency between cohorts reinforces the inconclusive finding.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds produced confidence intervals that included zero. This suggests that enforcing Frobenius norm alignment between query projections across depth does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this specific architecture and dataset. The results are consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

We measured accuracy, not attention map stability or feature learning dynamics directly. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings. While the intervention was designed to stabilize attention across depth, the observed accuracy contrast alone cannot prove attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. The detached reference tensor in the penalty stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. Thus, the null result does not prove the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct, though the control arm recorded zero activity.

This design establishes the effect on held-out accuracy but does not establish the mechanism. An alternative explanation is that the consistency constraint is too weak to influence the learned representations meaningfully, or that the optimal solution for subject-disjoint generalization requires divergent query projections at different depths. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not a fluke of a specific seed set, but it is not an independent replication in terms of data source or implementation.

These findings agree with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which found inconclusive results for spectral entropy minimization in a subject-disjoint setting [3]. They conflict with *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which noted improvements on machine translation tasks, suggesting consistency benefits may be task-dependent [17]. They are not comparable to *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation*, which addresses domain gaps in vision rather than subject-disjoint generalization in time series [18]. *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of Transformer-based solutions, which aligns with our finding that architectural modifications do not automatically yield gains [5].

What would settle the question next is direct measurement of attention maps across layers during training and evaluation. Future work should test whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks with larger models or different modalities.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether attention stability was achieved, as only accuracy was recorded. Claiming attention stability from an accuracy contrast is unsupported. The study is limited to the UCI HAR dataset and a two-block transformer architecture; results may not generalize to deeper models or other time-series domains. The registered margin reflects measurement precision and does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient. The power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter. The calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

=== conclusion ===
We found inconclusive evidence that cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Both primary and replication cohorts showed confidence intervals including zero. This changes the choice for someone choosing between these methods by indicating that cross-layer consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Layer-specific adaptation may remain essential. Future work should settle the question by directly measuring attention stability and testing on diverse benchmarks.
