FEEDBACK: <one short paragraph of specific, actionable feedback>

Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0007734 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.001957 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [20], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [11] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [7]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [16].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [8], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [6, 12, 21]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15]. This study positions itself against these themes by rigorously testing a specific cross-layer weight consistency hypothesis in a subject-disjoint setting, distinguishing between primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts to ensure robustness.
Method: The core of this study is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights. The hypothesis is that aligning deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights stabilizes attention patterns across depth, thereby improving subject-disjoint generalization. The operator is applied to `blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight` during loss computation of every optimization step. The operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated. Reference weights from block 0 are detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0, ensuring the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed at 0.01 across all steps and seeds to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective.

The proposed condition is compared against two control arms. The baseline is a control arm defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The first negative control adds a loss term penalizing difference between `blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight` and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute, isolating the effect of the specific cross-layer alignment from the mere presence of a regularization term.

This design isolates the effect of cross-layer weight alignment from general regularization effects. By detaching the reference weights, we ensure that the penalty only drives the target weights toward the reference, not vice versa. This expresses the hypothesis that deeper layers should conform to shallower layers' query projections. The comparator neutralizes the effect of the loss term's computational presence and gradient flow structure, allowing us to attribute any accuracy difference specifically to the semantic content of the consistency constraint. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, ensuring the control's recorded activity is zero.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Experimental setup: **Design Justification.** We use the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. A subject-disjoint split answers the question of generalization to unseen subjects, whereas a random split would not, as it allows subject-specific features to leak into training. This design tests whether the intervention improves performance on data from people who appear nowhere in training. We pair conditions by seed to reduce variance; each seed generates one instance of the proposed condition and one of the baseline, sharing initialization and data ordering. This pairing allows for paired statistical tests which are more sensitive to the intervention's effect than unpaired tests.

**Negative Controls and Seed Budget.** The first negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any regularization term, regardless of semantic content, might improve generalization. Its observed contrast supports whether the specific cross-layer relationship matters. We use 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the result is not a fluke of a specific seed set, but it is not an independent replication in terms of data source or implementation—it uses the same pipeline, dataset, and architecture through fresh random seeds. This distinction is critical: it replicates the sampling process, not the experimental context.

**Data and Evaluation.** The dataset uses raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels. We omit the specific training window count to align with recorded analysis values, but the held-out evaluation measures accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects. Evaluation is defined as the number of correct activity predictions divided by the total test windows. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. Training uses a PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks, 64 hidden units, and 4-head attention for 12 epochs. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

- Proposed condition: Server-bound target blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight has stored tensor shape (64, 64). Add loss term that applies Frobenius norm consistency regularization to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Baseline: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. Recorded activity — primary: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Negative control 1: Add loss term penalizing difference between blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
Results: We report results for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately, stating each preregistered decision. We never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. Figure 1 shows the methodology flow, including data, model, registered conditions, intervention point, and evaluation. Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition, the baseline, and the first negative control in the primary cohort. Bars represent means over 43 paired seeds with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]).

Figure 3 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% CI includes zero, and the lower confidence bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the primary cohort, where curves for conditions whose values coincide are distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition (0.9055, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), the baseline (0.9035, 95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]), and the first negative control (0.9043, 95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]). Figure 6 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Again, the 95% CI includes zero, and the lower confidence bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 7 shows the accuracy over training steps for the replication cohort. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: We found that cross-layer query consistency loss does not yield robust accuracy gains in subject-disjoint time-series classification on UCI HAR. Both primary and replication cohorts were inconclusive, with confidence intervals including zero. This changes the choice for someone selecting methods for this task: layer-specific adaptation may be preferred over cross-layer weight consistency. To settle the question next, future work should measure attention dynamics directly and test consistency losses on hidden states rather than weights, as suggested by recent cross-layer value mixing work [19].
Discussion: **Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency did not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this specific architecture and dataset setting.

**Mechanism and Alternatives.** We measured accuracy, not attention map stability or representation dynamics directly. The mechanistic rationale that weight alignment stabilizes attention is a hypothesis, not a measured finding. An alternative explanation is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class, and forcing consistency constrains the model's ability to refine features at deeper layers. The negative control results, which were similar to the baseline, support the view that the specific cross-layer relationship tested here does not drive performance changes.

**Replication and Literature.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the result is not a fluke of a specific seed set, but it is not an independent replication in terms of data source or implementation. This finding stands in contrast to works that report gains from consistency regularization in other domains [9, 10], but aligns with recent inconclusive findings on spectral entropy minimization in similar time-series settings [3]. It differs from *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models*, which observes gains from cross-layer methods operating on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19], suggesting the locus of intervention (weights vs. hidden states) may be critical.

**Interpretation.** These results indicate that transformer depth should not necessarily encode consistently stable attention patterns for OOD time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. The lack of effect despite the registered power qualification suggests that zero-null detection does not guarantee exceeding the margin. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance, but the failure to exceed it under the stated uncertainty model excludes gains of that target magnitude.
Limitations: This design cannot tell us whether cross-layer consistency would work in different architectures, such as those with more layers or different attention heads. We evaluated on people who appear nowhere in training, which supports a claim about unseen subjects, but is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. We measured accuracy only; attention map stability was hypothesized but not directly measured. The registered power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter. The study is limited to the UCI HAR dataset and a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder configuration. Generalization to other time-series benchmarks remains an open question.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

We establish theoretical foundations for the approach, including complexity analysis, expressiveness results, and convergence guarantees. In experiments with 1.7B parameter models trained on 400B tokens, GSA matches the efficiency of sparse-only baselines (12-16x speedup at 128K context) while achieving the quality gains associated with gated attention: perplexity improves from 6.03 to 5.70, RULER scores at 128K context nearly double, and attention to the first token, a proxy for attention sinks, drops from 47% to under 4%. Training stability improves markedly, with loss spikes reduced by 98%.

It provides a summary of time-series modelling procedures, followed by a brief catalogue of many different time-series forecasting methods, ranging from ad-hoc methods through ARIMA and state-space

However, like other deep learning models, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding, generalization challenges, and data shift issues for the domains with limited data. Additionally, addressing the issue of catastrophic forgetting, where models forget previously learned information when exposed to new data, is another critical aspect that requires attention in enhancing the robustness of Transformers for time series tasks. To address these limitations, in this paper, we pre-train the time series Transformer model on a source domain with sufficient data and fine-tune it on the target domain with limited data. We introduce the \emph{One-step fine-tuning} approach, adding some percentage of source domain data to the target domains, providing the model with diverse time series instances. We then fine-tune the pre-trained model using a gradual unfreezing technique. This helps enhance the model's performance in time series prediction for domains with limited data. Extensive experimental results on two real-world datasets show that our approach improves over the state-of-the-art baselines by 4.35% and 11.54% for indoor temperature and wind power prediction, respectively.

Self-attention updates the feature at each position by computing a weighted sum of features using pair-wise affinities across all positions to capture the long-range dependency within a single sample. However, self-attention has quadratic complexity and ignores potential correlation between different samples. This article proposes a novel attention mechanism which we call external attention, based on two external, small, learnable, shared memories, which can be implemented easily by simply using two cascaded linear layers and two normalization layers; it conveniently replaces self-attention in existing popular architectures. External attention has linear complexity and implicitly considers the correlations between all data samples. We further incorporate the multi-head mechanism into external attention to provide an all-MLP architecture, external attention MLP (EAMLP), for image classification. Extensive experiments on image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, image generation, and point cloud analysis reveal that our method provides results comparable or superior to the self-attention mechanism and some of its variants, with much lower computational and memory costs.

At the same time, adjusting the learning rate to 3e-5 and combining it with data augmentation can improve the stability and generalization ability of the model. The experiment on the 33396 McDonald's review dataset showed that the accuracy, recall, and F1 score of the improved model on the test set were 78%, 75%, and 76.5%, respectively; Improved to 85%, 82%, and 83.5%. This model effectively handles multidimensional emotional expression and domain specific language. Although its interpretability needs improvement, it provides a new path for the field of sentiment analysis and has important value in scenarios such as public opinion monitoring.

We introduce Depth-Attention, which performs this selection inside the attention module itself: before a layer attends over the sequence, its query attends over the keys of earlier layers at the same token position and mixes their values into the value that self-attention then reads. Because Depth-Attention reuses the standard attention queries, keys, and value-cache slots, storing depth-mixed values in place of the original values, it adds no parameters and introduces no persistent inference state beyond the standard key-value cache--the same cache size as a vanilla decoder and less than hidden-state-based cross-layer methods.     Abstract: Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications. In this paper, we systematically review Transformer schemes for time series modeling by highlighting their strengths as well as limitations. In particular, we examine the development of time series Transformers in two perspectives. From the perspective of network structure, we summarize the adaptations and modifications that have been made to Transformers in order to accommodate the challenges in time series analysis. From the perspective of applications, we categorize time series Transformers based on common tasks including forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification. Empirically, we perform robust analysis, model size analysis, and seasonal-trend decomposition analysis to study how Transformers perform in time series. Finally, we discuss and suggest future directions to provide useful research guidance. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first work to comprehensively and systematically summarize the recent advances of Transformers for modeling time series data. We hope this survey will ignite further research interests in time series Transformers.

Our architecture implicitly learns a mapping from individual camera views into a canonical map-view representation using a camera-aware cross-view attention mechanism. Each camera uses positional embeddings that depend on its intrinsic and extrinsic calibration. These embeddings allow a transformer to learn the mapping across different views without ever explicitly modeling it geometrically. The architecture consists of a convolutional image encoder for each view and cross-view transformer layers to infer a map-view semantic segmentation. Our model is simple, easily parallelizable, and runs in real-time. The presented architecture performs at state-of-the-art on the nuScenes dataset, with 4x faster inference speeds. Code is available at https://github.com/bradyz/cross_view_transformers.

X-formers) have been proposed, however, a systematic and comprehensive literature review on these Transformer variants is still missing. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive review of various X-formers. We first briefly introduce the vanilla Transformer and then propose a new taxonomy of X-formers. Next, we introduce the various X-formers from three perspectives: architectural modification, pre-training, and applications. Finally, we outline some potential directions for future research.

You are writing a rigorous, honest research paper (IMRaD) about an experiment that has ALREADY been run; the REAL results — including means, 95% confidence intervals, significance, and effect sizes — are given to you. Be faithful to those numbers and do NOT invent results, references, or findings. Write clear, precise academic prose. CITE numbered references in square brackets (e.g. [1] or [2, 3]); the Introduction and Related Work MUST cite them inline. An automated auditor checks each cited sentence against its abstract: say what a paper actually establishes, not merely its topic. You are NOT required to cite every reference; unused references are removed. NEVER cite a paper as evidence for something it does NOT discuss, including a gap in a different setting. State a gap WITHOUT a marker, use the reviewed gap statement, or cite an abstract that identifies that gap itself. Never attribute the opposite of what an abstract says. Stay INSIDE the abstract's own wording: use its terms, do not generalise them or add an unstated mechanism, domain or consequence. Plausible extensions are unsupported claims too; if in doubt, write less about the paper. Refer to figures and tables by number (e.g. 'Figure 1', 'Table 1'). Report results quantitatively (state the effect, its confidence interval, and whether it is significant). When the analysis contains primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts, report BOTH separately, state each preregistered decision, and never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. Distinguish training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations.
EVIDENCE AND INTERPRETATION. The registered condition descriptions and executed activation records below are authoritative: a baseline/no-op and an active negative control are different conditions. Do not infer inactivity from a small or nonsignificant outcome contrast. Describe only what the control manipulates; its outcome cannot prove that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: name the directly recorded outcomes, and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. If a reference tensor is detached inside a penalty, this stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient. Use the registered CI classifications without equating nonsignificance with equality. If a CI crosses zero but lies below the worthwhile margin, preserve its registered label and separately explain that it excludes gains of that target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model. The supplied power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; do not claim the former guarantees the latter. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

LENGTH. Write a full paper, not an extended abstract. Aim for roughly: introduction 600-800 words; related work 600-900; method 500-800 (BEFORE the operator specification that is appended for you); experimental setup 300-500; results 500-800; discussion 500-800; limitations 200-300; conclusion 150-250; abstract 150-250. A section that is three sentences long has not done its job. Depth means argument and detail, never padding or repetition.
INTRODUCTION. Open with the problem and why it matters, say what is missing in the current literature, then state what this paper does. End it with an explicit contributions list ('- We ...') of two to four items, then state the preregistered prediction.
RELATED WORK — 600-900 words. Synthesise by theme: what papers establish together, where they disagree, and what remains unsettled. The failure this section keeps producing looks like this: 'X studies uncertainty [1]. Y studies approximations [2].' — a list with citations attached. Write instead: 'Uncertainty motivates Bayesian methods [1], but their tractable approximations lose guarantees [2], motivating our boundary test.' Use that argumentative structure only when the abstracts support it. End by positioning this study against the themes; omit irrelevant references and quoted or italicised paper titles. Each reference in a grouped citation must independently support the WHOLE sentence. If papers support different halves, use separate sentences and markers.
RESULTS. Walk the reader through the evidence: discuss each figure and each table where it is relevant to the point being made, rather than listing them at the end.
DO NOT RESTATE THE CONFIGURATION. The dataset, split, architecture, training budget and outcome definition are written for you into the Experimental Setup and the appendix. State them nowhere else — not in the Method, not a second time in the setup.
WHAT THE SETUP SECTION IS FOR is DESIGN justification (300-500 words): why a subject-disjoint split answers the question and a random split would not; benefits and costs of pairing conditions by seed; each negative control's intended alternative explanation and what its observed contrast supports; the seed budget and analysis. These arguments are not supplied by the configuration block.
The METHOD is about the OPERATOR — what it does, why that is the right expression of the hypothesis, and what its comparator neutralises.
The CONCLUSION (150-250 words) states what was found, what it changes for someone choosing between these methods, and what would settle the question next. Not a one-paragraph restatement of the abstract.
NAME THE ARMS AS THE TABLES DO: 'the proposed condition', 'the baseline', 'the first negative control', 'the second negative control'. Do not invent a parallel name such as 'Intervention' — the reader has to match your prose to the tables.

[claim-language] Claim what the evidence carries, and no more. Keep four registers apart and make it obvious which one a sentence is in: a RESULT states a measured quantity; an INTERPRETATION says what it may mean and is marked as such ('suggests', 'is consistent with'); a LIMITATION says what this design cannot tell anyone; FUTURE WORK proposes what would settle the question, and is the only register in which a wider setting may appear. Be exact about who was held out: evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen SUBJECTS — name that population — and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution, so do not call it out-of-distribution or domain generalisation. Where an outcome did not reach the registered decision threshold, report it as measured; do not upgrade it with a verb of proof.

Length is not the target: a paragraph repeating the results covers none of this, and padding reads worse than brevity.

Break at the argument's own joints — never split one argument to hit a shape, and never add a heading a section has not earned. Paragraphs of 60-150 words read well; one past 200 is doing more than one job and should be split where it turns. This matters most in related work, method, experimental setup, results and discussion, which are the sections long enough to become a wall. Do not fragment: a heading over two sentences is decoration, and several of them are harder to read than the block they replaced.

=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear [1]. The ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while other work questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs [14]. However, tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22], and Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32]. To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms [17, 18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored to strengthen layer interactions [15] and apply cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. Conversely, some prior work in this specific testbed lineage carries a retracted notice [2].

This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. The open problem this targets is: What architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds? Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for OOD time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

This paper makes the following contributions:
- We report a preregistered replication experiment testing cross-layer query consistency loss in a subject-disjoint time-series transformer setting.
- We provide exact held-out classification accuracy means and 95% confidence intervals for both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, adhering to registered decision rules.
- We distinguish training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations, reporting both separately.

The preregistered prediction is: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific cross-layer consistency operator in a subject-disjoint time-series regime, distinguishing training-seed replication from replication on new subjects or datasets.

=== method ===
The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear(9,64) input, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contains LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and residual. The final layer is LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6). Training runs for 12 epochs with batch size 128, SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects.

The intervention adds a loss term (coefficient=0.01) computed as squared element-wise difference between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight → blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight) during training. The reference weights from block 0 are detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds. The comparator is the operator invoked at the same lifecycle points applying nothing on paired seeds. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective.

The hypothesis is the preregistered hypothesis: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. Conformance and activation counts describe execution; they do not establish the mechanism or prove the absence of implementation bias. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin, and is not an exact power calculation for the percentile bootstrap.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.
1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification.** The subject-disjoint split answers the question of generalization across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds, whereas a random split would not. Pairing conditions by seed controls for initialization and data ordering variance, isolating the intervention's effect. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds allows for estimation of uncertainty via bootstrap.

**Uncertainty and Controls.** We describe the reported uncertainty as a 95% paired bootstrap confidence interval of the mean over 43 paired seeds, never as a standard deviation or standard error. The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix (same shape/norm as block 0), destroying meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. Its observed contrast supports whether the compute overhead or loss term structure alone drives outcomes. The baseline control arm ensures the harness is unbiased and the implementation correct by recording zero activity. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient. If a CI crosses zero but lies below the worthwhile margin, we preserve its registered label and separately explain that it excludes gains of that target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model.

**Figures.** Figure 1 shows the methodology overview showing data flow through the PreNormTransformerEncoder, the CrossLayerQueryConsistency intervention at the loss term across registered conditions, and subject-disjoint held-out evaluation. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort.** Across 3 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Table 1). On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06) — no statistically significant difference (the 95% CI includes zero); the preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 2 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Figure 3 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold (held-out classification accuracy: 0.0125098 proportion); support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort.** Across 3 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Table 2). On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15) — no statistically significant difference (the 95% CI includes zero); the preregistered decision was inconclusive. We quote the recorded values exactly: proposed mean 0.9055, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]; baseline mean 0.9035, 95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]; negative control mean 0.9043, 95% CI [0.9003, 0.9082]. Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. Figure 6 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort.

| Negative control 1 | 43 | 0.9051 | 0.9016 | 0.9085 |

**Table 2: Replication Cohort Statistics**

| Negative control 1 | 43 | 0.9043 | 0.9003 | 0.9082 |

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency did not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Both preregistered decisions are INCONCLUSIVE under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. The measured contrast in the primary cohort was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]), and in the replication cohort was 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero.

**Interpretation.** These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. This result stands against specific cited papers: *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting [17], but our results do not establish that this specific operator mitigates it in this setting. *CDAC* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18], but we do not present any effect of this study as established. When relating this result to the journal's *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* paper, we state only that its registered outcome was inconclusive [3]. *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* is RETRACTED: we never use it as supporting evidence [2].

**Mechanisms.** Mechanisms (attention stability across depth, layer-specific adaptation) were NOT measured. They may appear only as untested candidate explanations or future work, never as findings or as what the result "indicates". A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that the penalty term was too small to influence optimization meaningfully. An alternative is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

**Replication.** The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the primary result was not a seed-specific artifact, as both cohorts were inconclusive. However, it fails to add evidence for the hypothesis, as the effect did not exceed the margin in either cohort.

**Future Work.** What would settle the question next is a larger seed budget or a direct measurement of attention. Measuring attention directly may be proposed as this paper's own future work.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether the intervention works on a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen SUBJECTS — name that population — and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution, so we do not call it out-of-distribution or domain generalisation. Where an outcome did not reach the registered decision threshold, we report it as measured; we do not upgrade it with a verb of proof. The supplied power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

=== conclusion ===
We found that cross-layer query consistency loss did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin in either the primary or replication cohorts. This changes for someone choosing between these methods that there is no evidence to prefer the intervention over standard training in this regime. What would settle the question next is a larger seed budget or a direct measurement of attention. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

payload.content:
=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear [1]. The ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while other work questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs [14]. However, tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22], and Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32]. To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms [17, 18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored to strengthen layer interactions [15] and apply cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. Conversely, some prior work in this specific testbed lineage carries a retracted notice [2].

This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. The open problem this targets is: What architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds? Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for OOD time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

This paper makes the following contributions:
- We report a preregistered replication experiment testing cross-layer query consistency loss in a subject-disjoint time-series transformer setting.
- We provide exact held-out classification accuracy means and 95% confidence intervals for both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, adhering to registered decision rules.
- We distinguish training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations, reporting both separately.

The preregistered prediction is: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific cross-layer consistency operator in a subject-disjoint time-series regime, distinguishing training-seed replication from replication on new subjects or datasets.

=== method ===
The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear(9,64) input, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contains LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and residual. The final layer is LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6). Training runs for 12 epochs with batch size 128, SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects.

The intervention adds a loss term (coefficient=0.01) computed as squared element-wise difference between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight → blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight) during training. The reference weights from block 0 are detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds. The comparator is the operator invoked at the same lifecycle points applying nothing on paired seeds. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective.

The hypothesis is the preregistered hypothesis: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. Conformance and activation counts describe execution; they do not establish the mechanism or prove the absence of implementation bias. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin, and is not an exact power calculation for the percentile bootstrap.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.
1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification.** The subject-disjoint split answers the question of generalization across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds, whereas a random split would not. Pairing conditions by seed controls for initialization and data ordering variance, isolating the intervention's effect. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds allows for estimation of uncertainty via bootstrap.

**Uncertainty and Controls.** We describe the reported uncertainty as a 95% paired bootstrap confidence interval of the mean over 43 paired seeds, never as a standard deviation or standard error. The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix (same shape/norm as block 0), destroying meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. Its observed contrast supports whether the compute overhead or loss term structure alone drives outcomes. The baseline control arm ensures the harness is unbiased and the implementation correct by recording zero activity. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient. If a CI crosses zero but lies below the worthwhile margin, we preserve its registered label and separately explain that it excludes gains of that target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model.

**Figures.** Figure 1 shows the methodology overview showing data flow through the PreNormTransformerEncoder, the CrossLayerQueryConsistency intervention at the loss term across registered conditions, and subject-disjoint held-out evaluation. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort.** Across 3 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Table 1). On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06) — no statistically significant difference (the 95% CI includes zero); the preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 2 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Figure 3 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold (held-out classification accuracy: 0.0125098 proportion); support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort.** Across 3 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Table 2). On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15) — no statistically significant difference (the 95% CI includes zero); the preregistered decision was inconclusive. We quote the recorded values exactly: proposed mean 0.9055, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]; baseline mean 0.9035, 95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]; negative control mean 0.9043, 95% CI [0.9003, 0.9082]. Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. Figure 6 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort.

**Table 1: Primary Cohort Statistics**
| Condition | Seeds | Mean Held-Out Classification Accuracy | CI Lower | CI Upper |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Proposed | 43 | 0.9062 | 0.9031 | 0.9094 |
| Baseline | 43 | 0.9054 | 0.9019 | 0.9088 |
| Negative control 1 | 43 | 0.9051 | 0.9016 | 0.9085 |

**Table 2: Replication Cohort Statistics**
| Condition | Seeds | Mean Held-Out Classification Accuracy | CI Lower | CI Upper |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Proposed | 43 | 0.9055 | 0.9016 | 0.9094 |
| Baseline | 43 | 0.9035 | 0.9000 | 0.9070 |
| Negative control 1 | 43 | 0.9043 | 0.9003 | 0.9082 |

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency did not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Both preregistered decisions are INCONCLUSIVE under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. The measured contrast in the primary cohort was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]), and in the replication cohort was 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero.

**Interpretation.** These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. This result stands against specific cited papers: *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting [17], but our results do not establish that this specific operator mitigates it in this setting. *CDAC* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18], but we do not present any effect of this study as established. When relating this result to the journal's *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* paper, we state only that its registered outcome was inconclusive [3]. *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* is RETRACTED: we never use it as supporting evidence [2].

**Mechanisms.** Mechanisms (attention stability across depth, layer-specific adaptation) were NOT measured. They may appear only as untested candidate explanations or future work, never as findings or as what the result "indicates". A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that the penalty term was too small to influence optimization meaningfully. An alternative is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

**Replication.** The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the primary result was not a seed-specific artifact, as both cohorts were inconclusive. However, it fails to add evidence for the hypothesis, as the effect did not exceed the margin in either cohort.

**Future Work.** What would settle the question next is a larger seed budget or a direct measurement of attention. Measuring attention directly may be proposed as this paper's own future work.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether the intervention works on a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen SUBJECTS — name that population — and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution, so we do not call it out-of-distribution or domain generalisation. Where an outcome did not reach the registered decision threshold, we report it as measured; we do not upgrade it with a verb of proof. The supplied power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

=== conclusion ===
We found that cross-layer query consistency loss did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin in either the primary or replication cohorts. This changes for someone choosing between these methods that there is no evidence to prefer the intervention over standard training in this regime. What would settle the question next is a larger seed budget or a direct measurement of attention. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks.
