Abstract: Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00133 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546). Second, the efficient frequency transformer (EFT) is proposed to deeply mine global information, local spatial features, and edge detail information. Finally, the graph-aware fusion (GAF) module is proposed to model the relationships among regions in the feature graph by graph convolutional network (GCN), which enhances the intra-class feature consistency. A wide range of experiments have been carried out on three publicly accessible RS scene datasets. Positive results show that our CLFETNet framework outperforms many existing methods, has high robustness and superiority in remote sensing scene classification tasks, and can effectively handle complex scenes and meet multi-scale feature challenges.

We then fine-tune the pre-trained model using a gradual unfreezing technique. This helps enhance the model's performance in time series prediction for domains with limited data. External attention has linear complexity and implicitly considers the correlations between all data samples. We further incorporate the multi-head mechanism into external attention to provide an all-MLP architecture, external attention MLP (EAMLP), for image classification. Extensive experiments on image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, image generation, and point cloud analysis reveal that our method provides results comparable or superior to the self-attention mechanism and some of its variants, with much lower computational and memory costs.

Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4, 20]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [11] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [7]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [16].

Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Registered conditions.
- Proposed condition: Server-bound target blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight has stored tensor shape (64, 64). Add loss term that applies Frobenius norm consistency regularization to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Baseline: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. Recorded activity — primary: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Negative control 1: Add loss term penalizing difference between blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.

On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06) — no statistically significant difference (the 95% CI includes zero); the preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 2 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Figure 3 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold (held-out classification accuracy: 0.0125098 proportion); support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort.** Across 3 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Table 2). On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15) — no statistically significant difference (the 95% CI includes zero); the preregistered decision was inconclusive. We quote the recorded values exactly: proposed mean 0.9055, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]; baseline mean 0.9035, 95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]; negative control mean 0.9043, 95% CI [0.9003, 0.9082]. Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. Figure 6 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort.

| Condition | Seeds | Mean Held-Out Classification Accuracy | CI Lower | CI Upper |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Proposed | 43 | 0.9062 | 0.9031 | 0.9094 |
| Baseline | 43 | 0.9054 | 0.9019 | 0.9088 |
| Negative control 1 | 43 | 0.9051 | 0.9016 | 0.9085 |

**Table 2: Replication Cohort Statistics**
| Condition | Seeds | Mean Held-Out Classification Accuracy | CI Lower | CI Upper |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Baseline | 43 | 0.9035 | 0.9000 | 0.9070 |
| Negative control 1 | 43 | 0.9043 | 0.9003 | 0.9082 |

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: We found that cross-layer query consistency loss did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin in either the primary or replication cohorts. This changes for someone choosing between these methods that there is no evidence to prefer the intervention over standard training in this regime. What would settle the question next is a larger seed budget or a direct measurement of attention. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks.
Discussion: **Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency did not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Both preregistered decisions are INCONCLUSIVE under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. The measured contrast in the primary cohort was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]), and in the replication cohort was 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero.

**Interpretation.** These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. This result stands against specific cited papers: *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting [9], but our results do not establish that this specific operator mitigates it in this setting. *CDAC* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [10], but we do not present any effect of this study as established. When relating this result to the journal's *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* paper, we state only that its registered outcome was inconclusive [3]. *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* is RETRACTED: we never use it as supporting evidence [2].

**Mechanisms.** Mechanisms (attention stability across depth, layer-specific adaptation) were NOT measured. They may appear only as untested candidate explanations or future work, never as findings or as what the result "indicates". A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that the penalty term was too small to influence optimization meaningfully. An alternative is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

**Replication.** The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the primary result was not a seed-specific artifact, as both cohorts were inconclusive. However, it fails to add evidence for the hypothesis, as the effect did not exceed the margin in either cohort.

**Future Work.** What would settle the question next is a larger seed budget or a direct measurement of attention. Measuring attention directly may be proposed as this paper's own future work.
Limitations: This design cannot tell anyone whether the intervention works on a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen SUBJECTS — name that population — and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution, so we do not call it out-of-distribution or domain generalisation. Where an outcome did not reach the registered decision threshold, we report it as measured; we do not upgrade it with a verb of proof. The supplied power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

You are writing a rigorous, honest research paper (IMRaD) about an experiment that has ALREADY been run; the REAL results — including means, 95% confidence intervals, significance, and effect sizes — are given to you. Be faithful to those numbers and do NOT invent results, references, or findings. Write clear, precise academic prose. CITE numbered references in square brackets (e.g. [1] or [2, 3]); the Introduction and Related Work MUST cite them inline. An automated auditor checks each cited sentence against its abstract: say what a paper actually establishes, not merely its topic. You are NOT required to cite every reference; unused references are removed. NEVER cite a paper as evidence for something it does NOT discuss, including a gap in a different setting. State a gap WITHOUT a marker, use the reviewed gap statement, or cite an abstract that identifies that gap itself. Never attribute the opposite of what an abstract says. Stay INSIDE the abstract's own wording: use its terms, do not generalise them or add an unstated mechanism, domain or consequence. Plausible extensions are unsupported claims too; if in doubt, write less about the paper. Refer to figures and tables by number (e.g. 'Figure 1', 'Table 1'). Report results quantitatively (state the effect, its confidence interval, and whether it is significant). When the analysis contains primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts, report BOTH separately, state each preregistered decision, and never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. Distinguish training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations.
EVIDENCE AND INTERPRETATION. The registered condition descriptions and executed activation records below are authoritative: a baseline/no-op and an active negative control are different conditions. Do not infer inactivity from a small or nonsignificant outcome contrast. Describe only what the control manipulates; its outcome cannot prove that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: name the directly recorded outcomes, and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. If a reference tensor is detached inside a penalty, this stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient. Use the registered CI classifications without equating nonsignificance with equality. If a CI crosses zero but lies below the worthwhile margin, preserve its registered label and separately explain that it excludes gains of that target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model. The supplied power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; do not claim the former guarantees the latter. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

LENGTH. Write a full paper, not an extended abstract. Aim for roughly: introduction 600-800 words; related work 600-900; method 500-800 (BEFORE the operator specification that is appended for you); experimental setup 300-500; results 500-800; discussion 500-800; limitations 200-300; conclusion 150-250; abstract 150-250. A section that is three sentences long has not done its job. Depth means argument and detail, never padding or repetition.
INTRODUCTION. Open with the problem and why it matters, say what is missing in the current literature, then state what this paper does. End it with an explicit contributions list ('- We ...') of two to four items, then state the preregistered prediction.
RELATED WORK — 600-900 words. Synthesise by theme: what papers establish together, where they disagree, and what remains unsettled. The failure this section keeps producing looks like this: 'X studies uncertainty [1]. Y studies approximations [2].' — a list with citations attached. Write instead: 'Uncertainty motivates Bayesian methods [1], but their tractable approximations lose guarantees [2], motivating our boundary test.' Use that argumentative structure only when the abstracts support it. End by positioning this study against the themes; omit irrelevant references and quoted or italicised paper titles. Each reference in a grouped citation must independently support the WHOLE sentence. If papers support different halves, use separate sentences and markers.
RESULTS. Walk the reader through the evidence: discuss each figure and each table where it is relevant to the point being made, rather than listing them at the end.

The METHOD is about the OPERATOR — what it does, why that is the right expression of the hypothesis, and what its comparator neutralises.
The CONCLUSION (150-250 words) states what was found, what it changes for someone choosing between these methods, and what would settle the question next. Not a one-paragraph restatement of the abstract.
NAME THE ARMS AS THE TABLES DO: 'the proposed condition', 'the baseline', 'the first negative control', 'the second negative control'. Do not invent a parallel name such as 'Intervention' — the reader has to match your prose to the tables.

Keep four registers apart and make it obvious which one a sentence is in: a RESULT states a measured quantity; an INTERPRETATION says what it may mean and is marked as such ('suggests', 'is consistent with'); a LIMITATION says what this design cannot tell anyone; FUTURE WORK proposes what would settle the question, and is the only register in which a wider setting may appear. Be exact about who was held out: evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen SUBJECTS — name that population — and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution, so do not call it out-of-distribution or domain generalisation. === abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. The ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while recent work questions the validity of this research line for forecasting tasks [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation and representing multivariate series as graphs [14, 20]. However, tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones, and transformers face limitations in time series prediction including generalization challenges [22, 32]. This uncertainty motivates a rigorous test of specific architectural modifications under controlled conditions.

One proposed mechanism for improving generalization is stabilizing attention patterns across network depth. Deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data, and domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [17, 18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in recent work to strengthen layer interactions or refine activation steering [15, 34]. However, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. This work addresses this gap by testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. Clarifying whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting is critical. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

This paper reports a preregistered experiment evaluating the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator. We compare the proposed condition against a baseline and a negative control using a subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset. The design isolates the effect of the regularization term from implementation bias by pairing conditions by seed and verifying operator activity. We report results for both a primary cohort and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds.

Our contributions are:
- We execute a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency loss on subject-disjoint time-series generalization.
- We report inconclusive results in both primary and replication cohorts, with confidence intervals including zero.
- We provide verified activation records confirming the intervention executed as specified without control arm contamination.

The preregistered prediction stated: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14, 20]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [15, 34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight-space consistency constraint rather than activation mixing or external attention, using a subject-disjoint protocol to assess generalization claims directly.

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency between query projection weights of successive transformer blocks. The hypothesis is that stabilizing query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization by reducing overfitting to subject-specific temporal patterns. The operator adds a loss term during training that penalizes the element-wise squared difference between the query weights of block 1 and the detached query weights of block 0. This formulation targets the weight geometry directly, distinct from methods that mix hidden states or values across layers [37].

The comparator neutralizes the intervention by executing the identical code path but returning a zero loss term. This control arm ensures that any observed contrast arises from the regularization term itself, not from implementation artifacts such as graph construction or optimizer state changes. The harness records operator activity for every seed and condition, refusing results where the control arm records non-zero activity. This design distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations; here, we employ disjoint seeds through the same pipeline to confirm the primary result was not a seed-specific artifact.

The operator specification defines the exact computational graph. Reference weights from block 0 are detached to prevent gradients flowing to block 0, ensuring the penalty only trains the target parameters in block 1. The coefficient is fixed at 0.01 to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment; this operator regularizes parameters, not activations. If a reference tensor is detached inside a penalty, this stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient.

**Operator Specification**
Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification**
We use a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization to unseen subjects, which a random split would not. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance attributable to initialization and data ordering, allowing a more precise estimate of the intervention effect. Each negative control's intended alternative explanation is that compute overhead or loss term addition alone drives changes; the observed contrast supports whether the specific cross-layer relationship matters. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds provides the registered power to detect the worthwhile margin.

**Data and Evaluation**
The dataset is the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Training runs for 12 epochs with batch size 128, SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects. We describe the reported uncertainty as a 95% bootstrap confidence interval of the mean over 43 paired seeds, never as a standard deviation or standard error. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. Figure 1 illustrates the methodology flow showing data entry, transformer model, registered conditions, CrossLayerQueryConsistency intervention at the loss term, and subject-disjoint evaluation, meaning the pipeline enforces condition isolation before evaluation on held-out subjects.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). This result is not statistically significant as the 95% CI includes zero. Table 3 reports the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed (0.9062, 95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), baseline (0.9054, 95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]), and first negative control (0.9051, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]) conditions. Figure 2 visualizes these means with error bars, showing overlapping intervals. Figure 3 plots the paired mean difference, where the confidence interval crosses zero and lies below the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098. Figure 4 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions; the learning curves for the proposed and baseline conditions coincide closely, indicating no divergence in optimization dynamics during training. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). This result is also not statistically significant. Table 5 reports the replication cohort means: proposed (0.9055, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.909]), baseline (0.9035, 95% CI [0.9000, 0.907]), and first negative control (0.9043, 95% CI [0.9003, 0.908]). Figure 5 shows these bars, and Figure 6 plots the paired difference, which again includes zero. Figure 7 shows the replication learning curves, which similarly overlap. Table 4 details the primary outcome differences for reference. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the primary result was not a seed-specific artifact, as both cohorts were inconclusive. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding and Interpretation**
The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency loss did not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. The measured contrast in the primary cohort was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]), and in the replication cohort was 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Both intervals include zero, and neither lower bound exceeds the worthwhile margin. This suggests that enforcing weight alignment between query projections across depth does not improve subject-disjoint generalization for this architecture and task. The result is consistent with findings that spectral entropy minimization of input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime [3].

**What This Design Does and Does Not Establish**
This design establishes that the specific operator tested does not improve held-out classification accuracy under the registered conditions. It does not establish that attention stability is irrelevant to generalization; mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings. We did not measure attention maps, feature learning, or layer specialization directly. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. The experiment does not establish transfer to other domains, sensors, or architectures. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

**Mechanism and Alternatives**
A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class, as suggested by prior work [1]. An alternative explanation is that the coefficient (0.01) was too small to influence optimization meaningfully, though the penalty was recorded as active. The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the primary result was not a seed-specific artifact, as both cohorts were inconclusive. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds confirms the stability of the null result across sampling.

**Relation to Cited Work**
These findings agree with [1] which suggests cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. They conflict with hypotheses that cross-layer consistency universally improves stability [15, 34], though those works operate in different settings (vision, activation steering). The result is not comparable to [17] which focuses on output consistency rather than weight geometry. The null result clarifies the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks [3].

**Future Work**
What would settle the question next is testing larger margins, different coefficients, or direct attention-map measurements. Future work should investigate whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks or requires architectural changes beyond weight regularization.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to the UCI HAR dataset and a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture. The margin justification relies on a versioned policy accuracy_fraction_v1; a margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision and does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin; it does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. We did not measure attention maps directly, so claims about attention stability remain hypothetical. The study does not address computational cost differences between arms.

=== conclusion ===
We found that cross-layer query consistency loss did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers under the registered conditions. Both primary and replication cohorts yielded inconclusive results with confidence intervals including zero. This changes the choice for someone choosing between these methods by indicating that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential. The finding stands against specific cited papers [1] agreeing that robust accuracy gains are not yielded in this regime. What would settle the question next is direct measurement of attention stability or testing on larger margins. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime.

Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line. === abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. The ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while recent work questions the validity of this research line for forecasting tasks [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation and representing multivariate series as graphs [14, 20]. However, tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones, and transformers face limitations in time series prediction including generalization challenges [22, 32]. This uncertainty motivates a rigorous test of specific architectural modifications under controlled conditions.

One proposed mechanism for improving generalization is stabilizing attention patterns across network depth. Deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data, and domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [17, 18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in recent work to strengthen layer interactions or refine activation steering [15, 34]. However, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. This work addresses this gap by testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. Clarifying whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting is critical. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

This paper reports a preregistered experiment evaluating the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator. We compare the proposed condition against a baseline and a negative control using a subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset. The design isolates the effect of the regularization term from implementation bias by pairing conditions by seed and verifying operator activity. We report results for both a primary cohort and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds.

Our contributions are:
- We execute a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency loss on subject-disjoint time-series generalization.
- We report inconclusive results in both primary and replication cohorts, with confidence intervals including zero.
- We provide verified activation records confirming the intervention executed as specified without control arm contamination.

The preregistered prediction stated: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14, 20]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [15, 34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight-space consistency constraint rather than activation mixing or external attention, using a subject-disjoint protocol to assess generalization claims directly.

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency between query projection weights of successive transformer blocks. The hypothesis is that stabilizing query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization by reducing overfitting to subject-specific temporal patterns. The operator adds a loss term during training that penalizes the element-wise squared difference between the query weights of block 1 and the detached query weights of block 0. This formulation targets the weight geometry directly, distinct from methods that mix hidden states or values across layers [37].

The comparator neutralizes the intervention by executing the identical code path but returning a zero loss term. This control arm ensures that any observed contrast arises from the regularization term itself, not from implementation artifacts such as graph construction or optimizer state changes. The harness records operator activity for every seed and condition, refusing results where the control arm records non-zero activity. This design distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations; here, we employ disjoint seeds through the same pipeline to confirm the primary result was not a seed-specific artifact.

The operator specification defines the exact computational graph. Reference weights from block 0 are detached to prevent gradients flowing to block 0, ensuring the penalty only trains the target parameters in block 1. The coefficient is fixed at 0.01 to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment; this operator regularizes parameters, not activations. If a reference tensor is detached inside a penalty, this stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient.

**Operator Specification**
Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification**
We use a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization to unseen subjects, which a random split would not. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance attributable to initialization and data ordering, allowing a more precise estimate of the intervention effect. Each negative control's intended alternative explanation is that compute overhead or loss term addition alone drives changes; the observed contrast supports whether the specific cross-layer relationship matters. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds provides the registered power to detect the worthwhile margin.

**Data and Evaluation**
The dataset is the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Training runs for 12 epochs with batch size 128, SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects. We describe the reported uncertainty as a 95% bootstrap confidence interval of the mean over 43 paired seeds, never as a standard deviation or standard error. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. Figure 1 illustrates the methodology flow showing data entry, transformer model, registered conditions, CrossLayerQueryConsistency intervention at the loss term, and subject-disjoint evaluation, meaning the pipeline enforces condition isolation before evaluation on held-out subjects.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). This result is not statistically significant as the 95% CI includes zero. Table 3 reports the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed (0.9062, 95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), baseline (0.9054, 95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]), and first negative control (0.9051, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]) conditions. Figure 2 visualizes these means with error bars, showing overlapping intervals. Figure 3 plots the paired mean difference, where the confidence interval crosses zero and lies below the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098. Figure 4 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions; the learning curves for the proposed and baseline conditions coincide closely, indicating no divergence in optimization dynamics during training. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). This result is also not statistically significant. Table 5 reports the replication cohort means: proposed (0.9055, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.909]), baseline (0.9035, 95% CI [0.9000, 0.907]), and first negative control (0.9043, 95% CI [0.9003, 0.908]). Figure 5 shows these bars, and Figure 6 plots the paired difference, which again includes zero. Figure 7 shows the replication learning curves, which similarly overlap. Table 4 details the primary outcome differences for reference. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the primary result was not a seed-specific artifact, as both cohorts were inconclusive. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding and Interpretation**
The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency loss did not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. The measured contrast in the primary cohort was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]), and in the replication cohort was 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Both intervals include zero, and neither lower bound exceeds the worthwhile margin. This suggests that enforcing weight alignment between query projections across depth does not improve subject-disjoint generalization for this architecture and task. The result is consistent with findings that spectral entropy minimization of input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime [3].

**What This Design Does and Does Not Establish**
This design establishes that the specific operator tested does not improve held-out classification accuracy under the registered conditions. It does not establish that attention stability is irrelevant to generalization; mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings. We did not measure attention maps, feature learning, or layer specialization directly. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. The experiment does not establish transfer to other domains, sensors, or architectures. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

**Mechanism and Alternatives**
A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class, as suggested by prior work [1]. An alternative explanation is that the coefficient (0.01) was too small to influence optimization meaningfully, though the penalty was recorded as active. The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the primary result was not a seed-specific artifact, as both cohorts were inconclusive. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds confirms the stability of the null result across sampling.

**Relation to Cited Work**
These findings agree with [1] which suggests cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. They conflict with hypotheses that cross-layer consistency universally improves stability [15, 34], though those works operate in different settings (vision, activation steering). The result is not comparable to [17] which focuses on output consistency rather than weight geometry. The null result clarifies the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks [3].

**Future Work**
What would settle the question next is testing larger margins, different coefficients, or direct attention-map measurements. Future work should investigate whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks or requires architectural changes beyond weight regularization.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to the UCI HAR dataset and a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture. The margin justification relies on a versioned policy accuracy_fraction_v1; a margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision and does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin; it does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. We did not measure attention maps directly, so claims about attention stability remain hypothetical. The study does not address computational cost differences between arms.

=== conclusion ===
We found that cross-layer query consistency loss did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers under the registered conditions. Both primary and replication cohorts yielded inconclusive results with confidence intervals including zero. This changes the choice for someone choosing between these methods by indicating that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential. The finding stands against specific cited papers [1] agreeing that robust accuracy gains are not yielded in this regime. What would settle the question next is direct measurement of attention stability or testing on larger margins. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime.

Abstract: Transformer, first applied to the field of natural language processing, is a type of deep neural network mainly based on the self-attention mechanism. Thanks to its strong representation capabilities, researchers are looking at ways to apply transformer to computer vision tasks. The main categories we explore include the backbone network, high/mid-level vision, low-level vision, and video processing. We also include efficient transformer methods for pushing transformer into real device-based applications. Furthermore, we also take a brief look at the self-attention mechanism in computer vision, as it is the base component in transformer. The intra-series correlations are represented by nodes in a dynamic graph; a self-attention mechanism is modified to capture the inter-series correlations by using the super-empirical mode decomposition (SMD) module. We applied the embedded dynamic graphs to times series forecasting problems, including two real-world datasets and two benchmark datasets. Extensive experiments show that TSAT clearly outerperforms six state-of-the-art baseline methods in various forecasting horizons. We further visualize the embedded dynamic graphs to illustrate the graph representation power of TSAT. We share our code at https://github.com/RadiantResearch/TSAT.

A light-weighted version of MRLA is also proposed to reduce the quadratic computation cost. The proposed layer attention mechanism can enrich the representation power of many state-of-the-art vision networks, including CNNs and vision transformers. Its effectiveness has been extensively evaluated in image classification, object detection and instance segmentation tasks, where improvements can be consistently observed. For example, our MRLA can improve 1.6% Top-1 accuracy on ResNet-50, while only introducing 0.16M parameters and 0.07B FLOPs. Abstract: The large-scale and deep-layer deep neural network based on the Transformer model is very powerful in sequence tasks, but it is prone to overfitting for small-scale training data. Specifically, on the basis of the cross-entropy loss function, we build the mean model by integrating the model parameters of the previous rounds and measure the consistency between the models by calculating the KL divergence between the features of the encoder output and the probability distribution of the decoder output of the mean model and the base model so as to impose regularization constraints on the solution space of the model. We conducted extensive experiments on machine translation tasks, and the results show that the BLEU score increased by 2.60 on average, demonstrating the effectiveness of DOCR in improving model performance and its complementary impacts with other regularization techniques.

Specifically, we impose consistency between predictions from cross-domain attention and self-attention modules to encourage similar distributions across domains in both the attention and output of the model, i.e., attention-level and output-level alignment. We also enforce consistency in attention maps between different augmented views to further strengthen the attention-based alignment. Combining these two components, CDAC mitigates the discrepancy in attention maps across domains and further boosts the performance of the transformer under unsupervised domain adaptation settings. Our method is evaluated on various widely used benchmarks and outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines, including GTAV-to-Cityscapes by 1.3 and 1.5 percent point (pp) and Synthia-to-Cityscapes by 0.6 pp and 2.9 pp when combining with two competitive Transformer-based backbones, respectively. Our code will be publicly available at https://github.com/wangkaihong/CDAC.

[11] TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation
Abstract: Signal measurement appearing in the form of time series is one of the most common types of data used in medical machine learning applications. Such datasets are often small in size, expensive to collect and annotate, and might involve privacy issues, which hinders our ability to train large, state-of-the-art deep learning models for biomedical applications. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) can be utilized as another data augmentation tool. In this paper, we present TTS-CGAN, a transformer-based conditional GAN model that can be trained on existing multi-class datasets and generate class-specific synthetic time-series sequences of arbitrary length. We elaborate on the model architecture and design strategies. Synthetic sequences generated by our model are indistinguishable from real ones, and can be used to complement or replace real signals of the same type, thus achieving the goal of data augmentation. To evaluate the quality of the generated data, we modify the wavelet coherence metric to be able to compare the similarity between two sets of signals, and also conduct a case study where a mix of synthetic and real data are used to train a deep learning model for sequence classification. Together with other visualization techniques and qualitative evaluation approaches, we demonstrate that TTS-CGAN generated synthetic data are similar to real data, and that our model performs better than the other state-of-the-art GAN models built for time-series data generation.

Abstract: Astounding results from Transformer models on natural language tasks have intrigued the vision community to study their application to computer vision problems. Among their salient benefits, Transformers enable modeling long dependencies between input sequence elements and support parallel processing of sequence as compared to recurrent networks, e.g., Long short-term memory. Different from convolutional networks, Transformers require minimal inductive biases for their design and are naturally suited as set-functions. Furthermore, the straightforward design of Transformers allows processing multiple modalities (e.g., images, videos, text, and speech) using similar processing blocks and demonstrates excellent scalability to very large capacity networks and huge datasets. These strengths have led to exciting progress on a number of vision tasks using Transformer networks. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the Transformer models in the computer vision discipline. We start with an introduction to fundamental concepts behind the success of Transformers, i.e., self-attention, large-scale pre-training, and bidirectional feature encoding. We then cover extensive applications of transformers in vision including popular recognition tasks (e.g., image classification, object detection, action recognition, and segmentation), generative modeling, multi-modal tasks (e.g., visual-question answering, visual reasoning, and visual grounding), video processing (e.g., activity recognition, video forecasting), low-level vision (e.g., image super-resolution, image enhancement, and colorization), and three-dimensional analysis (e.g., point cloud classification and segmentation). We compare the respective advantages and limitations of popular techniques both in terms of architectural design and their experimental value. Finally, we provide an analysis on open research directions and possible future works. We hope this effort will ignite further interest in the community to solve current challenges toward the application of transformer models in computer vision.

[13] Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks
Abstract: Large pre-trained models have been vital in recent advancements in domains like language and vision, making model training for individual downstream tasks more efficient and provide superior performance. We propose Large Pre-trained Time-series Models (LPTM) that introduces a novel method of adaptive segmentation that automatically identifies optimal dataset-specific segmentation strategy during pre-training. This enables LPTM to perform similar to or better than domain-specific state-of-art model when fine-tuned to different downstream time-series analysis tasks and under zero-shot settings. LPTM achieves superior forecasting and time-series classification results taking up to 40% less data and 50% less training time compared to state-of-art baselines.
