This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. We distinguish between the measured weight consistency and the inferred attention stability, noting that the latter was not directly observed.

Introduction: Time-series classification using deep learning has become critical for applications ranging from healthcare monitoring to industrial predictive maintenance. Among architectural choices, Transformers have gained prominence due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies without the sequential constraints of recurrent networks [20]. However, their effectiveness in time-series domains, particularly regarding generalization to unseen subjects, remains a subject of active debate [4]. While Transformers excel in natural language processing, their application to sensor data involves distinct challenges, including varying movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds across individuals. The central open problem is identifying which architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across these subject-specific variations.

Current literature highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding Transformer effectiveness in time series. Surveys note that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [20], yet empirical studies question the validity of this research line compared to simpler linear models [4]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [11] and representing multivariate series as graphs [7], but the fundamental question of how to regularize depth for subject-disjoint tasks is unsettled. Some works propose consistency regularization to address stability and generalization [9], while others explore cross-layer mechanisms to strengthen interactions [8]. However, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. This gap motivates a rigorous test of whether enforcing weight consistency between layers yields measurable benefits in a controlled setting.

This paper reports a registered replication study testing the hypothesis that cross-layer query consistency improves generalization. We address the lack of independent verification by executing a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds, ensuring that any observed effects are not artifacts of a specific random initialization. The study utilizes the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, ensuring that evaluation is performed on unseen subjects rather than random windows from trained subjects. This design isolates the model's ability to generalize across individuals, which is the primary requirement for deployment in real-world monitoring scenarios.

The contributions of this work are as follows:
- We execute a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency loss in a time-series transformer, reporting both primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts.
- We provide exact quantitative results including means, 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, and effect sizes for held-out classification accuracy.
- We distinguish between the measured intervention (weight consistency) and the inferred mechanism (attention stability), clarifying the limits of the evidence.

The preregistered prediction was that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with the mean paired contrast in the hypothesised direction exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

Discussion: The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency loss did not yield robust accuracy gains in the tested regime. Both the primary and replication cohorts produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. This outcome suggests that, for this specific architecture and dataset, layer-specific adaptation may be as effective as cross-layer consistency. However, this is an interpretation of the outcome contrast, not a measured finding of the mechanism.

What this design does and does not establish is critical. The experiment establishes that the intervention did not improve held-out classification accuracy under the stated conditions. It does not establish that attention stability was achieved, as attention maps were not measured. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: we name the directly recorded outcomes (accuracy), and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient, and the observed null result could stem from the penalty being too weak to influence learning, or from the hypothesis being incorrect.

An alternative explanation for the null result is that the consistency constraint conflicts with the task objective. If deeper layers need to specialize to capture higher-level temporal features, forcing them to align with shallower layers might impede this specialization. This would be consistent with the finding that the baseline performed similarly to the proposed condition. The negative control results further suggest that the specific cross-layer relationship does not provide a unique benefit over generic regularization, as the negative control means were comparable to the baseline and proposed conditions.

Comparing this finding against specific cited papers, our results agree with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also reported inconclusive results for a weight regularization hypothesis in this setting [3]. They also align with the caution raised in *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* regarding the benefits of complex architectures over simpler ones [4]. Conversely, they do not support the positive claims of *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* in this specific replication context [1], highlighting the importance of independent verification. The result is not comparable to *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* [9] as that study focused on machine translation and encoder-decoder consistency, a different intervention and task.

The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the primary result was not a false positive due to seed selection. Both cohorts pointed in the same direction (small positive mean difference) but neither reached significance. This consistency across cohorts strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if it exists, is smaller than the worthwhile margin. What would settle the question next is a study that directly measures attention map stability alongside accuracy, or one that varies the consistency coefficient to determine if a stronger penalty yields different results. Until then, the evidence remains inconclusive.

Conclusion: This study found inconclusive evidence that cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The proposed condition scored higher under the tested conditions (difference 0.000773 in primary, 0.00196 in replication), but neither met the registered decision rule (95% CI lower bound > 0.0125098). This changes the choice for someone choosing between these methods by indicating that the intervention does not provide a guaranteed gain over standard training in this regime. One hypothesis is that layer-specific adaptation remains essential, though this is not established fact. Future work should directly measure attention stability and test stronger consistency coefficients to determine if the null result stems from the hypothesis or the implementation strength.

Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. We distinguish between the measured weight consistency and the inferred attention stability, noting that the latter was not directly observed.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [20], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line, showing that simple linear models can outperform sophisticated Transformer-based solutions in forecasting tasks [4]. This tension suggests that architectural complexity does not automatically translate to performance gains in temporal domains. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN* [11] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Time Series Attention Transformer* [7]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13], indicating a fragmentation in the field that complicates the identification of robust inductive biases. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [16].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data and proposes constraining encoder and decoder outputs [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, proposing consistency between predictions from cross-domain attention and self-attention modules [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions by sending query representations to previous layers [8]. *Global Evolutionary Steering* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering in language models [18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice, indicating that its conclusions may not be relied upon [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks, noting that self-attention has quadratic complexity [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [6], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [12], and *A survey of transformers* [21] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15].

Synthesizing these themes, the literature establishes that while Transformers are widely adopted, their specific inductive biases for time-series generalization are not fully understood. Consistency regularization is a common strategy to mitigate overfitting [9], and cross-layer mechanisms are proposed to enhance representation power [8]. However, disagreement remains on whether these mechanisms translate to subject-disjoint generalization in sensor data. Some studies report improvements in specific domains like segmentation [10] or remote sensing [14], but others find null results in time-series classification [1, 3]. This study positions itself against this unsettled background by providing a high-power replication of the cross-layer query consistency hypothesis, distinguishing between the operational definition of weight consistency and the theoretical goal of attention stability.
Method: The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces weight alignment between attention query projections in different transformer blocks. The hypothesis is that regularizing deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights will improve subject-disjoint generalization. This hypothesis rests on the assumption that stable attention patterns across depth are beneficial for temporal representation learning, though this mechanism is not directly measured. The operator is applied during the loss computation of every optimization step, adding a consistency term to the classification objective.

The intervention targets the query projection weights of the second attention block (blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight). It retrieves the weights from the first block (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight) as a reference. To prevent gradients from flowing back to the reference block, the reference weights are detached from the gradient graph. The operator computes the element-wise difference between the target and reference weights, squares these differences, and sums them to produce a raw loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed coefficient of 0.01 and added to the training objective. This design ensures that the consistency penalty is differentiable with respect to the target parameters only, while the reference parameters remain unaffected by this specific loss term. It is critical to note that detaching the reference tensor inside the penalty stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. The reference weights continue to be updated by the primary classification objective.

The comparator is the baseline condition, which executes the identical code path but returns a zero loss term for the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, ensuring that dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. This pairing controls for variance due to initialization and data sampling. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm, the intervention leaves the registered target parameter unchanged and adds nothing to the training objective. This design isolates the effect of the consistency loss term from other training dynamics.

A negative control is included to test whether the compute overhead or the presence of a loss term alone drives any observed effects. The negative control penalizes the difference between the target weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as the reference weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the computational cost of the proposed condition. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, it suggests that the specific cross-layer relationship matters, not just the regularization effect.

The operator specification is fixed before any compute was spent. The scope is the full weight matrix treated as flat parameter space. The ordering is element-wise subtraction then sum, which is order-invariant. No normalization is applied; the raw Frobenius norm squared is scaled by the fixed coefficient. Numerical safeguards include the coefficient 0.01 to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective. The following invariants hold throughout: reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients from this term; the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only; and the coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.
1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute in the training objective = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store in the training objective in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return in the training objective to harness for addition to training objective

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0

5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. Experimental setup: The experimental design uses a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization to unseen individuals. A random split would not suffice because it would allow the model to learn subject-specific features that do not transfer. By holding out entire subjects, we ensure that the evaluation measures the model's ability to generalize across different movement styles and sensor characteristics. This design choice is critical for claims about subject-disjoint generalization; evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task, or deployment distribution.

We use paired seeds for the proposed condition and the baseline. This pairing reduces variance in the contrast estimate by ensuring that both conditions see the exact same data order and initialization. The benefit is increased statistical power to detect small effects; the cost is that the seeds are not independent between conditions, which is accounted for in the paired statistical analysis. We report 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. We distinguish training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations; this study replicates on new seeds within the same dataset and architecture.

The negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any improvement comes from the regularization effect of adding a loss term, rather than the specific cross-layer alignment. If the negative control performs similarly to the proposed condition, it would suggest that the specific reference weights do not matter. The observed contrast supports or refutes this alternative. We describe the reported uncertainty as a 95% bootstrap confidence interval of the mean over 43 paired seeds, never as a standard deviation or standard error. This interval captures the uncertainty in the mean estimate due to seed sampling.

The seed budget was determined by a registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targeting 90% power to reject a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. The margin of 0.0125098 proportion was derived from a versioned policy based on calibration noise. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign. The analysis reports primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately and never pools them.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. Recorded activity — primary: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity.

Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.

The bars represent means over 43 paired seeds, and the error bars represent 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The figure shows the proposed condition against the baseline, with the dashed line marking the baseline mean as an ordering reference. The 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.

This changes the choice for someone choosing between these methods by indicating that the intervention does not provide a guaranteed gain over standard training in this regime. One hypothesis is that layer-specific adaptation remains essential, though this is not established fact. Future work should directly measure attention stability and test stronger consistency coefficients to determine if the null result stems from the hypothesis or the implementation strength.
Discussion: The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency loss did not yield robust accuracy gains in the tested regime. Both the primary and replication cohorts produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. This outcome suggests that, for this specific architecture and dataset, layer-specific adaptation may be as effective as cross-layer consistency. However, this is an interpretation of the outcome contrast, not a measured finding of the mechanism.

What this design does and does not establish is critical. The experiment establishes that the intervention did not improve held-out classification accuracy under the stated conditions. It does not establish that attention stability was achieved, as attention maps were not measured. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: we name the directly recorded outcomes (accuracy), and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient, and the observed null result could stem from the penalty being too weak to influence learning, or from the hypothesis being incorrect.

An alternative explanation for the null result is that the consistency constraint conflicts with the task objective. If deeper layers need to specialize to capture higher-level temporal features, forcing them to align with shallower layers might impede this specialization. This would be consistent with the finding that the baseline performed similarly to the proposed condition. The negative control results further suggest that the specific cross-layer relationship does not provide a unique benefit over generic regularization, as the negative control means were comparable to the baseline and proposed conditions.

Comparing this finding against specific cited papers, our results agree with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also reported inconclusive results for a weight regularization hypothesis in this setting [3]. They also align with the caution raised in *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* regarding the benefits of complex architectures over simpler ones [4]. Conversely, they do not support the positive claims of *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* in this specific replication context [1], highlighting the importance of independent verification. The result is not comparable to *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* [9] as that study focused on machine translation and encoder-decoder consistency, a different intervention and task.

The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the primary result was not a false positive due to seed selection. Both cohorts pointed in the same direction (small positive mean difference) but neither reached significance. This consistency across cohorts strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if it exists, is smaller than the worthwhile margin. What would settle the question next is a study that directly measures attention map stability alongside accuracy, or one that varies the consistency coefficient to determine if a stronger penalty yields different results. Until then, the evidence remains inconclusive.
Limitations: This study has several limitations that constrain the generalizability of the findings. First, the experiment was conducted on a single dataset (UCI HAR) and a specific transformer architecture (PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks). The results may not transfer to deeper models, different time-series domains, or datasets with different subject variability. Second, the mechanism of attention stability was not directly measured. We enforced weight consistency, but did not verify if this resulted in stable attention maps. Third, the registered margin was derived from calibration noise, which reflects measurement precision but does not by itself establish practical importance. A null result relative to this margin does not rule out smaller, practically useful gains. Finally, the study distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations; we only performed the former.

Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. We distinguish between the measured weight consistency and the inferred attention stability, noting that the latter was not directly observed.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [20], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line, showing that simple linear models can outperform sophisticated Transformer-based solutions in forecasting tasks [4]. This tension suggests that architectural complexity does not automatically translate to performance gains in temporal domains. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN* [11] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Time Series Attention Transformer* [7]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13], indicating a fragmentation in the field that complicates the identification of robust inductive biases. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [16].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data and proposes constraining encoder and decoder outputs [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, proposing consistency between predictions from cross-domain attention and self-attention modules [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions by sending query representations to previous layers [8]. *Global Evolutionary Steering* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering in language models [18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice, indicating that its conclusions may not be relied upon [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks, noting that self-attention has quadratic complexity [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [6], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [12], and *A survey of transformers* [21] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15].

Synthesizing these themes, the literature establishes that while Transformers are widely adopted, their specific inductive biases for time-series generalization are not fully understood. Consistency regularization is a common strategy to mitigate overfitting [9], and cross-layer mechanisms are proposed to enhance representation power [8]. However, disagreement remains on whether these mechanisms translate to subject-disjoint generalization in sensor data. Some studies report improvements in specific domains like segmentation [10] or remote sensing [14], but others find null results in time-series classification [1, 3]. This study positions itself against this unsettled background by providing a high-power replication of the cross-layer query consistency hypothesis, distinguishing between the operational definition of weight consistency and the theoretical goal of attention stability.
Method: The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces weight alignment between attention query projections in different transformer blocks. The hypothesis is that regularizing deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights will improve subject-disjoint generalization. This hypothesis rests on the assumption that stable attention patterns across depth are beneficial for temporal representation learning, though this mechanism is not directly measured. The operator is applied during the loss computation of every optimization step, adding a consistency term to the classification objective.

The intervention targets the query projection weights of the second attention block (blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight). It retrieves the weights from the first block (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight) as a reference. To prevent gradients from flowing back to the reference block, the reference weights are detached from the gradient graph. The operator computes the element-wise difference between the target and reference weights, squares these differences, and sums them to produce a raw loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed coefficient of 0.01 and added to the training objective. This design ensures that the consistency penalty is differentiable with respect to the target parameters only, while the reference parameters remain unaffected by this specific loss term. It is critical to note that detaching the reference tensor inside the penalty stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. The reference weights continue to be updated by the primary classification objective.

The comparator is the baseline condition, which executes the identical code path but returns a zero loss term for the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, ensuring that dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. This pairing controls for variance due to initialization and data sampling. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm, the intervention leaves the registered target parameter unchanged and adds nothing to the training objective. This design isolates the effect of the consistency loss term from other training dynamics.

A negative control is included to test whether the compute overhead or the presence of a loss term alone drives any observed effects. The negative control penalizes the difference between the target weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as the reference weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the computational cost of the proposed condition. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, it suggests that the specific cross-layer relationship matters, not just the regularization effect.

The operator specification is fixed before any compute was spent. The scope is the full weight matrix treated as flat parameter space. The ordering is element-wise subtraction then sum, which is order-invariant. No normalization is applied; the raw Frobenius norm squared is scaled by the fixed coefficient. Numerical safeguards include the coefficient 0.01 to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective. The following invariants hold throughout: reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients from this term; the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only; and the coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.
1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute in the training objective = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store in the training objective in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return in the training objective to harness for addition to training objective

Experimental setup: The experimental design uses a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization to unseen individuals. A random split would not suffice because it would allow the model to learn subject-specific features that do not transfer. By holding out entire subjects, we ensure that the evaluation measures the model's ability to generalize across different movement styles and sensor characteristics. This design choice is critical for claims about subject-disjoint generalization; evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task, or deployment distribution.

We use paired seeds for the proposed condition and the baseline. This pairing reduces variance in the contrast estimate by ensuring that both conditions see the exact same data order and initialization. The benefit is increased statistical power to detect small effects; the cost is that the seeds are not independent between conditions, which is accounted for in the paired statistical analysis. We report 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. We distinguish training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations; this study replicates on new seeds within the same dataset and architecture.

The negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any improvement comes from the regularization effect of adding a loss term, rather than the specific cross-layer alignment. If the negative control performs similarly to the proposed condition, it would suggest that the specific reference weights do not matter. The observed contrast supports or refutes this alternative. We describe the reported uncertainty as a 95% bootstrap confidence interval of the mean over 43 paired seeds, never as a standard deviation or standard error. This interval captures the uncertainty in the mean estimate due to seed sampling.

The seed budget was determined by a registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targeting 90% power to reject a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. The margin of 0.0125098 proportion was derived from a versioned policy based on calibration noise. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign. The analysis reports primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately and never pools them.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Results: We report the results for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately, stating each preregistered decision. We do not pool the cohorts or call a primary-only result replicated. The analysis uses 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for the mean over 43 paired seeds.

In the primary cohort, the proposed condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The first negative control achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for these three conditions in the primary cohort. The bars represent means over 43 paired seeds, and the error bars represent 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The figure shows the proposed condition against the baseline, with the dashed line marking the baseline mean as an ordering reference. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, the proposed condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). The first negative control achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9082]). Figure 5 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for these three conditions in the replication cohort. Similar to Figure 2, the bars represent means over 43 paired seeds with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The figure shows the proposed condition against the baseline. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

Table 5 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for all conditions across both cohorts. It allows for direct comparison of the primary and replication means. The proposed condition scored higher under the tested conditions in both cohorts (difference 0.000773 in primary, 0.00196 in replication), but neither difference met the registered decision rule. The confidence intervals in both cohorts exclude gains of the target magnitude (0.0125098) under the stated uncertainty model. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive regarding the hypothesis that cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This study found inconclusive evidence that cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The proposed condition scored higher under the tested conditions (difference 0.000773 in primary, 0.00196 in replication), but neither met the registered decision rule (95% CI lower bound > 0.0125098). This changes the choice for someone choosing between these methods by indicating that the intervention does not provide a guaranteed gain over standard training in this regime. One hypothesis is that layer-specific adaptation remains essential, though this is not established fact. Future work should directly measure attention stability and test stronger consistency coefficients to determine if the null result stems from the hypothesis or the implementation strength.
Discussion: The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency loss did not yield robust accuracy gains in the tested regime. Both the primary and replication cohorts produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. This outcome suggests that, for this specific architecture and dataset, layer-specific adaptation may be as effective as cross-layer consistency. However, this is an interpretation of the outcome contrast, not a measured finding of the mechanism.

What this design does and does not establish is critical. The experiment establishes that the intervention did not improve held-out classification accuracy under the stated conditions. It does not establish that attention stability was achieved, as attention maps were not measured. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: we name the directly recorded outcomes (accuracy), and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient, and the observed null result could stem from the penalty being too weak to influence learning, or from the hypothesis being incorrect.

An alternative explanation for the null result is that the consistency constraint conflicts with the task objective. If deeper layers need to specialize to capture higher-level temporal features, forcing them to align with shallower layers might impede this specialization. This would be consistent with the finding that the baseline performed similarly to the proposed condition. The negative control results further suggest that the specific cross-layer relationship does not provide a unique benefit over generic regularization, as the negative control means were comparable to the baseline and proposed conditions.

Comparing this finding against specific cited papers, our results agree with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also reported inconclusive results for a weight regularization hypothesis in this setting [3]. They also align with the caution raised in *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* regarding the benefits of complex architectures over simpler ones [4]. Conversely, they do not support the positive claims of *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* in this specific replication context [1], highlighting the importance of independent verification. The result is not comparable to *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* [9] as that study focused on machine translation and encoder-decoder consistency, a different intervention and task.

The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the primary result was not a false positive due to seed selection. Both cohorts pointed in the same direction (small positive mean difference) but neither reached significance. This consistency across cohorts strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if it exists, is smaller than the worthwhile margin. What would settle the question next is a study that directly measures attention map stability alongside accuracy, or one that varies the consistency coefficient to determine if a stronger penalty yields different results. Until then, the evidence remains inconclusive.
Limitations: This study has several limitations that constrain the generalizability of the findings. First, the experiment was conducted on a single dataset (UCI HAR) and a specific transformer architecture (PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks). The results may not transfer to deeper models, different time-series domains, or datasets with different subject variability. Second, the mechanism of attention stability was not directly measured. We enforced weight consistency, but did not verify if this resulted in stable attention maps. Third, the registered margin was derived from calibration noise, which reflects measurement precision but does not by itself establish practical importance. A null result relative to this margin does not rule out smaller, practically useful gains. Finally, the study distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations; we only performed the former.

This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). You are writing a rigorous, honest research paper (IMRaD) about an experiment that has ALREADY been run; the REAL results — including means, 95% confidence intervals, significance, and effect sizes — are given to you. Be faithful to those numbers and do NOT invent results, references, or findings. Write clear, precise academic prose. CITE numbered references in square brackets (e.g. [1] or [2, 3]); the Introduction and Related Work MUST cite them inline. An automated auditor checks each cited sentence against its abstract: say what a paper actually establishes, not merely its topic. You are NOT required to cite every reference; unused references are removed. NEVER cite a paper as evidence for something it does NOT discuss, including a gap in a different setting. State a gap WITHOUT a marker, use the reviewed gap statement, or cite an abstract that identifies that gap itself. Never attribute the opposite of what an abstract says. Stay INSIDE the abstract's own wording: use its terms, do not generalise them or add an unstated mechanism, domain or consequence. Plausible extensions are unsupported claims too; if in doubt, write less about the paper. Refer to figures and tables by number (e.g. 'Figure 1', 'Table 1'). Report results quantitatively (state the effect, its confidence interval, and whether it is significant). When the analysis contains primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts, report BOTH separately, state each preregistered decision, and never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. Distinguish training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations.
EVIDENCE AND INTERPRETATION. The registered condition descriptions and executed activation records below are authoritative: a baseline/no-op and an active negative control are different conditions. Do not infer inactivity from a small or nonsignificant outcome contrast. Describe only what the control manipulates; its outcome cannot prove that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: name the directly recorded outcomes, and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. If a reference tensor is detached inside a penalty, this stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient. Use the registered CI classifications without equating nonsignificance with equality. If a CI crosses zero but lies below the worthwhile margin, preserve its registered label and separately explain that it excludes gains of that target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model. The supplied power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; do not claim the former guarantees the latter. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

LENGTH. Write a full paper, not an extended abstract. Aim for roughly: introduction 600-800 words; related work 600-900; method 500-800 (BEFORE the operator specification that is appended for you); experimental setup 300-500; results 500-800; discussion 500-800; limitations 200-300; conclusion 150-250; abstract 150-250. A section that is three sentences long has not done its job. Depth means argument and detail, never padding or repetition.
INTRODUCTION. Open with the problem and why it matters, say what is missing in the current literature, then state what this paper does. End it with an explicit contributions list ('- We ...') of two to four items, then state the preregistered prediction.
RELATED WORK — 600-900 words. Synthesise by theme: what papers establish together, where they disagree, and what remains unsettled. The failure this section keeps producing looks like this: 'X studies uncertainty [1]. Y studies approximations [2].' — a list with citations attached. Write instead: 'Uncertainty motivates Bayesian methods [1], but their tractable approximations lose guarantees [2], motivating our boundary test.' Use that argumentative structure only when the abstracts support it. End by positioning this study against the themes; omit irrelevant references and quoted or italicised paper titles. Each reference in a grouped citation must independently support the WHOLE sentence. If papers support different halves, use separate sentences and markers.
RESULTS. Walk the reader through the evidence: discuss each figure and each table where it is relevant to the point being made, rather than listing them at the end.
DO NOT RESTATE THE CONFIGURATION. The dataset, split, architecture, training budget and outcome definition are written for you into the Experimental Setup and the appendix. State them nowhere else — not in the Method, not a second time in the setup.
WHAT THE SETUP SECTION IS FOR is DESIGN justification (300-500 words): why a subject-disjoint split answers the question and a random split would not; benefits and costs of pairing conditions by seed; each negative control's intended alternative explanation and what its observed contrast supports; the seed budget and analysis. These arguments are not supplied by the configuration block.
The METHOD is about the OPERATOR — what it does, why that is the right expression of the hypothesis, and what its comparator neutralises.
The CONCLUSION (150-250 words) states what was found, what it changes for someone choosing between these methods, and what would settle the question next. Not a one-paragraph restatement of the abstract.
NAME THE ARMS AS THE TABLES DO: 'the proposed condition', 'the baseline', 'the first negative control', 'the second negative control'. Do not invent a parallel name such as 'Intervention' — the reader has to match your prose to the tables.
REGISTER. Never enumerate random seeds in the prose — they are in the appendix. Never annotate a sentence with the subsystem that produced it.

PAPER-QUALITY SKILLS (only those relevant to this task are loaded; everything the system can decide for itself is checked, not asked for):
[claim-language] Claim what the evidence carries, and no more. Keep four registers apart and make it obvious which one a sentence is in: a RESULT states a measured quantity; an INTERPRETATION says what it may mean and is marked as such ('suggests', 'is consistent with'); a LIMITATION says what this design cannot tell anyone; FUTURE WORK proposes what would settle the question, and is the only register in which a wider setting may appear. Be exact about who was held out: evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen SUBJECTS — name that population — and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution, so do not call it out-of-distribution or domain generalisation. Where an outcome did not reach the registered decision threshold, report it as measured; do not upgrade it with a verb of proof.
[discussion-depth] The discussion is where the study is interpreted, not summarised again. Cover, in whatever order the argument wants: the principal finding; what it means; what this design does and does NOT establish; a mechanism that would produce the observed result and at least one alternative that would too; what the independent replication cohort adds or fails to add; and how the finding stands against specific cited papers [n] — agreeing, conflicting, extending, or not comparable because the intervention, task, data regime or evaluation differ. Judge that relation from what each abstract says, never from a title. Close with what would settle the question next. A null, refuted or inconclusive outcome owes the reader every one of those and is never rewritten as a positive finding. Length is not the target: a paragraph repeating the results covers none of this, and padding reads worse than brevity.
[paper-structure] Give a long section the internal structure its content earns. Where a section covers two or three distinct matters, open each with a short bold run-in heading (**Like this**) and keep one idea per paragraph; where it makes a single continuous argument, leave it undivided. Break at the argument's own joints — never split one argument to hit a shape, and never add a heading a section has not earned. Paragraphs of 60-150 words read well; one past 200 is doing more than one job and should be split where it turns. This matters most in related work, method, experimental setup, results and discussion, which are the sections long enough to become a wall. Do not fragment: a heading over two sentences is decoration, and several of them are harder to read than the block they replaced.
