=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, driven by their ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions [38]. Despite their success in natural language processing and computer vision, their effectiveness for time-series forecasting and classification remains a subject of active debate [5]. Specifically, it is unclear which architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. While large pre-trained models offer efficiency, the prevalence of separate models for specific tasks implies a fragmentation in the field that complicates the identification of robust inductive biases [13]. This fragmentation necessitates rigorous testing of specific architectural modifications to determine whether they provide genuine generalization benefits or merely add computational cost without performance gains.

One proposed inductive bias is cross-layer consistency, which hypothesizes that stabilizing attention patterns across network depth improves representation quality. In semantic segmentation and domain adaptation, attention consistency has been shown to mitigate discrepancies caused by domain gaps [18]. Similarly, cross-layer mechanisms have been devised to strengthen layer interactions in vision networks [15]. However, these methods often operate on hidden states or attention maps rather than weight structures, and their applicability to subject-disjoint time-series generalization is unverified. A recent study tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy, finding inconclusive results in a specific transformer regime [1]. This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether such consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling.

This paper presents a rigorous replication and extension of the cross-layer query consistency test. We distinguish between the enforced intervention (weight consistency via loss) and the inferred mechanism (attention stability), clarifying the limits of the evidence. Our study employs a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset, utilizing an official subject-disjoint split to evaluate generalization to unseen subjects. We report results from both a primary cohort and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, ensuring that findings are not artifacts of a specific random sample.

The contributions of this work are:
- We execute a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency loss on subject-disjoint time-series generalization, reporting exact means and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
- We provide a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to assess the stability of the primary finding under fresh sampling.
- We distinguish between the measured intervention (weight consistency enforced via loss) and the inferred mechanism (attention stability), noting that the latter was not directly observed.

The preregistered prediction states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 38]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation and representing multivariate series as graphs [14, 20]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones, indicating fragmentation [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including generalization challenges [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice, cautioning against relying on its conclusions [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28].

This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight-based consistency loss in a subject-disjoint setting. Unlike methods that modify attention maps or hidden states [15, 37], we regularize query projection weights directly. While [1] tested this intervention, our work provides a confirmatory replication to verify stability. We do not claim to solve the fragmentation noted in [13] but rather to test one specific bias within the current paradigm. The unsettled nature of Transformer effectiveness in time series [5] motivates this boundary test, as positive results would justify further testing while negative results suggest layer-specific adaptation is essential.

=== method ===
The core of this experiment is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces weight consistency between transformer blocks. The hypothesis is that regularizing deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights stabilizes attention patterns across depth, potentially improving generalization. The operator is applied to the query projection weights of the second attention block (blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight), regularizing them toward the weights of the first block (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight).

The operator specification is fixed and preregistered. During loss computation of every optimization step, the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph. The reference weights from block 0 are retrieved and detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients from flowing to block 0. This ensures that the consistency penalty only trains the target parameters in block 1. The difference is computed element-wise, squared, and summed to form a raw Frobenius norm squared loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01 and added to the training objective. The coefficient is chosen to prevent the consistency term from dominating the classification objective while still exerting regularization pressure.

The proposed condition implements this operator fully. The baseline condition serves as a control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, ensuring identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. In the baseline, the intervention code path is executed but returns zero loss, adding nothing to the training objective and leaving the target parameter unchanged. This design isolates the effect of the loss term itself.

A first negative control penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the computational cost of the proposed condition. If the proposed condition outperforms this negative control, it suggests the specific cross-layer relationship matters, not just the act of regularization. The harness records operator activity for every seed and condition, refusing results where the control arm acted at any registered point. This ensures the baseline remains a true no-op regarding the intervention.

The method distinguishes between the enforced intervention and the inferred mechanism. We enforce weight consistency via the loss term; we do not measure weight consistency as an outcome metric. Similarly, attention stability is a hypothesized mechanism resulting from weight consistency, but it was not directly observed or measured in this run. The method tests whether the enforced weight structure leads to accuracy gains, without claiming to verify the internal attention dynamics. This separation ensures claims remain within the bounds of the recorded evidence.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experimental design prioritizes validity in estimating subject-disjoint generalization. We use the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with its official subject-disjoint split, separating 7,352 training windows from 2,947 held-out windows from unseen subjects. A subject-disjoint split answers the question of generalization to new individuals, whereas a random split would leak subject-specific movement styles into training, inflating accuracy estimates. This design choice is critical for claims about OOD performance in this setting.

We employ 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance by ensuring the proposed and baseline conditions see the exact same data order and initialization. This pairing allows for a paired contrast analysis, increasing sensitivity to small effects. The confirmatory replication cohort uses a disjoint set of seeds through the same pipeline, providing a pre-specified check on the stability of the primary result. This is not an independent replication in the sense of a new pipeline or dataset, but a replication of the sampling process.

Uncertainty is reported as a 95% bootstrap confidence interval of the mean over the paired seeds. We do not report standard deviation or standard error as the primary uncertainty metric. This interval captures the uncertainty in the mean estimate under the stated uncertainty model. The registered decision rule compares the lower confidence bound to a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

The negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any regularization loss might improve accuracy simply by acting as a noise source or compute match. By comparing the proposed condition to a negative control that penalizes a random relationship, we test whether the specific cross-layer alignment matters. The seed budget and analysis plan were fixed before compute was spent. We describe the reported uncertainty as a 95% bootstrap confidence interval of the mean over 43 paired seeds, never as a standard deviation or standard error. This setup ensures that the reported contrasts reflect the intervention's effect rather than sampling variability.

=== results ===
We walk through the evidence from the primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, referencing the methodology flow in Figure 1. Table 1 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition, the baseline, and the first negative control across both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). Figure 2 visualizes these means with error bars representing the 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06).

Figure 3 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. The green dash-dot marker indicates the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion. The confidence interval includes zero and does not exceed the threshold. Figure 4 shows the learning curves over training steps, where the conditions' curves coincide closely, distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern. The preregistered decision for the primary cohort was inconclusive, as the 95% CI includes zero.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, the proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]), and the baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). Figure 5 displays these replication means. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 6 plots the paired mean differences for the replication cohort, again showing the interval crossing zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile threshold. Figure 7 presents the replication learning curves, which mirror the primary cohort's overlap. The registered decision for the replication cohort was also inconclusive.

Table 1 further details the negative control 1 performance, which achieved 0.9051 in the primary and 0.9043 in the replication cohort. The proposed condition's contrast against the negative control was similarly small and nonsignificant. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. We report these outcomes as measured, without upgrading them with a verb of proof. The experiment does not establish that the intervention improves accuracy; it establishes that under these conditions, the measured gain was inconclusive.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency loss did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. The mean differences were small (0.000773 and 0.00196), and the 95% bootstrap confidence intervals included zero in both cases. This result is consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation may be essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, as forcing deeper layers to mimic shallower layers might restrict the network's capacity to refine features progressively.

What this design does and does not establish requires careful distinction. We enforced weight consistency via the loss term; we did not measure weight consistency as an outcome metric, nor did we observe attention stability directly. The mechanism remains a hypothesis. An alternative explanation for the null result is that the coefficient (0.01) was too small to exert meaningful pressure, or that the Frobenius norm is too coarse a measure of functional consistency. However, the negative control matched the compute and loss magnitude without the semantic relationship, and it also failed to improve accuracy, suggesting the issue is not merely the presence of a penalty.

The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the primary result was not a false positive driven by a specific seed sample. Both cohorts pointed in the same direction (small positive mean difference) but neither reached significance. This consistency across 86 total seeds strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if it exists, is smaller than the registered worthwhile margin. This stands in contrast to works reporting gains from cross-layer mechanisms in vision or domain adaptation [15, 18], suggesting that time-series subject-disjoint generalization may rely on different inductive biases.

Comparing to specific cited papers, our findings agree with [1], which reported inconclusive results for this intervention. They also align with [3], which found spectral entropy minimization did not yield robust accuracy gains in a similar regime. However, they conflict with the general expectation from [17] that consistency regularization alleviates overfitting in deep transformers. This discrepancy may arise because the UCI HAR dataset, while subject-disjoint, may not present the same overfitting pressure as machine translation or small-scale vision tasks. The intervention, task, data regime, and evaluation differ from [18], making direct comparison difficult.

To settle the question next, future work should measure attention map stability directly to verify if the weight loss achieves the inferred mechanism. Additionally, testing on larger, more diverse time-series benchmarks would determine if the null result generalizes beyond UCI HAR. Until then, the evidence suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not provide a robust accuracy gain in this setting.

=== limitations ===
This study has several limitations that constrain the interpretation of the findings. First, the experiment was conducted on a single dataset (UCI HAR) with a specific transformer architecture (2-block PreNormTransformerEncoder). The results may not generalize to deeper networks, different time-series domains, or other modalities. Second, we enforced weight consistency but did not measure it as an outcome, nor did we measure attention stability. The mechanism linking the loss to accuracy remains inferred. Third, the registered worthwhile margin was derived from calibration noise, which reflects measurement precision but does not necessarily establish practical importance. Finally, the confirmatory replication cohort used the same pipeline and dataset, differing only in seeds; it does not test robustness to implementation changes or distribution shifts beyond subject disjointness.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The results were inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, with mean accuracy gains failing to exceed the registered worthwhile margin. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence suggests that this intervention does not justify the added complexity in the UCI HAR regime. Future work should measure attention dynamics directly and test on broader benchmarks to determine if consistency biases are viable for time-series generalization.

=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation

Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer*. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy. Hypothesis: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.
Open problem this targets: What architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds?
Why it matters (impact): Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for OOD time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

REGISTERED OPERATOR (including gradient handling; do not infer that detaching one loss term freezes ordinary task-loss learning):
Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer*. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it.

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance.

=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% bootstrap confidence interval [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% bootstrap confidence interval [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [38]. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling [38]. However, recent work questions the validity of Transformer-based solutions for time series forecasting, noting that permutation-invariant self-attention may result in temporal information loss compared to linear models [5]. Despite this uncertainty, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges for domains with limited data [32]. What architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds remains an open problem.

Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. Large pre-trained models have been vital in recent advancements in domains like language and vision, but tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model from scratch [22]. This fragmentation complicates the identification of robust inductive biases [22]. This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling.

We distinguish between the enforced intervention (weight consistency via loss) and the inferred mechanism (attention stability), clarifying the limits of the evidence. We do not claim attention stability was directly observed, as no such measurement was recorded. This paper makes the following contributions:
- We preregister and execute a calibrated testbed to evaluate cross-layer query consistency in time-series transformers under subject-disjoint generalization.
- We report results from both a primary cohort and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, ensuring robustness against sampling variance.
- We provide null results regarding accuracy gains, suggesting layer-specific adaptation may be necessary in this regime.

The preregistered prediction states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [11], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [21], and *A survey of transformers* [41] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight consistency operator in a subject-disjoint time-series setting, distinct from domain adaptation or activation engineering.

=== method ===
The method focuses on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces weight consistency between attention query projections across layers. Figure 1 illustrates the methodology flow showing data input, transformer model, registered conditions with CrossLayerQueryConsistency intervention at the loss term, and held-out evaluation. The operator is applied to the query projection weight matrix of the second attention block (blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight). The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent.

The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. The operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The scope covers the full weight matrix treated as flat parameter space. The ordering involves element-wise subtraction then sum, which is order-invariant due to commutativity of addition. There is no normalization; the raw Frobenius norm squared is scaled by a fixed coefficient. Numerical safeguards include a coefficient of 0.01 to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective.

Algorithm 1 details the operator: retrieve reference weights from the first block's query projection; detach reference weights from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0; compute the element-wise difference; square the elements; sum over all elements; scale by the consistency coefficient; and return the loss term for addition to the training objective. The following invariants hold throughout: reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients; the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only; and the coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

The control arm is defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experimental design prioritizes validity in subject-disjoint generalization testing. We use a subject-disjoint split because a random split would allow subject-specific movement styles to leak between training and testing, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to answer the question of generalization to unseen subjects. Pairing conditions by seed ensures that variance due to initialization and data ordering is controlled, allowing the paired contrast to isolate the intervention's effect. This pairing is critical for detecting small effects against the noise of stochastic training.

We describe the reported uncertainty as a 95% bootstrap confidence interval of the mean over 43 paired seeds, never as a standard deviation or standard error. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds provides power to detect effects exceeding the registered margin. The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix, destroying meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This control supports the alternative explanation that any observed effect is due to compute overhead or regularization generally, rather than specific cross-layer consistency. The second negative control (baseline) ensures the harness itself introduces no bias. The observed contrast between the proposed condition and the baseline supports claims about the specific consistency operator, while the contrast with the first negative control supports claims about the meaningfulness of the cross-layer relationship.

The analysis distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations. Here, the confirmatory cohort uses disjoint seeds through the same generated pipeline on the same subject-disjoint split. This distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance. The registered condition descriptions and executed activation records are authoritative: a baseline/no-op and an active negative control are different conditions. We do not infer inactivity from a small or nonsignificant outcome contrast.

=== results ===
We report results for the primary cohort and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds separately. Table 1 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for the proposed condition, the baseline, and the first negative control. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). Figure 2 displays these means with error bars, showing the proposed condition against the baseline. The dashed line marks the baseline mean as an ordering reference only.

The paired mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 3 plots these paired differences, with the green dash-dot marker showing the registered worthwhile threshold. Support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it, which it does not. The 43 individual paired differences are plotted behind the interval at their exact values. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the primary cohort. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. Series encoding distinguishes conditions whose curves coincide by marker shape and dash pattern as well as by colour.

In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, the proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). Figure 5 displays these means for the replication cohort. The paired mean difference was 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 6 plots these replication paired differences against the registered threshold. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. Figure 7 shows the learning curves for the replication cohort. The preregistered decision was inconclusive for both cohorts. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not improve held-out classification accuracy under the stated conditions. The results are inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. This means the evidence does not support the hypothesis that the intervention yields accuracy gains exceeding the worthwhile margin. What this design does establish is that any effect size is likely smaller than the registered margin of 0.0125098 proportion under the stated uncertainty model. It does not establish that the effect is zero, only that it was not detected with sufficient magnitude to meet the support rule.

A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, and constraining deeper layers to match shallower layers restricts this necessary flexibility. An alternative mechanism is that the consistency penalty was too weak to overcome the classification objective's gradient, or that the detachment of reference weights prevented meaningful co-adaptation. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the primary result was not a false positive due to seed selection, as the replication effect direction was consistent but similarly inconclusive.

These findings agree with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which found null results for spectral entropy minimization in this regime [3]. They conflict with *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* if that study claimed positive gains, but align if it reported inconclusive results [1]. They are not comparable to *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* because the intervention, task, data regime or evaluation differ [18]. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes overfitting on small-scale data, but our null result suggests consistency alone does not solve generalization here [17].

What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks with larger datasets or different architectures. A negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. We distinguish between the enforced intervention (weight consistency via loss) and the inferred mechanism (attention stability), clarifying the limits of the evidence. We do not claim attention stability was directly observed.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency improves generalization on different corpora, sensors, tasks, or deployment distributions. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects in the UCI HAR population, and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution, so we do not call it out-of-distribution or domain generalisation. The margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. Conformance and activation counts describe execution; they do not establish the mechanism or prove the absence of implementation bias. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

=== conclusion ===
The experiment found that cross-layer query consistency did not improve held-out classification accuracy in the primary or replication cohorts. This changes the choice for someone choosing between these methods by indicating that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks in this regime. The findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains. What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks. A negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks.

REGISTERED OPERATOR (including gradient handling; do not infer that detaching one loss term freezes ordinary task-loss learning):
Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer*. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it.

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance.

=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% bootstrap confidence interval [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% bootstrap confidence interval [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [38]. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling [38]. However, recent work questions the validity of Transformer-based solutions for time series forecasting, noting that permutation-invariant self-attention may result in temporal information loss compared to linear models [5]. Despite this uncertainty, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges for domains with limited data [32]. What architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds remains an open problem.

Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. Large pre-trained models have been vital in recent advancements in domains like language and vision, but tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model from scratch [22]. This fragmentation complicates the identification of robust inductive biases [22]. This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling.

We distinguish between the enforced intervention (weight consistency via loss) and the inferred mechanism (attention stability), clarifying the limits of the evidence. We do not claim attention stability was directly observed, as no such measurement was recorded. This paper makes the following contributions:
- We preregister and execute a calibrated testbed to evaluate cross-layer query consistency in time-series transformers under subject-disjoint generalization.
- We report results from both a primary cohort and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, ensuring robustness against sampling variance.
- We provide null results regarding accuracy gains, suggesting layer-specific adaptation may be necessary in this regime.

The preregistered prediction states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [11], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [21], and *A survey of transformers* [41] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight consistency operator in a subject-disjoint time-series setting, distinct from domain adaptation or activation engineering.

=== method ===
The method focuses on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces weight consistency between attention query projections across layers. Figure 1 illustrates the methodology flow showing data input, transformer model, registered conditions with CrossLayerQueryConsistency intervention at the loss term, and held-out evaluation. The operator is applied to the query projection weight matrix of the second attention block (blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight). The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent.

The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. The operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The scope covers the full weight matrix treated as flat parameter space. The ordering involves element-wise subtraction then sum, which is order-invariant due to commutativity of addition. There is no normalization; the raw Frobenius norm squared is scaled by a fixed coefficient. Numerical safeguards include a coefficient of 0.01 to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective.

Algorithm 1 details the operator: retrieve reference weights from the first block's query projection; detach reference weights from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0; compute the element-wise difference; square the elements; sum over all elements; scale by the consistency coefficient; and return the loss term for addition to the training objective. The following invariants hold throughout: reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients; the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only; and the coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

The control arm is defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experimental design prioritizes validity in subject-disjoint generalization testing. We use a subject-disjoint split because a random split would allow subject-specific movement styles to leak between training and testing, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to answer the question of generalization to unseen subjects. Pairing conditions by seed ensures that variance due to initialization and data ordering is controlled, allowing the paired contrast to isolate the intervention's effect. This pairing is critical for detecting small effects against the noise of stochastic training.

We describe the reported uncertainty as a 95% bootstrap confidence interval of the mean over 43 paired seeds, never as a standard deviation or standard error. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds provides power to detect effects exceeding the registered margin. The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix, destroying meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This control supports the alternative explanation that any observed effect is due to compute overhead or regularization generally, rather than specific cross-layer consistency. The second negative control (baseline) ensures the harness itself introduces no bias. The observed contrast between the proposed condition and the baseline supports claims about the specific consistency operator, while the contrast with the first negative control supports claims about the meaningfulness of the cross-layer relationship.

The analysis distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations. Here, the confirmatory cohort uses disjoint seeds through the same generated pipeline on the same subject-disjoint split. This distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance. The registered condition descriptions and executed activation records are authoritative: a baseline/no-op and an active negative control are different conditions. We do not infer inactivity from a small or nonsignificant outcome contrast.

=== results ===
We report results for the primary cohort and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds separately. Table 1 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for the proposed condition, the baseline, and the first negative control. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). Figure 2 displays these means with error bars, showing the proposed condition against the baseline. The dashed line marks the baseline mean as an ordering reference only.

The paired mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 3 plots these paired differences, with the green dash-dot marker showing the registered worthwhile threshold. Support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it, which it does not. The 43 individual paired differences are plotted behind the interval at their exact values. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the primary cohort. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. Series encoding distinguishes conditions whose curves coincide by marker shape and dash pattern as well as by colour.

In the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, the proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). Figure 5 displays these means for the replication cohort. The paired mean difference was 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 6 plots these replication paired differences against the registered threshold. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. Figure 7 shows the learning curves for the replication cohort. The preregistered decision was inconclusive for both cohorts. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not improve held-out classification accuracy under the stated conditions. The results are inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. This means the evidence does not support the hypothesis that the intervention yields accuracy gains exceeding the worthwhile margin. What this design does establish is that any effect size is likely smaller than the registered margin of 0.0125098 proportion under the stated uncertainty model. It does not establish that the effect is zero, only that it was not detected with sufficient magnitude to meet the support rule.

A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, and constraining deeper layers to match shallower layers restricts this necessary flexibility. An alternative mechanism is that the consistency penalty was too weak to overcome the classification objective's gradient, or that the detachment of reference weights prevented meaningful co-adaptation. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the primary result was not a false positive due to seed selection, as the replication effect direction was consistent but similarly inconclusive.

These findings agree with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which found null results for spectral entropy minimization in this regime [3]. They conflict with *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* if that study claimed positive gains, but align if it reported inconclusive results [1]. They are not comparable to *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* because the intervention, task, data regime or evaluation differ [18]. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes overfitting on small-scale data, but our null result suggests consistency alone does not solve generalization here [17].

What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks with larger datasets or different architectures. A negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. We distinguish between the enforced intervention (weight consistency via loss) and the inferred mechanism (attention stability), clarifying the limits of the evidence. We do not claim attention stability was directly observed.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency improves generalization on different corpora, sensors, tasks, or deployment distributions. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects in the UCI HAR population, and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution, so we do not call it out-of-distribution or domain generalisation. The margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. Conformance and activation counts describe execution; they do not establish the mechanism or prove the absence of implementation bias. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

=== conclusion ===
The experiment found that cross-layer query consistency did not improve held-out classification accuracy in the primary or replication cohorts. This changes the choice for someone choosing between these methods by indicating that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks in this regime. The findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains. What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks. A negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks.

We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would exceed a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion in accuracy gain.
