Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet it remains unclear whether architectural inductive biases, such as cross-layer attention stability, improve generalization to unseen subjects. This preregistered study tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and an active negative control across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on 43 disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, though this mechanism was not directly measured.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [20], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line, showing that simple linear models can outperform sophisticated Transformer-based solutions on long-term forecasting tasks [3]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation using Transformer-based GANs [11] and representing multivariate series as graphs to capture inter-dependencies [6]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [16].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data and proposes constraining encoder and decoder outputs [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, proposing consistency between predictions from cross-domain attention and self-attention modules [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions by retrieving query-related information from previous layers [7]. *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering, exploiting global signals to rectify steering vectors [18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it due to implementation discrepancies, highlighting the need for rigorous verification in this area [1].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements, improving performance and efficiency [4]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks, offering linear complexity [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow, proposing a method to mix values inside the attention module [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [5, 12, 21]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance, finding that query and key content comparison is negligible for self-attention in some contexts [15]. *Transformer in Transformer* explores nesting local patches within visual transformers to excavate features at different scales, demonstrating effectiveness on image benchmarks [2]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing whether a specific cross-layer consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in a time-series setting, where evidence remains unsettled.
Method: The core of this study is the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency between attention query projection weights in different transformer blocks. The hypothesis is that regularizing deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights stabilizes attention patterns across depth, thereby improving generalization to unseen subjects. This operator is applied to the query projection weight matrix of the second attention block (blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight), regularizing it toward the corresponding weights of the first block (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight).

The operator is invoked during the loss computation of every optimization step. Its term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, meaning the combined objective is differentiated, and the operator-owned parameters are trained by it. The algorithm retrieves the reference weights from the first block and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients from flowing back to the shallower layer. It then computes the element-wise difference between the target weights and the detached reference weights. The squared elements are summed to produce a raw loss, which is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01. This coefficient was chosen to prevent the consistency term from dominating the classification objective while still exerting a regularizing influence. The resulting loss term is stored for harness aggregation and returned to be added to the training objective.

This design ensures that the reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients from this specific loss term, while the loss term remains differentiable with respect to the target parameters in block 1. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds. The registered comparator holds the architecture and training procedure fixed, differing only in the absence of this loss term. This allows us to isolate the effect of the cross-layer consistency constraint on the held-out classification accuracy.

The intervention is distinct from standard weight decay or dropout; it explicitly couples the optimization of two different layers. By detaching the reference weights, we ensure that the penalty acts as a one-way constraint, pulling the deeper layer's query projections toward the shallower layer's configuration without altering the shallower layer via this specific mechanism. This tests whether aligning query projections across depth provides an inductive bias beneficial for subject-disjoint generalization, or whether layer-specific adaptation is necessary for the model to capture the temporal dynamics of different subjects.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Experimental setup: The experiment uses the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. This design choice is critical: a random split would allow data from the same subject to appear in both training and testing, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to measure generalization to new individuals. The subject-disjoint split ensures that the 2,947 held-out windows come from subjects who appear nowhere in the training set, supporting claims about unseen subjects rather than merely unseen windows.

We distinguish three conditions: the proposed condition, the baseline, and the first negative control. The baseline is a control arm defined by what the harness guarantees: it executes the identical code path but returns a zero loss term. The harness records zero operator activations for the baseline (0/43 seeds), confirming it acts as a no-op. In contrast, the first negative control is an active condition. It adds a loss term penalizing the difference between the target weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as the reference weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the computational cost and gradient flow of the proposed condition. The harness recorded operator activity for all 43 seeds in this condition. This distinction allows us to determine whether any observed effect is due to the specific cross-layer consistency or merely the presence of an additional loss term.

All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. We used 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance in the contrast estimate by controlling for random initialization and data ordering effects. The seed budget was determined by a preregistered power analysis targeting 90% power to detect an effect at the worthwhile margin, though this power calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null and does not guarantee power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin.

The analysis plan distinguishes the primary cohort from the confirmatory-replication cohort. We report results for each separately and do not pool them. The confirmatory cohort is not an independent replication in the sense of a new dataset or architecture; it is a replication on new seeds within the same experimental setting. This design allows us to assess the stability of the effect estimate under fresh sampling while holding the data and model constant.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Registered conditions.
- Proposed condition: Server-bound target blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight has stored tensor shape (64, 64). Add loss term that applies Frobenius norm consistency regularization to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Baseline: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. Recorded activity — primary: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Negative control 1: Add loss term penalizing difference between blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
Results: We report the held-out classification accuracy for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]), as shown in Table 2. The first negative control achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 1 visualizes these means with error bars representing the 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The figure shows the proposed condition against the baseline, with the dashed line marking the baseline mean for reference. The overlapping intervals suggest no clear separation between conditions.

The primary contrast is detailed in Table 3. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 2 plots the paired mean difference over the 43 seeds, with the green dash-dot marker indicating the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098. The confidence interval includes zero and lies well below the threshold. Figure 3 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all three conditions in the primary cohort. The curves for the proposed, baseline, and negative control conditions coincide closely, indicating similar learning dynamics.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, the proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]), and the baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]), as shown in Table 4. The first negative control achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9082]). Figure 4 displays these means. The replication contrast, detailed in Table 5, shows the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 5 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The points represent the paired mean difference over 43 seeds, and the error bars show the 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The green dash-dot marker again shows the registered worthwhile threshold. The figure supports the comparison of the intervention effect against the threshold, showing that the lower confidence bound does not exceed it. Figure 6 plots the training curves for the replication cohort, which again show coincident performance across conditions.

In both cohorts, the 95% confidence intervals included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive for both the primary and replication cohorts. The variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This preregistered study found no evidence that cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers on the UCI HAR dataset. Both primary and replication cohorts yielded inconclusive results, with effect sizes small and confidence intervals including zero. For someone choosing between these methods, the measured outcome licenses the conclusion that this intervention does not provide a robust accuracy gain in this regime. One possible explanation, which this experiment did not test, is that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. Future work should test whether this finding holds for larger models, different time-series domains, or alternative consistency metrics that directly measure attention stability.
Discussion: The principal finding of this study is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not yield a statistically significant or practically worthwhile improvement in subject-disjoint generalization on the UCI HAR dataset. Both the primary and replication cohorts produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals spanning zero and failing to exceed the registered margin. One possibility, which this experiment did not test, is that that, in this specific regime, the inductive bias provided by aligning query projections across depth does not robustly enhance accuracy.

One possible explanation, which this experiment did not test, is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. Transformers may require the flexibility to learn distinct attention patterns at different depths to capture the complex temporal dynamics of human movement. Enforcing consistency might constrain this flexibility without providing sufficient regularization benefit to offset the loss of expressivity. Alternatively, the consistency coefficient of 0.01 may have been too small to exert a meaningful influence, or the Frobenius norm penalty may not align with the geometric properties of the attention space that matter for generalization. These are hypotheses; the experiment measured the registered outcome (accuracy), not the stability of attention maps or the geometry of the weight space.

The independent replication cohort adds weight to the inconclusive finding. The effect size in the replication cohort (dz=0.15) was slightly larger than in the primary cohort (dz=0.06), but the confidence interval remained wide and included zero. This consistency in null results across 86 total seeds suggests that the lack of effect is not merely a sampling artifact of the primary run. However, because the replication used the same dataset and architecture, it does not establish generalizability to other time-series domains or model sizes.

These findings stand in contrast to works that report benefits from consistency regularization in other contexts. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* found improvements in machine translation by constraining encoder and decoder outputs [9], and *CDAC* reported gains in domain adaptive semantic segmentation by aligning attention maps [10]. The discrepancy may arise from the task difference: subject-disjoint time-series classification may rely on different features than sequence-to-sequence translation or pixel-level segmentation. Furthermore, *Global Evolutionary Steering* applied cross-layer consistency to activation engineering in LLMs [18], a different mechanism than weight regularization during training. Our results do not contradict these papers but indicate that the benefit of cross-layer consistency does not automatically transfer to subject-disjoint time-series transformers with this specific operator.
Limitations: This study has several limitations. First, the findings are specific to the UCI HAR dataset and the PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture used. We cannot claim that cross-layer consistency is ineffective for all time-series tasks or all transformer variants. Second, the experiment measured held-out classification accuracy, not attention stability or feature geometry. We cannot conclude that the consistency loss failed to align weights, only that any alignment did not translate to accuracy gains. Third, the worthwhile margin was derived from calibration noise, which reflects measurement precision but does not by itself establish practical importance. Finally, the confirmatory replication cohort is not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets; it is a replication on new seeds within the same setting.

Declared scope. payload.content:
=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The registered decision for both cohorts was inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [38]. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications [38]. However, recent work questions the validity of this research line, noting that permutation-invariant self-attention mechanisms may result in temporal information loss compared to simpler linear models [5]. Despite this debate, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [32]. Addressing these limitations often involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones, or employing domain adaptation techniques [22, 32].

A critical open problem is identifying what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Specifically, it remains unclear whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks. Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization [38, 5]. To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms [17, 18]. For instance, deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data, motivating regularization strategies [17]. Cross-layer interactions are explored to strengthen layer interactions or apply consistency to activation engineering [15, 34]. However, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization.

This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. We conduct a calibrated testbed experiment using the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block query projection weights during training. We compare the proposed condition against a baseline control arm and an active negative control.

Our contributions are as follows:
- We execute a preregistered replication study testing cross-layer query consistency loss in a subject-disjoint time-series setting.
- We report results from both a primary cohort and a confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, adhering to registered decision rules.
- We provide empirical evidence regarding the efficacy of weight alignment across depth for generalization in this specific architecture and data regime.

The preregistered prediction is: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [38], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28].

This study positions itself against these themes by independently verifying the cross-layer consistency hypothesis in a subject-disjoint setting. While prior work explores cross-layer mechanisms for representation power or domain adaptation [15, 18], few isolate the effect of query weight alignment on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Unlike works that propose new architectures for specific tasks like segmentation or forecasting [23, 32], this experiment tests a specific regularization operator within a fixed architecture. The inconclusive results of related regularization tests, such as spectral entropy minimization, motivate this boundary test [3].

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator applied to the query projection weights of the second attention block. The hypothesis posits that enforcing consistency between the query weights of the first and second blocks improves generalization. The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step, adding a term to the classification objective inside the autograd graph. The specification is fixed before any compute was spent. The scope covers the full weight matrix of shape [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space. The ordering of operations is element-wise subtraction then sum, which is order-invariant due to commutativity of addition. There is no normalization; the raw Frobenius norm squared is scaled by a fixed coefficient of 0.01. Numerical safeguards rely on this coefficient to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective.

The algorithm retrieves reference weights from the first block's query projection and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. It computes the element-wise difference between the target weights (block 1) and the reference weights. The squared elements are summed over all elements to produce a raw loss, which is then multiplied by the consistency coefficient. This loss term is stored for harness aggregation and returned for addition to the training objective. The invariants hold throughout: reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients, the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only, and the coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

The control arm is defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

The first negative control adds a loss term penalizing difference between the target weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This condition tests whether the mere presence of a regularization term, rather than the specific cross-layer alignment, drives any observed effects. The proposed condition is the server-bound target where the operator applies Frobenius norm consistency regularization to the second block's query weights.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification for Subject-Disjoint Split.** The experiment uses the official subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset. This design answers the question of generalization to unseen subjects, which a random split would not. A random split allows windows from the same subject to appear in both training and testing, inflating accuracy estimates by capturing subject-specific idiosyncrasies rather than activity patterns. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. Therefore, the subject-disjoint split is necessary to test the hypothesis regarding architectural inductive biases for cross-subject generalization.

**Pairing Conditions by Seed.** Both the proposed condition and the baseline are trained from the same paired seed. The dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. This pairing reduces variance in the paired contrast by controlling for initialization and data ordering effects. The analysis uses paired statistics to detect the effect of the intervention against the noise of stochastic training. The seed budget consists of 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. Reporting both cohorts separately allows us to distinguish training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations; the confirmatory cohort is never an independent replication of the dataset, but it is an independent replication of the training process.

**Negative Control Purpose.** The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. This active condition tests the alternative explanation that any regularization term, regardless of its semantic content, improves generalization by acting as a regularizer. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, it suggests the cross-layer relationship is specific and meaningful. If both perform similarly, the effect may be due to generic regularization. The baseline is the inert comparator. The design does not isolate the effect of the constraint from computational overhead, as per-step cost was deliberately not held equal. The recorded activity confirms the harness executed the operator in the proposed and negative control conditions and remained inert in the baseline.

**Analysis Plan.** The primary outcome is held-out classification accuracy. The registered decision rule requires the lower confidence bound of the paired contrast to exceed the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The planning target power was 90% with a planning SD of 0.0250196. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

=== results ===
We report results for the primary and confirmatory replication cohorts separately. In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition mean was 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]). The baseline condition mean was 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The first negative control mean was 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 2 displays these means with error bars. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 3 plots the paired mean difference with the registered worthwhile threshold. The 95% CI includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition mean was 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]). The baseline condition mean was 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). The first negative control mean was 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9082]). Figure 5 displays these means. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 6 plots the paired mean difference. The 95% CI includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

Figure 4 and Figure 7 show the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. The curves for the proposed, baseline, and negative control conditions track closely throughout training, with no condition consistently separating from the others. The variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive in both cohorts. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks. The registered condition descriptions and executed activation records confirm the operator acted in the proposed and negative control conditions and remained inert in the baseline.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not yield a statistically significant or practically worthwhile improvement in subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. The registered decision for both the primary and replication cohorts was inconclusive. The measured contrast in the primary cohort was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]), and in the replication cohort was 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). These intervals include zero and lie below the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. This outcome suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

This design establishes the effect of the specific operator on held-out accuracy but does not establish the mechanism. Mechanistic rationales such as attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization are hypotheses, not measured findings. We name the directly recorded outcomes, and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. An alternative explanation is that the regularization coefficient was too small to influence the optimization trajectory meaningfully, or that the task does not benefit from query weight similarity across depth. The negative control, which penalized deviation from a random matrix, also did not significantly differ from the baseline, suggesting generic regularization of this form may not aid generalization in this setting.

The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the primary result was not a false positive due to seed selection. Both cohorts produced inconclusive decisions with overlapping confidence intervals. This consistency across 86 total seeds strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if it exists, is smaller than the registered margin. This finding stands against specific cited papers that propose cross-layer mechanisms for representation power [15, 34]. While those works report improvements in classification or steering tasks, the intervention, task, data regime or evaluation differ. For example, *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention* improves accuracy on image classification tasks [15], which may not transfer to subject-disjoint time-series data. Similarly, *Global Evolutionary Steering* applies consistency to activation engineering in language models [34], a different modality and intervention type.

The results are consistent with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which found inconclusive results for spectral regularization in a similar setting [3]. Both studies suggest that weight geometry constraints may not robustly improve generalization in finite-width time-series transformers. Conversely, *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting [17], but our results do not confirm that this specific consistency loss mitigates that risk in the subject-disjoint UCI HAR setting. Future work would settle the question by testing larger coefficients, different layers, or direct measurements of attention map stability.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether the intervention works in different domains, such as language or vision, or with different architectures. The subject-disjoint split supports a claim about unseen subjects in the UCI HAR population and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. We do not call it out-of-distribution or domain generalisation beyond this scope. Mechanisms such as attention stability were not measured; we mention them only as untested candidate explanations. The study does not isolate the effect of the constraint from computational overhead, as per-step cost was deliberately not held equal. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance. The registered power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter. If a CI crosses zero but lies below the worthwhile margin, we preserve its registered label and separately explain that it excludes gains of that target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model.

=== conclusion ===
This study found that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin for subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The registered decision for both primary and replication cohorts was inconclusive, with mean contrasts of 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]) and 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]) respectively. This outcome licenses the conclusion that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. It does not prove the mechanism is ineffective, only that this implementation did not improve accuracy under these conditions. Future work should test whether direct measurements of attention stability correlate with generalization or whether alternative consistency losses yield different results.

=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The registered decision for both cohorts was inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [38]. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications [38]. However, recent work questions the validity of this research line, noting that permutation-invariant self-attention mechanisms may result in temporal information loss compared to simpler linear models [5]. Despite this debate, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [32]. Addressing these limitations often involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones, or employing domain adaptation techniques [22, 32].

A critical open problem is identifying what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Specifically, it remains unclear whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks. Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization [38, 5]. To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms [17, 18]. For instance, deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data, motivating regularization strategies [17]. Cross-layer interactions are explored to strengthen layer interactions or apply consistency to activation engineering [15, 34]. However, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization.

This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. We conduct a calibrated testbed experiment using the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block query projection weights during training. We compare the proposed condition against a baseline control arm and an active negative control.

Our contributions are as follows:
- We execute a preregistered replication study testing cross-layer query consistency loss in a subject-disjoint time-series setting.
- We report results from both a primary cohort and a confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, adhering to registered decision rules.
- We provide empirical evidence regarding the efficacy of weight alignment across depth for generalization in this specific architecture and data regime.

The preregistered prediction is: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [38], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28].

This study positions itself against these themes by independently verifying the cross-layer consistency hypothesis in a subject-disjoint setting. While prior work explores cross-layer mechanisms for representation power or domain adaptation [15, 18], few isolate the effect of query weight alignment on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Unlike works that propose new architectures for specific tasks like segmentation or forecasting [23, 32], this experiment tests a specific regularization operator within a fixed architecture. The inconclusive results of related regularization tests, such as spectral entropy minimization, motivate this boundary test [3].

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator applied to the query projection weights of the second attention block. The hypothesis posits that enforcing consistency between the query weights of the first and second blocks improves generalization. The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step, adding a term to the classification objective inside the autograd graph. The specification is fixed before any compute was spent. The scope covers the full weight matrix of shape [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space. The ordering of operations is element-wise subtraction then sum, which is order-invariant due to commutativity of addition. There is no normalization; the raw Frobenius norm squared is scaled by a fixed coefficient of 0.01. Numerical safeguards rely on this coefficient to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective.

The algorithm retrieves reference weights from the first block's query projection and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. It computes the element-wise difference between the target weights (block 1) and the reference weights. The squared elements are summed over all elements to produce a raw loss, which is then multiplied by the consistency coefficient. This loss term is stored for harness aggregation and returned for addition to the training objective. The invariants hold throughout: reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients, the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only, and the coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

The control arm is defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

The first negative control adds a loss term penalizing difference between the target weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This condition tests whether the mere presence of a regularization term, rather than the specific cross-layer alignment, drives any observed effects. The proposed condition is the server-bound target where the operator applies Frobenius norm consistency regularization to the second block's query weights.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification for Subject-Disjoint Split.** The experiment uses the official subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset. This design answers the question of generalization to unseen subjects, which a random split would not. A random split allows windows from the same subject to appear in both training and testing, inflating accuracy estimates by capturing subject-specific idiosyncrasies rather than activity patterns. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. Therefore, the subject-disjoint split is necessary to test the hypothesis regarding architectural inductive biases for cross-subject generalization.

**Pairing Conditions by Seed.** Both the proposed condition and the baseline are trained from the same paired seed. The dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. This pairing reduces variance in the paired contrast by controlling for initialization and data ordering effects. The analysis uses paired statistics to detect the effect of the intervention against the noise of stochastic training. The seed budget consists of 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. Reporting both cohorts separately allows us to distinguish training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations; the confirmatory cohort is never an independent replication of the dataset, but it is an independent replication of the training process.

**Negative Control Purpose.** The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. This active condition tests the alternative explanation that any regularization term, regardless of its semantic content, improves generalization by acting as a regularizer. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, it suggests the cross-layer relationship is specific and meaningful. If both perform similarly, the effect may be due to generic regularization. The baseline is the inert comparator. The design does not isolate the effect of the constraint from computational overhead, as per-step cost was deliberately not held equal. The recorded activity confirms the harness executed the operator in the proposed and negative control conditions and remained inert in the baseline.

**Analysis Plan.** The primary outcome is held-out classification accuracy. The registered decision rule requires the lower confidence bound of the paired contrast to exceed the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The planning target power was 90% with a planning SD of 0.0250196. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

=== results ===
We report results for the primary and confirmatory replication cohorts separately. In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition mean was 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]). The baseline condition mean was 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The first negative control mean was 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 2 displays these means with error bars. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 3 plots the paired mean difference with the registered worthwhile threshold. The 95% CI includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition mean was 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]). The baseline condition mean was 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). The first negative control mean was 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9082]). Figure 5 displays these means. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 6 plots the paired mean difference. The 95% CI includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

Figure 4 and Figure 7 show the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. The curves for the proposed, baseline, and negative control conditions track closely throughout training, with no condition consistently separating from the others. The variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive in both cohorts. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks. The registered condition descriptions and executed activation records confirm the operator acted in the proposed and negative control conditions and remained inert in the baseline.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not yield a statistically significant or practically worthwhile improvement in subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. The registered decision for both the primary and replication cohorts was inconclusive. The measured contrast in the primary cohort was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]), and in the replication cohort was 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). These intervals include zero and lie below the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. This outcome suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

This design establishes the effect of the specific operator on held-out accuracy but does not establish the mechanism. Mechanistic rationales such as attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization are hypotheses, not measured findings. We name the directly recorded outcomes, and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. An alternative explanation is that the regularization coefficient was too small to influence the optimization trajectory meaningfully, or that the task does not benefit from query weight similarity across depth. The negative control, which penalized deviation from a random matrix, also did not significantly differ from the baseline, suggesting generic regularization of this form may not aid generalization in this setting.

The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the primary result was not a false positive due to seed selection. Both cohorts produced inconclusive decisions with overlapping confidence intervals. This consistency across 86 total seeds strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if it exists, is smaller than the registered margin. This finding stands against specific cited papers that propose cross-layer mechanisms for representation power [15, 34]. While those works report improvements in classification or steering tasks, the intervention, task, data regime or evaluation differ. For example, *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention* improves accuracy on image classification tasks [15], which may not transfer to subject-disjoint time-series data. Similarly, *Global Evolutionary Steering* applies consistency to activation engineering in language models [34], a different modality and intervention type.

The results are consistent with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which found inconclusive results for spectral regularization in a similar setting [3]. Both studies suggest that weight geometry constraints may not robustly improve generalization in finite-width time-series transformers. Conversely, *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting [17], but our results do not confirm that this specific consistency loss mitigates that risk in the subject-disjoint UCI HAR setting. Future work would settle the question by testing larger coefficients, different layers, or direct measurements of attention map stability.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether the intervention works in different domains, such as language or vision, or with different architectures. The subject-disjoint split supports a claim about unseen subjects in the UCI HAR population and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. We do not call it out-of-distribution or domain generalisation beyond this scope. Mechanisms such as attention stability were not measured; we mention them only as untested candidate explanations. The study does not isolate the effect of the constraint from computational overhead, as per-step cost was deliberately not held equal. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance. The registered power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter. If a CI crosses zero but lies below the worthwhile margin, we preserve its registered label and separately explain that it excludes gains of that target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model.

=== conclusion ===
This study found that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin for subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The registered decision for both primary and replication cohorts was inconclusive, with mean contrasts of 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]) and 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]) respectively. This outcome licenses the conclusion that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. It does not prove the mechanism is ineffective, only that this implementation did not improve accuracy under these conditions. Future work should test whether direct measurements of attention stability correlate with generalization or whether alternative consistency losses yield different results.

Related-work section:
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [38], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28].

This study positions itself against these themes by independently verifying the cross-layer consistency hypothesis in a subject-disjoint setting. While prior work explores cross-layer mechanisms for representation power or domain adaptation [15, 18], few isolate the effect of query weight alignment on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Unlike works that propose new architectures for specific tasks like segmentation or forecasting [23, 32], this experiment tests a specific regularization operator within a fixed architecture. The inconclusive results of related regularization tests, such as spectral entropy minimization, motivate this boundary test [3].

Abstract: Recently, there has been a surge of Transformer-based solutions for the long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) task. Specifically, on the basis of the cross-entropy loss function, we build the mean model by integrating the model parameters of the previous rounds and measure the consistency between the models by calculating the KL divergence between the features of the encoder output and the probability distribution of the decoder output of the mean model and the base model so as to impose regularization constraints on the solution space of the model. We conducted extensive experiments on machine translation tasks, and the results show that the BLEU score increased by 2.60 on average, demonstrating the effectiveness of DOCR in improving model performance and its complementary impacts with other regularization techniques.

Specifically, we impose consistency between predictions from cross-domain attention and self-attention modules to encourage similar distributions across domains in both the attention and output of the model, i.e., attention-level and output-level alignment. We also enforce consistency in attention maps between different augmented views to further strengthen the attention-based alignment. Combining these two components, CDAC mitigates the discrepancy in attention maps across domains and further boosts the performance of the transformer under unsupervised domain adaptation settings. Our method is evaluated on various widely used benchmarks and outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines, including GTAV-to-Cityscapes by 1.3 and 1.5 percent point (pp) and Synthia-to-Cityscapes by 0.6 pp and 2.9 pp when combining with two competitive Transformer-based backbones, respectively. We evaluate ABN on several image recognition tasks such as image classification, fine-grained recognition, and multiple facial attribute recognition. Experimental results indicate that ABN outperforms the baseline models on these image recognition tasks while generating an attention map for visual explanation. Our code is available.

This enables LPTM to perform similar to or better than domain-specific state-of-art model when fine-tuned to different downstream time-series analysis tasks and under zero-shot settings.
