To overcome the above limitations, this paper proposes a novel end-to-end learning model, called cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network (CLFETNet), for remote sensing scene classification. Firstly, we utilize the FPN to extract multi-scale features and design a fine feature aggregation module (RFA) to integrate complementary information from different layers to obtain more reliable and accurate features. Second, the efficient frequency transformer (EFT) is proposed to deeply mine global information, local spatial features, and edge detail information. Finally, the graph-aware fusion (GAF) module is proposed to model the relationships among […abstract truncated here]

[24] Shape analysis for time series
Abstract: Analyzing inter-individual variability of physiological functions is particularly appealing in medical and biological contexts to describe or quantify health conditions. Once the deformations and the reference time series are learned, the vector representations of individual time series are given by the parametrization of their corresponding deformation. At the crossroads between URL for time series and shape analysis, the proposed algorithm handles irregularly sampled multivariate time series of variable lengths and provides shape-based representations of temporal data.In this work, we establish a representation theorem for the graph of a time series and derive its consequences on the LDDMM framework. By constraining features from the same location to be closer than those from different ones, it implicitly ensures the result to take content from the source. However, previous work uses the features from random locations to impose the constraint, which may not be appropriate since some locations contain less information of source domain. Moreover, the feature itself does not reflect the relation with others. This paper deals with these problems by intentionally selecting significant anchor points for contrastive learning. We design a query-selected attention (QS-Attn) module, which compares feature distances in the source domain, giving an attention matrix with a probability distribution in each row. Then we select queries according to their measurement of significance, computed from the distribution. The selected ones are regarded as anchors for contrastive loss. At the same time, the reduced attention matrix is employed to route features in both domains, so that source relations maintain in the synthesis. Abstract: The discovery of knowledge by analyzing time series is an important field of research. There are several approaches which make use of the granger causality or the cross correlation in order to analyze the influence of time series on each other. In this paper we extend the idea of mutual influence and present FCSETS (Fuzzy Clustering Stability Evaluation of Time Series), a new approach which makes use of the membership degree produced by the fuzzy c-means (FCM) algorithm. We first cluster time series per timestamp and then compare the relative assignment agreement (introduced by Eyke Hüllermeier and Maria Rifqi) of all subsequences. This leads us to a stability score for every time series which itself can be used to evaluate single time series in the data set. It is then used to rate the stability of the entire clustering. The stability score of a time series is higher the more the time series sticks to its peers over time. This not only reveals a new idea of mutual time series impact but also enables the identification of an optimal amount of clusters per timestamp. We applied our model on different data, such as financial, country related economy and generated data, and present the results.

[28] An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks

Conducted on a variety of applications, the study yields significant findings about spatial attention in deep networks, some of which run counter to conventional understanding. For example, we find that the query and key content comparison in Transformer attention is negligible for self-attention, but vital for encoder-decoder attention. A proper combination of deformable convolution with key content only saliency achieves the best accuracy-efficiency tradeoff in self-attention. Our results suggest that there exists much room for improvement in the design of attention mechanisms.

The second improves the eﬃciency of cross-encoders by deactivating the attention between various sub-sequences, such as between query and document tokens. The third improves the eﬀectiveness of cross-encoders by allowing multiple documents to attend to one another via an additional interaction token. Our analyses show that our attention adaptations lead to substantial eﬀectiveness and eﬃciency improvements. The ﬁrst is LightningIR, a framework that uniﬁes the implementation of various model variants, and the second is Rank-DistiLLM, a set of high-quality distillation datasets for ﬁne-tuning. Abstract: The computational burden of attention in long-context language models has motivated two largely independent lines of work: sparse attention mechanisms that reduce complexity by attending to selected tokens, and gated attention variants that improve training sta-bility while mitigating the attention sink phenomenon. GSA incorporates a gated lightning indexer with sigmoid activations that produce bounded, interpretable selection scores, an adaptive sparsity controller that modulates the number of attended tokens based on local uncertainty, and dual gating at the value and output stages. We establish theoretical foundations for the approach, including complexity analysis, expressiveness results, and convergence guarantees. In experiments with 1.7B parameter models trained on 400B tokens, GSA matches the efficiency of sparse-only baselines (12-16x speedup at 128K context) while achieving the quality gains associated with gated attention: perplexity improves from 6.03 to 5.70, RULER scores at 128K context nearly double, and attention to the first token, a proxy for attention sinks, drops from 47% to under 4%. Training stability improves markedly, with loss spikes reduced by 98%.

[31] Time-Series Forecasting
Abstract: From the author of the bestselling "Analysis of Time Series," Time-Series Forecasting offers a comprehensive, up-to-date review of forecasting methods. It provides a summary of time-series modelling procedures, followed by a brief catalogue of many different time-series forecasting methods, ranging from ad-hoc methods through ARIMA and state-space

[32] Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning
Abstract: The recent breakthrough of Transformers in deep learning has drawn significant attention of the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies. However, like other deep learning models, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding, generalization challenges, and data shift issues for the domains with limited data. Additionally, addressing the issue of catastrophic forgetting, where models forget previously learned information when exposed to new data, is another critical aspect that requires attention in enhancing the robustness of Transformers for time series tasks. To address these limitations, in this paper, we pre-train the time series Transformer model on a source domain with sufficient data and fine-tune it on the target domain with limited data. We introduce the \emph{One-step fine-tuning} approach, adding some percentage of source domain data to the target domains, providing the model with diverse time series instances. We then fine-tune the pre-trained model using a gradual unfreezing technique. This helps enhance the model's performance in time series prediction for domains with limited data. Extensive experimental results on two real-world datasets show that our approach improves over the state-of-the-art baselines by 4.35% and 11.54% for indoor temperature and wind power prediction, respectively.

Abstract: Attention mechanisms, especially self-attention, have played an increasingly important role in deep feature representation for visual tasks. However, self-attention has quadratic complexity and ignores potential correlation between different samples. This article proposes a novel attention mechanism which we call external attention, based on two external, small, learnable, shared memories, which can be implemented easily by simply using two cascaded linear layers and two normalization layers; it conveniently replaces self-attention in existing popular architectures. External attention has linear complexity and implicitly considers the correlations between all data samples. We further incorporate the multi-head mechanism into external attention to provide an all-MLP architecture, external attention MLP (EAMLP), for image classification. Extensive experiments on image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, image generation, and point cloud analysis reveal that our method provides results comparable or superior to the self-attention mechanism and some of its variants, with much lower computational and memory costs.

[34] Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency
Abstract: Activation engineering enables precise control over Large Language Models (LLMs) without the computational cost of fine-tuning. However, existing methods deriving vectors from static activation differences are susceptible to high-dimensional noise and layer-wise semantic drift, often capturing spurious correlations rather than the target intent. To address this, we propose Global Evolutionary Refined Steering (GER-steer), a training-free framework that grounded in the geometric stability of the network's representation evolution. GER-steer exploits this global signal to rectify raw steering vectors, effectively decoupling robust semantic intent from orthogonal artifacts. Extensive evaluations confirm that GER-steer consistently outperforms baselines, delivering superior efficacy and generalization without layer-specific tuning, establishing a universal solution for reliable model alignment.

We first lift PT into the Spatial-Temporal Probabilistic Transformer (ST-PT) to repair PT's missing channel axis and weak per-step semantics, and adopt ST-PT as a shared cornerstone backbone. We then identify three distinct properties that PT/ST-PT offers as a factor-graph model and derive three Research Questions, one per property, that probe how each property can be exploited in time series: RQ1. The graph topology and potentials are direct programmable primitives. Can this be used to inject symbolic time-series priors into ST-PT through structural graph modifications, especially under data scarcity and noise? RQ2. The CRF's factor matrices are the operator's potentials. Can an external condition program these factor matrices on a per-sample basis, so that conditional generation becomes structural rather than feature-level modulation of a fixed one? RQ3. [36] Research on sentiment analysis model improved based on Transformer attention mechanism
Abstract: In response to the limitations of traditional sentiment analysis models, this paper proposes an improved sentiment analysis model based on Transformer attention mechanism. This model enhances contextual semantic modeling capability by optimizing self attention and multi head attention mechanisms; Increase the number of multi head attention heads in the BERT architecture from 12 to 16 to capture multi-level emotional features; Introducing dynamic position encoding to enhance modeling of long-distance dependencies. At the same time, adjusting the learning rate to 3e-5 and combining it with data augmentation can improve the stability and generalization ability of the model. The experiment on the 33396 McDonald's review dataset showed that the accuracy, recall, and F1 score of the improved model on the test set were 78%, 75%, and 76.5%, respectively; Improved to 85%, 82%, and 83.5%. This model effectively handles multidimensional emotional expression and domain specific language. Although its interpretability needs improvement, it provides a new path for the field of sentiment analysis and has important value in scenarios such as public opinion monitoring.

We introduce Depth-Attention, which performs this selection inside the attention module itself: before a layer attends over the sequence, its query attends over the keys of earlier layers at the same token position and mixes their values into the value that self-attention then reads. Because Depth-Attention reuses the standard attention queries, keys, and value-cache slots, storing depth-mixed values in place of the original values, it adds no parameters and introduces no persistent inference state beyond the standard key-value cache--the same cache size as a vanilla decoder and less than hidden-state-based cross-layer methods. On Qwen3-style decoders at 1.5B and 3B parameters, Depth-Attention attains the lowest perplexity and the highest average downstream accuracy, improving over the vanilla Transformer by up to 2.3 accuracy points and surpassing strong cross-layer baselines in perplexity and average accuracy, while adding under 0.01% extra arithmetic FLOPs and no additional persistent inference state. [38] Transformers in Time Series: A Survey
Abstract: Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications. In this paper, we systematically review Transformer schemes for time series modeling by highlighting their strengths as well as limitations. In particular, we examine the development of time series Transformers in two perspectives. From the perspective of network structure, we summarize the adaptations and modifications that have been made to Transformers in order to accommodate the challenges in time series analysis. From the perspective of applications, we categorize time series Transformers based on common tasks including forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification. Empirically, we perform robust analysis, model size analysis, and seasonal-trend decomposition analysis to study how Transformers perform in time series. Finally, we discuss and suggest future directions to provide useful research guidance. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first work to comprehensively and systematically summarize the recent advances of Transformers for modeling time series data. We hope this survey will ignite further research interests in time series Transformers.

[39] Cross-view Transformers for real-time Map-view Semantic Segmentation
Abstract: We present cross-view transformers, an efficient attention-based model for map-view semantic segmentation from multiple cameras. Our architecture implicitly learns a mapping from individual camera views into a canonical map-view representation using a camera-aware cross-view attention mechanism. Each camera uses positional embeddings that depend on its intrinsic and extrinsic calibration. These embeddings allow a transformer to learn the mapping across different views without ever explicitly modeling it geometrically. The architecture consists of a convolutional image encoder for each view and cross-view transformer layers to infer a map-view semantic segmentation. Our model is simple, easily parallelizable, and runs in real-time. The presented architecture performs at state-of-the-art on the nuScenes dataset, with 4x faster inference speeds. Code is available at https://github.com/bradyz/cross_view_transformers.

[41] A survey of transformers
Abstract: Transformers have achieved great success in many artificial intelligence fields, such as natural language processing, computer vision, and audio processing. Therefore, it is natural to attract lots of interest from academic and industry researchers. Up to the present, a great variety of Transformer variants (a.k.a. X-formers) have been proposed, however, a systematic and comprehensive literature review on these Transformer variants is still missing. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive review of various X-formers. We first briefly introduce the vanilla Transformer and then propose a new taxonomy of X-formers. Next, we introduce the various X-formers from three perspectives: architectural modification, pre-training, and applications. Finally, we outline some potential directions for future research.

We restore these priors in STructure-AwaRe (STAR) Set Transformer by adding parameter-efficient soft attention biases: a temporal locality penalty $-|Δt|/τ$ with learnable timescales and a variable-type affinity $B_{s_i,s_j}$ from a learned feature-compatibility matrix. We benchmark 10 depth-wise fusion schedules (Fig.2). On three ICU prediction tasks, STAR-Set achieves AUC/APR of 0.7158/0.0026 (CPR), 0.9164/0.2033 (mortality), and 0.8373/0.1258 (vasopressor use), outperforming regular-grid, event-time grid, and prior set baselines. Learned $τ$ and $B$ provide interpretable summaries of temporal context and variable interactions, offering a practical plug-in for context-informed time-series models.

Introduction: Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [38]. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications [38]. However, recent work questions the validity of this research line, noting that permutation-invariant self-attention mechanisms may result in temporal information loss compared to simpler linear models [5]. Despite this debate, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [32]. Addressing these limitations often involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones, or employing domain adaptation techniques [22, 32].

A critical open problem is identifying what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Specifically, it remains unclear whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks. Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization [38, 5]. To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms [17, 18]. For instance, deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data, motivating regularization strategies [17]. Cross-layer interactions are explored to strengthen layer interactions or apply consistency to activation engineering [15, 34]. However, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization.

This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. We conduct a calibrated testbed experiment using the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block query projection weights during training. We compare the proposed condition against a baseline control arm and an active negative control.

Our contributions are as follows:
- We execute a preregistered replication study testing cross-layer query consistency loss in a subject-disjoint time-series setting.
- We report results from both a primary cohort and a confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, adhering to registered decision rules.
- We provide empirical evidence regarding the efficacy of weight alignment across depth for generalization in this specific architecture and data regime.

The preregistered prediction is: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean paired contrast in the hypothesised direction H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

Discussion: The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not yield a statistically significant or practically worthwhile improvement in subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. The registered decision for both the primary and replication cohorts was inconclusive. The measured contrast in the primary cohort was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]), and in the replication cohort was 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). These intervals include zero and lie below the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. This outcome suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

This design establishes the effect of the specific operator on held-out accuracy but does not establish the mechanism. Mechanistic rationales such as attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization are hypotheses, not measured findings. We name the directly recorded outcomes, and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. An alternative explanation is that the regularization coefficient was too small to influence the optimization trajectory meaningfully, or that the task does not benefit from query weight similarity across depth. The negative control, which penalized deviation from a random matrix, also did not significantly differ from the baseline, suggesting generic regularization of this form may not aid generalization in this setting.

The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort adds confidence that the primary result was not a false positive due to seed selection. Both cohorts produced inconclusive decisions with overlapping confidence intervals. This consistency across 86 total seeds strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if it exists, is smaller than the registered margin. This finding stands against specific cited papers that propose cross-layer mechanisms for representation power [15, 34]. While those works report improvements in classification or steering tasks, the intervention, task, data regime or evaluation differ. For example, *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention* improves accuracy on image classification tasks [15], which may not transfer to subject-disjoint time-series data. Similarly, *Global Evolutionary Steering* applies consistency to activation engineering in language models [34], a different modality and intervention type.

The results are consistent with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which found inconclusive results for spectral regularization in a similar setting [3]. Both studies suggest that weight geometry constraints may not robustly improve generalization in finite-width time-series transformers. Conversely, *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting [17], but our results do not confirm that this specific consistency loss mitigates that risk in the subject-disjoint UCI HAR setting. Future work would settle the question by testing larger coefficients, different layers, or direct measurements of attention map stability.

Conclusion: This study found that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin for subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The registered decision for both primary and replication cohorts was inconclusive, with mean contrasts of 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]) and 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]) respectively. This outcome licenses the conclusion that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. It does not prove the mechanism is ineffective, only that this implementation did not improve accuracy under these conditions. Future work should test whether direct measurements of attention stability correlate with generalization or whether alternative consistency losses yield different results.

Paper to review:
Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The registered decision for both cohorts was inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [38], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28].

This study positions itself against these themes by independently verifying the cross-layer consistency hypothesis in a subject-disjoint setting. While prior work explores cross-layer mechanisms for representation power or domain adaptation [15, 18], few isolate the effect of query weight alignment on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Unlike works that propose new architectures for specific tasks like segmentation or forecasting [23, 32], this experiment tests a specific regularization operator within a fixed architecture. The inconclusive results of related regularization tests, such as spectral entropy minimization, motivate this boundary test [3].
Method: The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator applied to the query projection weights of the second attention block. The hypothesis posits that enforcing consistency between the query weights of the first and second blocks improves generalization. The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step, adding a term to the classification objective inside the autograd graph. The specification is fixed before any compute was spent. The scope covers the full weight matrix of shape [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space. The ordering of operations is element-wise subtraction then sum, which is order-invariant due to commutativity of addition. There is no normalization; the raw Frobenius norm squared is scaled by a fixed coefficient of 0.01. Numerical safeguards rely on this coefficient to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective.

The algorithm retrieves reference weights from the first block's query projection and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. It computes the element-wise difference between the target weights (block 1) and the reference weights. The squared elements are summed over all elements to produce a raw loss, which is then multiplied by the consistency coefficient. This loss term is stored for harness aggregation and returned for addition to the training objective. The invariants hold throughout: reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients, the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only, and the coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

The control arm is defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

The first negative control adds a loss term penalizing difference between the target weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This condition tests whether the mere presence of a regularization term, rather than the specific cross-layer alignment, drives any observed effects. The proposed condition is the server-bound target where the operator applies Frobenius norm consistency regularization to the second block's query weights.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Experimental setup: **Design Justification for Subject-Disjoint Split.** The experiment uses the official subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset. This design answers the question of generalization to unseen subjects, which a random split would not. A random split allows windows from the same subject to appear in both training and testing, inflating accuracy estimates by capturing subject-specific idiosyncrasies rather than activity patterns. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. Therefore, the subject-disjoint split is necessary to test the hypothesis regarding architectural inductive biases for cross-subject generalization.

**Pairing Conditions by Seed.** Both the proposed condition and the baseline are trained from the same paired seed. The dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. This pairing reduces variance in the paired contrast by controlling for initialization and data ordering effects. The analysis uses paired statistics to detect the effect of the intervention against the noise of stochastic training. The seed budget consists of 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. Reporting both cohorts separately allows us to distinguish training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations; the confirmatory cohort is never an independent replication of the dataset, but it is an independent replication of the training process.

**Negative Control Purpose.** The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix. This active condition tests the alternative explanation that any regularization term, regardless of its semantic content, improves generalization by acting as a regularizer. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, it suggests the cross-layer relationship is specific and meaningful. If both perform similarly, the effect may be. This experiment did not test whether this was due to generic regularization. The baseline is the inert comparator. The design does not isolate the effect of the constraint from computational overhead, as per-step cost was deliberately not held equal. The recorded activity confirms the harness executed the operator in the proposed and negative control conditions and remained inert in the baseline.

**Analysis Plan.** The primary outcome is held-out classification accuracy. The registered decision rule requires the lower confidence bound of the paired contrast to exceed the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The planning target power was 90% with a planning SD of 0.0250196. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Registered conditions.

Add loss term that applies Frobenius norm consistency regularization to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Baseline: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. Results: We report results for the primary and confirmatory replication cohorts separately. In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition mean was 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]). The baseline condition mean was 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The first negative control mean was 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 2 displays these means with error bars. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 3 plots the paired mean difference with the registered worthwhile threshold. The 95% CI includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition mean was 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]). The baseline condition mean was 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). The first negative control mean was 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9082]). Figure 5 displays these means. The proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 6 plots the paired mean difference. The 95% CI includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

Figure 4 and Figure 7 show the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. The curves for the proposed, baseline, and negative control conditions track closely throughout training, with no condition consistently separating from the others. The variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive in both cohorts. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks. The registered condition descriptions and executed activation records confirm the operator acted in the proposed and negative control conditions and remained inert in the baseline.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This study found that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin for subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The registered decision for both primary and replication cohorts was inconclusive, with mean contrasts of 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]) and 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]) respectively. This outcome licenses the conclusion that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. It does not prove the mechanism is ineffective, only that this implementation did not improve accuracy under these conditions. Future work should test whether direct measurements of attention stability correlate with generalization or whether alternative consistency losses yield different results.
Discussion: The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not yield a statistically significant or practically worthwhile improvement in subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. The registered decision for both the primary and replication cohorts was inconclusive. The measured contrast in the primary cohort was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]), and in the replication cohort was 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). These intervals include zero and lie below the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. This outcome suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

This design establishes the effect of the specific operator on held-out accuracy but does not establish the mechanism. Mechanistic rationales such as attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization are hypotheses, not measured findings. We name the directly recorded outcomes, and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. An alternative explanation is that the regularization coefficient was too small to influence the optimization trajectory meaningfully, or that the task does not benefit from query weight similarity across depth. The negative control, which penalized deviation from a random matrix, also did not significantly differ from the baseline, suggesting generic regularization of this form may not aid generalization in this setting.

The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort adds confidence that the primary result was not a false positive due to seed selection. Both cohorts produced inconclusive decisions with overlapping confidence intervals. This consistency across 86 total seeds strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if it exists, is smaller than the registered margin. This finding stands against specific cited papers that propose cross-layer mechanisms for representation power [15, 34]. While those works report improvements in classification or steering tasks, the intervention, task, data regime or evaluation differ. For example, *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention* improves accuracy on image classification tasks [15], which may not transfer to subject-disjoint time-series data. Similarly, *Global Evolutionary Steering* applies consistency to activation engineering in language models [34], a different modality and intervention type.

The results are consistent with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which found inconclusive results for spectral regularization in a similar setting [3]. Both studies suggest that weight geometry constraints may not robustly improve generalization in finite-width time-series transformers. REGISTERED OPERATOR (including gradient handling; do not infer that detaching one loss term freezes ordinary task-loss learning):
Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer*. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it.

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance.

=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The registered decisions are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [36]. However, their effectiveness and generalization capabilities, particularly across subjects with different movement styles and sensor characteristics, remain subjects of debate [5]. While architectural modifications such as consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms have been proposed to address stability and generalization [17, 18], independent verification regarding whether these biases improve subject-disjoint generalization is lacking. Specifically, it is unclear whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections stabilizes attention across depth to benefit generalization in time-series transformers [1].

This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. The open problem this targets is identifying what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects. Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

This paper reports the results of a preregistered experiment testing the hypothesis that the intervention yields higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. We contribute the following:
- We execute a calibrated testbed with 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds to evaluate cross-layer query consistency.
- We report exact held-out classification accuracy means, 95% confidence intervals, and registered decisions for both cohorts separately.
- We provide an independent verification of whether cross-layer consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in this regime.

The preregistered prediction is that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report the outcomes honestly against this prediction, labeling any unforeseen finding as exploratory.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [36], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [30].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [32]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [31]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [35]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [11], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [21], and *A survey of transformers* [39] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [26]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific cross-layer consistency intervention in a subject-disjoint time-series setting, distinct from domain adaptation or visual tasks.

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights during training. The hypothesis is that regularizing deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights improves subject-disjoint generalization by stabilizing attention patterns across depth. The operator is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight, with reference weights retrieved from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight. These reference weights are detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0, ensuring the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The loss term is computed as the squared element-wise difference scaled by a fixed coefficient of 0.01, added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph.

The registered comparator is the baseline control arm, which executes identical code paths but returns a zero loss term. This design isolates the effect of the constraint from the computational graph structure, though per-step cost was deliberately not held equal between the arms. The first negative control penalizes the difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This active condition destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute, testing whether any regularization effect arises from the loss term structure rather than the specific cross-layer alignment.

The operator specification is fixed before any compute was spent. Scope covers the full weight matrix treated as flat parameter space. Applied during loss computation of every optimization step, the operator's term is added to the classification objective. Ordering is element-wise subtraction then sum, invariant due to commutativity. No normalization is applied; raw Frobenius norm squared is scaled by the fixed coefficient. Numerical safeguards include the coefficient preventing the loss term from dominating the classification objective. Invariants hold throughout: reference weights from block 0 are detached, the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only, and the coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds. The control arm leaves the registered target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, adding nothing to the training objective.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experimental design uses a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization across unseen subjects, which a random split would not address. The UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset provides an official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows, ensuring evaluation occurs on people who appear nowhere in training. This supports a claim about unseen subjects, not a different corpus or deployment distribution. Pairing conditions by seed controls for variance due to initialization and data ordering, allowing paired contrasts to detect smaller effects than independent samples would.

The seed budget comprises 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. This allows separate reporting of primary and replication cohorts, distinguishing training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects. The confirmatory cohort is never an independent replication of the dataset, but it tests stability across fresh sampling. Each negative control's intended alternative explanation is tested by its observed contrast: the first negative control tests whether the loss term structure alone drives effects, while the baseline tests the inert comparator. The analysis reports means with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for each condition and cohort. Per-step computational cost was deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study, so we do not claim the design isolates the effect of the constraint from computational overhead.

=== results ===
We report results for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately, stating each preregistered decision. In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), compared to 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]) for the baseline (Figure 1). The hypothesis-positive paired contrast was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06) (Figure 2). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The preregistered decision is inconclusive. The first negative control achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]), showing no substantial deviation from the baseline. Training curves for all conditions coincide closely over steps (Figure 3).

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]), compared to 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]) for the baseline (Figure 4). The hypothesis-positive paired contrast was 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15) (Figure 5). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile margin. The preregistered decision is inconclusive. The first negative control achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9082]). Training curves again show close alignment across conditions (Figure 6). Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. Neither cohort provides evidence that the intervention exceeds the worthwhile margin under the stated uncertainty model.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that both preregistered decisions are inconclusive, with confidence intervals in both cohorts including zero and failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. This outcome suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, though the intervals do not license a claim that no effect exists. The measured contrast in the primary cohort was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]), and in the replication cohort 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). These results are consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, as the intervention did not improve generalization over the baseline.

This design does not establish the mechanism by which the operator acts, as attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization were not measured. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses; the directly recorded outcomes are accuracy contrasts. An alternative explanation for the null result is that the coefficient of 0.01 was insufficient to influence the optimization trajectory meaningfully, or that the detachment of reference weights prevented the necessary gradient flow for alignment. The independent replication cohort adds stability to the estimate but fails to provide an independent replication on new datasets or architectures, as it uses the same held-out split.

Comparing these findings to specific cited papers, the inconclusive result aligns with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found null results for spectral regularization in this setting [3]. It contrasts with *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which reported improvements in machine translation tasks, suggesting the effect may be task-dependent [17]. The result is not comparable to *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation*, as that work addresses domain adaptation in vision, not subject-disjoint time-series classification [18]. Future work would settle the question by testing different coefficients, architectures, or datasets where attention stability is more critical.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether the intervention works on different corpora, sensors, tasks, or deployment distributions, as evaluation was limited to the UCI HAR subject-disjoint split. Mechanisms such as attention stability or layer-specific adaptation were not measured, so claims about them remain untested hypotheses. The confirmatory cohort is not an independent replication of the dataset, limiting generalization claims to this specific data regime. Per-step computational cost was not held equal, so we cannot isolate the effect of the constraint from overhead. The registered power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

=== conclusion ===
We found that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin in either the primary or replication cohorts. The measured outcomes license the conclusion that the registered decisions are inconclusive, with confidence intervals including zero. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence does not support adopting the intervention for subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. What would settle the question next is testing whether different regularization coefficients or architectures yield measurable gains, or whether attention stability can be directly measured to correlate with accuracy.

REGISTERED OPERATOR (including gradient handling; do not infer that detaching one loss term freezes ordinary task-loss learning):
Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer*. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it.
