=== abstract ===
Transformers are prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [36]. However, their effectiveness and generalization capabilities in this domain remain uncertain [5]. Specific applications range from biosignal data augmentation [20] to representing multivariate series as graphs [14], yet tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including generalization challenges and data shift issues [30]. A critical open problem is identifying what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting.

Current literature lacks independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. While consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms have been proposed to address stability and generalization [17, 18], and cross-layer interactions have been explored to strengthen layer interactions [15, 32], the specific impact of cross-layer query consistency on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers remains unsettled. This work addresses the lack of independent verification, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling.

This paper reports a rigorous experiment testing whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization. We manipulate the query projection weights of the deeper transformer block, regularizing them toward the shallower block's weights, and measure the outcome via held-out classification accuracy. We do not measure attention patterns directly; rather, we test the hypothesis that weight consistency yields accuracy gains.

- We report a preregistered replication of the cross-layer query consistency loss intervention on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset using a subject-disjoint split.
- We provide separate analyses for a primary cohort and a confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, adhering to registered decision thresholds.
- We evaluate the intervention against a baseline and a negative control to isolate the effect of meaningful cross-layer relationships from compute-matched penalties.

The preregistered prediction states that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Specifically, we predict the lower confidence bound of the accuracy difference will exceed this margin. This study tests whether this prediction holds under fresh sampling in the same testbed.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [36], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [30]. These works collectively establish that while transformers are widely applied, their generalization mechanisms in time-series domains require further validation.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [32]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2]. These studies suggest that regularization strategies are actively investigated, but their efficacy varies by task and implementation.

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [31]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [35]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [11], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [21], and *A survey of transformers* [39] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [26]. This body of work underscores that attention modifications are common, yet their impact on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers remains an open empirical question. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight-regularization hypothesis in a controlled, subject-disjoint setting, distinguishing our measured accuracy outcomes from unmeasured attention constructs.

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between the query projection weights of the first and second transformer blocks. The hypothesis is that regularizing `blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight` toward `blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight` improves subject-disjoint generalization as measured by held-out classification accuracy. This operator expresses the hypothesis by directly penalizing divergence between deeper and shallower layer weights, operationalizing the concept of cross-layer stability through weight alignment rather than attention-map similarity.

The operator is applied during the loss computation of every optimization step. It retrieves the reference weights from `model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight` and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients from flowing to block 0. It then computes the element-wise difference between the target weights (`blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight`) and the reference weights. The squared elements are summed to produce a raw loss, which is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01. This loss term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, ensuring the combined objective is differentiated. The specification ensures that the reference weights receive no gradients, while the loss term remains differentiable with respect to the target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds to maintain consistency.

The registered comparator is the baseline condition, which executes the identical code path but returns a zero loss term. This control arm leaves the registered target parameter unchanged, leaves that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and adds nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. This design ensures that any observed contrast in accuracy is attributable to the presence of the consistency loss term, not to implementation artifacts or data ordering differences. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms.

A first negative control penalizes the difference between `blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight` and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This condition destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the compute cost of the proposed condition. If the proposed condition outperforms the baseline but not the negative control, it would suggest that the penalty term itself, rather than the specific cross-layer alignment, drives any observed effect. The method distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations; the confirmatory cohort is never an independent replication of the dataset or architecture, but rather a replication of the sampling process within the same testbed.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 on the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K). The data consists of raw inertial signals in 128-timestep windows over 9 channels, with an official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear(9,64) input projection, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contains LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connections, and a feed-forward network (Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64)). Training proceeds for 12 epochs with batch size 128 using SGD(lr=0.05, momentum=0.9). Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on the 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects.

**Design Justification**. The subject-disjoint split answers the question of generalization to new subjects, which a random split would not. A random split would allow the model to memorize subject-specific movement styles, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to test robustness to distribution shift across individuals. Pairing conditions by seed controls for variance introduced by initialization and data ordering, ensuring that the paired contrast isolates the intervention's effect. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds provides sufficient power to detect effects exceeding the registered margin, distinguishing zero-null detection from exceeding the margin.

**Negative Controls**. The first negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any loss penalty, regardless of its target, might regularize the model simply by adding noise or constraint to the optimization trajectory. Its observed contrast supports the claim that the specific cross-layer relationship is necessary if the proposed condition outperforms it. The baseline control ensures the harness is unbiased and the implementation correct, though its outcome cannot prove the absence of implementation bias alone. The analysis separates the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts to verify stability across fresh sampling, without pooling them or calling a primary-only result replicated.

=== results ===
We report results for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately, stating each preregistered decision. Table 1 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline, and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Figure 2 visualizes these means with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, showing the proposed condition against the baseline. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The negative control 1 achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for these conditions, illustrating that learning curves coincide closely across conditions.

Table 2 reports the outcome contrast for the primary cohort. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 3 plots the paired mean difference over 43 seeds with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The zero line marks no directional effect, and the green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion. The confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the threshold. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, Table 4 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the three conditions. Figure 5 visualizes these means with error bars. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]), the baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]), and the negative control 1 achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9082]). Figure 7 shows the learning curves for the replication cohort, which again show close alignment between conditions.

Table 3 reports the outcome contrast for the replication cohort. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 6 plots the paired mean difference with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. Neither cohort provides evidence that the intervention exceeds the margin.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency via weight regularization did not yield robust accuracy gains in this subject-disjoint time-series setting. Both the primary and replication cohorts produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. This outcome suggests that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class, rather than cross-layer weight stability. The measured outcome licenses a choice against this intervention for someone choosing between these methods in the UCI HAR setting, as it does not demonstrate a reliable benefit over standard training.

**Mechanism and Alternatives**. The hypothesis posited that regularizing deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights improves generalization by stabilizing attention patterns across depth. However, we measured only held-out classification accuracy, not attention stability. An alternative explanation is that the penalty term constrains the optimization trajectory in a way that does not align with the task's generalization requirements. The negative control, which penalized deviation from a random matrix, performed similarly to the baseline, suggesting that the compute cost of the penalty itself is not the driver of the null result. The null result does not prove that attention patterns were unstable; it only indicates that this specific weight regularization did not improve accuracy.

**Replication Cohort**. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds stability to the estimate but does not constitute an independent replication on new datasets or architectures, as it uses the same held-out split within the uci_har_small_transformer_v1 testbed. The replication cohort failed to resolve the inconclusive primary result, with a slightly larger point estimate (0.00196 vs 0.000773) but still nonsignificant confidence intervals. This consistency across cohorts strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if any, is below the worthwhile margin in this setting.

**Relation to Literature**. These findings align with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found inconclusive results for weight-spectrum regularization in this regime [3]. They contrast with *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which reported gains on machine translation tasks [17], suggesting that consistency benefits may be task-dependent. The results are not comparable to *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* in terms of positive findings, as that study also reported inconclusive results [1]. The null result indicates that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, clarifying the mechanistic role of weight spectra and layer interactions in finite-width networks. Future work would need to settle the question by testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks with different architectures or data regimes.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell us whether cross-layer consistency improves generalization in datasets with different temporal characteristics, sensor modalities, or subject variability. The subject-disjoint split supports a claim about unseen subjects within the UCI HAR population, but is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task, or deployment distribution. We did not measure attention patterns directly, so we cannot confirm whether the intervention stabilized attention as hypothesized. The margin was derived from calibration noise, which reflects measurement precision but does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient, and we did not measure the magnitude of the penalty relative to the task loss. The confirmatory cohort is not an independent replication of the dataset or architecture, limiting generalizability beyond this testbed.

=== conclusion ===
This study found that enforcing cross-layer query consistency in transformer weights did not improve subject-disjoint generalization as measured by held-out classification accuracy. Both primary and replication cohorts yielded inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered margin. The measured outcome licenses a decision against adopting this intervention for UCI HAR subject-disjoint tasks, as it offers no demonstrated accuracy benefit over standard training. The findings suggest that layer-specific adaptation may be essential for this architecture class. Future work should test whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks to settle the question of its broader utility.

PAPER-QUALITY SKILLS (only those relevant to this task are loaded; everything the system can decide for itself is checked, not asked for):
[claim-language] Claim what the evidence carries, and no more. Keep four registers apart and make it obvious which one a sentence is in: a RESULT states a measured quantity; an INTERPRETATION says what it may mean and is marked as such ('suggests', 'is consistent with'); a LIMITATION says what this design cannot tell anyone; FUTURE WORK proposes what would settle the question, and is the only register in which a wider setting may appear. Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

=== abstract ===
Transformers are prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [36]. However, their effectiveness and generalization capabilities in this domain remain uncertain [5]. Specific applications range from biosignal data augmentation [20] to representing multivariate series as graphs [14], yet tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including generalization challenges and data shift issues [30]. A critical open problem is identifying what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting.

Current literature lacks independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. While consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms have been proposed to address stability and generalization [17, 18], and cross-layer interactions have been explored to strengthen layer interactions [15, 32], the specific impact of cross-layer query consistency on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers remains unsettled. This work addresses the lack of independent verification, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling.

This paper reports a rigorous experiment testing whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization. We manipulate the query projection weights of the deeper transformer block, regularizing them toward the shallower block's weights, and measure the outcome via held-out classification accuracy. We do not measure attention patterns directly; rather, we test the hypothesis that weight consistency yields accuracy gains.

- We report a preregistered replication of the cross-layer query consistency loss intervention on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset using a subject-disjoint split.
- We provide separate analyses for a primary cohort and a confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, adhering to registered decision thresholds.
- We evaluate the intervention against a baseline and a negative control to isolate the effect of meaningful cross-layer relationships from compute-matched penalties.

The preregistered prediction states that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Specifically, we predict the lower confidence bound of the accuracy difference will exceed this margin. This study tests whether this prediction holds under fresh sampling in the same testbed.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [36], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [30]. These works collectively establish that while transformers are widely applied, their generalization mechanisms in time-series domains require further validation.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [32]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2]. These studies suggest that regularization strategies are actively investigated, but their efficacy varies by task and implementation.

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [31]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [35]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [11], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [21], and *A survey of transformers* [39] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [26]. This body of work underscores that attention modifications are common, yet their impact on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers remains an open empirical question. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight-regularization hypothesis in a controlled, subject-disjoint setting, distinguishing our measured accuracy outcomes from unmeasured attention constructs.

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between the query projection weights of the first and second transformer blocks. The hypothesis is that regularizing `blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight` toward `blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight` improves subject-disjoint generalization as measured by held-out classification accuracy. This operator expresses the hypothesis by directly penalizing divergence between deeper and shallower layer weights, operationalizing the concept of cross-layer stability through weight alignment rather than attention-map similarity.

The operator is applied during the loss computation of every optimization step. It retrieves the reference weights from `model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight` and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients from flowing to block 0. It then computes the element-wise difference between the target weights (`blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight`) and the reference weights. The squared elements are summed to produce a raw loss, which is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01. This loss term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, ensuring the combined objective is differentiated. The specification ensures that the reference weights receive no gradients, while the loss term remains differentiable with respect to the target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds to maintain consistency.

The registered comparator is the baseline condition, which executes the identical code path but returns a zero loss term. This control arm leaves the registered target parameter unchanged, leaves that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and adds nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. This design ensures that any observed contrast in accuracy is attributable to the presence of the consistency loss term, not to implementation artifacts or data ordering differences. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering, and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms.

A first negative control penalizes the difference between `blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight` and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This condition destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching the compute cost of the proposed condition. If the proposed condition outperforms the baseline but not the negative control, it would suggest that the penalty term itself, rather than the specific cross-layer alignment, drives any observed effect. The method distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations; the confirmatory cohort is never an independent replication of the dataset or architecture, but rather a replication of the sampling process within the same testbed.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 on the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K). The data consists of raw inertial signals in 128-timestep windows over 9 channels, with an official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear(9,64) input projection, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contains LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connections, and a feed-forward network (Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64)). Training proceeds for 12 epochs with batch size 128 using SGD(lr=0.05, momentum=0.9). Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on the 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects.

**Design Justification**. The subject-disjoint split answers the question of generalization to new subjects, which a random split would not. A random split would allow the model to memorize subject-specific movement styles, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to test robustness to distribution shift across individuals. Pairing conditions by seed controls for variance introduced by initialization and data ordering, ensuring that the paired contrast isolates the intervention's effect. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds provides sufficient power to detect effects exceeding the registered margin, distinguishing zero-null detection from exceeding the margin.

**Negative Controls**. The first negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any loss penalty, regardless of its target, might regularize the model simply by adding noise or constraint to the optimization trajectory. Its observed contrast supports the claim that the specific cross-layer relationship is necessary if the proposed condition outperforms it. The baseline control ensures the harness is unbiased and the implementation correct, though its outcome cannot prove the absence of implementation bias alone. The analysis separates the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts to verify stability across fresh sampling, without pooling them or calling a primary-only result replicated.

=== results ===
We report results for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately, stating each preregistered decision. Table 1 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline, and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Figure 2 visualizes these means with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, showing the proposed condition against the baseline. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The negative control 1 achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for these conditions, illustrating that learning curves coincide closely across conditions.

Table 2 reports the outcome contrast for the primary cohort. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 3 plots the paired mean difference over 43 seeds with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The zero line marks no directional effect, and the green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion. The confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the threshold. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, Table 4 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the three conditions. Figure 5 visualizes these means with error bars. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]), the baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]), and the negative control 1 achieved 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9082]). Figure 7 shows the learning curves for the replication cohort, which again show close alignment between conditions.

Table 3 reports the outcome contrast for the replication cohort. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 6 plots the paired mean difference with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the registered worthwhile threshold. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. Neither cohort provides evidence that the intervention exceeds the margin.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency via weight regularization did not yield robust accuracy gains in this subject-disjoint time-series setting. Both the primary and replication cohorts produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. This outcome suggests that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class, rather than cross-layer weight stability. The measured outcome licenses a choice against this intervention for someone choosing between these methods in the UCI HAR setting, as it does not demonstrate a reliable benefit over standard training.

**Mechanism and Alternatives**. The hypothesis posited that regularizing deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights improves generalization by stabilizing attention patterns across depth. However, we measured only held-out classification accuracy, not attention stability. An alternative explanation is that the penalty term constrains the optimization trajectory in a way that does not align with the task's generalization requirements. The negative control, which penalized deviation from a random matrix, performed similarly to the baseline, suggesting that the compute cost of the penalty itself is not the driver of the null result. The null result does not prove that attention patterns were unstable; it only indicates that this specific weight regularization did not improve accuracy.

**Replication Cohort**. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds stability to the estimate but does not constitute an independent replication on new datasets or architectures, as it uses the same held-out split within the uci_har_small_transformer_v1 testbed. The replication cohort failed to resolve the inconclusive primary result, with a slightly larger point estimate (0.00196 vs 0.000773) but still nonsignificant confidence intervals. This consistency across cohorts strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if any, is below the worthwhile margin in this setting.

**Relation to Literature**. These findings align with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found inconclusive results for weight-spectrum regularization in this regime [3]. They contrast with *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which reported gains on machine translation tasks [17], suggesting that consistency benefits may be task-dependent. The results are not comparable to *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* in terms of positive findings, as that study also reported inconclusive results [1]. The null result indicates that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, clarifying the mechanistic role of weight spectra and layer interactions in finite-width networks. Future work would need to settle the question by testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks with different architectures or data regimes.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell us whether cross-layer consistency improves generalization in datasets with different temporal characteristics, sensor modalities, or subject variability. The subject-disjoint split supports a claim about unseen subjects within the UCI HAR population, but is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task, or deployment distribution. We did not measure attention patterns directly, so we cannot confirm whether the intervention stabilized attention as hypothesized. The margin was derived from calibration noise, which reflects measurement precision but does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient, and we did not measure the magnitude of the penalty relative to the task loss. The confirmatory cohort is not an independent replication of the dataset or architecture, limiting generalizability beyond this testbed.

=== conclusion ===
This study found that enforcing cross-layer query consistency in transformer weights did not improve subject-disjoint generalization as measured by held-out classification accuracy. Both primary and replication cohorts yielded inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered margin. The measured outcome licenses a decision against adopting this intervention for UCI HAR subject-disjoint tasks, as it offers no demonstrated accuracy benefit over standard training. The findings suggest that layer-specific adaptation may be essential for this architecture class. Future work should test whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks to settle the question of its broader utility.

payload.title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers

Related-work section:
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [20], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [11] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [7]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [16]. These works collectively establish that while transformers are widely applied, their generalization mechanisms in time-series domains require further validation.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [8], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2]. These studies suggest that regularization strategies are actively investigated, but their efficacy varies by task and implementation.

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [6], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [12], and *A survey of transformers* [21] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15]. This body of work underscores that attention modifications are common, yet their impact on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers remains an open empirical question. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight-regularization hypothesis in a controlled, subject-disjoint setting, distinguishing our measured accuracy outcomes from unmeasured attention constructs.

Cited papers and their abstracts:
[1] Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00133 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by -0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

[2] Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness
Abstract: [EDITORIAL NOTICE — RETRACTED: this paper carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it. Stated reason: The numerical outputs reported in this paper remain computationally reproducible: an independent re-run from the archived reproducibility bundle reproduced all eight aggregate metrics within tolerance. A post-publication audit of the artifact source found that the executed intervention did not implement the preregistered intervention. The preregistration committed to a multiplicative weight perturbation applied BEFORE the forward pass, an entropy term added to the training OBJECTIVE, and a noise scale learned by BACKPROPAGATION, with held-out evaluation on the clean weights. The experiment har. Its conclusions may not be relied on; cite it only with its status stated.] Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic training often fails to provide calibrated confidence under distribution shift. This study investigates whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We preregistered a hypothesis that entropy maximization would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the baseline, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the intervention across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results refuted the preregistered hypothesis in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by 0.04805 proportion (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002) relative to the baseline. The replication cohort confirmed this degradation with a contrast of -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Negative controls involving entropy minimization and fixed noise performed comparably to the deterministic baseline. These findings indicate that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over explicit entropy maximization for robustness tasks in this regime.

[3] Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning
Abstract: Regularization design for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. This study tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy compared to standard weight decay in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would exceed a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion in accuracy gain. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset, we evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and two negative controls across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results were inconclusive: the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0004419 (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], p=0.75) in the primary cohort and 0.002549 (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], p=0.106) in the replication cohort. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. These findings suggest that spectral entropy minimization of input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks.

[4] Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?
Abstract: Recently, there has been a surge of Transformer-based solutions for the long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) task. Despite the growing performance over the past few years, we question the validity of this line of research in this work. Specifically, Transformers is arguably the most successful solution to extract the semantic correlations among the elements in a long sequence. However, in time series modeling, we are to extract the temporal relations in an ordered set of continuous points. While employing positional encoding and using tokens to embed sub-series in Transformers facilitate preserving some ordering information, the nature of the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss. To validate our claim, we introduce a set of embarrassingly simple one-layer linear models named LTSF-Linear for comparison. Experimental results on nine real-life datasets show that LTSF-Linear surprisingly outperforms existing sophisticated Transformer-based LTSF models in all cases, and often by a large margin. Moreover, we conduct comprehensive empirical studies to explore the impacts of various design elements of LTSF models on their temporal relation extraction capability. We hope this surprising finding opens up new research directions for the LTSF task. We also advocate revisiting the validity of Transformer-based solutions for other time series analysis tasks (e.g., anomaly detection) in the future.

[5] Selective Attention Improves Transformer
Abstract: Unneeded elements in the attention’s context degrade performance. We introduce Selective Attention, a simple parameter-free change to the standard attention mechanism which reduces attention to unneeded elements. Selective attention consistently improves language modeling and downstream task performance in a variety of model sizes and context lengths. For example, transformers trained with the language modeling objective on C4 with selective attention perform language modeling equivalently to standard transformers with ~2X more heads and parameters in their attention modules. Selective attention also allows decreasing the size of the attention’s context buffer, leading to meaningful reductions in the memory and compute requirements during inference. For example, transformers trained on C4 with context sizes of 512, 1,024, and 2,048 need 16X, 25X, and 47X less memory for their attention module, respectively, when equipped with selective attention, as those without selective attention, with the same validation perplexity.

[6] A Survey on Vision Transformer
Abstract: Transformer, first applied to the field of natural language processing, is a type of deep neural network mainly based on the self-attention mechanism. Thanks to its strong representation capabilities, researchers are looking at ways to apply transformer to computer vision tasks. Related-work section:
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [20], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [11] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [7]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [13]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [16]. These works collectively establish that while transformers are widely applied, their generalization mechanisms in time-series domains require further validation.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [9]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [10]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [8], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [18]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [14]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2]. These studies suggest that regularization strategies are actively investigated, but their efficacy varies by task and implementation.

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [17]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [19]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [6], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [12], and *A survey of transformers* [21] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [15]. This body of work underscores that attention modifications are common, yet their impact on subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers remains an open empirical question. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight-regularization hypothesis in a controlled, subject-disjoint setting, distinguishing our measured accuracy outcomes from unmeasured attention constructs.
