You are writing a rigorous, honest research paper (IMRaD) about an experiment that has ALREADY been run; the REAL results — including means, 95% confidence intervals, significance, and effect sizes — are given to you. Be faithful to those numbers and do NOT invent results, references, or findings. Write clear, precise academic prose. CITE numbered references in square brackets (e.g. [1] or [2, 3]); the Introduction and Related Work MUST cite them inline. An automated auditor checks each cited sentence against its abstract: say what a paper actually establishes, not merely its topic. You are NOT required to cite every reference; unused references are removed. NEVER cite a paper as evidence for something it does NOT discuss, including a gap in a different setting. State a gap WITHOUT a marker, use the reviewed gap statement, or cite an abstract that identifies that gap itself. Never attribute the opposite of what an abstract says. Stay INSIDE the abstract's own wording: use its terms, do not generalise them or add an unstated mechanism, domain or consequence. Plausible extensions are unsupported claims too; if in doubt, write less about the paper. Refer to figures and tables by number (e.g. 'Figure 1', 'Table 1'). Report results quantitatively (state the effect, its confidence interval, and whether it is significant). When the analysis contains primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts, report BOTH separately, state each preregistered decision, and never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. Distinguish training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations; the confirmatory cohort is never an independent replication.
EVIDENCE AND INTERPRETATION (never copy these instructions into the paper). The registered condition descriptions and executed activation records below are authoritative: a baseline/no-op and an active negative control are different conditions. Do not infer inactivity from a small or nonsignificant outcome contrast. Describe only what the control manipulates; its outcome cannot prove that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: name the directly recorded outcomes, and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. If a reference tensor is detached inside a penalty, this stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient. Use the registered CI classifications without equating nonsignificance with equality. If a CI crosses zero but lies below the worthwhile margin, preserve its registered label and separately explain that it excludes gains of that target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model. The supplied power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; do not claim the former guarantees the latter. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

LENGTH. Write a full paper, not an extended abstract. Aim for roughly: introduction 600-800 words; related work 600-900; method 500-800 (BEFORE the operator specification that is appended for you); experimental setup 300-500; results 500-800; discussion 500-800; limitations 200-300; conclusion 150-250; abstract 150-250. A section that is three sentences long has not done its job. Depth means argument and detail, never padding or repetition.
INTRODUCTION. Open with the problem and why it matters, say what is missing in the current literature, then state what this paper does. End it with an explicit contributions list ('- We ...') of two to four items, then state the preregistered prediction.
RELATED WORK — 600-900 words. Synthesise by theme: what papers establish together, where they disagree, and what remains unsettled. The failure this section keeps producing looks like this: 'X studies uncertainty [1]. Y studies approximations [2].' — a list with citations attached. Write instead: 'Uncertainty motivates Bayesian methods [1], but their tractable approximations lose guarantees [2], motivating our boundary test.' Use that argumentative structure only when the abstracts support it. End by positioning this study against the themes; omit irrelevant references and quoted or italicised paper titles. Each reference in a grouped citation must independently support the WHOLE sentence. If papers support different halves, use separate sentences and markers.
RESULTS. Walk the reader through the evidence: discuss each figure and each table where it is relevant to the point being made, rather than listing them at the end.
DO NOT RESTATE THE CONFIGURATION. The dataset, split, architecture, training budget and outcome definition are written for you into the Experimental Setup and the appendix. State them nowhere else — not in the Method, not a second time in the setup.
WHAT THE SETUP SECTION IS FOR is DESIGN justification (300-500 words): why a subject-disjoint split answers the question and a random split would not; benefits and costs of pairing conditions by seed; each negative control's intended alternative explanation and what its observed contrast supports; the seed budget and analysis. These arguments are not supplied by the configuration block.
The METHOD is about the OPERATOR — what it does, why that is the right expression of the hypothesis, and what its registered comparator holds fixed.
The CONCLUSION (150-250 words) states what was found, what the measured outcome licenses for someone choosing between these methods (never an unmeasured mechanism), and what would settle the question next. Not a one-paragraph restatement of the abstract.
NAME THE ARMS AS THE TABLES DO: 'the proposed condition', 'the baseline', 'the first negative control', 'the second negative control'. Do not invent a parallel name such as 'Intervention' — the reader has to match your prose to the tables.
REGISTER. Never enumerate random seeds in the prose — they are in the appendix. Never annotate a sentence with the subsystem that produced it.

[claim-language] Claim what the evidence carries, and no more. Keep four registers apart and make it obvious which one a sentence is in: a RESULT states a measured quantity; an INTERPRETATION says what it may mean and is marked as such ('suggests', 'is consistent with'); a LIMITATION says what this design cannot tell anyone; FUTURE WORK proposes what would settle the question, and is the only register in which a wider setting may appear. Be exact about who was held out: evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen SUBJECTS — name that population — and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution, so do not call it out-of-distribution or domain generalisation. Where an outcome did not reach the registered decision threshold, report it as measured; do not upgrade it with a verb of proof.
[discussion-depth] The discussion is where the study is interpreted, not summarised again. Cover, in whatever order the argument wants: the principal finding; what it means; what this design does and does NOT establish; a mechanism that would produce the observed result and at least one alternative that would too; what the independent replication cohort adds or fails to add; and how the finding stands against specific cited papers [n] — agreeing, conflicting, extending, or not comparable because the intervention, task, data regime or evaluation differ. A null, refuted or inconclusive outcome owes the reader every one of those and is never rewritten as a positive finding. Length is not the target: a paragraph repeating the results covers none of this, and padding reads worse than brevity.
[paper-structure] Give a long section the internal structure its content earns. Where a section covers two or three distinct matters, open each with a short bold run-in heading (**Like this**) and keep one idea per paragraph; where it makes a single continuous argument, leave it undivided. Break at the argument's own joints — never split one argument to hit a shape, and never add a heading a section has not earned. Paragraphs of 60-150 words read well; one past 200 is doing more than one job and should be split where it turns. This matters most in related work, method, experimental setup, results and discussion, which are the sections long enough to become a wall. Do not fragment: a heading over two sentences is decoration, and several of them are harder to read than the block they replaced.

The gains hold from 360M to 3B parameters and extend to looped Transformers.
[36] Qingsong Wen, Tian Zhou et al. Transformers in Time Series: A Survey (2022).
    Abstract: Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications. In this paper, we systematically review Transformer schemes for time series modeling by highlighting their strengths as well as limitations. In particular, we examine the development of time series Transformers in two perspectives. From the perspective of network structure, we summarize the adaptations and modifications that have been made to Transformers in order to accommodate the challenges in time series analysis. From the perspective of applications, we categorize time series Transformers based on common tasks including forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification. Empirically, we perform robust analysis, model size analysis, and seasonal-trend decomposition analysis to study how Transformers perform in time series. Finally, we discuss and suggest future directions to provide useful research guidance. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first work to comprehensively and systematically summarize the recent advances of Transformers for modeling time series data. We hope this survey will ignite further research interests in time series Transformers.
[37] Brady Zhou, Philipp Krähenbühl. Cross-view Transformers for real-time Map-view Semantic Segmentation (2022).
    Abstract: We present cross-view transformers, an efficient attention-based model for map-view semantic segmentation from multiple cameras. Our architecture implicitly learns a mapping from individual camera views into a canonical map-view representation using a camera-aware cross-view attention mechanism. Each camera uses positional embeddings that depend on its intrinsic and extrinsic calibration. These embeddings allow a transformer to learn the mapping across different views without ever explicitly modeling it geometrically. The architecture consists of a convolutional image encoder for each view and cross-view transformer layers to infer a map-view semantic segmentation. Our model is simple, easily parallelizable, and runs in real-time. The presented architecture performs at state-of-the-art on the nuScenes dataset, with 4x faster inference speeds. Code is available at https://github.com/bradyz/cross_view_transformers.
[38] Liangrui Pan, Wenjuan Liu et al. CVFC: Attention-Based Cross-View Feature Consistency for Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation of Pathology Images (2023).
    Abstract: Histopathology image segmentation is the gold standard for diagnosing cancer, and can indicate cancer prognosis. However, histopathology image segmentation requires high-quality masks, so many studies now use image-level labels to achieve pixel-level segmentation to reduce the need for fine-grained annotation. To solve this problem, we propose an attention-based cross-view feature consistency end-to-end pseudo-mask generation framework named CVFC based on the attention mechanism. Specifically, CVFC is a three-branch joint framework composed of two Resnet38 and one Resnet50, and the independent branch multi-scale integrated feature map to generate a class activation map (CAM); in each branch, through down-sampling and The expansion method adjusts the size of the CAM; the middle branch projects the feature matrix to the query and key feature spaces, and generates a feature space perception matrix through the connection layer and inner product to adjust and refine the CAM of each branch; finally, through the feature consistency loss and feature cross loss to optimize the parameters of CVFC in co-training mode. After a large number of experiments, An IoU of 0.7122 and a fwIoU of 0.7018 are obtained on the WSSS4LUAD dataset, which outperforms HistoSegNet, SEAM, C-CAM, WSSS-Tissue, and OEEM, respectively.
[39] Tianyang Lin, Yuxin Wang et al. A survey of transformers (2022).
    Abstract: Transformers have achieved great success in many artificial intelligence fields, such as natural language processing, computer vision, and audio processing. Therefore, it is natural to attract lots of interest from academic and industry researchers. Up to the present, a great variety of Transformer variants (a.k.a. X-formers) have been proposed, however, a systematic and comprehensive literature review on these Transformer variants is still missing. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive review of various X-formers. We first briefly introduce the vanilla Transformer and then propose a new taxonomy of X-formers. Next, we introduce the various X-formers from three perspectives: architectural modification, pre-training, and applications. Finally, we outline some potential directions for future research.
[40] Joohyung Lee, Kwanhyung Lee et al. Structure-Aware Set Transformers: Temporal and Variable-Type Attention Biases for Asynchronous Clinical Time Series (2026).
    Abstract: Electronic health records (EHR) are irregular, asynchronous multivariate time series. As time-series foundation models increasingly tokenize events rather than discretizing time, the input layout becomes a key design choice. Grids expose time$\times$variable structure but require imputation or missingness masks, risking error or sampling-policy shortcuts. Point-set tokenization avoids discretization but loses within-variable trajectories and time-local cross-variable context (Fig.1). We restore these priors in STructure-AwaRe (STAR) Set Transformer by adding parameter-efficient soft attention biases: a temporal locality penalty $-|Δt|/τ$ with learnable timescales and a variable-type affinity $B_{s_i,s_j}$ from a learned feature-compatibility matrix. We benchmark 10 depth-wise fusion schedules (Fig.2). On three ICU prediction tasks, STAR-Set achieves AUC/APR of 0.7158/0.0026 (CPR), 0.9164/0.2033 (mortality), and 0.8373/0.1258 (vasopressor use), outperforming regular-grid, event-time grid, and prior set baselines. Learned $τ$ and $B$ provide interpretable summaries of temporal context and variable interactions, offering a practical plug-in for context-informed time-series models.

You are writing a rigorous, honest research paper (IMRaD) about an experiment that has ALREADY been run; the REAL results — including means, 95% confidence intervals, significance, and effect sizes — are given to you. Be faithful to those numbers and do NOT invent results, references, or findings. Write clear, precise academic prose. CITE numbered references in square brackets (e.g. [1] or [2, 3]); the Introduction and Related Work MUST cite them inline. An automated auditor checks each cited sentence against its abstract: say what a paper actually establishes, not merely its topic. You are NOT required to cite every reference; unused references are removed. NEVER cite a paper as evidence for something it does NOT discuss, including a gap in a different setting. State a gap WITHOUT a marker, use the reviewed gap statement, or cite an abstract that identifies that gap itself. Never attribute the opposite of what an abstract says. Stay INSIDE the abstract's own wording: use its terms, do not generalise them or add an unstated mechanism, domain or consequence. Plausible extensions are unsupported claims too; if in doubt, write less about the paper. Refer to figures and tables by number (e.g. 'Figure 1', 'Table 1'). Report results quantitatively (state the effect, its confidence interval, and whether it is significant). When the analysis contains primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts, report BOTH separately, state each preregistered decision, and never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. Distinguish training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations; the confirmatory cohort is never an independent replication.
EVIDENCE AND INTERPRETATION (never copy these instructions into the paper). The registered condition descriptions and executed activation records below are authoritative: a baseline/no-op and an active negative control are different conditions. Do not infer inactivity from a small or nonsignificant outcome contrast. Describe only what the control manipulates; its outcome cannot prove that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: name the directly recorded outcomes, and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. If a reference tensor is detached inside a penalty, this stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient. Use the registered CI classifications without equating nonsignificance with equality. If a CI crosses zero but lies below the worthwhile margin, preserve its registered label and separately explain that it excludes gains of that target magnitude under the stated uncertainty model. The supplied power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; do not claim the former guarantees the latter. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance.

LENGTH. Write a full paper, not an extended abstract. Aim for roughly: introduction 600-800 words; related work 600-900; method 500-800 (BEFORE the operator specification that is appended for you); experimental setup 300-500; results 500-800; discussion 500-800; limitations 200-300; conclusion 150-250; abstract 150-250. A section that is three sentences long has not done its job. Depth means argument and detail, never padding or repetition.
INTRODUCTION. Open with the problem and why it matters, say what is missing in the current literature, then state what this paper does. End it with an explicit contributions list ('- We ...') of two to four items, then state the preregistered prediction.
RELATED WORK — 600-900 words. Synthesise by theme: what papers establish together, where they disagree, and what remains unsettled. The failure this section keeps producing looks like this: 'X studies uncertainty [1]. Y studies approximations [2].' — a list with citations attached. Write instead: 'Uncertainty motivates Bayesian methods [1], but their tractable approximations lose guarantees [2], motivating our boundary test.' Use that argumentative structure only when the abstracts support it. End by positioning this study against the themes; omit irrelevant references and quoted or italicised paper titles. Each reference in a grouped citation must independently support the WHOLE sentence. If papers support different halves, use separate sentences and markers.
RESULTS. Walk the reader through the evidence: discuss each figure and each table where it is relevant to the point being made, rather than listing them at the end.
DO NOT RESTATE THE CONFIGURATION. The dataset, split, architecture, training budget and outcome definition are written for you into the Experimental Setup and the appendix. State them nowhere else — not in the Method, not a second time in the setup.
WHAT THE SETUP SECTION IS FOR is DESIGN justification (300-500 words): why a subject-disjoint split answers the question and a random split would not; benefits and costs of pairing conditions by seed; each negative control's intended alternative explanation and what its observed contrast supports; the seed budget and analysis. These arguments are not supplied by the configuration block.
The METHOD is about the OPERATOR — what it does, why that is the right expression of the hypothesis, and what its registered comparator holds fixed.
The CONCLUSION (150-250 words) states what was found, what the measured outcome licenses for someone choosing between these methods (never an unmeasured mechanism), and what would settle the question next. Not a one-paragraph restatement of the abstract.
NAME THE ARMS AS THE TABLES DO: 'the proposed condition', 'the baseline', 'the first negative control', 'the second negative control'. Do not invent a parallel name such as 'Intervention' — the reader has to match your prose to the tables.

Keep four registers apart and make it obvious which one a sentence is in: a RESULT states a measured quantity; an INTERPRETATION says what it may mean and is marked as such ('suggests', 'is consistent with'); a LIMITATION says what this design cannot tell anyone; FUTURE WORK proposes what would settle the question, and is the only register in which a wider setting may appear. Be exact about who was held out: evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen SUBJECTS — name that population — and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution, so do not call it out-of-distribution or domain generalisation. payload.content:
=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projection weights improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Deep learning models for time-series analysis increasingly rely on Transformer architectures to capture long-range dependencies in sequential data [36]. However, the effectiveness of these models in generalizing across subjects with distinct movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds remains an open question [5]. Standard training objectives optimize for fit on the training distribution, which may not encourage representations that are invariant to subject-specific nuisance factors. Architectural inductive biases, such as cross-layer consistency, have been proposed to stabilize learning and improve generalization, but their impact on subject-disjoint performance lacks independent verification [17].

This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. Specifically, we investigate whether regularizing the query projection weights of deeper transformer blocks to match those of shallower blocks yields measurable improvements in held-out classification accuracy. This question matters because answering it clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

Current literature offers conflicting perspectives on Transformer efficacy in time series. While some surveys highlight the ability to capture long-range dependencies [36], others question the validity of this research line, noting that simple linear models can outperform sophisticated Transformer-based forecasting models [5]. Furthermore, domain adaptation for time-series Transformers often requires fine-tuning to address generalization challenges [30]. Consistency regularization has been proposed to mitigate overfitting in deep Transformer models [17], and cross-layer mechanisms have been explored to strengthen layer interactions [15]. However, whether enforcing weight consistency across layers specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in activity recognition remains untested in a registered setting.

This paper reports a registered replication experiment evaluating the effect of a Cross-Layer Query Consistency loss on subject-disjoint generalization. We contribute the following:
- We execute a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency on the UCI HAR dataset using a subject-disjoint split.
- We report exact held-out classification accuracy means and 95% confidence intervals for both primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts.
- We provide an inconclusive result where confidence intervals exclude gains exceeding the registered margin but include zero.

The preregistered prediction stated that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with the mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The observed confidence intervals in both cohorts exclude effects larger than this margin in both directions, but they also include zero, meaning smaller effects are not excluded. Thus, the statistical inference supports the conclusion that effects larger than the registered margin are excluded, while the presence of a smaller non-zero effect remains indeterminate.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [36], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [30].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [32]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [31]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [35]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [11], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [21], and *A survey of transformers* [39] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [26].

This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight-level consistency intervention in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. Unlike works that modify attention maps or hidden states [18, 35], we regularize the query projection weights directly. Unlike domain adaptation methods that rely on fine-tuning [30], we test a training-time regularization applied from scratch. The inconclusive results here contrast with positive findings in cross-layer fusion for remote sensing [23], suggesting that the benefit of cross-layer consistency may depend on the domain and the specific level of the architecture targeted.

=== method ===
The experiment employs the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, applied to the query projection weights of the second attention block (blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight). The operator enforces Frobenius norm consistency between these weights and the corresponding weights of the first block (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight). This manipulation targets the parameter space directly, rather than attention maps or activations, to test whether weight stability across depth improves generalization.

The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. The operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The reference weights from block 0 are retrieved and detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The difference is computed element-wise, squared, and summed to produce the raw loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01 and added to the training objective. This coefficient prevents the loss term from dominating the classification objective while ensuring it exerts a regularizing pressure.

The baseline condition executes the identical code path but returns a zero loss term. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective.

A negative control condition penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute, isolating the effect of the specific cross-layer relationship from the mere presence of a penalty term. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification.** We use the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset with the official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. A subject-disjoint split answers the question of generalization to unseen individuals, whereas a random split would allow subject-specific features to leak into the training set, inflating accuracy estimates. Pairing conditions by seed controls for variance introduced by initialization and data ordering, increasing the power to detect small effects. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds provides sufficient power to detect effects exceeding the registered margin. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin, and is not an exact power calculation for the percentile bootstrap.

**Uncertainty and Analysis.** We report bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for all mean estimates. These intervals quantify the uncertainty in the mean accuracy due to seed variation. We do not report standard deviations as the primary measure of uncertainty for the mean contrast. The analysis distinguishes between the primary cohort and the confirmatory-replication cohort. The confirmatory cohort is never an independent replication in the sense of a new dataset or architecture; it is a replication on new seeds within the same experimental design. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

**Conditions.** The proposed condition adds the consistency loss. The baseline adds no loss. The first negative control adds a loss against a random matrix. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. Training uses PreNormTransformerEncoder (2 blocks, 64 hidden, 4-head attention, 128 timesteps, 9 channels) on UCI HAR subject-disjoint split. Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects. Figure 1 illustrates the experimental flow from UCI HAR data through PreNormTransformerEncoder under three conditions to held-out accuracy, showing how the data propagates through the model and loss computation to the final metric.

=== results ===
We report results for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately. In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Table 5 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for each condition: Proposed (0.9062, 95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), Baseline (0.9054, 95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]), and Negative control 1 (0.9051, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

Figure 3 displays the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. Points are the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Zero marks no directional effect. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold (held-out classification accuracy: 0.0125098 proportion); support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it. The 43 individual paired differences are plotted behind the interval at their exact values. The interval lies entirely below the threshold, excluding gains of that target magnitude, but crosses zero.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Table 5 reports the replication means: Proposed (0.9055, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]), Baseline (0.9035, 95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]), and Negative control 1 (0.9043, 95% CI [0.9003, 0.9082]). Again, the 95% CI includes zero, and the decision is inconclusive.

Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. Bars are means over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimate is printed above each bar; the axis starts at zero, so the bar lengths are comparable. The figure shows the proposed condition against the baseline. The dashed line marks the baseline mean, as an ordering reference only. Visually, the bars overlap substantially, consistent with the non-significant contrast. Figure 6 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. Points are the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Zero marks no directional effect. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold. The interval again excludes the threshold but includes zero. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or replication cohorts. The confidence intervals in both cohorts exclude effects larger than the registered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion, but they also include zero. This outcome is consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class, rather than cross-layer weight stability. However, mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: we measured accuracy, not attention stability or feature learning. The observed contrast supports the conclusion that the specific weight regularization tested does not produce robust accuracy gains in this regime.

This design establishes that the intervention does not improve accuracy by the target margin under the stated uncertainty model. It does not establish that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct; the negative control's outcome merely supports that the compute-matched penalty itself is not the driver of any effect. The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is not a fluke of the primary seeds, as the effect direction and magnitude were similar (0.000773 vs 0.00196) and both intervals overlapped zero.

Comparing to specific cited papers, our null result contrasts with *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification*, which utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. This discrepancy may arise because that intervention operates on feature fusion rather than weight regularization, or because remote sensing scenes differ from human activity time series. Our findings align with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found inconclusive results for weight spectrum regularization in this setting [3]. Both studies suggest that weight-level constraints may not be the limiting factor for generalization in small time-series transformers.

Alternative explanations for the null result include the possibility that the consistency coefficient (0.01) was too small to exert sufficient pressure, or that the two-block architecture is too shallow to benefit from cross-layer constraints. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [35], suggesting that weight-level consistency might be too rigid compared to activation-level mixing. Future work should test whether activation-level consistency or deeper architectures yield different outcomes.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to the UCI HAR dataset and a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture with two blocks. The results may not generalize to other time-series domains, sensor modalities, or deeper transformer stacks. The consistency coefficient was fixed at 0.01; different coefficients might produce different effects, though the registered margin test was designed to detect worthwhile gains regardless of coefficient tuning. The negative control destroys the cross-layer relationship but does not test all possible alternative regularizations. Finally, we measured held-out classification accuracy; we did not measure attention maps or feature representations directly, so claims about attention stability remain hypothetical.

=== conclusion ===
We tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projection weights improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The intervention did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin in either the primary or replication cohorts, and confidence intervals included zero. The results are inconclusive regarding the presence of a small effect but exclude gains larger than 0.0125098 proportion. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence does not support adopting cross-layer query consistency loss for this task. Future work should investigate activation-level consistency or deeper architectures to settle whether cross-layer mechanisms can benefit subject-disjoint time-series classification.

6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projection weights improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Deep learning models for time-series analysis increasingly rely on Transformer architectures to capture long-range dependencies in sequential data [36]. However, the effectiveness of these models in generalizing across subjects with distinct movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds remains an open question [5]. Standard training objectives optimize for fit on the training distribution, which may not encourage representations that are invariant to subject-specific nuisance factors. Architectural inductive biases, such as cross-layer consistency, have been proposed to stabilize learning and improve generalization, but their impact on subject-disjoint performance lacks independent verification [17].

This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. Specifically, we investigate whether regularizing the query projection weights of deeper transformer blocks to match those of shallower blocks yields measurable improvements in held-out classification accuracy. This question matters because answering it clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

Current literature offers conflicting perspectives on Transformer efficacy in time series. While some surveys highlight the ability to capture long-range dependencies [36], others question the validity of this research line, noting that simple linear models can outperform sophisticated Transformer-based forecasting models [5]. Furthermore, domain adaptation for time-series Transformers often requires fine-tuning to address generalization challenges [30]. Consistency regularization has been proposed to mitigate overfitting in deep Transformer models [17], and cross-layer mechanisms have been explored to strengthen layer interactions [15]. However, whether enforcing weight consistency across layers specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in activity recognition remains untested in a registered setting.

This paper reports a registered replication experiment evaluating the effect of a Cross-Layer Query Consistency loss on subject-disjoint generalization. We contribute the following:
- We execute a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency on the UCI HAR dataset using a subject-disjoint split.
- We report exact held-out classification accuracy means and 95% confidence intervals for both primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts.
- We provide an inconclusive result where confidence intervals exclude gains exceeding the registered margin but include zero.

The preregistered prediction stated that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with the mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The observed confidence intervals in both cohorts exclude effects larger than this margin in both directions, but they also include zero, meaning smaller effects are not excluded. Thus, the statistical inference supports the conclusion that effects larger than the registered margin are excluded, while the presence of a smaller non-zero effect remains indeterminate.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [36], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [30].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [32]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [31]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [35]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [11], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [21], and *A survey of transformers* [39] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [26].

This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight-level consistency intervention in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. Unlike works that modify attention maps or hidden states [18, 35], we regularize the query projection weights directly. Unlike domain adaptation methods that rely on fine-tuning [30], we test a training-time regularization applied from scratch. The inconclusive results here contrast with positive findings in cross-layer fusion for remote sensing [23], suggesting that the benefit of cross-layer consistency may depend on the domain and the specific level of the architecture targeted.

=== method ===
The experiment employs the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, applied to the query projection weights of the second attention block (blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight). The operator enforces Frobenius norm consistency between these weights and the corresponding weights of the first block (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight). This manipulation targets the parameter space directly, rather than attention maps or activations, to test whether weight stability across depth improves generalization.

The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. The operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The reference weights from block 0 are retrieved and detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The difference is computed element-wise, squared, and summed to produce the raw loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01 and added to the training objective. This coefficient prevents the loss term from dominating the classification objective while ensuring it exerts a regularizing pressure.

The baseline condition executes the identical code path but returns a zero loss term. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective.

A negative control condition penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute, isolating the effect of the specific cross-layer relationship from the mere presence of a penalty term. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification.** We use the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset with the official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. A subject-disjoint split answers the question of generalization to unseen individuals, whereas a random split would allow subject-specific features to leak into the training set, inflating accuracy estimates. Pairing conditions by seed controls for variance introduced by initialization and data ordering, increasing the power to detect small effects. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds provides sufficient power to detect effects exceeding the registered margin. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin, and is not an exact power calculation for the percentile bootstrap.

**Uncertainty and Analysis.** We report bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for all mean estimates. These intervals quantify the uncertainty in the mean accuracy due to seed variation. We do not report standard deviations as the primary measure of uncertainty for the mean contrast. The analysis distinguishes between the primary cohort and the confirmatory-replication cohort. The confirmatory cohort is never an independent replication in the sense of a new dataset or architecture; it is a replication on new seeds within the same experimental design. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

**Conditions.** The proposed condition adds the consistency loss. The baseline adds no loss. The first negative control adds a loss against a random matrix. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. Training uses PreNormTransformerEncoder (2 blocks, 64 hidden, 4-head attention, 128 timesteps, 9 channels) on UCI HAR subject-disjoint split. Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects. Figure 1 illustrates the experimental flow from UCI HAR data through PreNormTransformerEncoder under three conditions to held-out accuracy, showing how the data propagates through the model and loss computation to the final metric.

=== results ===
We report results for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately. In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Table 5 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for each condition: Proposed (0.9062, 95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), Baseline (0.9054, 95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]), and Negative control 1 (0.9051, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

Figure 3 displays the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. Points are the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Zero marks no directional effect. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold (held-out classification accuracy: 0.0125098 proportion); support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it. The 43 individual paired differences are plotted behind the interval at their exact values. The interval lies entirely below the threshold, excluding gains of that target magnitude, but crosses zero.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Table 5 reports the replication means: Proposed (0.9055, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]), Baseline (0.9035, 95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]), and Negative control 1 (0.9043, 95% CI [0.9003, 0.9082]). Again, the 95% CI includes zero, and the decision is inconclusive.

Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. Bars are means over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimate is printed above each bar; the axis starts at zero, so the bar lengths are comparable. The figure shows the proposed condition against the baseline. The dashed line marks the baseline mean, as an ordering reference only. Visually, the bars overlap substantially, consistent with the non-significant contrast. Figure 6 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. Points are the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Zero marks no directional effect. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold. The interval again excludes the threshold but includes zero. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or replication cohorts. The confidence intervals in both cohorts exclude effects larger than the registered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion, but they also include zero. This outcome is consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class, rather than cross-layer weight stability. However, mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: we measured accuracy, not attention stability or feature learning. The observed contrast supports the conclusion that the specific weight regularization tested does not produce robust accuracy gains in this regime.

This design establishes that the intervention does not improve accuracy by the target margin under the stated uncertainty model. It does not establish that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct; the negative control's outcome merely supports that the compute-matched penalty itself is not the driver of any effect. The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is not a fluke of the primary seeds, as the effect direction and magnitude were similar (0.000773 vs 0.00196) and both intervals overlapped zero.

Comparing to specific cited papers, our null result contrasts with *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification*, which utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. This discrepancy may arise because that intervention operates on feature fusion rather than weight regularization, or because remote sensing scenes differ from human activity time series. Our findings align with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found inconclusive results for weight spectrum regularization in this setting [3]. Both studies suggest that weight-level constraints may not be the limiting factor for generalization in small time-series transformers.

Alternative explanations for the null result include the possibility that the consistency coefficient (0.01) was too small to exert sufficient pressure, or that the two-block architecture is too shallow to benefit from cross-layer constraints. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [35], suggesting that weight-level consistency might be too rigid compared to activation-level mixing. Future work should test whether activation-level consistency or deeper architectures yield different outcomes.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to the UCI HAR dataset and a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture with two blocks. The results may not generalize to other time-series domains, sensor modalities, or deeper transformer stacks. The consistency coefficient was fixed at 0.01; different coefficients might produce different effects, though the registered margin test was designed to detect worthwhile gains regardless of coefficient tuning. The negative control destroys the cross-layer relationship but does not test all possible alternative regularizations. Finally, we measured held-out classification accuracy; we did not measure attention maps or feature representations directly, so claims about attention stability remain hypothetical.

=== conclusion ===
We tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projection weights improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The intervention did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin in either the primary or replication cohorts, and confidence intervals included zero. The results are inconclusive regarding the presence of a small effect but exclude gains larger than 0.0125098 proportion. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence does not support adopting cross-layer query consistency loss for this task. Future work should investigate activation-level consistency or deeper architectures to settle whether cross-layer mechanisms can benefit subject-disjoint time-series classification.

payload.title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
