Related-work section:
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [19], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [3]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [10] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [6]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [12]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [15].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [8]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [9]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [7], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [17]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [13]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [2]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [1].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [4]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [16]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [18]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [5], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [11], and *A survey of transformers* [20] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [14].

This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight-level consistency intervention in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. Unlike works that modify attention maps or hidden states [9, 18], we regularize the query projection weights directly. Unlike domain adaptation methods that rely on fine-tuning [15], we test a training-time regularization applied from scratch. The inconclusive results here contrast with positive findings in cross-layer fusion for remote sensing [13], suggesting that the benefit of cross-layer consistency may depend on the domain and the specific level of the architecture targeted.

Cited papers and their abstracts:
[1] Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness
Abstract: [EDITORIAL NOTICE — RETRACTED: this paper carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it. Stated reason: The numerical outputs reported in this paper remain computationally reproducible: an independent re-run from the archived reproducibility bundle reproduced all eight aggregate metrics within tolerance. A post-publication audit of the artifact source found that the executed intervention did not implement the preregistered intervention. The preregistration committed to a multiplicative weight perturbation applied BEFORE the forward pass, an entropy term added to the training OBJECTIVE, and a noise scale learned by BACKPROPAGATION, with held-out evaluation on the clean weights. The experiment har. Its conclusions may not be relied on; cite it only with its status stated.] Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic training often fails to provide calibrated confidence under distribution shift. This study investigates whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We preregistered a hypothesis that entropy maximization would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the baseline, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the intervention across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results refuted the preregistered hypothesis in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by 0.04805 proportion (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002) relative to the baseline. The replication cohort confirmed this degradation with a contrast of -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Negative controls involving entropy minimization and fixed noise performed comparably to the deterministic baseline. These findings indicate that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over explicit entropy maximization for robustness tasks in this regime.

[2] Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning
Abstract: Regularization design for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. This study tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy compared to standard weight decay in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would exceed a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion in accuracy gain. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset, we evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and two negative controls across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results were inconclusive: the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0004419 (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], p=0.75) in the primary cohort and 0.002549 (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], p=0.106) in the replication cohort. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. These findings suggest that spectral entropy minimization of input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks.

[3] Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?
Abstract: Recently, there has been a surge of Transformer-based solutions for the long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) task. Despite the growing performance over the past few years, we question the validity of this line of research in this work. Specifically, Transformers is arguably the most successful solution to extract the semantic correlations among the elements in a long sequence. However, in time series modeling, we are to extract the temporal relations in an ordered set of continuous points. While employing positional encoding and using tokens to embed sub-series in Transformers facilitate preserving some ordering information, the nature of the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss. To validate our claim, we introduce a set of embarrassingly simple one-layer linear models named LTSF-Linear for comparison. Experimental results on nine real-life datasets show that LTSF-Linear surprisingly outperforms existing sophisticated Transformer-based LTSF models in all cases, and often by a large margin. Moreover, we conduct comprehensive empirical studies to explore the impacts of various design elements of LTSF models on their temporal relation extraction capability. We hope this surprising finding opens up new research directions for the LTSF task. We also advocate revisiting the validity of Transformer-based solutions for other time series analysis tasks (e.g., anomaly detection) in the future.

[4] Selective Attention Improves Transformer
Abstract: Unneeded elements in the attention’s context degrade performance. We introduce Selective Attention, a simple parameter-free change to the standard attention mechanism which reduces attention to unneeded elements. Selective attention consistently improves language modeling and downstream task performance in a variety of model sizes and context lengths. For example, transformers trained with the language modeling objective on C4 with selective attention perform language modeling equivalently to standard transformers with ~2X more heads and parameters in their attention modules. Selective attention also allows decreasing the size of the attention’s context buffer, leading to meaningful reductions in the memory and compute requirements during inference. For example, transformers trained on C4 with context sizes of 512, 1,024, and 2,048 need 16X, 25X, and 47X less memory for their attention module, respectively, when equipped with selective attention, as those without selective attention, with the same validation perplexity.

[5] A Survey on Vision Transformer
Abstract: Transformer, first applied to the field of natural language processing, is a type of deep neural network mainly based on the self-attention mechanism. Thanks to its strong representation capabilities, researchers are looking at ways to apply transformer to computer vision tasks. In a variety of visual benchmarks, transformer-based models perform similar to or better than other types of networks such as convolutional and recurrent neural networks. Given its high performance and less need for vision-specific inductive bias, transformer is receiving more and more attention from the computer vision community. In this paper, we review these vision transformer models by categorizing them in different tasks and analyzing their advantages and disadvantages. The main categories we explore include the backbone network, high/mid-level vision, low-level vision, and video processing. We also include efficient transformer methods for pushing transformer into real device-based applications. Furthermore, we also take a brief look at the self-attention mechanism in computer vision, as it is the base component in transformer. Toward the end of this paper, we discuss the challenges and provide several further research directions for vision transformers.

[6] Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer
Abstract: A reliable and efficient representation of multivariate time series is crucial in various downstream machine learning tasks. In multivariate time series forecasting, each variable depends on its historical values and there are inter-dependencies among variables as well. Models have to be designed to capture both intra- and inter-relationships among the time series. To move towards this goal, we propose the Time Series Attention Transformer (TSAT) for multivariate time series representation learning. Using TSAT, we represent both temporal information and inter-dependencies of multivariate time series in terms of edge-enhanced dynamic graphs. The intra-series correlations are represented by nodes in a dynamic graph; a self-attention mechanism is modified to capture the inter-series correlations by using the super-empirical mode decomposition (SMD) module. We applied the embedded dynamic graphs to times series forecasting problems, including two real-world datasets and two benchmark datasets. Extensive experiments show that TSAT clearly outerperforms six state-of-the-art baseline methods in various forecasting horizons. We further visualize the embedded dynamic graphs to illustrate the graph representation power of TSAT. We share our code at https://github.com/RadiantResearch/TSAT.

[7] Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention
Abstract: More and more evidence has shown that strengthening layer interactions can enhance the representation power of a deep neural network, while self-attention excels at learning interdependencies by retrieving query-activated information. Motivated by this, we devise a cross-layer attention mechanism, called multi-head recurrent layer attention (MRLA), that sends a query representation of the current layer to all previous layers to retrieve query-related information from different levels of receptive fields. A light-weighted version of MRLA is also proposed to reduce the quadratic computation cost. The proposed layer attention mechanism can enrich the representation power of many state-of-the-art vision networks, including CNNs and vision transformers. Its effectiveness has been extensively evaluated in image classification, object detection and instance segmentation tasks, where improvements can be consistently observed. For example, our MRLA can improve 1.6% Top-1 accuracy on ResNet-50, while only introducing 0.16M parameters and 0.07B FLOPs. Surprisingly, it can boost the performances by a large margin of 3-4% box AP and mask AP in dense prediction tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/joyfang1106/MRLA.

[8] Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks
Abstract: The large-scale and deep-layer deep neural network based on the Transformer model is very powerful in sequence tasks, but it is prone to overfitting for small-scale training data. Moreover, the prediction result of the model with a small disturbance input is significantly lower than that without disturbance. In this work, we propose a double consistency regularization (DOCR) method for the end-to-end model structure, which separately constrains the output of the encoder and decoder during the training process to alleviate the above problems. Specifically, on the basis of the cross-entropy loss function, we build the mean model by integrating the model parameters of the previous rounds and measure the consistency between the models by calculating the KL divergence between the features of the encoder output and the probability distribution of the decoder output of the mean model and the base model so as to impose regularization constraints on the solution space of the model. We conducted extensive experiments on machine translation tasks, and the results show that the BLEU score increased by 2.60 on average, demonstrating the effectiveness of DOCR in improving model performance and its complementary impacts with other regularization techniques.

[9] CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation
Abstract: While transformers have greatly boosted performance in semantic segmentation, domain adaptive transformers are not yet well explored. We identify that the domain gap can cause discrepancies in self-attention. Due to this gap, the transformer attends to spurious regions or pixels, which deteriorates accuracy on the target domain. We propose Cross-Domain Attention Consistency (CDAC), to perform adaptation on attention maps using cross-domain attention layers that share features between source and target domains. Specifically, we impose consistency between predictions from cross-domain attention and self-attention modules to encourage similar distributions across domains in both the attention and output of the model, i.e., attention-level and output-level alignment. We also enforce consistency in attention maps between different augmented views to further strengthen the attention-based alignment. Combining these two components, CDAC mitigates the discrepancy in attention maps across domains and further boosts the performance of the transformer under unsupervised domain adaptation settings. Our method is evaluated on various widely used benchmarks and outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines, including GTAV-to-Cityscapes by 1.3 and 1.5 percent point (pp) and Synthia-to-Cityscapes by 0.6 pp and 2.9 pp when combining with two competitive Transformer-based backbones, respectively. Our code will be publicly available at https://github.com/wangkaihong/CDAC.

[10] TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation
Abstract: Signal measurement appearing in the form of time series is one of the most common types of data used in medical machine learning applications. Such datasets are often small in size, expensive to collect and annotate, and might involve privacy issues, which hinders our ability to train large, state-of-the-art deep learning models for biomedical applications. For time-series data, the suite of data augmentation strategies we can use to expand the size of the dataset is limited by the need to maintain the basic properties of the signal. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) can be utilized as another data augmentation tool. In this paper, we present TTS-CGAN, a transformer-based conditional GAN model that can be trained on existing multi-class datasets and generate class-specific synthetic time-series sequences of arbitrary length. We elaborate on the model architecture and design strategies. Synthetic sequences generated by our model are indistinguishable from real ones, and can be used to complement or replace real signals of the same type, thus achieving the goal of data augmentation. To evaluate the quality of the generated data, we modify the wavelet coherence metric to be able to compare the similarity between two sets of signals, and also conduct a case study where a mix of synthetic and real data are used to train a deep learning model for sequence classification. Together with other visualization techniques and qualitative evaluation approaches, we demonstrate that TTS-CGAN generated synthetic data are similar to real data, and that our model performs better than the other state-of-the-art GAN models built for time-series data generation.

[11] Transformers in Vision: A Survey
Abstract: Astounding results from Transformer models on natural language tasks have intrigued the vision community to study their application to computer vision problems. Among their salient benefits, Transformers enable modeling long dependencies between input sequence elements and support parallel processing of sequence as compared to recurrent networks, e.g., Long short-term memory. Different from convolutional networks, Transformers require minimal inductive biases for their design and are naturally suited as set-functions. Furthermore, the straightforward design of Transformers allows processing multiple modalities (e.g., images, videos, text, and speech) using similar processing blocks and demonstrates excellent scalability to very large capacity networks and huge datasets. Related-work section:
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [19], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [3]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [10] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [6]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [12]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [15].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [8]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [9]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [7], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [17]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [13]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [2]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [1].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [4]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [16]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [18]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [5], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [11], and *A survey of transformers* [20] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [14].

This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight-level consistency intervention in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. Unlike works that modify attention maps or hidden states [9, 18], we regularize the query projection weights directly. Unlike domain adaptation methods that rely on fine-tuning [15], we test a training-time regularization applied from scratch. The inconclusive results here contrast with positive findings in cross-layer fusion for remote sensing [13], suggesting that the benefit of cross-layer consistency may depend on the domain and the specific level of the architecture targeted.

Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [7], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [17]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [13]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [2]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [1].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [4]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [16]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [18]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [5], *Transformers in Vision: A Survey* [11], and *A survey of transformers* [20] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [14].

This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight-level consistency intervention in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. Unlike works that modify attention maps or hidden states [9, 18], we regularize the query projection weights directly. Unlike domain adaptation methods that rely on fine-tuning [15], we test a training-time regularization applied from scratch. The inconclusive results here contrast with positive findings in cross-layer fusion for remote sensing [13], suggesting that the benefit of cross-layer consistency may depend on the domain and the specific level of the architecture targeted.
Method: The experiment employs the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, applied to the query projection weights of the second attention block (blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight). The operator enforces Frobenius norm consistency between these weights and the corresponding weights of the first block (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight). This manipulation targets the parameter space directly, rather than attention maps or activations, to test whether weight stability across depth improves generalization.

The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. The operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The reference weights from block 0 are retrieved and detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The difference is computed element-wise, squared, and summed to produce the raw loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01 and added to the training objective. This coefficient prevents the loss term from dominating the classification objective while ensuring it exerts a regularizing pressure.

The baseline condition executes the identical code path but returns a zero loss term. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective.

A negative control condition penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute, isolating the effect of the specific cross-layer relationship from the mere presence of a penalty term. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Experimental setup: **Design Justification.** We use the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset with the official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. A subject-disjoint split answers the question of generalization to unseen individuals, whereas a random split would allow subject-specific features to leak into the training set, inflating accuracy estimates. Pairing conditions by seed controls for variance introduced by initialization and data ordering, increasing the power to detect small effects. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds provides sufficient power to detect effects exceeding the registered margin. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin, and is not an exact power calculation for the percentile bootstrap.

**Uncertainty and Analysis.** We report bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for all mean estimates. These intervals quantify the uncertainty in the mean accuracy due to seed variation. We do not report standard deviations as the primary measure of uncertainty for the mean contrast. The analysis distinguishes between the primary cohort and the confirmatory-replication cohort. The confirmatory cohort is a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds within the same experimental design. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

**Conditions.** The proposed condition adds the consistency loss. The baseline adds no loss. The first negative control adds a loss against a random matrix. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. Training uses PreNormTransformerEncoder (2 blocks, 64 hidden, 4-head attention, 128 timesteps, 9 channels) on UCI HAR subject-disjoint split. Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects. Figure 1 illustrates the experimental flow from UCI HAR data through PreNormTransformerEncoder under three conditions to held-out accuracy, showing how the data propagates through the model and loss computation to the final metric.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Results: We report results for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately. In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Table 5 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for each condition: Proposed (0.9062, 95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), Baseline (0.9054, 95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]), and Negative control 1 (0.9051, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

Figure 3 displays the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. Points are the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Zero marks no directional effect. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold (held-out classification accuracy: 0.0125098 proportion); support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it. The 43 individual paired differences are plotted behind the interval at their exact values. The interval lies entirely below the threshold, excluding gains of that target magnitude, but crosses zero.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Table 5 reports the replication means: Proposed (0.9055, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]), Baseline (0.9035, 95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]), and Negative control 1 (0.9043, 95% CI [0.9003, 0.9082]). Again, the 95% CI includes zero, and the decision is inconclusive.

Bars are means over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimate is printed above each bar; the axis starts at zero, so the bar lengths are comparable. The figure shows the proposed condition against the baseline. The dashed line marks the baseline mean, as an ordering reference only. Visually, the bars overlap substantially, consistent with the non-significant contrast. Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: We tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projection weights improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The intervention did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin in either the primary or replication cohorts, and confidence intervals included zero. The results are inconclusive regarding the presence of a small effect but exclude gains larger than 0.0125098 proportion. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence does not support adopting cross-layer query consistency loss for this task. Future work should investigate activation-level consistency or deeper architectures to settle whether cross-layer mechanisms can benefit subject-disjoint time-series classification.
Discussion: The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or replication cohorts. The confidence intervals in both cohorts exclude effects larger than the registered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion, but they also include zero. This outcome is consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class, rather than cross-layer weight stability. However, mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: we measured accuracy, not attention stability or feature learning. The observed contrast supports the conclusion that the specific weight regularization tested does not produce robust accuracy gains in this regime.

This design establishes that the intervention does not improve held-out classification accuracy by the target margin. It does not establish that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct; the negative control's outcome merely supports that the compute-matched penalty itself is not the driver of any effect. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is not a fluke of the primary seeds, as the effect direction and magnitude were similar (0.000773 vs 0.00196) and both intervals overlapped zero.

Comparing to specific cited papers, our null result contrasts with *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification*, which utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [13]. This discrepancy may arise because that intervention operates on feature fusion rather than weight regularization, or because remote sensing scenes differ from human activity time series. Our findings align with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found inconclusive results for weight spectrum regularization in this setting [2], although this mechanism was not tested in this study. Both studies suggest that weight-level constraints may not be the limiting factor for generalization in this setting.

Alternative explanations for the null result include the possibility that the consistency coefficient (0.01) was too small to exert sufficient pressure, or that the two-block architecture is too shallow to benefit from cross-layer constraints. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [18], suggesting that weight-level consistency might be too rigid compared to activation-level mixing. Future work should test whether activation-level consistency or deeper architectures yield different outcomes.
Limitations: This study is limited to the UCI HAR dataset and a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture with two blocks. The results may not generalize to other time-series domains, sensor modalities, or deeper transformer stacks. The consistency coefficient was fixed at 0.01; different coefficients might produce different effects, though the registered margin test was designed to detect worthwhile gains regardless of coefficient tuning. The negative control destroys the cross-layer relationship but does not test all possible alternative regularizations. Finally, we measured held-out classification accuracy; we did not measure attention maps or feature representations directly, so claims about attention stability remain hypothetical.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

Method: The experiment employs the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, applied to the query projection weights of the second attention block (blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight). The operator enforces Frobenius norm consistency between these weights and the corresponding weights of the first block (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight). This manipulation targets the parameter space directly, rather than attention maps or activations, to test whether weight stability across depth improves generalization.

The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. The operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it. The reference weights from block 0 are retrieved and detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The difference is computed element-wise, squared, and summed to produce the raw loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01 and added to the training objective. This coefficient prevents the loss term from dominating the classification objective while ensuring it exerts a regularizing pressure.

The baseline condition executes the identical code path but returns a zero loss term. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective.

A negative control condition penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute, isolating the effect of the specific cross-layer relationship from the mere presence of a penalty term. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Experimental setup: **Design Justification.** We use the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset with the official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. A subject-disjoint split answers the question of generalization to unseen individuals, whereas a random split would allow subject-specific features to leak into the training set, inflating accuracy estimates. Pairing conditions by seed controls for variance introduced by initialization and data ordering, increasing the power to detect small effects. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds provides sufficient power to detect effects exceeding the registered margin. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin, and is not an exact power calculation for the percentile bootstrap.

**Uncertainty and Analysis.** We report bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for all mean estimates. These intervals quantify the uncertainty in the mean accuracy due to seed variation. We do not report standard deviations as the primary measure of uncertainty for the mean contrast. The analysis distinguishes between the primary cohort and the confirmatory-replication cohort. The confirmatory cohort is a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds within the same experimental design. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

**Conditions.** The proposed condition adds the consistency loss. The baseline adds no loss. The first negative control adds a loss against a random matrix. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. Training uses PreNormTransformerEncoder (2 blocks, 64 hidden, 4-head attention, 128 timesteps, 9 channels) on UCI HAR subject-disjoint split. Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects. Figure 1 illustrates the experimental flow from UCI HAR data through PreNormTransformerEncoder under three conditions to held-out accuracy, showing how the data propagates through the model and loss computation to the final metric.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive.

Figure 3 displays the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. Points are the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Zero marks no directional effect. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold (held-out classification accuracy: 0.0125098 proportion); support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it. The 43 individual paired differences are plotted behind the interval at their exact values. The interval lies entirely below the threshold, excluding gains of that target magnitude, but crosses zero.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Table 5 reports the replication means: Proposed (0.9055, 95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]), Baseline (0.9035, 95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]), and Negative control 1 (0.9043, 95% CI [0.9003, 0.9082]). Again, the 95% CI includes zero, and the decision is inconclusive.

Bars are means over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimate is printed above each bar; the axis starts at zero, so the bar lengths are comparable. The figure shows the proposed condition against the baseline. The dashed line marks the baseline mean, as an ordering reference only. Visually, the bars overlap substantially, consistent with the non-significant contrast. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: We tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projection weights improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The intervention did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin in either the primary or replication cohorts, and confidence intervals included zero. The results are inconclusive regarding the presence of a small effect but exclude gains larger than 0.0125098 proportion. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence does not support adopting cross-layer query consistency loss for this task. Future work should investigate activation-level consistency or deeper architectures to settle whether cross-layer mechanisms can benefit subject-disjoint time-series classification.
Discussion: The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or replication cohorts. The confidence intervals in both cohorts exclude effects larger than the registered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion, but they also include zero. This outcome is consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class, rather than cross-layer weight stability. However, mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings: we measured accuracy, not attention stability or feature learning. The observed contrast supports the conclusion that the specific weight regularization tested does not produce robust accuracy gains in this regime.

This design establishes that the intervention does not improve held-out classification accuracy by the target margin. It does not establish that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct; the negative control's outcome merely supports that the compute-matched penalty itself is not the driver of any effect. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is not a fluke of the primary seeds, as the effect direction and magnitude were similar (0.000773 vs 0.00196) and both intervals overlapped zero.

Comparing to specific cited papers, our null result contrasts with *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification*, which utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [13]. This discrepancy may arise because that intervention operates on feature fusion rather than weight regularization, or because remote sensing scenes differ from human activity time series. Our findings align with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found inconclusive results for weight spectrum regularization in this setting [2], although this mechanism was not tested in this study. Both studies suggest that weight-level constraints may not be the limiting factor for generalization in this setting.

Alternative explanations for the null result include the possibility that the consistency coefficient (0.01) was too small to exert sufficient pressure, or that the two-block architecture is too shallow to benefit from cross-layer constraints. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [18], suggesting that weight-level consistency might be too rigid compared to activation-level mixing. Future work should test whether activation-level consistency or deeper architectures yield different outcomes.
Limitations: This study is limited to the UCI HAR dataset and a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture with two blocks. The results may not generalize to other time-series domains, sensor modalities, or deeper transformer stacks. The consistency coefficient was fixed at 0.01; different coefficients might produce different effects, though the registered margin test was designed to detect worthwhile gains regardless of coefficient tuning. The negative control destroys the cross-layer relationship but does not test all possible alternative regularizations. Finally, we measured held-out classification accuracy; we did not measure attention maps or feature representations directly, so claims about attention stability remain hypothetical.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance).     Abstract: Self-attention selects information freely across the sequence, but across depth, Transformers merely add each layer's output to the residual stream, so later layers cannot selectively reuse earlier-layer representations. === abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projection weights improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Time-series classification using deep learning often requires models to generalize across subjects who exhibit different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Transformers have emerged as a powerful architecture for sequence modeling due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [36]. However, their effectiveness in time-series forecasting and classification remains a subject of debate, with some evidence suggesting simpler linear models may outperform them in certain forecasting tasks [5]. In subject-disjoint settings, where training and testing data come from different individuals, the risk of overfitting to subject-specific artifacts is high. Architectural inductive biases, such as cross-layer consistency, have been proposed to stabilize learning and improve generalization, but empirical verification in this specific regime is limited.

One possible explanation, which this experiment did not test, is that enforcing consistency between query projection weights across transformer layers could reduce overfitting by constraining the hypothesis space. However, it is also possible that layer-specific adaptation is necessary to capture the hierarchical temporal features present in inertial sensor data. This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. The open problem this targets is identifying what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects.

This paper makes three contributions. First, we execute a preregistered replication of a cross-layer consistency intervention on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset using a subject-disjoint split. Second, we report exact held-out classification accuracy means, 95% confidence intervals, and significance tests for both primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts. Third, we evaluate the results against a fixed worthwhile margin to determine if the intervention offers practical utility. The preregistered prediction states that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report the outcomes honestly against this hypothesis, labeling any unforeseen finding as exploratory.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community [36], while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [10] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [30].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [32]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [31]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [35]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer* [11] and *A survey of transformers* [20] document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [26]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight-level consistency constraint in a subject-disjoint time-series setting, distinguishing it from activation engineering [32] or domain adaptation [18].

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces weight similarity between transformer blocks. The hypothesis is that regularizing deeper layer query projections toward shallower layer weights may improve generalization by reducing layer-wise divergence. The operator is applied to the target parameter blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight, which has a stored tensor shape of (64, 64). During loss computation of every optimization step, the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph. This ensures the combined objective is differentiated and the operator-owned parameter is trained by it.

The operator retrieves reference weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. It computes the element-wise difference between the target and reference weights, squares these differences, and sums them to produce a raw loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01 to prevent the term from dominating the classification objective. The resulting loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients from this term, though they still receive gradients from the task loss. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

The baseline condition serves as the comparator. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. In the control arm the intervention leaves the registered target parameter unchanged, leaves that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and adds nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them.

The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This control tests whether any regularization effect, rather than the specific cross-layer relationship, drives outcomes. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. Training uses PreNormTransformerEncoder on UCI HAR subject-disjoint split. Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification**. The experimental design prioritizes external validity regarding subject generalization. We use the official subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset, where 7,352 training windows come from a set of subjects and 2,947 held-out windows come from unseen subjects. A random split would mix subjects between training and testing, inflating accuracy by allowing the model to learn subject-specific artifacts rather than activity patterns. The subject-disjoint split answers the question of whether the intervention improves generalization to new people, which is the relevant deployment scenario for wearable sensing.

**Pairing and Controls**. We pair conditions by seed to reduce variance arising from initialization and data ordering. Each of the 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds generates a paired comparison between the proposed condition and the baseline. This pairing allows us to compute paired differences and confidence intervals that account for seed-specific noise. The baseline control arm ensures that any observed difference is due to the loss term and not implementation artifacts, as the harness guarantees the control arm adds no term and modifies no parameters. The first negative control matches the compute cost of the intervention but applies the penalty against a random matrix. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, it suggests the cross-layer relationship specifically matters, rather than just the act of regularizing weights.

**Power and Analysis**. The planning target power was 90% with a planning SD of 0.0250196 and a registered margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. We report held-out classification accuracy as the primary metric. The seed identities are recorded in the appendix. We distinguish training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects; here, the confirmatory cohort uses new seeds on the same subject-disjoint split, serving as a robustness check rather than an independent dataset replication.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**. In the primary cohort, we evaluated the proposed condition, the baseline, and the first negative control across 43 seeds. Table 1 reports the mean held-out classification accuracy for each condition. The proposed condition achieved a mean of 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9031, 0.9094]), while the baseline achieved 0.9054 (95% CI [0.9019, 0.9088]). The first negative control achieved 0.9051 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9085]). Figure 2 visualizes these means with error bars, showing the proposed condition against the baseline. The mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions was 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06), as detailed in Table 2. Figure 3 plots the paired mean difference with the registered worthwhile threshold. The 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the lower bound does not exceed the margin of 0.0125098. Figure 4 shows the learning curves over training steps, where the conditions track closely throughout training. The preregistered decision for the primary cohort was inconclusive.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**. The replication cohort used 43 disjoint seeds to verify stability. Table 3 reports the accuracy means: proposed condition 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), baseline 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]), and first negative control 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9080]). Figure 5 displays these bars. The mean difference was 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15), shown in Table 4 and Figure 6. Again, the confidence interval includes zero and fails to exceed the worthwhile margin. Figure 7 presents the replication learning curves, which mirror the primary cohort's stability. The preregistered decision for the replication cohort was also inconclusive.

**Combined Analysis**. Table 3 and Table 4 summarize the outcomes across both cohorts. Neither cohort showed a statistically significant difference, and neither excluded the possibility of no effect. The variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results do not support the hypothesis that the mean contrast exceeds the fixed worthwhile margin.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding**. The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency loss did not improve held-out classification accuracy by the target margin in either the primary or replication cohorts. Both 95% confidence intervals included zero, and the lower bounds remained well below the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. This design does not establish that the intervention cannot improve accuracy, but rather that under the stated uncertainty model, the observed data exclude gains of the target magnitude. The registered decision for both cohorts was inconclusive.

**Mechanism and Interpretation**. The intervention manipulated query projection weights, not attention maps directly. While one hypothesis is that weight consistency stabilizes attention across depth, this experiment did not measure attention stability. The outcome contrast is evidence about the accuracy, not about why the result occurred. An alternative explanation is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class to capture hierarchical temporal features, and constraining weights across layers restricts this capacity. The negative control results suggest that the specific cross-layer relationship did not drive performance, as the negative control performed similarly to the baseline.

**Comparison to Literature**. These findings align with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found inconclusive results for weight regularization in this setting [3]. They contrast with *Global Evolutionary Steering*, which reported success with cross-layer consistency in activation engineering [32], suggesting that weight-level constraints may differ in effect from activation-level constraints. The results also support the caution raised in *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* regarding architectural complexity [5]. Unlike *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks*, which found gains in machine translation [17], we observed no robust gains in time-series classification, highlighting domain differences.

**Future Work**. To settle the question, future work should measure attention maps directly to test the stability hypothesis. Additionally, testing on different time-series benchmarks or with larger models may reveal regimes where consistency is beneficial. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance, so future margins should be justified by task requirements.

=== limitations ===
This study has several limitations. First, it evaluates a single architecture (PreNormTransformerEncoder) on a single dataset (UCI HAR). The findings may not generalize to other time-series domains, sensor types, or model sizes. Second, the mechanism—attention stability—was not directly measured. We inferred it from accuracy outcomes, which is insufficient to confirm the hypothesis. Third, the subject-disjoint split, while rigorous for subject generalization, does not test domain generalization across different sensor placements or activities. Finally, the inconclusive decision means we cannot rule out small effects below the margin, only that the target margin was not exceeded.

=== conclusion ===
This replication study tested whether cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Across 43 primary and 43 replication seeds, the proposed condition did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 in held-out classification accuracy. Both cohorts yielded inconclusive decisions with confidence intervals including zero. For someone choosing between these methods, the measured outcome licenses no preference for the intervention over the baseline in this regime. The findings suggest that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. Future work should directly measure attention mechanisms and explore alternative consistency constraints to clarify the role of architectural inductive biases in this domain.
