Title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4, 21]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [6] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [8]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [14]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [17].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [10]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [11]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [9], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [19]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [15]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [18]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [20]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [7, 13, 22]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [16]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight regularization intervention in a subject-disjoint time-series setting, distinct from activation engineering or domain adaptation tasks.
Method: The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between query projection weights of successive attention blocks. The hypothesis is that regularizing deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights may improve generalization by reducing representational divergence across depth. The operator is applied to `blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight` during the loss computation of every optimization step. The operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated.

The operator retrieves reference weights from `model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight`. These reference weights are detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The operator computes the element-wise difference between the target weights (block 1) and the reference weights. It then squares these differences element-wise and sums them over all elements to compute the raw loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01 to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective. The resulting loss term is stored for harness aggregation and returned to the harness for addition to the training objective. The reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients, ensuring the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

The baseline condition serves as a control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation.

The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This condition tests whether the observed contrast is due to the specific cross-layer relationship or merely the presence of a regularization term. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients

Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. However, the experiment measured the registered outcome, not this mechanism. Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.
Related work: Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [4, 21]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [6] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [8]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [14]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [17].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [10]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [11]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [9], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [19]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [15]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [5]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [18]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [20]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [7, 13, 22]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [16]. Method: The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between query projection weights of successive attention blocks. The hypothesis is that regularizing deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights may improve generalization by reducing representational divergence across depth. The operator is applied to `blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight` during the loss computation of every optimization step. The operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated.

The operator retrieves reference weights from `model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight`. These reference weights are detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The operator computes the element-wise difference between the target weights (block 1) and the reference weights. It then squares these differences element-wise and sums them over all elements to compute the raw loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed consistency coefficient of 0.01 to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective. The resulting loss term is stored for harness aggregation and returned to the harness for addition to the training objective. The reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients, ensuring the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

The green dash-dot marker in Figure 3 shows the registered worthwhile threshold of 0.0125098 proportion. The lower confidence bound does not exceed this threshold. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 4 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the primary cohort. The learning curves for the proposed and baseline conditions coincide closely, distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, Table 3 reports the condition means. The proposed condition achieved 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9094]), the baseline 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]), and the first negative control 0.9043 (95% CI [0.9003, 0.9082]). Figure 5 visualizes these replication means. Table 4 presents the replication contrast. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Again, the 95% CI includes zero. Figure 6 plots these replication differences against the worthwhile threshold. The lower confidence bound does not exceed the margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 7 shows the learning curves for the replication cohort, where conditions whose curves coincide are distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern as well as by colour. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: We found that cross-layer query consistency regularization did not improve held-out classification accuracy beyond the preregistered margin in either the primary or replication cohorts. The measured outcome licenses the conclusion that the intervention does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence suggests that the proposed method did not demonstrate a clear advantage in the tested setting. What would settle the question next is direct measurement of attention stability, and a positive result would justify testing whether this extends to diverse time-series domains.
Discussion: The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer query consistency did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or replication cohorts. The measured outcome licenses the conclusion that the intervention does not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion under the stated uncertainty model. This design establishes that the intervention does not improve held-out classification accuracy by the target margin, though the registered decision was inconclusive regarding the zero-null. The confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero (primary 95% CI [-0.002707, 0.004356], replication 95% CI [-0.001957, 0.005714]), leading to inconclusive registered decisions.

One possible explanation, which this experiment did not test, is that architectural inductive biases, such as cross-layer consistency, stabilize learning. However, the experiment measured the registered outcome, not this mechanism. An alternative explanation is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, and forcing consistency constrains the model's ability to fit subject-specific variations. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is not a sampling artifact of the primary seeds, as both cohorts showed inconclusive decisions with CIs crossing zero.

These findings agree with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which also found inconclusive results for weight regularization in this setting [3]. They conflict with the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency universally improves generalization, as suggested by work in activation engineering [19]. However, that work applies cross-layer consistency to activation steering, not weight regularization during training, making the interventions not comparable. The result extends the evidence from *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers*, confirming the inconclusive decision under fresh sampling [1].

A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that the regularization coefficient (0.01) was too small to influence the optimization trajectory meaningfully. However, a small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient. Another mechanism is that the subject-disjoint shift requires flexible, layer-specific features rather than consistent ones. What would settle the question next is an experiment that varies the consistency coefficient or measures attention map stability directly, rather than inferring it from accuracy. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance, so future work should justify margins based on task requirements.
Limitations: This design cannot tell us whether the intervention affects attention stability directly, as we did not measure attention maps. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings. We name the directly recorded outcomes, and do not claim attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization from an accuracy contrast alone. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. The study is limited to the UCI HAR dataset and the PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture; results may not generalize to other time-series benchmarks or model sizes. The confirmatory cohort is a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, not an independent replication in terms of dataset or architecture. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects, and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer*. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction.

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy. === abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series classification, yet whether specific architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study replicates a test of cross-layer query consistency loss, which regularizes deeper attention query projection weights toward shallower layer weights, to determine if it improves held-out classification accuracy. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss term during training. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and a negative control across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on 43 disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query weight consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [36]. However, their effectiveness in generalizing across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds remains uncertain [5]. While architectural modifications such as consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms have been proposed to enhance stability and generalization [17, 18], independent verification of their impact on subject-disjoint performance is lacking. Specifically, it is unknown whether enforcing consistency in attention query projection weights across depth improves held-out classification accuracy in time-series transformers.

This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization. We test if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. The open problem this work addresses is identifying whether regularizing query projection weights across transformer blocks enables transformers to achieve higher held-out classification accuracy on unseen subjects. Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode consistently stable query weights or layer-specific adaptations for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

This paper makes the following contributions:
- We conduct a preregistered replication of the cross-layer query consistency loss intervention on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset using a subject-disjoint split.
- We evaluate the intervention across 43 primary seeds and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds, reporting held-out classification accuracy with 95% confidence intervals.
- We provide a rigorous design justification for the subject-disjoint split and paired-seed analysis, distinguishing training-seed replication from independent replication.

The preregistered prediction is that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 36]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [30].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [32]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [31]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [35]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 39]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [26]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight regularization hypothesis in a subject-disjoint time-series setting, distinguishing measured accuracy outcomes from unmeasured attention mechanisms.

=== method ===
The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear(9,64) input, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block consists of LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and residual. The final layer is LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6). Training proceeds for 12 epochs with batch size 128, SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects.

The intervention enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight → blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight) during training. The intervention adds a loss term (coefficient=0.01) computed as squared element-wise difference, detached from block 0 to prevent gradient flow. This operator is applied during loss computation of every optimization step, added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph. The control arm executes identical code path but returns zero loss term. The negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix (same shape/norm as block 0), destroying meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters.

The CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent. Scope is the full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space. It is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. Ordering is element-wise subtraction then sum. Normalisation is raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient. Numerical safeguards include coefficient 0.01 to prevent loss_term from dominating classification objective. Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients. Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification**. The subject-disjoint split answers the question of generalization to unseen subjects, which a random split would not. A random split allows the model to memorize subject-specific features, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to test robustness to movement styles or sensor characteristics. The subject-disjoint split ensures that training and testing subjects are mutually exclusive, providing a valid estimate of out-of-subject performance.

**Pairing and Controls**. Pairing conditions by seed reduces noise in the contrast estimate, increasing power to detect the preregistered margin under the assumed variance model. This pairing ensures that differences in accuracy are attributed to the intervention rather than seed-specific initialization or data ordering. The first negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any loss term addition improves accuracy; its observed contrast supports whether the specific cross-layer relationship matters. The second negative control (not used in this specific run description but registered) would test compute matching. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 replication seeds provides 90% planning target power for detecting the margin, distinguishing zero-null detection from exceeding the margin.

**Analysis**. The analysis distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations. The confirmatory cohort is never an independent replication but a fresh sampling of seeds on the same dataset split. We report both cohorts separately, state each preregistered decision, and never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**. Figure 1 illustrates the methodology flow showing data input, model architecture, registered conditions, intervention point at loss term, and subject-disjoint evaluation. In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 5). On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 2 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Bars are means over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimate is printed above each bar. The figure shows the proposed condition against the baseline. The 95% CI includes zero; the preregistered decision was inconclusive.

**Replication Cohort**. In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 5). On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. Bars are means over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The 95% CI includes zero; the preregistered decision was inconclusive.

**Comparison**. Table 5 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for all conditions in both cohorts. The proposed condition mean was 0.9062 (Primary) and 0.9055 (Replication). The baseline mean was 0.9054 (Primary) and 0.9035 (Replication). The negative control 1 mean was 0.9051 (Primary) and 0.9043 (Replication). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding**. The principal finding is that the cross-layer query consistency loss intervention did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or replication cohorts. The measured outcome licenses the conclusion that, under the stated uncertainty model, the intervention does not improve accuracy by the target margin. This design establishes that the intervention does not improve held-out classification accuracy by the target margin, though the registered decision was inconclusive regarding the zero-null.

**Interpretation**. This result suggests that cross-layer query weight consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, and forcing consistency constrains the model's ability to refine features across depth. An alternative mechanism is that the regularization coefficient (0.01) was too small to influence optimization meaningfully, or that the Frobenius norm penalty does not align with the geometric properties required for generalization.

**Comparison to Literature**. These findings agree with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which found inconclusive results for spectral entropy minimization [3]. They conflict with the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency generally improves stability, as suggested by *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* [17], though that work focused on small-scale training data overfitting rather than subject-disjoint generalization. The result is not comparable to *CDAC* [18] as the intervention, task, and data regime differ.

**What This Design Does Not Establish**. This experiment does not establish that attention stability is irrelevant, as attention maps were not measured. It does not establish that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct, as the control's outcome cannot prove that. It does not support claims about domain generalisation to different corpora, sensors, or tasks.

**Future Work**. What would settle the question next is measuring attention map stability directly to determine if weight consistency translates to attention consistency. Testing larger coefficients or alternative norms might clarify if the penalty strength was the limiting factor. Independent replication on different subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks would test transferability.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset and the specific PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture. The results support a claim about unseen subjects in this setting but are not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. The registered decision was inconclusive, meaning we cannot reject the zero-null hypothesis with the specified power. The calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings; we name the directly recorded outcomes and do not claim attention stability from an accuracy contrast alone.

=== conclusion ===
This study replicated a test of cross-layer query consistency loss on subject-disjoint time-series classification. The intervention did not improve held-out classification accuracy by the preregistered margin in either the primary or replication cohorts. The measured outcome suggests that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class in this regime. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence does not support adopting the intervention for accuracy gains. Future work should measure attention mechanisms directly and test alternative regularization strengths to settle the question of weight consistency versus layer-specific refinement.

=== appendix ===
**Operator Specification**. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight.
1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

**Seed Identities**. 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds (identities recorded in the run's own records).

| Baseline | 0.9054 | 0.9035 |
| Negative control 1 | 0.9051 | 0.9043 |

=== abstract ===
Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series classification, yet whether specific architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study replicates a test of cross-layer query consistency loss, which regularizes deeper attention query projection weights toward shallower layer weights, to determine if it improves held-out classification accuracy. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss term during training. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and a negative control across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on 43 disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query weight consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [36]. However, their effectiveness in generalizing across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds remains uncertain [5]. While architectural modifications such as consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms have been proposed to enhance stability and generalization [17, 18], independent verification of their impact on subject-disjoint performance is lacking. Specifically, it is unknown whether enforcing consistency in attention query projection weights across depth improves held-out classification accuracy in time-series transformers.

This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization. We test if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. The open problem this work addresses is identifying whether regularizing query projection weights across transformer blocks enables transformers to achieve higher held-out classification accuracy on unseen subjects. Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode consistently stable query weights or layer-specific adaptations for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

This paper makes the following contributions:
- We conduct a preregistered replication of the cross-layer query consistency loss intervention on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset using a subject-disjoint split.
- We evaluate the intervention across 43 primary seeds and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds, reporting held-out classification accuracy with 95% confidence intervals.
- We provide a rigorous design justification for the subject-disjoint split and paired-seed analysis, distinguishing training-seed replication from independent replication.

The preregistered prediction is that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 36]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [30].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [32]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [31]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [35]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 39]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [26]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight regularization hypothesis in a subject-disjoint time-series setting, distinguishing measured accuracy outcomes from unmeasured attention mechanisms.

=== method ===
The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear(9,64) input, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block consists of LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and residual. The final layer is LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6). Training proceeds for 12 epochs with batch size 128, SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects.

The intervention enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights (blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight → blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight) during training. The intervention adds a loss term (coefficient=0.01) computed as squared element-wise difference, detached from block 0 to prevent gradient flow. This operator is applied during loss computation of every optimization step, added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph. The control arm executes identical code path but returns zero loss term. The negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix (same shape/norm as block 0), destroying meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters.

The CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent. Scope is the full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space. It is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. Ordering is element-wise subtraction then sum. Normalisation is raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient. Numerical safeguards include coefficient 0.01 to prevent loss_term from dominating classification objective. Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients. Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification**. The subject-disjoint split answers the question of generalization to unseen subjects, which a random split would not. A random split allows the model to memorize subject-specific features, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to test robustness to movement styles or sensor characteristics. The subject-disjoint split ensures that training and testing subjects are mutually exclusive, providing a valid estimate of out-of-subject performance.

**Pairing and Controls**. Pairing conditions by seed reduces noise in the contrast estimate, increasing power to detect the preregistered margin under the assumed variance model. This pairing ensures that differences in accuracy are attributed to the intervention rather than seed-specific initialization or data ordering. The first negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any loss term addition improves accuracy; its observed contrast supports whether the specific cross-layer relationship matters. The second negative control (not used in this specific run description but registered) would test compute matching. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 replication seeds provides 90% planning target power for detecting the margin, distinguishing zero-null detection from exceeding the margin.

**Analysis**. The analysis distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations. The confirmatory cohort is never an independent replication but a fresh sampling of seeds on the same dataset split. We report both cohorts separately, state each preregistered decision, and never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**. Figure 1 illustrates the methodology flow showing data input, model architecture, registered conditions, intervention point at loss term, and subject-disjoint evaluation. In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 5). On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). Figure 2 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Bars are means over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimate is printed above each bar. The figure shows the proposed condition against the baseline. The 95% CI includes zero; the preregistered decision was inconclusive.

**Replication Cohort**. In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 5). On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. Bars are means over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The 95% CI includes zero; the preregistered decision was inconclusive.

**Comparison**. Table 5 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for all conditions in both cohorts. The proposed condition mean was 0.9062 (Primary) and 0.9055 (Replication). The baseline mean was 0.9054 (Primary) and 0.9035 (Replication). The negative control 1 mean was 0.9051 (Primary) and 0.9043 (Replication). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding**. The principal finding is that the cross-layer query consistency loss intervention did not yield a statistically significant improvement in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or replication cohorts. The measured outcome licenses the conclusion that, under the stated uncertainty model, the intervention does not improve accuracy by the target margin. This design establishes that the intervention does not improve held-out classification accuracy by the target margin, though the registered decision was inconclusive regarding the zero-null.

**Interpretation**. This result suggests that cross-layer query weight consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks, and forcing consistency constrains the model's ability to refine features across depth. An alternative mechanism is that the regularization coefficient (0.01) was too small to influence optimization meaningfully, or that the Frobenius norm penalty does not align with the geometric properties required for generalization.

**Comparison to Literature**. These findings agree with *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning*, which found inconclusive results for spectral entropy minimization [3]. They conflict with the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency generally improves stability, as suggested by *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* [17], though that work focused on small-scale training data overfitting rather than subject-disjoint generalization. The result is not comparable to *CDAC* [18] as the intervention, task, and data regime differ.

**What This Design Does Not Establish**. This experiment does not establish that attention stability is irrelevant, as attention maps were not measured. It does not establish that the harness is unbiased or the implementation correct, as the control's outcome cannot prove that. It does not support claims about domain generalisation to different corpora, sensors, or tasks.

**Future Work**. What would settle the question next is measuring attention map stability directly to determine if weight consistency translates to attention consistency. Testing larger coefficients or alternative norms might clarify if the penalty strength was the limiting factor. Independent replication on different subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks would test transferability.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset and the specific PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture. The results support a claim about unseen subjects in this setting but are not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. The registered decision was inconclusive, meaning we cannot reject the zero-null hypothesis with the specified power. The calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings; we name the directly recorded outcomes and do not claim attention stability from an accuracy contrast alone.

=== conclusion ===
This study replicated a test of cross-layer query consistency loss on subject-disjoint time-series classification. The intervention did not improve held-out classification accuracy by the preregistered margin in either the primary or replication cohorts. The measured outcome suggests that layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for this architecture class in this regime. For someone choosing between these methods, the evidence does not support adopting the intervention for accuracy gains. Future work should measure attention mechanisms directly and test alternative regularization strengths to settle the question of weight consistency versus layer-specific refinement.

=== appendix ===
**Operator Specification**. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight.
1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store loss_term in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return loss_term to harness for addition to training objective

**Seed Identities**. 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds (identities recorded in the run's own records).

Related-work section:
Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* notes that the ability to capture long-range dependencies has triggered interest in the time series community, while *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this research line [5, 36]. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation in *TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation* [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs in *Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer* [14]. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning* states that Transformers face limitations in time series prediction [30].

To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. *Double Consistency Regularization for Transformer Networks* notes that deep Transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. *CDAC: Cross-domain Attention Consistency in Transformer for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation* identifies that domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [32]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [31]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [35]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 39]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [26]. This study positions itself against these themes by testing a specific weight regularization hypothesis in a subject-disjoint time-series setting, distinguishing measured accuracy outcomes from unmeasured attention mechanisms.

Cited papers and their abstracts:
[1] Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00133 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by -0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

[2] Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness

The preregistration committed to a multiplicative weight perturbation applied BEFORE the forward pass, an entropy term added to the training OBJECTIVE, and a noise scale learned by BACKPROPAGATION, with held-out evaluation on the clean weights. The experiment har. Its conclusions may not be relied on; cite it only with its status stated.] Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic training often fails to provide calibrated confidence under distribution shift. This study investigates whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We preregistered a hypothesis that entropy maximization would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the baseline, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the intervention across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. [3] Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning
Abstract: Regularization design for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. This study tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy compared to standard weight decay in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would exceed a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion in accuracy gain. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset, we evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and two negative controls across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results were inconclusive: the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0004419 (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], p=0.75) in the primary cohort and 0.002549 (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], p=0.106) in the replication cohort. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. These findings suggest that spectral entropy minimization of input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks.

[4] Transformer in Transformer
Abstract: Transformer is a new kind of neural architecture which encodes the input data as powerful features via the attention mechanism. Basically, the visual transformers first divide the input images into several local patches and then calculate both representations and their relationship. Since natural images are of high complexity with abundant detail and color information, the granularity of the patch dividing is not fine enough for excavating features of objects in different scales and locations. In this paper, we point out that the attention inside these local patches are also essential for building visual transformers with high performance and we explore a new architecture, namely, Transformer iN Transformer (TNT). Specifically, we regard the local patches (e.g., 16$\times$16) as "visual sentences" and present to further divide them into smaller patches (e.g., 4$\times$4) as "visual words". The attention of each word will be calculated with other words in the given visual sentence with negligible computational costs. Features of both words and sentences will be aggregated to enhance the representation ability. Experiments on several benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed TNT architecture, e.g., we achieve an 81.5% top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet, which is about 1.7% higher than that of the state-of-the-art visual transformer with similar computational cost. The PyTorch code is available at https://github.com/huawei-noah/CV-Backbones, and the MindSpore code is available at https://gitee.com/mindspore/models/tree/master/research/cv/TNT.

[5] Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?
Abstract: Recently, there has been a surge of Transformer-based solutions for the long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) task. Despite the growing performance over the past few years, we question the validity of this line of research in this work. Specifically, Transformers is arguably the most successful solution to extract the semantic correlations among the elements in a long sequence. However, in time series modeling, we are to extract the temporal relations in an ordered set of continuous points. While employing positional encoding and using tokens to embed sub-series in Transformers facilitate preserving some ordering information, the nature of the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss. To validate our claim, we introduce a set of embarrassingly simple one-layer linear models named LTSF-Linear for comparison. Experimental results on nine real-life datasets show that LTSF-Linear surprisingly outperforms existing sophisticated Transformer-based LTSF models in all cases, and often by a large margin. Moreover, we conduct comprehensive empirical studies to explore the impacts of various design elements of LTSF models on their temporal relation extraction capability. We hope this surprising finding opens up new research directions for the LTSF task. We also advocate revisiting the validity of Transformer-based solutions for other time series analysis tasks (e.g., anomaly detection) in the future.

[6] Point Transformer
Abstract: Self-attention networks have revolutionized natural language processing and are making impressive strides in image analysis tasks such as image classification and object detection. Inspired by this success, we investigate the application of self-attention networks to 3D point cloud processing. We design self-attention layers for point clouds and use these to construct self-attention networks for tasks such as semantic scene segmentation, object part segmentation, and object classification. Our Point Transformer design improves upon prior work across domains and tasks. For example, on the challenging S3DIS dataset for large-scale semantic scene segmentation, the Point Transformer attains an mIoU of 70.4% on Area 5, outperforming the strongest prior model by 3.3 absolute percentage points and crossing the 70% mIoU threshold for the first time.

[7] Time Series
Abstract: Abstract Time series analysis is one of several branches of statistics whose practical importance has increased with the availability of powerful computing tools. Methodology originally developed for specialized applications, for example in business forecasting or geophysical signal processing, is now widely available in general statistical packages. These computing developments have helped to bring the subject closer to the mainstream of applied statistics. This book is an introductory account of time-series analysis, written from the perspective of an applied statistician with a particular interest in biological applications. Separate chapters cover exploratory methods, the theory of stationary random processes, spectral analysis, repeated measurements, ARIMA modelling, forecasting, and bivariate time-series analysis. Throughout, analyses of data-sets drawn from the biological and medical sciences are integrated with the methodological development. The book is unique in its emphasis on biological and medical applications of time-series analysis. Nevertheless, its methodological content is more widely applicable, and it should be useful to both students and practitioners of applied statistics, whatever their specialization.

[8] Selective Attention Improves Transformer
Abstract: Unneeded elements in the attention’s context degrade performance. We introduce Selective Attention, a simple parameter-free change to the standard attention mechanism which reduces attention to unneeded elements. Selective attention consistently improves language modeling and downstream task performance in a variety of model sizes and context lengths. For example, transformers trained with the language modeling objective on C4 with selective attention perform language modeling equivalently to standard transformers with ~2X more heads and parameters in their attention modules. Selective attention also allows decreasing the size of the attention’s context buffer, leading to meaningful reductions in the memory and compute requirements during inference. For example, transformers trained on C4 with context sizes of 512, 1,024, and 2,048 need 16X, 25X, and 47X less memory for their attention module, respectively, when equipped with selective attention, as those without selective attention, with the same validation perplexity.

[9] Time Series Momentum
Abstract: We document significant “time series momentum” in equity index, currency, commodity, and bond futures for each of the 58 liquid instruments we consider. We find persistence in returns for 1 to 12 months that partially reverses over longer horizons, consistent with sentiment theories of initial under-reaction and delayed over-reaction. A diversified portfolio of time series momentum strategies across all asset classes delivers substantial abnormal returns with little exposure to standard asset pricing factors and performs best during extreme markets. Examining the trading activities of speculators and hedgers, we find that speculators profit from time series momentum at the expense of hedgers.

[10] CSWin Transformer: A General Vision Transformer Backbone with Cross-Shaped Windows
Abstract: We present CSWin Transformer, an efficient and effective Transformer-based backbone for general-purpose vision tasks. A challenging issue in Transformer design is that global self-attention is very expensive to compute whereas local self-attention often limits the field of interactions of each token.
